1. on the matter and essence of the Element of Earth, etc.

4. on the generation of Herbs possessing medicinal power.

### XVII.
### From the manuscripts of Dr. Johann Montanus and others.
### SAGACIOUS PHILOSOPHY, <note>original: "PHILOSOPHIA SAGAX"</note> or the Great Astronomy. 338. This is divided into four books according to the number of the four types of astronomy:

In the First Book, the entire <term>NATURAL Astronomy</term> <note>original: "Astronomia NATURALIS"</note> is theoretically described: that is, all the works and arts which are accomplished in a natural way through the power and potential of the firmament, placed there by God the Father according to the first and ancient creation. These natural effects <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term> divides into two kinds. The first is of those which man may perform and accomplish by his own art, skill, and knowledge through the power, influence, and means of the firmament above. <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term> describes nine of these works or arts, which he calls the <term>MEMBERS of Astronomy</term> <note>original: "MEMBRA Astronomiæ"</note> or <term>Astronomical Sciences</term>, each of which in turn has its certain parts or species beneath it: as can be clearly seen from the inserted table on page 360. The other kind of natural powers and effects are those which the firmament or heaven exercises and uses for itself: some of which are accomplished through man (though without his art and skill), and some of which show themselves and become manifest through other creatures. These workings and effects <term>THEOPHRASTUS</term> calls the <term>GIFTS of the Firmament</term> <note>original: "DONA des Firmaments"</note>, of which he mentions ten, where each likewise has other species beneath it, as seen in the Table on leaf 396.

In the Second Book (the beginning of which is on page 427), the entire <term>CELESTIAL Astronomy</term> <note>original: "Astronomia COELESTIS"</note> or <term>Supernatural Astronomy</term> is described, under which Theo-

<column-break/>
<meta>Catchword: phrastus</meta>

phrastus includes all works and deeds which are used and accomplished in a heavenly manner through the power and potential of the New Creature (proceeding from God the Son <term>JESUS CHRIST</term>, according to the second and New Creation). These works <term>Theophrastus</term> likewise divides into two kinds: namely into 9 Members and 10 Gifts, each of which includes just as many species and parts beneath it as was presented in the distribution of the Natural Astronomies.

In the Third Book is included the <term>ASTRONOMY OF FAITH</term> <note>original: "ASTRONOMIA FIDEI"</note> or of the <term>NEW OLYMPUS</term> <note>original: "OLYMPI NOVI"</note>, which <term>Theophrastus</term> mentions at the beginning of the fourth book, page 471 (noting that he had also described it). In this Astronomy, he would undoubtedly have described the power and effect of strong faith and intense imagination as necessity required, and also divided it according to the aforementioned arrangement into 9 Members and 10 Gifts: but it has not yet come to light.

->From Theophrastus's own handwriting.<-

In the Fourth Book (page 471), the <term>SATANIC</term> or <term>Infernal Astronomy</term> <note>original: "Astronomia SATHANICA oder Infernalis"</note> is theoretically described, in which are included all powers and effects which the devil uses and accomplishes, either for himself or through sorcerous people (though also through the power of nature). It was undoubtedly fully described by <term>Theophrastus</term> according to the aforementioned distribution: but at this time no more is available than what is included here.

The practice of these four astronomies is mentioned by <term>Theophrastus</term> in many places in these books, noting that he had also described them: but so far nothing of them has come to light.

# THE PHILOSOPHY OF THEOPHRA-
## STUS BOMBAST VON HOHENHEIM
### THE SWABIAN ARPINAS, GER-
#### MAN HERMIT.
## TO THE ATHENIENSES.
<note>original: "Ad Athenienses" - This is one of Paracelsus’s most famous works on cosmology. By addressing the "Athenians," he is not writing to Greeks, but symbolically addressing the learned scholars of his time, whom he often criticized.</note>

->Preface<-

### In the Second Part <note>original: "Paras," likely referring to a section or paragraph of the larger work</note> of the Prince
#### THEOPHRASTUS.

<margin>B</margin>Herein the Prince Theophrastus describes the second part, comprising three books of the first volume of his Philosophy. Within it, he reports the origin of all creatures from their first beginning. He calls this first beginning the **Mysterium Magnum** <term>Mysterium Magnum: The "Great Mystery," a term Paracelsus used to describe the primordial, undifferentiated matter from which God created the universe.</term> and asserts that all creatures were born and sprouted from this *Mysterio Magno*. He further gives us to understand that these creatures were not born <note>in the biological sense</note> but are here as a result of a single birth, and he divides them into the "Four Mothers" <note>The four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note> from which all things are born. However, he never validates the origin of these four mothers as a birth itself. In this part, he intends for all things to return to their first essence and demonstrates the reason why. It is found through his writing that this is caused by the Eternal, which is related to the Perishable. Here he gives us to understand a "fabric" <note>original: "Gemäch," referring to the structure of creation</note> of Eternity that is entirely hidden from us mortals. He provides an indication of the soul’s journey—where it comes from and where it goes—and what its nature is. Through the description in this part, Prince Theophrastus may be called a "guidepost" of all philosophy and an indicator of philosophical truth with a complete natural foundation; for he alone establishes that validation is sufficient for the Truth.

---

# THE TEXT OF THE PHILOSOPHY
## OF THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS
### BOMBAST VON HO-
### HENHEIM,

<margin>a</margin>For all created things that exist in a perishable state, there was a single beginning in which all creatures were enclosed and contained, caught between the **Ethers** <note>In the cosmology of the time, the "Ethers" referred to the upper reaches of the heavens or the substance of the stars.</note>. It should be understood that all creatures come from one single matter and were not given their own individual origins. This matter of all things is the *Mysterium Magnum*; it is not a tangible entity established in any specific essence, nor is it formed into any image. It is also not inclined toward any property, being likewise without color and without an elemental nature. As far as the Ethers have extended themselves, so far was the circle of the *Mysterii Magni*. This **Mysterium Magnum** was a mother of all elements, and likewise, it was also a grandmother of all stars, trees, and the creatures of the flesh. For just as children are born from a mother, so also from the *Mysterio Magno* were born all creatures, both the sentient and the non-sentient, and all others in the same way. The *Mysterium Magnum* is the sole mother of all mortal things, and they took their origin in her—not one after another, but they were given in a single creation, substance, matter, form, essence, nature, and inclination.

->The Second Text<-

Since there was such a Mystery, which looked like no other creature and which did not yet exist <note>as a physical form</note>, and yet it was the first matter from which all mortals have their origin: this is to be understood in no other way than how a human "cheese" <note>original: "Brin" or "Prün," an archaic term for curds or cheese. Paracelsus frequently used the metaphor of milk curdling into cheese to explain how the physical world "coagulated" out of the formless Great Mystery.</note> comes out of the water,

# PHILOSOPHY TO THE ATHENIANS.
<sig>A, B, C</sig>

...air, earth, and fire become, and look like their seed, and yet are not. All elements, along with other births, may spring from this into the third generation. Although urine is a creature <note>Paracelsus often viewed biological waste as a "creature" because it was a product of the body's internal alchemical processes</note>, a division occurs between it and its source. Thus, the Great Mystery <term>Mysterium Magnum: The primordial, undifferentiated substance from which God created all things.</term> is prepared, uncreated, by the Highest Artist, and nothing will ever be its equal again, nor will it ever return. For just as cheese never turns back into milk, the process of generation will never return to its first matter. It is true that all things return to their first essence, but not into the Mystery itself: for what is consumed cannot be brought back, nor does it happen. But things do return to that state which existed before the Mystery.

### The Third Text.

<margin>f. *
Dung <note>original: "Stercus"</note></margin>
And although the Great Mystery is a mother to all creatures, both sentient and insentient, not all plants were already formed within her, nor animals, nor many other such things. Rather, it should be understood that she has left behind all general mysteries: to humans, their mystery; to animals, the ability to multiply in their own form; to the flowing things, their essence; and similarly, she assigned other specific mysteries to their own forms. Thus, in this way, a mystery takes its origin from that which may be born from it, just as the mystery has ordained. For the star <note>The original text uses "Stern" (star) but lists it alongside animals, perhaps suggesting a celestial influence on biological forms</note> is a mystery of the horse, the beetle, the gnat, and the fly. Milk is the mystery of cheese, butter, and whey, and such things. Cheese is the mystery of the maggots and worms that grow within it; and in turn, the maggot is the mystery of its waste <note>original: "Fæcuræ," referring to excrement or byproduct</note>. Thus there are two kinds of mysteries: the great one, known as the uncreated mystery <note>original: "Mysterium increatum"</note>, and the others, called special mysteries, which are like grandchildren.

### The Fourth Text.

Since all other mortal things have grown and sprung from the uncreated mystery, it is now to be understood that no creature was created more freely, later, or more specifically than any other, but rather all together. For the highest secret <term>Arcanum: In Paracelsian philosophy, an Arcanum is the "secret" or "virtue"—the celestial, life-giving essence of a substance.</term> and great good of the Creator placed all things into the Uncreated, not in their final form, essence, or quality. Instead, they were in the Uncreated like a statue is inside a piece of wood: although the image is not seen, it is there, until the excess wood is cut away, after which the statue is recognized. Thus, the Uncreated Mystery is not to be understood as anything other than this: that the fleshly and the insentient, through their separation, each came into its own form and shape. No "wood chip" was thrown away; rather, everything became form and essence. No woodcarver will ever be found, through all eternity, who can turn even the smallest and most useless grain into something useful and living in such a way.

### The Fifth Text.

Thus it should be understood that no "house" was built out of the Great Mystery, nor were animals gathered or "made up," nor were the other plants. Instead, it is like a physician who mixes a compound <note>original: "Compositum"</note> of many virtues; although it is a single matter, none of the individual virtues appear the same as they lie hidden within it. Therefore, one should remember that all kinds of creatures contained in the ethers <note>original: "Etheren"</note> are ordered together in the Great Mystery. They were not perfect in their substance, form, and essence, but existed in a perfectly subtle way that is unknown to us mortals, enclosed within the one. For we are all created from the mortal, grown in no other way than the procreations of Saturn <note>original: "Procreationes Saturni." In alchemy, Saturn often represents the leaden, dark, or initial stage of transformation that contains all hidden colors and potentials.</note>, which in its separation gives all colors and forms, though none are visible within it. And if the mysteries of Saturn show such procreations, how much more does the great wonder, the Great Mystery, hold within it? In its separation, all things are carved from their remainders, and yet nothing is found to be leftover, like a work in which nothing goes to waste; it gives birth to another plant or matter after it.

### The Sixth Text.

It should be recognized that in the carving-work of the Great Mystery, there were many kinds of "off-cuts": some into flesh, and that in wonderfully many shapes and forms; some into sea monsters, with many kinds of forms and appearances; some into herbs, some into wood; some into stone and metals. For it cannot be measured how Almighty God carved these, other than what is found: that He brought His art into two ways and two paths. One way was that He ordained for things to cease living and growing. The other way was that they are not just a single matter. For when a statue is carved from wood, the chips are all still wood—which was not the case here—but He gave them His handiwork, form, and movement.

<meta>This page continues the cosmological explanation of the "Great Mystery," focusing on the process of "Separation" (Separatio) as the primary force that transformed the primordial chaos into specific, physical forms like elements, plants, and minerals.</meta>

BOOK ONE.

## The Seventh Text.

<margin>A</margin>
**T**hus the Great Mystery <note>original: "Mysterium Magnum"</note> was divided, and from it was carved that which remained from the other. From what remained, something else became: for the Great Mystery was not made of elements, even though all elements were within it. It was also not made of flesh, even though all types of humanity were contained within it. It was also not made of wood or stone; rather, it was a Matter <note>meaning the "prime matter" or fundamental substance</note> that was able to contain all mortal things within itself, without any recognition of its own essence, and through the division, it gave each thing its own essence and form. Just as food that is eaten is taken in by a person and becomes flesh—yet it looks nothing like flesh—or if it is taken as manure <note>original: "Feilung," likely referring to "Fäulung" or decay/refuse</note>, it becomes grass, which it also does not resemble. Even more so is this wonder to be understood in the Great Mystery, for the mysteries reveal themselves thus: one into stone, another into flesh, the third into herbs, and all in many wonderful forms.

## The Eighth Text.

<margin>B</margin>
**A**nd when each thing was separated into its own form and property, standing in its own free will and its own nature, then the Substantial Matter was recognized. For that which was meant for compaction <term>Compaction: The process of becoming solid or dense matter.</term> became compacted; the rest remained empty, in terms of its substance. For when the compactions gathered together, not everything could be made solid; rather, the greater part remained empty. This is seen in water: when it coagulates, only a small quantity is compacted; the same occurs in the separation of the elements. For all compaction became stone, metal, wood, and flesh, and the like; the rest remained empty, each according to its essence and the properties of the planets. And such a Great Mystery was, in its compaction, no different than a smoke that is large and wide, which has nothing of substance in itself except a tiny quantity of soot; the other vastness which the smoke occupies is pure air, as is seen in the separation of smoke from soot.

## The Ninth Text.

**I**n the beginning of all birth was the mother and producer: SEPARATION <note>original: "SEPARATIO"</note>. For the Separation of the philosophies is the greatest wonder. Although it is not for humans to philosophize about such things—as it contains more than human, mortal reason can hold—nonetheless, to understand in what way such a thing happened and continues to happen, it is thus: it is no different than vinegar being mixed into lukewarm milk, causing a separation to arise in many ways. Or like a <margin>* Refining cupel.</margin> * cupel <note>original: "Traphat," an alchemical vessel used for refining metals</note> of ore, which strikes and brings each metal into its own essence. So too was there something. For just as a tincture of silver is etched in, so it also passed through the Great Mystery and ordained each thing into its own being, and separated them so wonderfully that every form is in its own essence. But what such Magic <note>original: "Magy," referring to a natural or divine transformative power</note> was, which had such an entry, was a singular wonder. If it happened divinely through His Godhead, we will not philosophize on it, for the Godhead does not allow us to know such things. But if that Magic was natural, then it was a wonder-bearing Magic, a swift passage during a separation, and of great virtue, the likes of which it is impossible for Nature to give or make again. For there, one part was separated into elements, the second into the invisible, and the third into the vegetable, which is indeed a special miracle and sign.

## The Tenth Text.

<margin>C</margin>
**A**nd now that the Great Mystery was full in such Essence and Deity, with an inclusion of the greatest eternity, the Separation of all creatures began first of all. And when this occurred, every creature was found in its own majesty, power, and free will, which will remain so until the end of all things—that is, in the Great Harvest, when all things will bear fruit and cut down their growth. For the Harvest is the end of its growth, and signifies nothing other than the mortal destruction of all things. Although there are many such things, there is nonetheless only one Harvest, in which all the things of the creatures are cut and led into the barn. And just as the Great Mystery is wonderful in the beginning, so too is the Harvest of all things wonderful in its end. And although the free will of things may harm one another—for nothing is without a friend, and nothing without an enemy—free will floats alone in virtue, and the friend or enemy in the works. Thus, this does not affect the Separation, for it is a distribution to give each thing its own form and essence.

## The Eleventh Text.

**A**nd in the beginning of the separation of the Great Mystery, the separation of the elements came forth first, so that the elements came into being. The Fire became the heavens and a chest <note>i.e., a container or treasury</note> of the firmament. The Air became an emptiness in which nothing is to be seen, nor can be seen, at the ends where no substance or corporeal matter was placed; it is a chest of the fatalistic invisible ones. The Water became a liquid <note>original: "Liquor"</note> and settled itself around the center in its hollows, between the other elements and the ethers, and is a chest...

PHILOSOPHY TO THE ATHENIANS.

...of the nymphs and sea monsters. The Earth has been coagulated into a land, which is supported not by the other elements, but by the **Pillars of Archaltis** <term>Archaltis: In Paracelsian cosmology, these are the invisible spiritual pillars or foundations that uphold the physical world.</term>, and these are the **Great Works of God** <note>original: "Magnalia Dei"</note>. The Earth serves as a chest for the plants that nourish themselves from the soil: and such **Separation** <note>The process of "Separation" is the central theme here, describing how the distinct forms of nature were distilled out of the primordial "Great Mystery."</note> was the beginning of all creatures, and the first distribution of all these things and others.

# The Twelfth Text.

<margin>A</margin>
Once the elements were separated into their own essences and divided from one another—each to its own place, one without harm to the other—then the second Separation occurred after the first, proceeding out of the elements themselves. When everything was thus contained within the Fire, it was transformed into the Heavens; one part served as a "chest" or container, while the other part grew out of this, just as a flower shoots out from a stem. In this way, the stars, planets, and everything that touches the whole **Firmament** <note>The sphere of the stars and heavens.</note> grew. This happened out of the element of Fire—not in the same way a stem grows from the earth with its flowers, for the stem grows *from* the earth—but rather, the stars were born *from* the heavens solely through Separation, just as **silver flowers** <note>An alchemical reference to the way silver crystallizes into tree-like or flower-like shapes, known as the "Tree of Diana."</note> rise and separate themselves. Therefore, all Firmaments are separated from the Fire; and before the Firmament was separated from the Fire, it was all a single element of Fire. Just as in winter a tree is merely a tree, but in summer, when it separates from itself that which is to be separated, it gives forth leaves, fruit, and blossoms—for that is its "harvest" time to separate itself. In the same way, there was a "harvest" in the separation of the **Great Mystery** <note>original: "Mysterium Magnum"</note>, which could no longer contain itself; this is to be understood similarly in all things.

# The Thirteenth Text.

<margin>B</margin>
And after the separation of the elements, the second Separation out of the Air was distributed at the same time and moment as the Fire: for all Air is **predestined** <note>Meaning it has a pre-ordained purpose or path within the divine plan.</note> into all elements. It is not that it exists in the other elements as a mixture—that is not the case—but rather it takes up a variety of roles in all elements and possesses them, yet it does not possess that which was already possessed. Also, no mixture of the elements remained together; rather, each element exists in its own free will, entirely "unmarried" to any other element. Thus, as soon as this element [Air] was separated from the others out of the Great Mystery, there were immediately divided out of it the **Fates**, **Impressions**, **Incantations**, **Superstitions**, **Wicked Spells**, **Dreams**, **Divinations**, **Sorceries**, **Visions**, **Apparitions**, **Fata-Cesten**, **Melusines** <note>original: "Melosiniæ"; water-spirits or spirits who take on human form.</note>, **Spirits**, **Stone-Dwellers** <note>original: "Diemeæ"</note>, **Tree-Dwellers** <note>original: "Durdales"</note>, and **Earth-Pore-Dwellers** <note>original: "Neufareni"</note>. And after such separation, each of the aforementioned was assigned its own seat and its essence was predestined; this is why they are invisible, yet they can be felt by us. For no more subtle element was created by the highest **Secrets** <note>original: "Arcanen"</note> than the Air. The **Diemeæ** live in hard stones, for they were separated into the void along with the Air. The **Durdales** live in the trees, for their separation occurred within the substance of such things. The **Neufareni** live in the "air of the earth," that is, in the **pores of the Earth** <note>original: "poris Terræ"</note>. The **Melusines** enter into human blood, for their separation in the Air occurred within bodies and flesh. The **Spirits** were separated into the Air that exists within the **Chaos** <note>In this context, "Chaos" likely refers to the atmosphere or the vast, unformed space between the elements.</note>. All others dwell and exist in the particular essence of the Air, each in the place where it was assigned and divided from the element of Air, and yet it must remain within that element and cannot change it.

# The Fourteenth Text.

<margin>C</margin>
And in the separation of the elements, the Water was set apart to its own place and end, as it was predestined in the **Secret Plan** <note>original: "Arcano"</note>. In this, everything that was in its elemental power and property was separated during the first division; and thus the Water was divided into many **special mysteries** <note>original: "specialia Mysteria"</note>, all of which took their Mother from the element of Water. Some parts in this separation were ordained to become fish, and those in many forms. Some parts became animals with flesh, some became salt, some became sea-plants—such as corals, **Trina**, and **Citrones**. Some parts became sea monsters, following a course contrary to the nature of all elements. Some parts became **Nymphs**, some **Sirens**, some **Drames**, some **Lorind**, some **Nelder** <note>These terms refer to various classes of elemental spirits or mythological creatures specific to the author's folklore and cosmology.</note>; some became rational creatures who are endowed with an **Eternal** part in their bodies and reproduce themselves. Some are subject to total death, while others are yet to be separated in time. For the perfect separation of the element of Water has not yet fully occurred; rather, it comes into the "great harvest," where every year new growths must spring forth in the Water element. And such separation occurred at the same moment as the separation of the other elements in a "day's work" and through the movement of **Sequestration** <note>original: "Sequestrierung"; the act of setting apart or withdrawing.</note>. And so every thing that is in the water was created and revealed in that hour through a separation.

# The Fifteenth Text.

And in the same way, when the element of **Earth** <note>original: "Terræ"</note> was separated from the others, the earthly separation also occurred—that is, the separation of all things that are in the earth or spring forth from it. For the four elements were all equal in their first creation within the **Great Mystery**; they were also divided equally and in a single moment. Likewise, they were also divided into one another in their second division, which is then called the "elemental divisions." And in such elemental division, out of the element of Earth, there were separated the sensible and the insensible, the eternal and the non-eternal, and each came into its essence and free will...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Separation" of the elements, moving from the initial formation of the heavens to the specific categorization of minerals, plants, animals, and elemental spirits born from the Earth and Water. It explores the "complexions" (qualities) of the four elements and how they manifest in physical matter.</meta>

<header>BOOK ONE</header>

<margin>A</margin>...ordained: That which was of a woody nature became wood; another became metallic ore; a third became marcasites, talc, bismuth, garnet, cobalt, pyrite, and many others; a fourth became gems, and these in many shapes and various forms. Some became stone, sand, and lime; the fifth became fruits, flowers, herbs, and seeds; the sixth became sentient animals—some with the eternal <note>Refers to the soul or spirit.</note>, such as humans, and some with the mortal, such as calves, etc., and these in many ways and forms. More was separated out in the Earthly element than in any other, for there all things are born with seed, all things with two—mother and father—which is not divided or predetermined in the other elements in the same way. For there, also, **gnomes** <term>Gnomi: In Paracelsian philosophy, these are elemental spirits of the Earth who live within the rocks and soil.</term>, and **wild folk**, and **night-women** <note>original: "Nachtfrawen." Likely referring to spirits of the night or nymphs.</note> were created and divided: some into the mountains, some into the forests, and some only into the night. There, giants were also separated into the third generation; there also great **monstrous creatures** <note>original: "Ellentiz." Refers to strange or marvelous beings.</note> were distributed, along with such great miracles among humans, livestock, and all growth, which are wondrous for any **philosopher** <note>Here, "philosophy" refers to the study of nature and alchemy.</note> to understand, and all are to be recognized as having happened unnaturally.

### The Sixteenth Text.

It is mentioned here that the four elements were separated from the beginning, initially from one another out of a single Matter, in which their **complexion** <term>Complexion: The specific balance of qualities (hot, dry, cold, moist) that defines the nature of a substance.</term> and essence were not yet present. Thus, complexions and nature arose along with the separation: the **Hot and Dry** <note>original: "Heiß vnnd Trocken"</note> was ordained to the Heavens and Firmaments, each spread out and commanding in its own property; the **Hot and Moist** was ordained to the Air, out of which the Hot and Moist were then invisibly separated; **Cold and Wet** to a Sea, along with its appendages; the **Cold and Dry** to an Earth, and to all that is within it. Yet, contrary things have grown and been separated out of the elements which <margin>B</margin> are not like their own element: such as limestone, which is not Fire in its nature, even though it comes from fire. This is because the disruption in the separation of the element caused this, and it came too far from the nature of Fire. For Fire itself can be cold, hard, and wet; for there are four kinds of Fire. Likewise, the colors of Fire are not all the same: for one fire creates white and blue—the dry fire creates red and green; the wet creates gray and black; the cold fire creates yellow and red. For this reason, one **offspring** <note>original: "Procreatz"</note> is hotter than another, because one fire was more **refined** <note>original: "gradiert," referring to alchemical degrees of intensity.</note> than the other. For there was not just one Fire, but many hundreds of kinds of fire, where no two stood at the same degree; therefore, each ordained its own special offspring as its own **Mystery** <term>Mysterium: A hidden spiritual essence or "seed" from which a physical thing grows.</term> and was separated from it.

### The Seventeenth Text.

Furthermore, Water was not of a single form in its complexion: for there were many thousands of kinds of water in the **element of Water** <note>original: "Element Aquæ"</note>, and yet all are water. It is not for the philosopher to recognize the element of Water as being solely cold and moist in itself, but rather many hundreds of times colder and not wetter, and not inclined toward heat as much as toward cold. For the element of Water does not live or exist in the cold and wet on only one degree, but rather not on a single degree at all: some waters are springs, and those are manifold; some are seas, and the seas are wondrous; some are streams, and no two are alike. Some of the Water element is ordained to become stones, such as beryls, crystals, chalcedonies, and amethysts; some to plants, such as corals and **amber** <note>original: "Carabe," an old term for amber.</note>; some in the **chemistry** <note>original: "Chimū" / Chymia.</note> as the **liquor of life** <note>original: "Liquor vitæ"</note>; some in the soil as the **liquor of the earth** <note>original: "Liquor terræ"</note>. And these are the element of Water, and yet in many forms. <margin>C</margin> Some grow entirely from the earth with abandoned seeds and are also from the element of Water; some become flesh, such as **nymphs** <term>Nymphs: Elemental spirits of the water, often called Undines in other texts by Paracelsus.</term>, and are also of the element of Water. Though it should be understood that the element of Water is changed into another complexion, it still does not depart from the element from which it came. For what is from Water becomes Water again; and what is from Fire becomes Fire again; and what is from Earth becomes Earth again; and likewise, those of the Air become Air again.

### The Eighteenth Text.

Similarly, it is to be recognized concerning the **element of Earth** <note>original: "Element Terræ"</note> that all the soils which have come from the element of Earth possess its nature; although the "liquors of minerals" are regarded and recognized as fire, they are nevertheless not Fire. For **sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphur"</note> does not burn because it belongs to the **element of Fire** <note>original: "Elementū Ignis"</note>; rather, cold burns just as well as heat. And that which burns to ashes is not the element of Fire, but rather the **Fire of the Earth** <note>original: "Ignis Terræ"</note>. And that same fire should not be recognized as the element, for it is no element; it is solely the consumption of the Earth, or of that same substance. For Water may burn just as well and be brought to a blaze as any other; but when it burns, it is **Watery Fire** <note>original: "Ignis Aqueus"</note>. Fire should not be considered certain just because the Fire of the Earth burns and is hot—that it is therefore "fiery"—even though it looks like it. For the philosopher is one-sided who names the element only by how he perceives it; rather, he should think more deeply: the element is much different than such a fire. For why? Not everything that wets is the element of Water, for the element of Earth can be brought to a liquid state and yet remains Earth all the while. Likewise, everything in the Earth is of the element of Earth; it is recognized by the property born from it, or if it is born from that which it resembles. Hard **flint** <note>original: "Kirsting." A dialect/archaic word for Kiesel or flint stone.</note> and chalcedony give off fire; such a fire is not elemental Fire, but a **forceful expression** <note>original: "forcis expressio"</note> of great hardness.

<header>PHILOSOPHY TO THE ATHENIANS</header>
<sig>A</sig>

## The Nineteenth Text

Just as the element of Air contains within it many kinds of **procreations** <term>Procreationes: Natural births or generations produced within a specific element.</term>, these are all simply Air. Every **philosopher** <note>In this context, a "philosopher" refers to a student of nature and alchemy.</note> must know that no element procreates anything different from itself; like is always born from like. Since Air is invisible, it gives nothing visible; it cannot be grasped, and so it gives nothing tangible. **Melusina-like beings** <note>original: "Melosinirt." Refers to spirits similar to the legendary Melusina, often described by Paracelsus as spirits who live in the elements but seek human contact.</note>, although they are of the Air and are nothing but Air, may undergo a **conjunction** <note>original: "Conjunctio." A joining or union.</note> with another element, namely Earth. Such a joining can happen between the Air and humankind, as is seen in all **malefice** <note>original: "Maleficien." Harmful magic or witchcraft.</note> and **incantations** <note>original: "Incantationibus." Spells or ritual chanting.</note> performed through **spirits** <note>original: "Spiritus."</note>. In the same way, one should understand the **water-women** <note>original: "Wasserfrawen." Nymphs or undines.</note>, who belong solely to the element of **Water** <note>original: "Aquæ."</note> and no other; they may mingle among those of the Earth and bear children with them. Thus, a **compaction** <note>A solidification or densification.</note> also arises from the Air that is visible and tangible—not as a primary birth of the first division, but as a **consequence** <note>original: "Consequentia." An after-effect or secondary result.</note>. Just as a beetle arises from dung, so too can a "misgrowth" from the aerial elements take on a physical shape, with aerial speech, thoughts, and deeds, through mingling with the Earthly. Yet, such miracles and consequences turn back into Air, and the **nymphs** <note>original: "Nymphen."</note> back into water, just as a human—who comes from the Earth—rots and is consumed back into the Earth.

<margin>* Caterpillars.</margin>

## The Twentieth Text

Thus the procreations have arisen, one from the other, through the great Separation. From these procreations follow other births, which have their **Mystery** <note>original: "Mysterium." In Paracelsian thought, a hidden source or potentiality.</note> within these very procreations. This is not a separation in the same form as mentioned before, but rather a "straying" or a "miscarriage," or an "overflow," or a "harvest." Thunder comes from the procreations of the **Firmament** <note>original: "Firmamenti." The heavens or sky.</note>, which comes from the element of Fire. This is a "harvest" of the **star** <note>original: "Sidus." Astral influence.</note> at the time when the thunder is ripened to perform its nature. But magical storms arise from the Air and vanish again into the Air; not because the element of Air gives them, but the spirits of the Air. Some things are conceived physically from Fire, just as the **gnomes** <term>Gnomi: Elemental spirits of the Earth who dwell within rocks and soil.</term> are from the Earth. Similarly, **waste** <note>original: "Stercora." Excrement or dregs.</note> comes from humans and animals and not directly from the Earth. The **Lorind** <note>A Paracelsian term for a specific meteor or spiritual emanation.</note> comes from the "nativity" of the Water, yet it is not from the Water. From such overflow, error, and harvest, many other things are born: for from **impressions** <note>original: "Impressionibus." Astral or spiritual influences that shape matter.</note> come twisted humans, worms, and many such growths. From **fateful storms** <note>original: "Fatalischen Gewittern." Storms or events dictated by fate/providence.</note> grow the poisoning of lands, great mortality, and many hindrances to good years. From waste, the beetles and **giants** <note>original: "Risen."</note> and **Dalni** <note>Likely another class of elemental spirits or specialized beings.</note> take their origin. From the *Lorind* appears a prophet of that same region, serving as a sign of a great new history or a strange matter, as something unheard of in the future.

## The Twenty-First Text

Now that three kinds of separation have occurred from the **Mystery** <note>original: "Mysterio."</note> in three forms, as has been understood, the fourth separation is now to be recognized. This is the last, and after it, none work anymore. The others will also break apart, and no Mystery will remain. For through this, all things return to their first beginning, and only that remains which existed before the **Great Mystery** <note>original: "Mysterio Magno." The primordial state of all potentiality.</note> and which is Eternal. This is not to be understood as if I "become" something, or that something becomes of me after the final separation, such as through death. For I become nothing; I am from nothing, according to the first beginning. And although all things return to their first state, it happens thus: when they come to nothing, they are at their first state, for the first is to be sought in the first beginning. But what it is that "comes to nothing" are the **Secrets** <note>original: "Arcana."</note>. The Soul in me has become out of *Something*, therefore it does not come to *Nothing*, for it comes from "Somewhere." But from such a "Nothing," nothing becomes, and nothing more is born from it. A picture painted on a tablet exists and is made of something. But we are not made into the **ethers** <note>original: "Etheren."</note> out of "something" in the way a picture is. Why? Because we come from the *Great Mystery* and not from the *Procreated*. But we become nothing, like a picture that is wiped away until nothing is there anymore; thus the tablet is back in its first form. So all creatures shall come to their first place, which is to Nothing. But know this: the reason all physical bodies must become nothing again is solely because of the Eternal which is found in the unreasoning bodies; and such a last separation is the **Ultimate Matter** <note>original: "Vltima Materia." The final state of matter.</note>. Then many procreations, **mixtures** <note>original: "Permixtiones."</note>, **conversions** <note>original: "Conuersiones."</note>, **transmutations** <note>original: "Transmutationes."</note>, **alterations** <note>original: "Alterationes."</note>, and many other such things will happen, which we do not consider humanly possible to know.

## The Twenty-Second Text

And although a philosopher may recognize that everything which is helpful and at hand for the perishable is also itself perishable, so too that which is divided cannot come together again—just like curdled milk, which can never again become whole. Thus we must also philosophize that the *Great Mystery* does not return into that from which it came. Therefore, it is to be understood that all creatures are a "painting" of the highest **Secret** <note>original: "Arcanen."</note>, and a color cast upon the wall...

<meta>catchword: The wall/</meta>

<summary>This page discusses how the element of Air produces invisible beings like Melusinae, explains the origins of phenomena like thunder and "waste-born" creatures, and details the final "fourth separation" where all physical creation returns to a state of nothingness, leaving only the Eternal.</summary>

<header>BOOK ONE</header>
<sig>a iiii</sig>

<margin>A</margin> ...is no different than a wall: For we stand among the **ethers** <term>Etheren: Refers to the subtle, celestial regions or the spirits inhabiting the air.</term>, destined like everything else to be wiped out and brought to nothing. Even the tablets where the image is set are perishable and can be burned; so too is our **Great Mystery** <term>Mysterium Magnum: In Paracelsian thought, the "Great Mystery" is the primordial, chaotic source from which all specific forms of matter and life were separated by the Creator.</term>, and we along with them. And so, as all things among the creatures pass away with this Mystery, they are wiped out and diminished like a great forest that is reduced to a few ashes; and those same ashes become a little **glass** <note>original: "Vitrum."</note>, and that same glass becomes a small **beryl** <note>original: "Berillen." Likely referring to a crystalline or highly refined state of matter.</note>, and the beryl becomes a wind. In this way, we will be consumed from one state to another, for as long as nothing of us remains. For just as the origin of all creatures is, so too is their passing. If a great **cypress** tree can grow from a tiny grain, it can just as easily become small again, back to its first grain. For the grain and the beryl are held to be alike: as the seed begins, so the beryl ends. And once this separation has occurred, and each thing is in its own essence, it is as it was in the first beginning—as nothing. Then there is nothing transient left among the ethers, but only the eternal. For that which comes from the eternal will establish itself there more firmly than before the beginning of creation, and it has no decay within it. Like a glass that cannot be consumed by the creaturely world, so too that same eternal essence cannot be brought to nothing by the eternal realm.

### The Twenty-third Text.

And because the last separation is a breaking of all creations, where one is consumed after another and passes away, the time of such things is recognized. After the birth of these creations, there will be no decay within them, because the seed fills the place of the old things that have passed. Thus, the eternal remains within the transient without diminishing, to renew the seed of another.
<margin>B</margin> This is something the **philosopher** <note>In this context, a "Philosophus" is a student of the hidden laws of nature and alchemy.</note> does not know. For no seed can abandon the eternal, though it may certainly rot. When that which is eternal is ordained toward the eternal, then man alone among all creatures has the eternal within him inside the transient. Since the transient and the eternal stand beside one another, it is to be understood that the transient prepares an essence for the "stomach" and bears the merit of the body. This comes solely from the origin: that the eternal part of man lives eternally, and the transient part dies a mortal death. As is the body, so is the eternal that comes from it. It is a wonder of all **philosophy** <note>original: "Philosophiæ."</note> that a transient thing should master and lead the eternal according to its pleasure, and thus man looks upon his own free home. Therefore, he has more power over his eternal part than the one from whom the transient and his eternal part here come. By this, it is to be noted that the transient parts of all creatures dwell together—the rational and the irrational—each serving the other; and everything transient is given to the eternal and is in its power, dwelling together as equals. Therefore, Philosophy teaches that all which dwells together without strife, war, falsehood, or deceit—the good and the evil—cannot be consumed except one against the other. Yet for those in whom the eternal is not present, no judgment is found; but in those where the eternal is, it cannot pass without judgment. So, when this discord exists, one eternal part must give an accounting to the other and satisfy the debts for what was done by one to the other. And because this debt belongs to the eternal, it does not happen through the transient. For although bodies tolerate each other and unite, whatever remains is eternal. Therefore, only the eternal in us judges; so when an accounting must happen, one to the other, all transient things that have the eternal within them are forced to die, so that only the 
<margin>C</margin> eternal remains without the body and thus appears at the Judgment. For that alone is eternal and nothing more; that is the final death of everything at the end. Now, when those who have the eternal within them have died, nothing remains but the thing that held, guided, and nourished that eternal part. For what is not useful does not remain in the creature; they are only there for the sake of the eternal. Therefore, it follows that along with that which has the eternal within it, all things that contained it pass away and die; but the eternal alone does not. Thus, the "end" of bodily things is found—that is, the "nothing" into which all things come. For they are separated from their essence into nothing—that is, from "something" into **nothingness** <note>original: "nihilum."</note>. But in man, the perfect separation is missing—that is, the separation of the eternal from the mortal. For there the Judgment is found, which shows the decay of all things to everyone dwelling among the ethers. And if no accounting were found regarding the transient, then there would be no decay in the creatures, but all would be eternal. But this is the cause: because we mortals do not dwell in justice and do not give right judgment among ourselves, and have no power to judge the eternal, this must happen in the eternal realm. Because this must happen, we must all come together; and so the **dissolution** <term>Zergehung: The process of melting away, dissolving, or passing from a material state into a spiritual one.</term> of all things is found.

### The Twenty-fourth Text.

Now, since all things were created out of the first **Great Mystery** and thus pass away, it is subsequently to be noted that it is a "Great Mystery." Although it is nothing—just as if a house were made out of a word—this is to be understood as belonging to the Highest alone. It is like a man making a fire where there is none, and out of no fire. For the **flint** <note>original: "Kisslung."</note> has no fire, even though it gives fire. So it is to be recognized that in the Great Mystery, all mysteries...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Great Mystery" and the dissolution of elements, specifically focusing on the categorization of created things—plants, elements, and various forms of humanity—before concluding the second part of the work and introducing the third part, which deals with the First Matter and the origins of supernatural beings.</meta>

# THE PHILOSOPHY TO THE ATHENIANS

<margin>A</margin>
First they lay and were, and that in three ways: Upon the **Vegetable** <term>Vegetabilischen: Refers to the life-force of plants and the process of growth.</term>, upon the **Elements**, and upon the **Sensible** <note>original: "Sensibilia." Beings possessing the power of perception and sensation.</note>. Upon the **Vegetable** there were many hundreds and many thousands: for every species had its own particularity in the **Great Mystery** <term>Mysterium Magnum: The primordial, chaotic source or "womb" from which God separated all specific forms of matter and life.</term>. Thus, there were only four upon the **Elements**, for those have only four beginnings, but many hundreds upon **Humans**. For the **Loripedes** <term>Loripedes: Literally "strap-footed." In the folklore of the time, these were considered a "monstrous" race of humans with flexible or crawling limbs.</term> are a special kind, the **Cyclopes** a special kind, the **Giants** a special kind, the **Mechili** <note>original: "Mechili." Likely referring to a class of monstrous or hybrid beings described in Paracelsian biology.</note> a special kind; likewise those who dwell in the **Earth**, those who dwell in the **Air**, those who dwell in the **Water**, and those in the **Fire**. And especially all plants: every species had its own particular **Mystery** in the **Great Mystery**, and all manner of creatures were there. For as many kinds of trees as there are, so many kinds of humans, and so many **Mysteries**. And yet, the eternal alone reigns in man and in all their **Mysteries**, no more in one than in another. There was no **Species** <note>original: "Genus."</note> in the **Great Mystery** that was not formed and colored in a hundredfold way or more, unlike one another, yet all such things must pass away. But what may further become of them, that we shall let be: for it is insane to speculate on a new **Great Mystery**, unless it becomes much stranger, so that we cannot contemplate it for the sheer wonder of it.

### Conclusion of the second Part of the Prince THEOPHRASTUS
### on the creation of all things, and the separation of the 
### creatures, with the use of the Mysteries.

<margin>B</margin>
And as mentioned, the Prince **Theophrastus** <note>The author, Paracelsus, whose full name was Theophrastus von Hohenheim.</note> in this second part of the first volume **On the Generation of Things** <note>original: "de Generatione Rerum."</note>—so he concludes therein, that all things which are transient were created at one single point: and after that, no further species was created. He sets down first the **Elements**, thereafter how the **Procreations** <note>The various offspring or specialized forms of life.</note> were separated out of the four elements: thereafter the final **Mysteries**, which grow and are separated out of the procreations. And finally, he concludes that in the rational being there is an eternal element: wherein he acknowledges a **Last Judgment**, and an **Eternal Life**, and a perishing and consumption of all things, and an end to the world: he also indicates that every **Species** is here from a particular **Mystery**, and that no **Mystery** has left behind more than one **Species**, and he sets an end to all things.

### Preface to the third Part of the Great Prince
### THEOPHRASTUS.

<margin>C</margin>
<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'I' depicting a person in a landscape with buildings and foliage.</image-desc>
In this part, the Prince **Theophrastus** shows us the **First Matter** <term>Prima Materia: The original, undifferentiated substance from which the elements were formed.</term> of the four elements, each one contained in particular: what **Fire** is, and what **Air**, what **Water**, and what **Earth** is: how they became elements, and in what way they are elements. Thereafter he describes what the **First Matter** is of the **Firmament**, stars, planets, and all heavenly things that are transient. After that, the **Principles of Spirits and Fates** <note>original: "Principia Spirituum vnd Fatorum."</note>, how they received their birth in the separation. Following that, he sets down the origin of the **Nymphs**, **Lorind** <term>Lorind: A Paracelsian term for water spirits, often associated with sirens.</term>, **Sea-monsters**, and all flesh that is generated in the water, what their **Beginning and End** <note>original: "Principium vnnd Finis."</note> contain. After that, the earthly **Mysteries** of the minerals, the various forms of humans, of rational animals, of herbs, of trees, of stones: likewise of the **Dwarves** <note>original: "Zwergel." In Paracelsian thought, dwarves or gnomes were the elemental spirits of the Earth.</note>, of the natural ones. And so he concludes the third part with this **First Matter**, wherein he acknowledges from the **Philosophical Nature** an eternal and a transient part, and the mixing of the transient and the eternal. Likewise, he mentions the birth of **CHRIST**, and of the **Virgin MARY**: he gives us to understand how the transient may become untransient, with a wonderful interpretation; he gives us to recognize a distinction of the world, one eternal, and one transient: and how the transient becomes an eternal one: and thus concludes the final text with this.

It introduces the third part, which focuses on the First Matter of the elements and the transformation of the transient into the eternal through spiritual and philosophical means.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the introductory discussion on the "Great Mystery" (Mysterium Magnum) and the various classes of created beings, moving now into "The Second Book," which details the separation of elements and the nature of the creators behind mortal and immortal forms.</meta>

<center>BOOK TWO <note>original: "LIBER SECUNDUS"</note></center>

# The Second Book.

### The First Text.

<margin>A</margin>
Since something existed that came to a separation <term>Scheidung: The alchemical process of "separating" or "distilling" distinct forms out of the initial chaos.</term>, and through which all things were created: it is first to be understood that there is a distinction among the gods, and it is así. Since the creation is divided—one part into the eternal, the other into the perishable—it follows that there was another Creator of the Mysteries <note>original: "Mysteriorum." Referring to the hidden forces of nature.</note>, and not the highest and greatest. For the highest and greatest shall be a Judge of all creation and a punisher of the same; and He recognizes what is permitted to those creatures, and that it is in their power to do good and evil, which was not born out of Him. Furthermore, the creature is incited, tempted, provoked, compelled, and forced toward evil by the Stars, by Fate <note>original: "Fatum."</note>, and by the Infernal <note>original: "Infernale."</note>. Yet, if the creature came from Him, the Highest, it could not be that anything should force its nature toward good or evil; rather, it would be free and its own master without any interference. Likewise, the creature does not have sufficient understanding to recognize evil and good, or to distinguish the eternal from the mortal. For some are fools and simpletons, and among a thousand there is scarcely one wise man; instead, there are many false prophets, lying doctors, and ignorant masters. Yet, they are clearly regarded by the creation as the prominent ones, though they are not. This is a significant cause: because we are such a creation, we do not come from masters who are perfectly good, but are rather made by perishable gods who held power in the Great Mystery <term>Mysterio Magno: The primordial "womb" of all matter.</term>, and yet through the Eternal, a judgment was set for them and for us.

### The Second Text.

<margin>B</margin>
Thus, as was recognized in the Separation, all creatures must consist of and come forth from only four things; so these four are the Mothers of all creatures and are called Elements. And although every creature is an element, or has an attachment to an element, it is not an element in the sense of its mass, but rather as a Spirit of the Element. Nothing can exist without it; it must have an element. They also cannot stand together, for there is nothing that consists of four elements, nor three, nor two; rather, an element stands alone, and every creature has only one element. It is a blind understanding to think that "wetness" is recognized as the element of Water, or "burning" as the element of Fire. For the element should not be understood according to the body, or out of the substance, or according to its outward character. For that which is visible is merely the enclosure <note>The physical shell or "casing" of an object.</note>, and the element is a Spirit and lives within things just as a soul lives in a body. This is the First Matter <note>original: "Prima Materia."</note> of the elements—invisible and impalpable, yet present in all things. For the First Matter of the elements is nothing other than the Life that is within the creatures. And that which is dead is no longer in any element, but in the Final Matter <note>original: "ultima materia." The state of matter after it has lost its vital spark.</note>, wherein there is no longer any value, virtue, or power.

### The Third Text.

<margin>C</margin>
Now, since the four Mothers—the four elements—were empowered to create all things, it is further to be noted that the four elements were sufficient for all things; there could have been no more and no fewer. This is because in mortal things, no more than four natures can exist. In immortal things, however, the "Temperaments" <note>original: "Temperament." A balanced state of qualities found in the divine or celestial realm.</note> may exist, but not the elements. For whatever is of an Elemental Nature <note>original: "Elementur."</note> is fragile and breakable. But whatever is of the "Temperature" <note>original: "Temperatur."</note> has no fragility within it; it is so fashioned that nothing leaves it and nothing is added to it; it neither rots nor perishes. But since the mortal is created thus, it is to be recognized that they all stand under four names, and every nature has the name of its element. For instance: the Hot is an element of Fire; the Cold is an element of Earth; the Wet is an element of Water; the Dry is an element of Air. It should be understood that these four natures are each distinct: Fire is only hot, and neither dry nor moist; Earth is only cold, and neither dry nor moist; Water is only wet, and neither hot nor cold; Air is only dry, and neither hot nor cold. They are called Elements for this reason: they exist only in a single nature and are not twofold. However, their manifestation in all creatures should be recognized by how an element behaves with the substance and the body, and how it works therein. And the highest understanding of the elements is that they have a single nature, unblemished by additions of moisture or cold, dryness or heat. This is possible for spirits, and every spirit is singular in its nature and not divided, just as the elements are.
