--- Page 22 ---
<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s radical redefinition of the four elements. Having previously established the "Mysterium Magnum" (Great Mystery) as the source of all things, he now challenges the traditional medical theories of his time—specifically the Galenic view that elements and human complexions are combinations of qualities like "Hot and Dry" or "Cold and Moist."</meta>

# PHILOSOPHY TO THE ATHENIANS <note>original: "PHILOSOPHIÆ AD ATHEN."</note>

### The Fourth Text.

<margin>A</margin>
And although within us mortals there are **Composites** <term>Composita: Mixtures or combinations of different qualities.</term>, such as Warm and Moist, this is not to be understood in the way the old physicians defined it. For **Colic** <note>original: "Colica." Paracelsus often attributes diseases to elemental imbalances rather than just digestive issues.</note> comes from the **Element of Fire**, and it has no doubling, such as being both Hot and Dry; rather, it is solely Hot. The same applies to the other **Complexions** <term>Complexiones: The "humors" or temperaments of the body.</term>. Therefore, if a disease is noticed with Heat and Dryness, one should consider instead that two elements are present in that place—one in the liver, the other in the spleen, or likewise in other limbs—and not that two elements are within a single limb. For it is possible that a particular element dwells in each individual limb (which we leave to the physicians to determine). But it cannot be said that two elements may stand together, or that one element could be both Hot and Moist. It is not possible for a **Composite** to occur in that way, for the elements exist without being compounded, for the reasons stated before. For where there is Heat, there is no Cold, no Dryness, no Wetness; likewise, where there is Cold, none of the others are present. So it is also with Wetness and Dryness. For each element stands simply within itself, and only in combination does it appear twofold. But to understand what our philosophy attributes to the possibility of the elements regarding their **Conjunction**: a pairing such as Heat with Wetness cannot exist. For no **Element of Water** <note>original: "Elementum Aquæ."</note> tolerates Heat. Nor can any Heat stand within Wetness, for each is a distinct element. Likewise, Cold in itself cannot suffer Dryness; rather, Cold is unstained <note>original: "unbesleckt," meaning pure or unmixed.</note> within itself. This is said regarding the true nature of the elements; and any Dryness is a breaking 
<margin>B</margin>
of Cold. For just as little as Wetness and Dryness can agree, so too can Cold and Dryness, or Wetness, or Warmth, or Heat not come together or stay as one. For just as Heat and Cold hold themselves in discord, so too do Cold and Heat hold themselves in discord against Wetness and Dryness.

### The Fifth Text.

But to think that because all things are created from the four elements, they must therefore stand in **Conjunction**, is false. For every conjunction is a composition. So long as they are composed, they cannot be a **Mystery** <term>Mysterium: In this context, a pure, primordial essence or a singular state of being.</term>; for every Mystery is singular and a single element. But the difference between elements and composites is this: The element, like a Mystery, has the power to generate a **Divertallum** <term>Divertallum: A Paracelsian term for the diverse individual forms or "offshoots" that emerge from a single element.</term>. But a composite could generate nothing except its own likeness <note>original: "simile."</note>; just as humans make humans. But the Mystery does not give rise to another Mystery like itself, but rather to something diverse, like a *Divertallum*. The **Element of Fire** is the mother of the stars, planets, and the entire firmament, and yet none of these are formed exactly like it or are singular in the same way. The **Element of Water** <note>original: "Elementum Aqua."</note> has given us "substantial" water, which is entirely contrary to the *Element of Water* itself; for it is less wet than the *Element of Water* is in its own nature. For the *Element of Water* is such a wetness that it softens stones and the hardest metals; such great softening power is taken away from it by "substantial" water, so that its power is not complete. The **Element of Air** is so dry that it withers all water in an instant; but this power is taken from it and mixed with the "substantial" parts of the air. The **Element of Earth** is so cold that it brings all creatures to an **ultimate matter** <note>original: "vltimam materiam."</note>: it turns water into crystals, <note>Footnote marker in text</note>(*) [it turns minerals] into tufa stone, animals into marble, and trees into flint <note>original: "Kiſern." While "Kiefern" means pines, in the context of petrification (marble, tufa, crystal), it likely refers to "Kiesel" or silica/flint.</note>. This is the basis for recognizing the elements: they exist in such powerful operations that their equal cannot be found or known. And the things in which they dwell are drawn to them and taken like a **Fate** <note>original: "Fatum."</note> that becomes corporeal, and has no more power beyond this.

### The Sixth Text.

For a greater understanding of what an element is: an element is nothing other than a **Soul**. Although its essence is not exactly like a soul, it is uniform with the soul. For there is a difference between the soul of the element and the Eternal Soul. The soul of the element is the life of all creatures. The fire that burns there is not the **Element of Fire** <note>original: "Elementum Ignis"</note> as we see it; rather, the soul that is within it, invisible to us, is the *Element of Fire* and its life. Now, the *Element of Fire* may well be in green wood just as it is in the fire; but the life is not there as it is in the fire. Therefore, there is a difference between the soul and the life. For when the fire lives, it burns; but when it is in the soul—that is, in its element—it is without burning. And it is not the case that because a thing is cold, it must be from the cold element; it may rather be from the hot one, and much cold comes from the **Element of Fire**. For whatever grows, grows out of the *Element of Fire*, but in another form. Whatever is fixed <note>original: "Fir," likely "fix" or "firm."</note> comes from the **Element of Earth**. Whatever nourishes comes from the **Element of Air**. And whatever consumes comes from the **Element of Water**. For growth belongs solely to the **Element of Fire**, and where that is not present, there is no growth. And if the **Element of Earth** were not there, there would be no stopping of growth; for it **fixes** <note>original: "figirt."</note>, that is, it gives an end to the *Element of Fire*. Likewise, if the **Element of Air** were not there, nothing could be moved; for through the air alone are all things driven. Also, nothing could be broken or consumed if the **Element of Water** were not there; for through the *Element of Water* all things are reduced <note>original: "gerödt," meaning dissolved, rotted, or cleared away.</note> or brought to nothing.

### The Seventh Text.

But since the elements are thus entirely invisible and imperceptible, hidden within one another, they nonetheless have other mysteries to distribute. Just as the **Element of Fire** has distributed from itself the...

<meta>The text cuts off here, with the catchword "jhm das" (from itself the...) indicating the start of the next page's specific elemental distributions.</meta>

<summary>This page presents Paracelsus’s theory of the elements as pure, singular "souls" or invisible forces rather than mixed physical qualities. He argues that elements do not combine into "hot and dry" pairs but act as distinct life-forces responsible for specific functions like growth (Fire), fixing (Earth), movement (Air), and dissolution (Water).</summary>
<keywords>Elements, Fire, Water, Air, Earth, Soul, Mysterium, Divertallum, Petrification, Physiology, Pathology, Growth, Paracelsus</keywords>

--- Page 23 ---
<meta>This page continues Paracelsus's exploration of the four elements. Having argued that elements are simple and uncompounded, he now describes how each element—Fire, Air, Water, and Earth—serves as a "mother" or source for specific created things and inhabitants, ranging from the sun and stars to spiritual beings and minerals.</meta>

# BOOK THE SECOND
<note>original: "LIBER SECVNDVS"</note>

<margin>▲</margin>
The firmament belongs to it: but not with physical bodies, but only with the elemental essence. The Sun has a different body, coming from the element of Fire; but within it, the element is substantial with heat. Not that its heat has an origin from its motion <note>Paracelsus rejects the Aristotelian view that the movement of celestial spheres creates heat through friction.</note>, but from itself: even if it stands still and never moves, it still possesses its radiance along with its heat. For the crystals <note>original: "Crystallen"; likely referring to the luminous bodies or "stars" within the fire element.</note> from the element of Fire were given to the Sun: and although no other body is in it except what it received from the element of Fire, for the elements were incorporated out of that same source. The Moon and other stars have their origin likewise from the elements of Fire: but only in the ruby-colored shades, in which there is no heat nor burning nature, but rather a dead glow. And although there are many kinds of signs according to the forms and shapes in the heavens, which we do not mention here: yet such a form is to be understood just as it is with us on Earth, for there is not just one eternal thing, but many—both known and unknown to us. Because the Mystery of the element of Fire has been divided, each thing has stood and become as we see it: therefore, the stars are a daughter of the elements of Fire, and the heaven is nothing but a vapor <note>original: "Chay," a Paracelsian term for a chaotic, misty, or vaporous substance from which things are formed.</note>, that is, the steam from the firmament, so hot that it is beyond description. And that same heat gives the heavens their colors and shape: for it is the pure element of Fire <note>original: "Ignis"</note> at those ends, as will be further mentioned in its proper place.

### The Eighth Text.

<margin>B</margin>
And in like form, with the diversity of shapes and beings, just as Fire has provided, so in such a manner has the element of Air <note>original: "Aëris"</note> also provided. But although there is a distinction between the four kinds of elements in those who are born from them: each one has procreated something special. The Firmament is like none of the other three; the Fate <term>Fatum: In this context, Paracelsus refers to the specific destiny or spiritual inhabitants belonging to the element of Air.</term> from the Air is also not like the other three. The Signatures <note>original: "Signata"</note> of the Earth are not to be compared to the other three at all: likewise, the water-wonders <note>Likely referring to nymphs, undines, or other elemental beings of water.</note> are just as little similar to these three. For each element has born within it rational and irrational things: just as the heavens have intelligent creatures in the firmament, so does the element of Earth <note>original: "Terræ"</note>. Likewise, the Fate of the Air is endowed with reason and unreason in its signature: and the same applies to the water and earth. Now, who will grant us the truth to know which among the signatures of the four elements are those commanded to have faith, the right path, or which alone possess eternity—or if it is in all four? This we shall let pass for now. Now, it cannot be otherwise than that there are people in all four, just as in this one, which is the Earth. But to recognize the "Fate," its birth has been shown to be manifold from the element, and yet without any physical bodies or substance, according to the quality of the Air, which is not corporeal, along with its dwellings: for some have it corporeally, some intangibly <note>original: "intangibiliter"</note>, according to how it is understood.

### The Ninth Text.

<margin>C</margin>
For in the same way that from a seed the root goes out into many fibers, then the stalk with many branches, then the leaves, the blossom, the fruit, and the seed: just as that has happened, so it must also happen with the many kinds of procreations from the four elements: and all these that are in one element hang together, like a plant from one seed. And although it does not look like the seed: for those created from water, some are people, some animals, some for their health and sustenance. For an element has left its signature, its necessity and sustenance: it has also given indications of its course and future, which is most easily recognized through the stars: not that the stars rule or incline us, but only that they run parallel to us, with the internal course of our body. In the same way, all things happen in the water as in the element of Earth: for the *Lorind* <term>Lorind: A Paracelsian term for a meteorological sign or "comet" occurring within the element of water.</term> is a movement of the change of that same element of Water <note>original: "Aquæ"</note>. And when such a thing moves in the element of Water, the element of Earth also moves toward a change. For *Lorind* is to be noted just like a comet: and a water-wonder is to be understood just like an anomaly of the firmament. And thus, in the water, a special world is to be recognized, together with its Mystery, until the end of the world: for there is no other beginning in them than in the other elements: there is also no other end in them than what is noted in the other elements. There is only a difference of forms, beings, and natures, which exists between the elements with their signatures. Therefore, we are to recognize four worlds, according to the four elements and four ancestral dwellings: but according to the truth, only one eternal thing is to be recognized equally in all four.

### The Tenth Text.

In the element of Earth, we have great understanding, because we are from the element of Earth: for "like understands its like" <note>original: "simile verstehet sein simile"</note>. But to understand other elements comes from philosophy: but that is a "likeness" that comes from experience, from which philosophy follows afterward: and yet, not otherwise than how the element of Earth has procreated the Signature, so have the others procreated. The stones that we have exist just as well in the other elements as with us: although they are not stones in our form, but rather in their own form. The mineral among them is the same as among us, for the heavenly firmament gives blossoms and mineral stones, which we consider a miracle <note>original: "Miracul"</note>.

<summary>Paracelsus describes how each of the four elements (Fire, Air, Water, Earth) produces its own unique inhabitants, "people," and minerals, asserting that the stars are "daughters" of Fire and that each element constitutes its own distinct world.</summary>
<keywords>elemental beings, firmament, sun, stars, Chay, Fatum, water-wonders, Lorind, signatures, like understands like, mineral stones</keywords>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the four elements (Fire, Air, Water, and Earth), specifically focusing on how they act as distinct worlds or "mothers" for different types of beings, and how the "Great Mystery" will eventually be revealed at the end of time.</meta>

# PHILOSOPHY TO THE ATHENIANS
<note>original: "PHILOSOPHIÆ AD ATHEN."</note>
<meta>catchword: likewise-</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
Although we are mistaken, nothing is more contrary to us than our desire to regard the natural courses of the world as miraculous signs, or to prophesy as the prophets do. All that the heaven and its firmament signify has a different meaning; they indicate nothing to us except that their course is simply as it is. And if something follows us thereafter, let it be noted that our own course was such. But even though an element may suffer an error <note>In this context, an "error" refers to an anomaly or deviation from the natural order.</note>, it weakens the others: for they should all run perfectly and maintain their path. And although it is true that the other three elements serve us for our nourishment, the other three serve just as well the firmament, the air, the water, and those who dwell therein; and each is nourished by the other, like the many types of trees belonging to a gardener. The lack and error of the firmament may be seen and noted by us just as well as the firmament sees our own lack. Likewise, such an understanding applies to the others.

### The Eleventh Text.

Thus, it is a simple philosophy to place all bliss and eternity solely in our element of Earth; and it is a foolish opinion that we should consider ourselves alone to be the noblest of creatures, since there are more worlds than ours alone. Also, it is even more of a folly that we do not recognize those who come from our element and are also people, such as the <term>Nocturnals</term> <note>original: "Nocturnaliſchen"; beings or spirits associated with the night</note> and the <term>Gnomes</term> <note>elemental spirits of the earth</note>. And although they do not dwell in the sun’s shine, nor make use of the light from the firmament, but rather hate what we love, and we love what they hate—likewise regarding our form and essence, they are maintained, but not in the same likeness as us. So we should not wonder at this, for the reason that they are so created in the <term>Great Mystery</term> <note>original: "Mysterio Magno"; the primordial, undifferentiated source of all creation in Paracelsian thought</note>; and not only we, but many more exist whom we do not recognize. Therefore, it is to be understood that more bodies existed in the Great Mystery than just one kind: but yet only one Eternal thing is contained in all, and one Perishable thing. <margin>B</margin> And thus, as they have created the elements in many kinds of forms and many strange shapes, it is not possible to recount everything. But it will undoubtedly be known at the End, when the eternity of all such things shall come together. At the End, much that was unknown will be recognized, and will appear in many ways: not only from those who possess eternity within them, but also from those who have contained, nourished, and shown that which has an eternity in it. For the Eternal is to be understood in two ways: one to rule and govern, the other to serve as a witness to the same. For it is against philosophy to say that little flowers should be without eternity: although they perish, they will yet appear at the gathering of all generations. For nothing is created out of the Great Mystery that will not have an image outside of the <term>Ethers</term> <note>original: "Etheren"; the celestial or spiritual realms</note>.

### The Twelfth Text.

But from this, and as all <term>Procreations</term> <note>original: "Procreationes"; the beings or substances generated by the elements</note> indicate, there must have been four Mothers over all things, no more and no less. But this cannot be understood from the foundational ground according to a complete indication of the present Great Mystery as it appears in the beginning of its properties: rather, the first Great Mystery is recognized and understood through the last mysteries and through the procreations that have gone out and grown from the first. For the beginning does not make the philosopher, but the end makes the master: to know a thing in its perfect nature is found only at the end of its being. <margin>C</margin> Perhaps more elements were possible than were given to us: yet in the final knowledge, only four are found in all things. And although we consider that it would have been possible for the Creator to do more, who then created only four: yet because such a perishable world is created in only four, we consider that more could not have stood. We may rightly think it true that other elements will be born after these four cease, unlike these four in all their essence: and that after the perishing of this now-created world, a new Great Mystery will be made, which will possess a greater understanding than that of the past. However, we do not intend to set down the origin of that future state; it is for everyone who wishes to be skilled in the beginning of the world to recognize that the origin of the world comes from the elements, and of those there are four, and thus also four worlds; and in each one a special being and race, according to its necessity and need.

### The Thirteenth Text.

And although all things stand within the four elements, we do not posit that the four elements are in all things, or that the four elements dwell in everything. The reason is this: The world which is separated and procreated from the element of Fire, that same world needs no air, water, nor earth at all: likewise also the world of Air is in no way dependent on the other three: the Earth and Water are also in such a form. For the foundation of the elements does not imply that the world must be maintained by four elements together, but each by one element—that is, by that from which it originated. And although it is true that the firmament <note>Here referring to the starry, fiery heaven</note> nourishes the world through its elemental power, which goes forth from it entirely fiery upon the earth: yet that same nourishment is not necessary. For the world will not perish by itself; it is sufficient to nourish itself, just as another world nourishes itself without the earth. As with Water, the Earth contributes nothing fruitful to its own essence: also the Water contributes nothing to the Earth, nor the Air likewise...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that each of the four elements constitutes its own self-sufficient world inhabited by unique beings like Gnomes and Nocturnals, and asserts that the true nature of the Great Mystery is revealed only at the end of a thing's existence.</summary>
<keywords>elements, Great Mystery, Gnomes, Nocturnals, four worlds, procreation, eternity, firmament, Paracelsian philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the four elements (Fire, Air, Water, and Earth). It transitions from describing elements as physical "mothers" to explaining the "Arcanum"—the hidden, spiritual essence within each element that governs life, light, and the preservation of creatures beyond their physical death.</meta>

BOOK TWO
<note>original: "LIBER SECVNDVS"</note>
Vol, II. b
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
In the same way, it is sufficient for us to know that each world stands alone in its own element. Moreover, the light from heaven is an outflowing from the four elements, and the noblest part of their perfect character. Man should not understand this to mean that the sun took its shine and its path from the physical element of Fire, nor the planets likewise; rather, they exist through the <term>Arcanum</term> <note>From the Latin "arcanum," meaning "secret." In this context, it refers to the hidden, spiritual virtue or "inner stars" that give life and power to the physical elements.</note>. Therefore, the shine of the firmament upon the world does not come from the element of Fire itself, but from the Arcanum. For the Earth gives its <term>Tronum</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for the specific spiritual influence or "star" of the Earth.</note>, the Water its <term>Turas</term> <note>The spiritual influence or inner essence of Water.</note>, and the Air its <term>Samies</term> <note>The spiritual influence or inner essence of Air.</note>. These do not originate from the physical element but from the Arcanum, and yet they reside within the element. From these Arcana, the four worlds harmonize in such a way that they are useful to one another, helping and sustaining each other—but this is not by the physical nature of the elements, for they are simply the elemental containers.

# The Fourteenth Text.

That man lives, sees, hears, and the like, is not due to the elements, but comes from the Arcana, and even more so from the <term>Monarchy</term> <note>The divine, overarching order or spiritual government of the universe.</note>. All creatures are the same; only their shelter and nourishment are elemental. Understand also that everything eternal comes from the Arcanum and is the Arcanum itself. Dogs die, but their Arcanum remains; man dies, but his Arcanum remains—and his soul even more so, which makes him so much nobler than a dog. This is true for all growing things. From this arises the potential for error: in the <term>Great Ultimate Mystery</term> <note>original: "Mysterio Magno vltimo"; the final state of the world or the "Last Day" in Paracelsian theology.</note>, all creatures that have ever been will appear—not in their physical substance as they are now, but Arcanically. We do not say that the Arcanum is a physical being like that which has not yet died, but rather that it is the perfect version of it. The element of Fire has within it an Arcanum, and from this Arcanum comes the light, the shine, the influence, and the growth for the other three elements, rather than from the physical element of fire itself. For these Arcana could well exist without the physical element, just as the element could exist without them. But note further: the element of Air <note>original: "Aeris"</note> has within it an Arcanum, and from it comes the nourishment of all the other three worlds and itself. This does not pass from one element into the others in a physical way, but Arcanically, through the element.

<margin>B</margin>
The element of Earth <note>original: "Terræ"</note> has within it the Arcanum of persistence and stability, giving the others the power of their permanence and their ability to bring forth life so that they do not fail. The element of Water <note>original: "Aquæ"</note> gives the Arcanum that sustains all elements and what lies within them, allowing them to progress and remain without being destroyed. Thus, there is a distinction between the elements and the Arcana: one is perishable (the element), while the other is a permanence that remains in the Great Ultimate Mystery, in which all things are renewed, and yet they are nothing other than what they have always been.

# The Fifteenth Text.

It must be recognized that the elements do not stand mixed together; they are entirely Airy, Fiery, Earthly, or Aquatic, and are not blended. Furthermore, an element nourishes only its own, so that from it comes its own world. For this reason, medicine from the element of Water does not help those who are from the element of Earth or the others; it helps only the Nymphs, sea monsters, and the like. Earthly medicine also does not help the other three worlds, only the animals in its own world. The Air is the same: for in the Air there are also diseases, physicians, the learned, and the unlearned, within their own world and their own course. It is the same in the element of Fire. And although it happens that Nymphs dwell among earthly people and bear children, this is possible because <term>Rapture</term> <note>original: "Raptus"; a state of being "snatched" or transported from one elemental realm to another.</note> allows it. The same applies to beings of the air, such as when <term>Melusine</term> <note>original: "Melosin"; a legendary female spirit of fresh water, often depicted as a mermaid or serpent-woman.</note> came to the earthly people; all such things are the result of Rapture.

<margin>C</margin>
Likewise, those who are raptured from the Fire to us are called <term>Tristeres</term> <note>Paracelsian name for fire-spirits or beings belonging to the element of fire.</note>. When these three foreign worlds mingle with ours, as seen above, they are to be recognized in their whole being as "Gods" compared to us, because of the great strangeness and the alien nature they possess. If one of us were raptured to them, that person would be understood by them in the same way we understand those who are raptured to us. Thus, the elements do not need one another, except that each one serves as a "box" or container for the others, or holds the others together like a heap. Just as Water and Earth separate from one another, so do the Air and the Fire; each possesses its own separate part and reaches no further than the walls and the mutual inclination of the Arcana from all four.

# The Sixteenth Text.

Since it follows thereafter that there will be a joining together, and all things will return in measure according to the essence they once had, that state is "Arcanic" and according to the appearance of the elements. For in that state, nothing corporeal can appear from birth; instead, the "face" <note>the spiritual appearance or image</note> and the presence of all completed births will suffice to stand there. In this way, everything that happened before and after a person will be known to them, and this will be visible and known to everyone. But in this, there is a secret understanding of the Great Ultimate Mystery. This is not drawn from nature, but from the knowledge of causes—the final separation of the elements and all creatures—wherein an answer will be given to everyone regarding their death. This is the cause of both the perishable and the living or remaining. For there will be a single Judge, who has held power from the beginning, and has been the one and only Judge forever and ever. And this is the origin of faiths and the many kinds of servants of the gods, all of which are a false practice. For there has never been any God other than He who has always been the Judge. And it is a false folly to recognize the—

<margin>A</margin>

### The Seventeenth Text.

Now, having come to all predestination <note>In Paracelsian thought, "Predestination" refers to the pre-determined ultimate state or "final form" toward which a natural object evolves or decays.</note>, which is thus constituted, there arises an **Arcanum**: for Predestination is the ultimate matter <note>original: "lezt Materia"</note> which shall exist without the elements and without its current essence; instead, it will subsequently be a thing tempered and incorruptible <note>original: "Temporatum & Incorruptum"</note>. For this is not understood through the spirit, but through Nature, with the proof that an eternal state follows the mortal one. For when an unfeeling plant passes away, an eternal thing takes its place; and there is nothing on Earth among these perishable things that does not leave an eternal thing in its place. For nothing is empty; nothing among the perishable is created without leaving an eternal essence behind. For after the end of all creatures, such eternal things shall come together—not merely as a form of nourishment, but rather as a mastery of Nature within both the perishable and the eternal. Thus, the eternal is a sign of the breaking of Nature, and not a beginning of creation, but an end in all things, except for that which possesses no Nature. Although even the fatal beings <note>original: "Fatales," likely referring to spirits of destiny or the Fates</note> shall leave behind an eternal essence, as will the Melusines <note>Water spirits or mermaids from European folklore</note> and the Nymphs; yet we wish to mention nothing here of their corruption. For in that state, many kinds of decay <note>original: "Feule," referring to the alchemical process of putrefaction or breaking down</note> are understood, according to the four worlds: such as Earthly decay, Airy decay, and Aquatic decay. For each thing, together with its fellow creatures, is turned toward perishability within the abandoned eternal and is brought to that point. But these four decays shall bring their eternal essence into a comparison, known and visible, not through works but through being: for the eternal dwelling is an eternal thing, yet with many distinctions.
<margin>B</margin>

### The Eighteenth Text.

Now, we do not wish to dismiss the **EVESTRUM** <note>A Paracelsian term for the "sidereal body" or a spiritual double of a person or object that can mirror future events or provide omens.</note> in its essence, whether mortal or immortal. For the Evestrum is a thing like a shadow on the wall. The shadow grows and comes with the body, and remains with the same, even into its ultimate matter. The Evestrum takes its beginning with the first birth of every thing: for both the soulful and the soulless, the sensitive and the insensitive, have the Evestrum moving alongside them, as does everything that casts a shadow. **TRARAMES** <note>Another Paracelsian term, referring to an invisible spiritual essence or "ghost" of the senses and reason, distinct from the soul.</note>, however, is understood as a shadow of an invisible essence: for this reason, it is born with the reason and with the sensibility of the animals, both the rational and the irrational. To philosophize about the Evestrum and the Trarames belongs to the highest Wisdom <note>original: "Sophie"</note>: for the Evestrum gives prophecy, while the Trarames gives the sharpening of the mind. For the power to prophesy what is to come to man, animal, wood, or otherwise, comes from the shining Evestrum; that which comes from reason comes from the Trarames. Therefore, the Evestra are both beginning-having and beginningless: those with a beginning have perishability within them, along with an abandoned eternal essence. That which is beginningless has the beginning-having as a "Traranium," so as to sharpen the understanding. The mortal Evestrum recognizes the eternal; this recognition is the mother of the prophet. For the ground of all understanding is drawn from the Evestrum, as if with the light of Nature. Therefore, a prophet "evestrates"—that is, he speaks out of the Evestrum. But when the Spirit <note>Referring to the Holy Spirit or divine inspiration</note> prophesies, it is for us outside the Light of Nature; therefore, it is to us deceptive, false, and uncertain, as well as certain and true. So too the Trarames, the shadow of reason, desires to be divided.
<margin>D</margin>

### The Nineteenth Text.

And in the breaking of all things, the Evestrum and Trarames are also broken, yet not without leaving a remnant of their own. Thus the Evestrum is as extensive as the eternal essence of the firmament in the four worlds: for the firmament is fourfold according to the four worlds, and divided according to their perfect essences, each world perfect upon its own creature. It is also thus: one on Earth from the firmament, one upon the Water, the Air, and the Fire. But the firmament that is in the Evestrum is dispersed <note>original: "dispersum"</note>: not the stars as they are visible, but there are firmaments for the Nymphs, which are not stars. For they do not make use of the stars, but have a special firmament, as do the Fates <note>original: "Fata"</note>; those of fire <note>original: "Ignische"</note> each have their own special Heaven and Earth, Essence and Dwelling, Firmament, Stars, Planets, and the like, which do not appear at all similar to the others. Just as Water and Fire, a substance and an intangible thing, and as a visible and an invisible thing: so are these as well. In such things, the Evestrum is divided among the Fatal beings, and its shadow remains according to its essence after the breaking; and one Evestrum attaches to the Igneous, the fiery people; and then that which attaches to the watery ones; and likewise the earthly ones. This Evestrum befuddles and makes a fool of the world; it shadows itself with deception from one world into the other; it gives visions, it gives appearances, it gives signs, it gives form, it gives shape. For from this come Evestrum Comets, Evestrum 
<margin>

### The Twentieth Text.

To understand the Prophetic Evestrum <note>original: "Evestrum Prophetum"</note> is the most necessary task of all: For the Great Turban <note>original: "Turban magna"; in Paracelsian philosophy, this refers to the collective "Great Mystery" or a cosmic spirit that contains the archetypes of all events</note> is such an essence that it presages everything that happens in the four worlds. And whatever wonder occurs, whether against Nature or against common thought and life, is recognized through the Prophetic Evestrum, which is taken from and foreshadowed by the Great Turban. And it is necessary for the prophet to recognize the Great Turban, for it possesses great reason and unites itself with reason. Therefore, it is possible for a mortal <gloss>to recognize the Great Turban</gloss> until his final passing. From it, all prophets have spoken, for within it are all the signs of the world. All Evestra come from it; from it the comets are cast as shadows, as well as the significant stars that arise against the course of the heavens; and all impressions <note>original: "Impressiones"; referring to meteorological or astrological phenomena that leave a "mark" or sign on the world</note> take their beginning from the Turban and not from the firmament or the stars. For when an unheard-of, strange thing is to happen, heralds go forth to make such things known to the people, from which a following evil may be announced: these are not testimonies from Nature, but rather indicated by the Prophetic Evestrum. All deaths, all wars, all mutinies send their heralds before them, which arise from the Turban. And whoever is a knower of the property of the Evestra is a prophet and a soothsayer of all future things. For the Highest of all things does not speak with mortals, nor does He send 

<margin>
The Great Turban <note>original: "Turban magna"</note>. Held by Pagans, etc., to be God.
</margin>

His angels out from His dwelling to announce things; rather, such things are understood from the Great Turban, which many Pagans and Jews have held to be God, having been blinded in their understanding of the Godhead.

### The Twenty-First Text.

<margin>
B
</margin>

Since the overshadowed Evestrum <note>original: "Evester obumbratus"; the spiritual "double" or astral body that mirrors the physical person</note> grows and is born with every creature, it is further possible to predict the course and life of that same thing from its Evestrum. Just as when a child is born, the Evestrum is born with it, and is always formed within it, so that it shows all things concerning the child from infancy until its final days, and reveals what is to be done. For example, when someone dies, death does not occur unless the Evestrum first gives a sign: such as through knocking, shaking, falling, or some such sign related to that person's trade. If the Evestrum is noticed in this way, it may be understood as a herald of death, belonging to such a trade.

The Evestrum is also united with the eternal: for after the death of a human, the Evestrum remains on Earth and gives an indication of whether the person is in joy or pain through its manifestation. One should not say, as the simple-minded do, that these are spirits or souls, or that those who have died are walking there. It is the Evestrum of that same person, which does not depart until the "empty stable" <note>An idiomatic reference to the final judgment or the ultimate gathering of all things at the end of time</note> where all things come together. The Evestrum performs signs, for the Saints alone make understood and work miracles through their Evestrum. Just as the sun through its shine makes known its heat and its nature and essence: so are the presaging and prophetic Evestra <note>original: "Euestra præsagientia vnnd prophetica"</note> within us, and they are to be believed; for they govern sleep and dreams, prefiguring and portraying future things, indicating their nature, reason, essence, desires, and thoughts.

### The Twenty-Second Text.

<margin>
C
</margin>

Since future things are thus recognized in the elements, in which the Evestra have their dwelling: some Evestra are in water, some in mirrors, some in crystals, some from polished fingernails <note>original: "Vngues"; referring to onychomancy, the practice of divining the future by watching reflections on oiled fingernails</note>, some through the movement of waters, some through song, some through the mind—all of these may be "evestrated." For the highest and most benevolent God has a Mysterial Evestrum <note>original: "Evestrum mysteriale"</note> in which His essence and properties are seen; and through this Mysterial Evestrum, all good and all enlightenment are recognized. But on the other hand, the damned also has an Evestrum in the world, in which evil is recognized, and everything that then breaks the law of Nature, and the like. Although things are "evestrated" from these two, it is nothing other than their meeting our life: for only through our own Evestrum shall we recognize ourselves. In all creatures there are Evestra; alongside this, they are all prophets—rational and irrational, sentient and insentient. For the Evestrum is a spirit that teaches astronomy <note>In Paracelsian terms, this is "sidereal science," the knowledge of how celestial and spiritual forces influence the earthly realm</note>. Not that such things are recognized from nativities or prognostications from the stars, but they have their being <note>original: "Esse"</note> and their existence in the Evestra, like an image in a mirror, or a shadow in water, or on the earth. And in the same way that a plant grows and declines, and is meant to go, so the stars show themselves: not that they have their course thus by their own nature, or that moisture and cold are encountered from the earth, but only because the essence of the earth is such. Thus there are prefigurations in the heavens and in parts, but only as an Evestrum, and not as a power <note>original: "potentia"</note>.

Such Evestra shall also be broken, and yet they shall not pass away without an eternal element, and the Evestra shall not be looked upon [separately], but shall dwell entirely with all those to whom they belong. By this, everyone shall have the understanding to warn and recognize themselves above all things. For the great...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Evestrum" from the previous page, detailing its role as a universal prophetic force before concluding the third section (Paras) and introducing the fourth, which focuses on the nature of living things, the "Gubernator," and the path to the eternal.</meta>

PHILOSOPHY TO THE ATHENIANS, BOOK II.

<margin>A</margin> And the various types of Evestra <note>original: "Euestrorum"; in Paracelsian thought, an Evestrum is an invisible, prophetic shadow or astral body that exists for every object and person, conveying omens or dreams.</note> are innumerable: it guides the sleeper, it foretells good and evil, it seeks out thoughts, and it carries out work without physical movement. Thus it is wonderful, and a mother of all things, among prophets and astronomers, and likewise among physicians. And where understanding does not come from the Evestra, there is no knowledge of Nature. For just as stealing indicates a death by hanging, and a wet cloud indicates rain, and urine indicates a sickness: so the Evestrum indicates everything, with nothing excluded. For upon it the Sibyls and the prophets have spoken—but as if from sleep and dreams. And thus the Evestra are in the four worlds; each one gives a presage <note>original: "Præsagium"</note>, a precursor, and a wonder to the other: so through such breaking and rebirth, they shall be found more wonderful. We also do not wish to reject the idea that the Evestrum is the "abandoned eternal," a container of faith, and an operation of the heavenly. For we are moved to calculate against it only happiness <note>original: "fœlicitas"</note>, blessedness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note>, the highest good <note>original: "summum Bonum"</note>, and the Final Judgment, to more deeply and widely ground ourselves and experience the difference between the two—that is, the just and the false—which should be noted not spiritually, but naturally.

### The Conclusion of the Third Part <note>original: "Paras"; likely from the Greek "paratext" or a specific Paracelsian division of a book</note> of Prince THEOPHRASTUS.

In the preceding part, Prince THEOPHRASTUS clarifies and explains how, after the separation, there are four worlds, and what the Eternal is, and that nothing is created without an eternal aspect. In this is noted the Evestrum of God <note>original: "Euestrū Dei"</note> and likewise that of all things beneath Him: and it gives to understand the breaking of all things and the remaining of the eternal: and it is the third ground in all creatures, and ends with them. <margin>B</margin> That which, however, draws itself into a separation, as in Predestination <note>original: "Prædestinaz"</note>, there the fourth ground begins, acknowledging in it a Final Judgment, an eternal essence of all worlds: it gives to recognize that an Age <note>original: "Seculum"</note> is a world, as far and wide as it is comprised, and of such Ages there are four. And they should not be understood to have any other German meaning than four, as is shown in the elements, and from world to world—that is, from the mortal to the equality of the eternal assembly.

->Here ends the third part of Prince THEOPHRASTUS of Hohenheim, and the fourth part follows hereafter.<-

## Preface to the Fourth Part of the Great Prince THEOPHRASTUS.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'I' featuring a detailed landscape with rolling hills, leafy trees, and a small building or tower in the distance under a cloudy sky.</image-desc>

In this fourth part, Prince THEOPHRASTUS shows us the nature of everything that lives and everything that is dead, in what state each stands, what its appearance is, what its placement is, and what and how each thing comes into its essence—without substance, with substance, visible and invisible. Therein is understood what the Governor <note>original: "Gubernator"; the internal ruling spirit or guiding logic of a being</note> is, and how he is, and what his life is. Thereafter is understood herein what the highest good is, what the best good is, joy, and sorrow. Following that, understanding is given to men as to why the <margin>δ</margin> creatures exist, from whom, and from what, and for what purpose they come: therein is comprised what the body is, what the soul is, and what is eternal and non-eternal in its forms. And this part is a signifying and indicating of all figures <note>original: "Figuren"; the outward forms or signatures of things</note>, how each one stands and exists: and it is a "figural part" <note>original: "Paras figuralis"</note> because it gives to understand everything that adorns, polishes, makes, and changes the figures: therein he teaches how to do right, and what that is, and what it is good for: a complete philosophical understanding and ground for all those who desire to enter into the Eternal. Alongside this appears the explanation of why there are so many races of people, why so many languages, and why so many nations. Likewise, why there are so many faiths, and how there is one way to the Eternal, which comes not from faith, but comes alone from justice and piety. After that, how there is a way that goes alone to the heavenly, which comes out of faith, in which all sects of faiths and statutes, rules, and canons are comprised: what they are, what power and authority they have in men, what the vain and shameless life is, what unfaithfulness is, what falsehood is, and what is good and evil here and there. And this part is the greatest among the others, in indicating that Philosophy alone is the leader of man in all reason and understanding, and in her is the right life and the true life: not to regard gods, nor their law: everything is explained, why and how they are to be kept in their commandments, and without distinction, as according to Nature, and likewise what is then against Nature.

<meta>Vol. II. This page follows the discussion of the "Evestrum" by shifting focus to the material origins of the physical world. It introduces the concept of the "smoky spirit" as the invisible precursor to all physical substances, detailing how visible bodies "coagulate" from invisible sources.</meta>

# Book Three.

## The First Text.

<margin>A</margin>
Every thing that exists must have a body <note>original: "Corpus"</note>: but how that same body begins is to be understood as nothing other than a smoky spirit <note>original: "spiritus fumosus"</note>, which has no hard substance, is not yet a body, and is not tangible. and although it is none of these things, yet bodies and substance may be born out of it: Like arsenic <note>original: "Arsenicus"</note> which proceeds from it; there it is to be understood that after the birth of the body, nothing more of the smoky spirit will be seen, just as if it had all become one body: which is not the case, for the most subtle part still remains at the place of its birth. And thus a visible and an invisible thing are born together through a separation. All things are born in such a manner; wood still has a spirit from which it was separated; stones likewise; and so all things, with nothing excluded; its essence is still as it was when separated from it. Man likewise is nothing other than the remainder of the separated smoke. And note this: that there was a spirit, and from that same residue man arises, and the most subtle part is in the spirit: and it is a spirit that indicates two types of eternity. One is the Caleruthen <note>A Paracelsian term referring to the innate, natural destiny or "raw" eternal state of an object.</note>, the other is meritorious. The Caleruthen is an indicator in the first eternity: the other desires to reach the same; that is, to God. And that is a natural cause, that all things desire to return to that from which they came, and to the natures they have touched. For everything that the spirit was involved with, which it has made, also uses such things and goes back to them. And it is to be understood here, not that one desires the creator out of natural habit, but rather each thing desires that from which it comes. Thus the human body desires to return to the matter from which it was separated, and not to God, for it does not come from Him; and that same matter is a life and a dwelling in which the meritorious eternal remains: thus every thing returns again to its own essence.

<margin>B</margin>
## The Second Text.

Since every thing desires to return to its first place, that is, to the Mystery <note>original: "Mysterio"; the primordial source or hidden origin of all things.</note> from which it was separated: it is now to be recognized that this same thing is an eternal life, and that which comes from it is a mortal thing. Yet an eternal part remains in the mortal, which is the soul, as is understood elsewhere: and if a mortal thing is to return to its first place, this happens in no other way than this: that the parts which remain are joined together again, for then there is the assembly and unification of things. But the form and substance of the sentient and the non-sentient come from that same spirit of smoke <note>original: "spiritu Fumi"</note> in no other way than how hail or a lightning bolt comes from a cloud; the bolt is physical <note>original: "Corporalisch"</note>, but the matter from which it became remains invisible. Therefore it is to be understood that all things come from the invisible, and yet without harming the invisible, and that same matter always has the power to give birth to such things again. Thus it follows that the entire world will pass away like snow, and will return again into the same matter of the smoky spirit, and unite itself without any spiritual essence. After that, the first state may be born again. And it is also recognized there that there is no creature that is "born" <note>in the sense of being self-originated</note>, but rather well-created: For thus the Highest Good ordained it in the beginning of all things, that every thing comes from the invisible and thus becomes physical: and again it comes from the body and becomes invisible again: then they unite again and are brought into the first matter. But though they are thus united, they still have within them a distinction and a division: one is the lodging for the other, the other is an inhabitant of the lodging. For that is the dwelling of every thing, whether sentient or non-sentient, <margin>C</margin> everything must return to the end, whether in understanding or without understanding, so that nothing remains behind; it will appear again at its dwelling from which it was separated.

## The Third Text.

Likewise, every body or substance that is tangible is nothing other than a smoke that has coagulated. And it is to be understood that coagulation is of many kinds. One results in wood, one in stone, one in metals: but the body is nothing but a smoke <note>original: "Fumus"</note> that smokes up out of the matter or matrix in which it is contained. Just as what grows out of the earth is a smoke from the mercurial liquor <note>original: "liquore Mercurij"; the fundamental life-fluid in alchemy.</note>, which is manifold and gives manifold smoke, resulting in herbs, trees, and others. And as soon as that same smoke leaves its prime state <note>original: "Primum"</note>, as soon as it comes out of the matrix and touches the foreign air, or strikes against it, it is immediately coagulated: and it continually drives the smoke out, swelling in the same way as long as it "seethes"; as long as it seethes, it grows: and when it no longer seethes, it no longer smokes: thus the coagulation and the growth end. Wood is a smoke from the Oerles <note>A Paracelsian term for the prime matter of wood.</note>; in that same thing is this specific property from which wood becomes: not only from that same smoke, but possibly from other Dersic matter <note>Paracelsian term for specific terrestrial substances.</note>. Likewise, Lefkas <note>A Paracelsian term for the matrix of plants.</note> is a matter that exists, and from its smoke all herbs come: for only the herbal predestination is a Lefka, and in no other. For God is more wonderful in specific properties <note>original: "specificis"</note> than in all other natures. Scannar <note>A Paracelsian term for the matrix of metals.</note> is the mother of the metals, and gives the prime matter of metals <note>original: "primam materiam Metallorum"</note> out of her Vol. II.

<summary>This page explains that all physical matter originates from an invisible "smoky spirit" through a process of coagulation. It details how everything from trees to human bodies seeks to return to its original "Mystery" or primordial matter, emphasizing the cyclical nature of the visible and invisible worlds.</summary>

PHILOSOPHY TO THE ATHENIANS.

<margin>A</margin> Smoke. For all metals are nothing but a Coagulated Smoke from the Stannar <note>original: "Stannar"; in Paracelsian alchemy, this refers to the invisible "mother" or matrix of metals</note>. And Enuc <note>original: "Enuc"; a term for the internal "marrow" or essential spirit of stones</note> is the smoke of the stones. And thus that which is physical <note>original: "Corporalisch"</note> is viewed as nothing other than a Coagulated Smoke, within which is its specific predestination <note>original: "specifica prædestinatio"; the innate blueprint or purpose of a substance</note>, and all shall likewise dissolve again as smoke. For the specific thing that coagulates has no more power than for a perishable time: thus it is also to be understood in the coagulation: and all bodies shall at last dissolve into smoke and vanish, and end nowhere else but through the smoke, which is the consumption of living and dead physical things.

### The Fourth Text.

<margin>A</margin> Man is a Coagulated Smoke: For only out of the boiling vapors of the body and the generative members <note>original: "Samischen Gliedern"; referring to the reproductive organs</note> comes a coagulation of the spermatic matter <note>original: "Materiæ Spermaticæ"</note>: thus he shall also become a vapor again, and a smoke: he departs again just as he came. In addition, we see in ourselves nothing other than a human, Coagulated Smoke, formed out of human predestination. And everything that is taken in and eaten, that is all a Coagulated Smoke of liquids <note>original: "Liquoribus"</note>. Therefore, when that same thing is eaten, it is consumed by the life-force, in the manner that the coagulation is opened up and dissolved again, like ice in the sun, and thereafter vanishes away, like a smoke in the air. For life consumes all things, and is the spirit of consumption of all physical things and substances. And thus one must know of the separation of the mystery of digestion <note>original: "Mysterii digesti"</note>: For as each thing should return to its essence from which it came, and is eaten, it is consumed with the life-force: that same thing is only in those who are not transmuted. For transmutation <note>original: "Transmutierung"</note> cannot be driven backwards, and every transmutation happens through the life-force. Thus the transmuted thing changes into the perishability of the body: <margin>B</margin> But it is separated from the body again. For in its rotting <note>original: "Feulung"</note> the transmutation has no more power, and in the putrefaction <note>original: "Putrefaction"</note> the mystery of digestion follows: In this, all properties <note>original: "Proprietates"</note> that the human had from herbs, or other such things, separate from one another, each into its own essence. And that is a separation, just as ten or twelve different things are mixed together, and then drawn apart from one another again, each into its own special essence. Thus eating is nothing other than a dissolution of the bodies: Therefore the matter of the bodies is seen in the boiling and in the excrement: so that it is a stinking smoke, mixed with the good: And nature runs entirely toward the subtle part, and the coarse part she casts out. For stone, metals, and earth are all dissolved by the life-force, and otherwise there is no more dissolution of the body in them, except through the life-force.

### The Fifth Text.

This is likewise to be understood: how each thing takes its essence unto itself: It is to be compared to nothing else than how the fire that comes out of a hard stone and flames, and burns beyond all natural knowledge. Just as the hidden thing of the fire takes an origin, and thereafter comes into an effect: in such form and shape does the essence also come into nature. Recognize that in the beginning there was one thing without any inclination or genus, from which all things have sprung: This origin was nothing other than like a tempered color, which is brown in itself, and has no inclination in itself toward any other color, standing in complete balance <note>original: "Temperierung"</note>, and yet all colors are within it: <margin>C</margin> From which may be separated good Red, good Green, good Blue, good Yellow, good White, good Black: And of these colors each gives many dull colors, and each is well-colored within itself. And although the colors are many and contrary within themselves, yet they are all hidden under one color. So also each thing had its essence in the Great Mystery <note>original: "Mysterio magno"</note>, and was separated by the supreme Craftsman. The crystal gives fire, not out of a fiery nature, but through its strength with the hardness. It also has within it the other elements, not essentially <note>original: "Wesentlich"</note>, but materially <note>original: "Materialisch"</note>: a burning fire, a blowing air, a wet-black dry earth: Above all these, it has all colors in the mixture of its quality, but they are hidden within it, just like the fire in steel, which is not seen, neither by burning nor by its shine nor colors. In such a way all colors and elements lie in every thing, in their true essence, as they then show themselves in their works, nothing hidden. Now, how such things come into these objects, that same thing is to be recognized: that nothing else comes into them except through Him who is the maker of all things.

### The Six Text.

And although nature lies invisible in physical things and substances, as has been mentioned: yet note that the invisibility comes to visibility through the medium of the bodies: And as its essence is, so it will be visibly seen in virtues and colors. But the invisible bodies have no other understanding than such a physical one. Therefore note that the invisible ones have within them all elements, and they work in every element. They have to let out from them the fire and power of their element: the air likewise, like a human's breath: the water, like a human's urine: and they are also of an earthly nature, and take themselves from the earth. But understand that in this way: that the fluid of the earth <note>original: "Liquor Terræ"</note> moistens every day, and the most subtle spirit that is in it, from it

# THE ANATOMY OF THEOPHRASTUS: WHETHER HE COMPLETED IT ACCORDING TO THIS ARRANGEMENT IS UNKNOWN:

---

## GENERAL PROLOGUE TO ALL BOOKS
->*Of the Anatomy of Theophrastus.*<-

<margin>A</margin>Every anatomy, whether of the body or of the *Archeus* <note>original: "Archei"; the internal governing vital force or "inner chemist" that directs the body's functions</note>, is twofold: One is whole, the other is broken <note>or "dissected"</note>. That which is whole is of two kinds: one is *Idechtric* <note>original: "Idechtri"; likely referring to the essential, ideal image or "blueprints" of a thing</note>, the other is *Monstrous* <note>original: "Monstri"</note>, and both have their own anatomy. For the anatomy of the first creature is divided into the *Idechtric* and the *Monstrous*. The other, which is broken, is *Physical Anatomy* <note>original: "Anatomia Physica"</note>, and treats of the disease that burdens the *Idechtric*: For as is the *Anatomy of the Idechtric*, so is the *Anatomy of Disease* <note>original: "Anatomia Morbi"</note>. Now, however, to anatomize further, the first work is that one understands the *Anatomy of the Idechtric*, <margin>C</margin>thereafter the *Monstrous*, and these have their books in order in our volume. The second work is of the *Anatomy of Disease*, and has its rules <note>original: "Canones"</note> in its books, and is *Medical Anatomy* <note>original: "Anatomia Medica"</note>. The first, the *Physical*, as stated above, is spoken of as the *Anatomy of the Body* <note>original: "Anatomia Corporis"</note>, which comprises one volume.

Now, however, to speak of the *Anatomy of the Archeus*, it is the *Anatomy of Man* <note>original: "Anatomia Anthrotos"</note>, and I place that same one between the two anatomies as the middle point in the *Idechtric*.

Thus the First Anatomy is *PHYSICAL*, the Second is of *LIFE*, and the Third is *MEDICAL*: And *Medical* Anatomy is the *Anatomy of the Hand* <note>original: "Anatomia Cheros"; likely referring to surgical or practical medical application</note>, and has four anatomies within it, according to the four mothers of the elements. Thus there are seven kinds of Anatomy: One is equal to the *Idechtric*, the second is *Monstrous*, the third is of *Disease*, and four of the following elements. And the *Anatomy of Disease* is distinguished from the elements in that the *Anatomy of Disease* anatomizes the *disease*: And that which is anatomized by the anatomy of the four mothers is the *Anatomy of Practice* <note>original: "Anatomia Praxis"</note>, and of these there are seven. And of these seven alone, the beginning is *Experience*, then *KNOWLEDGE*, and then the Author.

->*END OF THE PROLOGUE.*<-

# TO THE READER.

<margin>D</margin>The anatomy as it flows from the *Idea* into the *Idechtric*, and thereafter the anatomy of the *Archeus*, of *Practice*, and of the elements—at that same thing, Reader, do not wonder at my style, if I present to you something new and different from the anatomy previously read by you and me. Some have been described, and yet the *Resolution of Nature* <note>original: "Relolteum Naturæ"; likely a corruption of "Resolutio Naturæ"</note> was not undertaken at that same place: and out of an incomplete anatomy, the physicians of the old and the new have stepped forward, and yet none the better; rather, as their anatomy appeared to them, they encountered the sick through it. I establish seven kinds of Anatomy: And though I did not prove them through your books, *Experience* and *Knowledge* prove them to me, and I as their author. A part of the...

The *Ideus*, or *Ideos* <note>the primordial "matrix" or "chaos" containing the seeds of all things</note> is the Portal out of which all creatures were created; it was contained in two essences: The Body of the creature is one, and the Life of the creature is the other. In the beginning, the *Yliaster* <note>the primeval force or substance from which the universe was molded</note> made the Bodies, and after this making, the Life was further assigned, and the *Ideos* was separated. The virtue hidden within it was drawn out, and it took on the name "Creature." Therefore, two anatomies follow: of the Body and of Life. But here we deal only with the Bodies, starting with the Anatomy of Man, then of Animals, then of Trees, then of Herbs, as each shall stand in its own chapter.

# THE PHILOSOPHY OF PHILIP
# THEOPHRASTUS PA-
# RACELSUS.

Before the four elements are explained to declare what philosophy contains, a philosopher must first know the beginning of every thing, as it is in itself. Then, entering into Nature and taking the light from her, he may philosophize on what the hand may prove, which is then found to be so in Nature. BOOK I OF PHILOSOPHY.

## Note.

<margin>A</margin>
Initially, before all elements, the Air was the very first to be extracted. It consists of the aerial Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt <note>original: "Mercurius, Sulphur vnnd Sal"</note>—not corporeal, not material, but invisible and intangible in its form. The beginning of this element is like the beginning of all elements in this way: Each element exists in Three Firsts <note>the *Tria Prima*: the three fundamental building blocks of matter in Paracelsian thought</note>; that is, in three things. From these three grow all the things that proceed from the elements—namely, Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt—for without these three, no element exists. These three constitute every element, and whatever grows from them remains within them. However, they are of various kinds, depending on the nature of the element: it is not that they take their nature from the element, but the element takes its nature from them. It is just like Wisdom <note>original Latin: "Sapientia"</note> that resides in a monk’s cell and provides many diverse judgments: so it is with these three "Firsts" as well.

# BOOK ONE: CONCERNING THE ELEMENT OF AIR.

### I.

<margin>B</margin>
First, the <term>Yliaster</term> <note>the primeval, undifferentiated substance of the universe</note> was divided—which in itself is nothing—and it yielded the four elements, making and ordering them. It is like a seed from which a trunk grows: for whatever the seed gives out, it does not take back into itself. But this Yliaster eventually draws the four elements back into itself; they dissolve and become as they were before the elements existed, once the <term>Year of the World</term> <note>original Latin: "Annus Mundi"; the duration of the current cosmic cycle</note> has passed. The trunk born from the Yliaster is the four elements; it provides no seed from which another child might come after this cosmic cycle to become something else. Rather, the four elements are both the mothers and the daughters; after the death of this world, nothing more of their lineage will be found. Just as they had a beginning, so shall they have an end, and everything within them passes away with them.

Although another world follows afterward, which is a daughter of this one in name—but not in form, essence, or the like. For that world shall not pass away, but remain like the soul that has come into being and been created as immortal. So it is in this world as well.

### II.

<margin>C</margin>
Now it follows that the Eternal Father—who is not only the Father of His Son, but of all things eternal and mortal, of those who remain and those who die, of the blessed and the damned—has created the <term>Houses</term> <note>original Latin: "Domos"</note>, that is, Heaven and Earth, Firmament and Water. He placed within them His Divine Will, of which we shall speak no further here, but will show in the <term>Paramirum</term> <note>referring to Paracelsus's major work, the *Opus Paramirum*</note>. He has made the natural out of the unnatural, out of that which no nature ever felt; and thus He let one nature be born after another, according to its kind, until its allotted time is up, so that the Divine Government may possess its Majesty itself, which man now possesses. Though the primary natures are diverse: so that from the earth a pear shall grow, from the sand a stalk, from the water the <term>Cachymia</term> <note>an alchemical term for mineral ores or the "flowers" of metals</note>, from the heaven the <term>Chaos</term> <note>here used to mean the atmosphere or air</note>, and from the fire the snow. Because this is so strange and unlike its origin, we must philosophize here: the element of water is not only water, but also a mineral; the element of earth is not only earth, but also a grape; and so with the others. For that philosophy is in vain which says that earth is an element but a nut is not; that fire is an element but snow is not; or he who says the four elements are present in every single thing—that is all in vain.

### III.

The earth is an element, and everything that grows from it; the water as well, and everything that comes from it; the firmament, and everything that comes from it. Thus, that which gives birth is an element, and an element is a mother. Of these there are four: Air, Fire, Water, and Earth. From these four mothers, all things of the whole world are born. It is useless talk to say that an element has only one temperament <note>original: "Complexion"; referring to the Galenic qualities of Hot, Cold, Moist, or Dry</note> such as Hot or Dry, Cold or Moist: for all four qualities are within it. Understand it thus: the earth is cold and dry, cold and moist, hot and dry, and hot and moist. Whatever grows from the earth that is hot and dry, grows from that part of the earth which is hot and dry. Likewise, what is cold and moist grows from the part of the element of Earth <note>original Latin: "Terræ"</note> that is cold and moist. Similarly, four such temperaments proceed from Fire: snow grows from that which is cold and dry in the element of Fire; the lightning bolt <note>original: "Strahl"</note> grows from that which is hot and dry, and so on with the others. Therefore, we initially give you to understand here that you should not categorize the elements according to their temperaments <note>original: "Complexionen"</note>, but according to their form—that is, what the four mothers possess within themselves. The earth is Material, Muddy <note>original: "Lutosisch"</note>, and Binding <note>original: "Conglutinosisch"</note>; whether it be hot or dry, cold or moist, it remains so. Water is wet, sensible, and tangible; but not corporeal nor material, and is

# CONCERNING THE ELEMENT OF AIR.
<page-num>23</page-num>

<margin>A</margin>An element, whether it be cold or hot. Fire is the firmament, and it is fire; although it is hot in one place, it is cold in another. The Air is the heaven <note>original: "Himmel"</note> which encloses everything, and it is hot and cold, dry and moist, as follows hereafter.

->IIII.<-

Now, to return to our beginning concerning the elements, it is to be understood that first, the <term>Yliaster</term> <note>the primeval, undifferentiated substance of the universe</note> was divided into four parts: Into the Air, which is the heaven that encloses all; into the Fire, which is the firmament that gives light and night, cold and warmth; into the Earth, which gives all fruit and provides the step for the foot; and into the Water, from which all minerals come and half the nourishment of living beings.

Two kinds of nourishment are here: one in the Air and in the Fire, the other in the Earth and in the Water. The upper two nourish us spiritually and invisibly; the lower two materially and corporeally. These four elements are divided into two parties: one is Air and Fire, the other is Earth and Water. The Air sustains the Fire, and the Earth sustains the Water. The Air and the Fire sustain the Earth and the Water, and they both sustain the Air and Fire. They are so fashioned that each one sustains, uses, and nourishes the other. Thus the Yliaster is divided so that it is within one House <note>original Latin: "Domo"</note> which has two globes: the outer and the inner, each with two elements. Outside, there is nothing known to us; inside is what we see and touch, and what the light of nature reveals to us. But He who created it is not with us, but outside; yet He is with us who was born of Him. Therefore, we wish to philosophize only about the four elements as nature demonstrates through its signs.

->V.<-

At the first of creation, the body <note>original Latin: "Corpus"</note> of the four elements was created in that form—the vastness drawn and taken from heaven and made perishable. Namely, as far as the <margin>B</margin><term>Aer</term> <note>the atmosphere or breathable air</note> encompasses was the throne of God and the center of His kingdom, from which center the world was created, so that it was made mortal and perishable by God.

Now, to understand this, it must be known that from this center the world came to be and was made material. Upon this throne Christ hung on the cross; upon this throne the prophets sat; and it is the footstool of His feet. That which has become material and bodily is God and His work—the center of His kingdom and His throne.

Thus, it is first to be known—before we reach the philosophers—that God made the center of His heaven perishable, and made it of Himself. For just as He is called a Son in the flesh, so the world is His house. Now, as it was thus created and came to be, it is to be known that it does not pass away as it came, but there shall remain the heart of man, and of the world, the <term>Geblüw</term> <note>the "blueness" or the celestial azure of the firmament</note>.

->VI.<-

Now, how God created the world is as follows: He made it into one body initially, as far as the four elements extended. This body He placed into three pieces: into Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt <note>original: "Mercurium Sulphur vnnd Sal"</note>, so that there are three things that make one body. These three things make everything that is and will be in the four elements. These three things have within them all the strength and power of perishable things. For within them lie the mornings, the day, night, warmth and cold, stone and fruit, and other things, but not yet formed. It is just like a piece of wood that lies there and is nothing but wood; but within it is every form of animal, every form of plant, every form of instrument. Whoever can take away the <margin>C</margin>excess that does not belong there will find that form within it. Thus, this first body of the Yliaster was like a lump <note>original: "Klotz"</note> in which all herbs, all waters, all gems, all minerals, all stones, all <term>Chaos</term> <note>here meaning the atmospheric void or space</note> lay, which only the Supreme <term>Fabricator</term> <note>the divine Craftsman or Creator</note> separated and formed so subtly that what was taken away became something else. First, He took away the Air, and from the remainder, three more were made: Fire, Water, and Earth. From these, He took the Fire; two remained: and so on until the end.

->VII.<-

Now that the four "fields" <note>original: "Aecker"</note> have been taken and separated, there remained four containers, in each of which the four elements stay: Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry; and each was as much as nothing.

Initially, the Air was ordered, then the Fire, then the Earth, then the Water. And it was thus: From the Air came the Chaos, the Throne, the Chains, and the Ground. From the Fire, Day and Night, Sun and Moon. From the Earth, Trees and Herbs, Grass and Fruit. From the Water, Minerals and Stones. They are so ordered that each remainder gave birth to another. That is: from the Yliaster of the Earth was drawn the beech wood, and the apple wood was put aside, each in its place, nothing spoiled or mixed. In the Water, gold was drawn from other metals, and the other metals from one another. In the Fire, the cold was separated from the warmth, the <term>Heytteri</term> <note>clarity or brightness</note> from the darkness. In the Air, the Chaos was ordained to maintain everything, to enclose the Earth from the Heaven. And now that these four Yliastri <note>the plural of Yliaster, referring to the primordial state of each element</note> are created and made into elements—that is, into the mothers of their fruits—the Air was prepared first, then the Fire. These two
