<margin>A</margin> They may know nothing more of this than what <term>Fatum</term> <note>original: "Fatum"; the predetermined course of events or Fate</note> mockingly allows them. Although they take it upon themselves to endure torments and turn him into an "Iron-eater" <note>original: "Eyßenbeiſſer"; a term for a brawler or a tough person, here linked to the metal iron</note>: they know this "Iron-eater" from the contempt of <term>Fatum</term> which is in <term>Marte</term> <note>original: "Marte"; the planet/god Mars</note>, who is called <term>Mars</term>. But he keeps his true tricks to himself and does not tell the good man what the true outcome shall be. He also has the choice to show himself as he wishes, differently today than tomorrow. Such an art takes its origin from <term>Fatum</term> and returns to that from which it came; therefore, no certain art exists there, nor may it be.

### III.

From all this it follows hereafter that <term>Fatum</term> reveals itself openly and understandably in its <term>præsagiren</term> <note>original: "præsagiren"; to presage or predict</note>, for that is what <term>Fatum</term> does. For every human being has a <term>Fatum</term>, every trade has its <term>Fatum</term>, every <term>Facultas</term> <note>original: "Facultas"; academic faculty or branch of knowledge</note> has its <term>Fatum</term>, every sect its <term>Fatum</term>, every faith has its <term>Fatum</term>, and every social rank its <term>Fatum</term>. These Fates stir and use themselves daily, more than is known to us. And whoever is experienced in <term>Fatamantia</term> <note>the art of divining or understanding Fate</note> may well indicate the <term>Præsagia</term> <note>omens or predictions</note> in what people encounter in their good or bad fortune, and the like. This <term>Fatum</term> is placed into the <term>Firmament</term> <note>the heavens or sky</note> through its <term>Adech</term> <note>a Paracelsian term for the inner spiritual power or "archetypal" force that shapes reality</note>, so that it shall have its effect therein, and it shows itself just like the <term>Firmament</term>. Although there are many of them, not only in this element but also in the others: they are spoken of by <term>Fatamantia</term> in their own chapters, according to the elements in which they reside. But those which are under the element of fire in the form of the firmament are as follows.

### IV.
### ON THE FIGURES.

<margin>B</margin> As for the figures that appear in the heavens—such as strange men, churches, and other unforeseen or recognized forms and shapes, with many colors and the like. Sometimes appearing as people, sometimes as war, sometimes as other likenesses. The likeness of earthly things takes its origin from the earth into the upper stars, so that the lower influence matches and unites with the upper; these are <term>Prognostica certa</term> <note>original: "Prognostica certa"; certain prognostications</note> of those things which they display in their form. Although sometimes this form is crude and incomprehensible: the reason is that they have joined together so crudely in the <term>Coniunction</term> <note>conjunction; the alignment of celestial bodies</note>, and the <term>Coniunction</term> is thus. Two kinds of spirits are in the <term>Influenz</term> <note>influence; the flowing of power from the stars</note>, below and above, from which the <term>Prognosticæ figuræ</term> <note>prognostic figures</note> emerge, and not from the material influence of the element of fire. But the reason we place them in this element is that they take their body from the element of fire. Therefore, as far as the body is concerned, it is the place of our philosophy. But what more is to be known of both spirits of the lower and upper influence is told in the section <term>de Fatis</term> <note>original: "de Fatis"; concerning Fates</note>. Regarding the figures, it is so: the lower Fates put on the upper ones and shape them according to their form, showing what shall happen in the future. Therefore, ultimately, what the form indicates occurs in its own time: and it does not happen in vain. It is the <term>Adech</term> who has covered himself with the cloak of <term>Mercurii</term>, <term>Salis</term>, and <term>Sulphuris</term> <note>Mercury, Salt, and Sulfur; the "Tria Prima" or three primary substances in alchemy</note>, and has formed the same according to the nature of his lament or joy.

### V.
### ON COMETS.

<margin>C</margin> The origin of <term>Cometen</term> <note>comets</note> is a <term>Fatum</term> of all peoples who lie beneath its path: signifying to them either misery and distress, or freedom, or some unheard-of new thing or being, and its servitude. It is born from the <term>Fatum</term> of the lords, the clergy, the laity, and the like. Some are born solely from the <term>Fatum</term> of the lords; these look like a new wonder among them and appear magnificent. Some come only from the clergy; these look wavering <note>original: "Schwenket"; perhaps flickering or like a swinging censer</note>. Some only from the peasants; these are coarse. And they take their form from what they signify: such as a star and a tail, because a long "tail" of events will come from the matter it signifies. If it is broad, it signifies a broad, extensive matter; and as it ends at the tail, whether fresh or joyful, so the matter ends as well. Therefore, nothing else is to be understood of comets except that they were born from the lower Fates into the upper, as a <term>Prognostication</term> to the world of a new report and event.

### VI.
### ON THE THREE SUNS AND MOONS.

Similarly, in place of comets, sometimes new suns are seen, and new moons, beyond those that are already there. These signify the state of the world that is beneath them, but not for the future—rather for what is currently happening and destined to occur that very day. They take their <term>Fatum</term> from the supreme <term>Heuptern</term> <note>heads or leaders</note> of the world, and it proceeds only from them: and it signifies nothing else but the very thing they contain, from which they emerge. And they are suns and moons because such superior powers signify error or the like, and only new, strange, and unheard-of things that rarely happen. And they signify, most of all, the great madness of the superiors, and folly, and foolish dealings. Therefore, suns are made from this, because there is as little need for three suns as there is for the things they signify. And just as one sun is enough, so would one person be enough for what it signifies. Therefore, just as two or three suns are an excess or a superfluity, so is that which they signify a superfluity and a vain thing.

### VII.
### ON NEW STARS.
<note>original: "DE NOVIS STELLIS"</note>

Similarly, strange stars are sometimes seen in the heavens—entirely new and previously unobserved. They signify the new birth of men, or perhaps a "new man" who is not currently recognized but is the one the star signifies. They also signify the downfall of such persons—that is, their decline, or that a powerful person shall be cast down from his throne. These stars take their <term>Fatum</term> <note>the predetermined destiny or course of events</note> from those they signify, and they take their path over the very place where those persons dwell or act. They take their <term>Corpus</term> <note>body or physical form</note> from the very <term>Ascendants</term> <note>the zodiacal sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment</note> of the planets and the Zodiac; therefore, they appear somewhat uniform to them, such that they resemble in form and movement those they signify, according to the harmony in which they were born.

Therefore, if the Ascendant and the planet of such a person are known, they may well be recognized through these stars. Thus, there are many such strange and different stars that arise from the planets of those they indicate, appearing with a hidden glow and form. And this never happens unless that person is something extraordinary or is destined to become so. And among all these stars, none are natural, but all are born from the Fates, and nothing comes from the nature of the upper heavens.

### VIII.
### ON THE CROSSES.
<note>original: "DE CRVCIBVS"</note>

<margin>B</margin>
Furthermore, the crosses that fall upon the people also take their origin from the Fates. They are <term>Prognostica</term> <note>foretelling signs or omens</note> and prophecies—likewise a sign of passing away, specifically for those who make frequent use of such forms or who sustain themselves through them. They give their indication strongly and terrifyingly, and in that same manner, it comes to pass: the event fashions itself after the time and hour it is meant to occur. Just as the crosses that fell in the year 100, etc.—that is, in the Jubilee Year <note>a special holy year in the Christian tradition, usually occurring every 25 or 50 years</note>—are indications of sorrow for the next Jubilee Year. The various forms they have taken indicated the decline of various classes of people. For example, a gridiron <note>original: "Rooßt"; likely a reference to the instrument of martyrdom of St. Lawrence</note> and similar signs of the saints with which they were martyred, signify that in such a manner those who serve those saints shall perish and fall from their throne, just as the signs fall from heaven. Crosses, roosters, ladders, dice, etc., signify that the <term>Vicars of Christ</term> <note>original: "Vicarij Christi"; the clergy or high-ranking church officials</note> shall suffer distress. And these fall upon the people, upon their clothes, because for them, this is the most punishing omen. They fall in the locations where such things will happen, or near them. Their origin is taken from Fate and materializes from the <term>Sulphur</term> <note>in Paracelsian alchemy, one of the three "Prime Materials," representing the principle of combustibility and structure</note> that flows out of the stars. It is formed by the power of the spirits in Fate and falls upon the people invisibly, as is the nature of Fate.

# BOOK THREE
# OF THE PHILOSOPHY OF THEOPHRASTUS,
## ON THE ELEMENT OF EARTH.
### TRACTATE THE FIRST.
### *On the Matter of the Element of EARTH & BEING.*

#### I.
#### ON EARTH IN ITSELF.
<note>original: "DE TERRA PER SE"</note>

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Yliast:</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' depicting a person, possibly a scholar or saint, seated in a landscape or study.</image-desc>To philosophize about the Element of Earth: its matter was created first, and in such a way that its "three firsts" <note>the Tria Prima: Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt</note> were separated from the great <term>Yliaster</term> <note>the primordial "prime matter" from which all things were fashioned</note>—unlike the first two elements—into a different form and essence. Initially, not only the Element of Earth but also the Element of Water was separated along with it, and both were joined together in a single globe, which is the center of the outer elements. Of these two elements, the Earth was filled first, then the Water. Now, concerning the Earth, it is important to know that all the power and nature that existed in the great <term>Yliaster</term> to nourish humans and cattle—with their food and necessary requirements—has come into the Element of Earth. This includes all trees, herbs, and other growths of the earth. These were thus separated away from the other three elements, so that this power resides only in the Element of Earth and in no other. Therefore, the Element of Earth has its own special <term>Yliaster</term>: to bring forth nourishment. It is an element for this reason: that the power of nourishing things, belonging to the living, resides within it.

<meta>This page transitions from the celestial portents of Book II into the foundational natural philosophy of Book III. Having discussed the "signs" in the heavens (stars and crosses), Paracelsus now moves to the terrestrial realm, specifically the Element of Earth, explaining its composition from the Three Primes and its role as a "matrix" for both natural and "Paradise-born" life.</meta>

<header>ON THE ELEMENT OF EARTH</header>
<note>original: "DE ELEMENTO TERRA"</note>

## II.

<margin>A</margin>
The Earths are three—Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury <note>original: "S. S. M." referring to the *Tria Prima*, the three primary substances Paracelsus believed composed all matter</note>—taken from the great Yliaster <note>The *Yliaster* is the Paracelsian term for the primeval, formless chaos from which the universe was fashioned</note>, from the nature where the Element of Earth resides. For therein existed this element and the other three as one Yliaster, in which all four elements stood together. But they were separated, and the Yliaster dissolved; therefore, the four elements no longer stand together nor can they be as one, for each is henceforth placed separately in its own stead. For this reason, those labor in vain who wish to separate the four elements <note>referring to alchemists trying to isolate pure elements from a mixture</note> or who seek the "fifth essence" <term>Quinta Essentia</term> <note>the supposed pure, celestial element beyond the four terrestrial ones</note> across that divide.

From these first three [the Primes], once they were separated from the other three elements, the Matter of the Earth was born as it is now shaped. Just as the Air became the Heavens, the Fire became the Firmament, and the Water became the Sea, so too did this separation cause this element to become Matter. It took the form of a sphere in its rotundity, placed in the center of the world, and within it were enclosed all the powers of trees, herbs, and fungi, so that from it every species in the world might be procreated from the seeds sown therein.

## III.

In this element of Earth lies the seed of wood, of roots, of herbs, and of fungi, and the power that allows the trunk to come to light and be carried according to the will of its husbandman, planted and cultivated. This seed lies invisible and comes from the nature of the Element, which is solely this seed, as well as its house and place where it is "cooked" <note>Alchemy often compared biological growth to a slow cooking or digestion process</note>. First, the power divides into its species, so that no two stay as one, but each species stands for itself: that which is wood, that which is herb, that which is fungus. And again, each within its own kind: that into Cedar <note>original: "Cedrum"</note>, that into Rosemary <note>original: "Anthos"</note>, that into Balsam <note>original: "Balsamum"</note>, that into Turpentine-resin <note>original: "Botin"</note>. Among the herbs: that into Lemon Balm <note>original: "Melissa"</note>, that into the Lily among the thorns <note>original: "Gilgen inter Spinas," a phrase evoking the Song of Solomon</note>, and so on from the others. Now, to rightly understand the seed 
<margin>B</margin>
in its division: in the separation of the great Aniadus <note>A Paracelsian term for the celestial or vital powers that direct the growth and destiny of plants</note>, the nature of trees was led to one place, the Turpentine-resin to another, and the Ebony <note>original: "Ebenus"</note> to a third. So it is with all others. Likewise with the herbs: the great Aniadus cast grass upon one land, clover upon another, and lavender upon a third, giving each land its own herbs and trees. Therefore, we should pay heed to these things, seeing how the Aniadus has fallen.

## IV.

Now, just as the Aniadus has fallen with the trees—so that Bitter Oranges <note>original: "Pomeranzen"</note> grow in one land and Sloes in another, Figs in one and Beech in another—the reason is that Figs and Oranges require their own particular soil that matches their growth, and the Heavens <note>the climate and astrological influence</note> must match as well. Therefore, if the Earth is unsuitable, or the Heavens are as well, this fruit cannot come forth; thus their seeds perish and do not emerge. Although the seed is there and present, the Heavens wither it, as does the adverse nature of the Earth, which is manifold because of the Heavens and not because of its own nature. For the Earth is one Earth everywhere, but there is a change caused by the Heavens, which either brings forth or hinders growth. Yet, on the other hand, there is Nature: while the Sun might burn away the nature of the Lily or other noble herbs, or if there is too little Sun, there is still the seed that Nature gives to the herb or tree. Thus, from that same material seed, the Sun—through the power of these flowers or trees—cannot burn or suppress it, but must let it turn green. Unless, however, the Sun is so lacking that its
<margin>C</margin>
fertility cannot be achieved. Thus, herbs and trees grow through planting which otherwise might not emerge from the Earth due to the aforementioned deficiencies.

## V.

If one is to philosophize further on the element of Earth, it is thus: two kinds of fruits come from the element of Earth. One which the Earth gives of itself, and one which it gives from seed. Thus all plants come out of the Earth through the element in two ways: from themselves, out of their own seeds, and one out of a given seed. The Earth's "own seed" is when an Earth produces a wild herb—that is, a self-grown herb. Beyond that is when one sows the seed, which is a "given seed." Therefore, there are two kinds of gifts of herbs. Grain grows from no earth, nor does wheat; it must be sown. Likewise lilies, and others of the kind, and pears. Now, here is the great philosophy of this treatise: from whence come the seeds that do not grow [naturally] out of the Earth? For if no grain or wheat is sown, then none grows; otherwise, only grass and hay grow. Therefore, grass and hay are the Earth’s own growth, out of itself, but no apples or cherries are. Therefore, there must be another philosophy here, from which grain, fruit trees, and the like were born. And it is this: that the seeds of all these things were born out of Paradise and sown here, and thus they grew and were further planted and cultivated. Their fruit is to be understood similarly to Paradise, just as Christ is God and yet is a mortal man.

## VI.

How the growth emerges from the seed is thus: one must know that the seed receives nothing from the Earth except growth alone and the power of its form; the rest is from Paradise, as is shown in the *Paramirum* <note>original: "Paramiro," referring to Paracelsus's work *Opus Paramirum*, which deals with the causes of diseases and the nature of life</note>. But what is of the Earth, concerning the element, is this: that initially the "three firsts" of the Earth mix themselves into the seed, wherein the wood and the herb reside, so that it reaches the end to which it belongs and becomes that which it was before. For the seed is that which...

# ON THE ELEMENT OF EARTH

<margin>A</margin> Of the Pine, and it lies in the wood / and because of its <term>subtlety<note>In alchemy, "subtlety" refers to a substance's ability to penetrate or flow, indicating a refined, less "gross" state of matter.</note></term> it penetrates out through the pores of the wood into the bark, or it melts / or dissolves in its place: and when an <term>Emunctorium<note>An "emunctorium" usually refers to an excretory organ or passage; here it describes the point where resin is expelled from the tree.</note></term> is formed / it exits at that same spot: this happens through a hole or a streak. In this, there is a distinction to be known: that the <term>Botin<note>original: "Botin"; likely referring to turpentine or a specific crude resin.</note></term> is more subtle in its <term>Sulphur<note>The principle of soul, flammability, and oily essence.</note></term> than the Fir or the Pine, and the Pine is more subtle than the Fir; yet all three have one generation / which proceeds from the <term>Aniadus<note>original: "Aniado"; a Paracelsian term for the celestial or spiritual power that directs growth and vital life in plants.</note></term> / and is compacted together by <term>Mercury<note>The principle of spirit, liquidity, and transformation.</note></term>.

Now, to speak of its bark / branches / and the like / it is this: the bark is also a coagulated Sulphur like the resin / but brought into that form by the Aniadus / for it is a congealed, hard Sulphur. And just as the tip of any body lacks hardness / so too is the end of the bark / which alone is hard / taken from the hardest Sulphur that lies within this plant. Its branches take themselves from the Aniadus, which is thus formed: the twigs likewise / and whatever else is therein. Its fruit / cones and stems / are also formed by the Aniadus in shape and figure / because it cannot give birth otherwise: and other trees are to be understood in the same way.

## ii.

## On the Stone Pine, Ash, and Maple.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>original: "Hoc caput medosu~ est." <note>This chapter is full of errors or corrupt.</note></margin> The nature of these three trees is a Sulphur / coagulated by the <term>wood-salt<note>Salt is the principle of body, solidity, and permanence.</note></term> / in the same manner as the Ash trees / except that they are much more subtle in their Sulphur and Salt: therefore their Salt is nobler and harder / because / in this way / their Salt is more noble / after the heavenly manner: therefore from their ashes, noble <term>Alkali<note>Potash used in early glass and soap making.</note></term> and glasses are made / and from their water a noble essence. For this reason, the Aniadus is also nobler in its growth than in the coarse Sulphur shown above / which is why it is of a special nature above other wood / such as the Fir. Now, as for its branches / because it is shaped in such a way / they go through and through its tree / into the trunk / and do not (simply) stick to the outside / as in other trees: and the reason is / that its branches grow from the core / therefore their branches are of the wood of which the seed is: for the power of the core makes the seed / and that same power also makes the branches. But whatever branches do not come from the core / those same branches are not like the wood of those trees. Also, those that have (spiral-like veins in the trunk): the reason is / that it has no other pores / than the streaks that it has here and there in a spiral: thus separated into such a form by the Aniadus / like a snail / and it has the nature of pores. The Maple in its <term>grain<note>original: "Flader"; the decorative, marbled pattern or "curly" figure found in wood like maple.</note></term> is such / that the Aniadus has flesh-like qualities within it / which it assumes in this Maple / and even more so in the grain. For the grain of this tree / or the grain of another tree / is nothing but the formative nature that the Aniadus possesses. And although it comes from the form / one more than the other / and does not remain exactly in the form as the Aniadus begins it: the reason is / that through growth (as it) drives it apart / it alters the form / and yet the likeness remains (But that such floral-work is not) possessed by all / is the image of the (spirit) Aniadus: for every form / that is on Earth / stands within it and proceeds from it. The special nature of these trees is born from the nature of the Sulphur and Salt / which is different there than in other trees: They also have a subtle Mercury / which is why they stand differently in their compaction than other trees. The Stone Pine has a brittle, hard Mercury: The Ash a tough / supple Mercury: The Maple a hard / firm Mercury: In these three natures, the trees are distinguished.

## iii.

## On the Cedar, Balsam, and Cypress.

<margin>C</margin> Another Sulphur proceeds from the Element of Earth / which is the noblest among all woods: from these come the Cedars, Balsams, and Cypresses: and it is the Sulphur that is the whitest / and with the most subtle Salt / and much of Mercury: and it divides itself initially into two forms / into a long form / and into a short nature of those first three / and not the Aniadus. On the other hand / the Sulphur-nature in them is also twofold: In Balsam there is a white Sulphur / which dissolves like the resin through the help (of the Influence). In Cedar and Cypress it is not so / but it dilutes itself into the trunk and branches / and grows along with the wood: and the Sulphur of the wood / and the Sulphur that dissolves / are one thing: therefore they are not separated / as in Balsam / for which they are separated. But in Turpentine they are like the Balsam. When the subtle Sulphur is separated from the Cedar and Cypress / it is the true Balsam just like the other: From this it follows / that the <term>Spagyrists<note>Alchemists who use the "spagyric" method of separating and recombining substances to create medicines.</note></term> look for Balsam in the wood / and wish to work with it. The Wood of the Fir is also like them / only with the distinction / that it has a different Salt / and a different Mercury / but the same Sulphur: The (Myrobalans) are similar in Sulphur / but in Salt and Mercury they are unlike them all. In these trees / Cedar, Balsam, Cypress, (Myrobalan), Aloes / there is a Sulphur / which is drawn from all three firsts of the Element of Earth / because of its nature and virtue / and all woods are (pervious) / except for the (Pomegranates): and it is the power of Sulphur / which does not allow rot / therefore all their nature and virtue / which they have / are to be attributed to the Sulphur that lies within them: therefore the Spagyrist well finds / he who seeks the Sulphur out of them.

### IV.
### On Ebony, Turbith, and Juniper.

<margin>The first half of this chapter is faulty.<note>original: "Huius Capitis pars prior dimidia mendosa est."</note></margin>
These three trees are also to be united as one generation within the three first principles; they consist of a coarse <term>Sulphur<note>The principle of soul, flammability, and oily essence.</note></term> and a coarse <term>Salt<note>The principle of body, solidity, and permanence.</note></term>, but a subtle <term>Mercury<note>The principle of spirit, liquidity, and transformation.</note></term>, and they are generated thus: In Ebony, the power remains within; in <term>Turbith<note>original: "Thurbit"; likely referring to the Turpeth plant (Ipomoea turpethum), often used as a purgative.</note></term>, it goes into the bark; in Juniper, it remains in both the wood and the bark. Thus they also differ in their properties: Ebony purges and constricts; Turbith purges alone; Juniper consolidates. Also, Ebony cures the "bad-paths" <note>likely referring to blockages or ulcers</note> in the body; Turbith the "flux-paths" <note>discharges or rheums</note>; and Juniper alone cures the blood. And regarding their virtue, it is to be noted—for from them their <term>First Matter<note>original: "prima Materia"; the original, undifferentiated substance from which all things grow.</note></term> is understood—as follows: Juniper consolidates phlegm and <term>Cholera<note>The humor of yellow bile.</note></term> and purges the blood; Ebony purges Cholera and constricts the blood and phlegm; Turbith purges phlegm and constricts the blood and Cholera. Although this is better demonstrated in the work *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: "de Natura rerum"; a reference to a foundational alchemical text</note>, it is nevertheless shown here because instruction must be given regarding Ebony: specifically, in the way that Mercury overcomes at the extremities, while Sulphur alone gives the body, and Salt gives the <term>congelation<note>The process of a liquid becoming solid.</note></term>. But Mercury gives the power of Ebony, such that it directs the Sulphur and the Salt, so that in Ebony the "Mercurial nature" alone remains; in Turbith, it drives it out into the bark; and in Juniper, into the wood and all its fruits. It is threefold in its operation, unique in each wood. They also possess other natures: Ebony has the Sulphur of Cedar and Cypress; Turbith has the Sulphur of <term>Myrobalan<note>A dried fruit used in traditional medicine as a purgative.</note></term> and Fir. Juniper has the nature of the <term>Aniadus<note>A Paracelsian term for the celestial or spiritual power that directs growth and vital life in plants.</note></term> of <term>Botin<note>A crude resin or turpentine.</note></term>, Pine, and <term>Cembra Pine<note>original: "Zirbo".</note></term>, because its Sulphur sometimes resembles the form of those, yet it falls short because it is not entirely of the same matter. Thus, many trees look somewhat alike because the Sulphur and similar components imitate one another’s nature; yet it is a distinct species, whatever is of this kind, and it comes from the Sulphur that is thus appropriated, and from the Aniadus, which is specially ordered into this resinous nature.

### V.
### On Boxwood, Savin, and Tamarind: Also Ivy, Laurel, and Wild Olive.

Boxwood, Savin, and Tamarind take their bodies from a very well-purified Sulphur and an almost subtle Salt, with a tough Mercury. Their generation is such that Boxwood has no nature of any other wood, but is an entirely unique being in its growth: for it has its own special Aniadus in its foliage, to which nothing among all trees can be compared except for the Laurel alone. However, it has a different Sulphur than the Laurel, which is somewhat like that of herbs such as Periwinkle and Ivy; therefore its Sulphur is like the Periwinkle-Sulphur and the Ivy-Sulphur. Savin also has a special nature above all other trees; it only resembles Juniper in its form. Otherwise, it belongs to the nature of Boxwood, and is distinct from other trees in that it does not have the strength of a tree in its growth, and is outside its usual nature. Tamarind is also thus distinguished; it is a type of Cembra Pine and <term>Betim<note>A Paracelsian term for a specific resinous plant or substance.</note></term>, and depends on the Sulphur of the Willows: for the Sulphur of Willows and the Sulphur of Tamarinds is one Sulphur, divided only in the Salt, the Mercury, and the Aniadus; and among the three, it is the coarsest. Many other trees can be compared to their nature which also stand alone: such as the Laurel, which is singular above the other tall trees; likewise the Wild Olive has a Sulphur within it that goes into the fruit, yet is of the same Sulphur as its trunk. The Laurel is the same; they are divided in their <term>Essence<note>original: "Essentia"; the inner nature or "being" of the plant.</note></term>, as stated in *On the Nature of Things*. It is also to be understood of them that their Sulphur produces many colors: in Boxwood, it is quite yellow, because it is a yellow Sulphur; and the green that lies within it goes into the leaf, which is why it has a very green leaf and a yellow wood. For in its Sulphur, there are only two colors: Yellow and Green. In Savin it is the same, but not so well-colored. In Tamarind it is somewhat white. Thus it is in the others as the colors of Sulphur manifest themselves, according to the nobility of that same Aniadus, just as the colors and essences are divided from one another.
<margin>C</margin>

### VI.
### On Sandalwood, Licorice, and Linden: Also on Beech, Oak, Alder, and Poplar.

The origin of Sandalwood and the others is a dry Sulphur with its own Salt, and Mercury in both. It differs in color, form, hardness, and essence, and yet it is all one origin and being of the three first principles. The redness of the Sulphur separates into a specific wood and is Red Sandalwood; this redness is the first and a distinct redness. After that, there are more reds from which <term>Brazilwood<note>A wood used since the Middle Ages to produce red dye.</note></term> is made, and its generation is like Sandalwood, except that this Sulphur stands in another color. After that, it produces a yellow, from which Yellow Sandalwood is made; then a white, which gives White Sandalwood; these differ in colors as much as the Sulphur has colors when it is of a dry nature, as in this generation.

However, more colors are present there, such as those of Licorice and Linden. Licorice is taken from the yellow Sulphur, and it is the Sulphur that has the Sulphuric sweetness within it, which is placed therein by Mercury...

...is contained within: for wherever <term>Mercury<note>In alchemical philosophy, Mercury represents the principle of fluidity, spirit, and volatile essence.</note></term> is present, there is a sweetness. Thus, in that place, there is a specific Mercury 
<margin>A</margin> in <term>licorice<note>original: "Liquiritien"</note></term>, and it is also in <term>white sandalwood<note>original: "Sandolo albo"</note></term>, though divided only within the Mercury. The <term>Linden<note>original: "Tilia"</note></term> is also of this same origin, except that it grows from the purest <term>Matter<note>original: "Materia"; the underlying substance of the Three Principles.</note></term> of these "three first" principles. The <term>Beech<note>original: "Fagus"</note></term> and the <term>Oak<note>original: "Quercus"</note></term> arise from the "Hardness" <note>the solid, salty aspect of the principles</note>, but the <term>Alder<note>original: "Alnus"</note></term> and <term>Poplar<note>original: "Populus"</note></term> do not; rather, they arise from the "Mildness" <note>the softer, more flexible aspect</note>. There are also many other trees of this kind (intertwined) whose names we do not mention, which are merely shrub-like or low-growing trees in their habit.

They also differ in their colors; this is caused by the <term>Aniadus<note>A Paracelsian term referring to the vital, formative power of nature or the celestial influence that gives form to living things.</note></term> and the property of the "three first," which remain within a single color. Because of this, there are two types of wood: these and others. Some have <term>Degrees<note>original: "Gradus"; likely referring to levels of intensity or specific medicinal virtues.</note></term>, and some do not—such as the <term>Fir<note>original: "Abies"</note></term>, which has veins that people call "years" <note>tree rings</note>. From this, an error follows: that as often as there is a year, there is a vein, which is not the case. For the cause is that as many veins as there are in the whole heart <note>the core of the wood</note> are also there on the first day, except that they are opened over time—not according to the year, but according to its growth, whether much or little.

Many trees, such as the Linden and Licorice, do not have these veins because there is a <term>Coagulation<note>A thickening or solidifying of the internal juices.</note></term> and a <term>Pore<note>original: "Por"</note></term>. Those that do have veins take them from the <term>Salt<note>The principle of stability and structure.</note></term>, similar to <term>Cachimia<note>An alchemical term for mineral ore or the "dross" of metals that has not yet reached a pure state.</note></term> and the mineral-like nature of the Element of Earth, which divides itself thus, always placing a "Mildness" between two parts and the "Hardness" into the veins.

### VII.

### On Peaches, Pears, and Apples: Also on Almonds, Walnuts, and Chestnuts: Also on Figs and others: Also on Pomegranates, Oranges, etc., also Cherries, Plums, and similar things:
<note>original: "Persica, Pyra, Poma: Item de Amygdalis, Nuce, item Castanea: Item Ficu & alijs: Item de Granato, Arantijs, &c, Item Cerasis, Prunis & similibus:"</note>

<margin>B</margin> Likewise, these trees and others take their wood, bark, and all their leaves, flowers, and fruit from <term>Sulphur<note>The principle of soul, oiliness, and flammability.</note></term>. Yet all is shaped so that the Sulphur, in its many forms within its "three first" principles of the Element of Earth along with its *Aniadus*, gives rise to various fruits and forms. Now, to philosophize regarding the fruits, leaves, flowers, and trees: it is thus that the Sulphur everywhere contains a surplus <term>Liquor<note>essence or fluid</note></term within it for the fruits. As in the <term>Peach<note>original: "Persica"</note></term>, there is a liquor that is not from Sulphur alone, but more from Mercury; therefore, peaches are watery and of a thin substance. In <term>Pears<note>original: "Pyris"</note></term> it is also like this, but not so quickly <term>Resolved<note>alchemically dissolved into liquid</note></term>, but rather of a greater Coagulation. In <term>Apples<note>original: "Oepffeln"</note></term> it is also thus. The power of the "three first" also divides itself into its substance and then into its skin. On the outside of the peach is a <term>Vinea<note>Latin for "vine"; here referring to a fuzzy or vine-like texture.</note></term>, because its Sulphur is of the "vine" kind. Pears and apples are not of this kind, but of a thick kind of Sulphur; therefore, the peels have a different taste and power compared to their fruits. This also appears in <term>Oranges<note>original: "Pomeranzen"</note></term> and <term>Pomegranates<note>original: "Granaten"</note></term>, where the Sulphur goes only into the rind with its substance and bodily nature, and encloses within it its "three first," resolved and more subtle—that is, the Salt and Mercury. But in the pomegranate, it has retained the redness from the Sulphur and coagulated it through the Salt-spirit in a pomegranate-like way, and placed behind it the fluidity of the "three first"—that which cannot be coagulated, but only <term>Conglutinated<note>stuck together or thickened into a pulp</note></term>, like the juice in which they lie. Thus wondrous is the great *Aniadus* in its <term>Spagyric<note>The art of separating and recombining the virtues of plants and minerals; Paracelsian chemistry.</note></term> nature and art.

In the same way, you have this in cherries, so that the Sulphur is the skin, and the internal part of the cherry is the flesh of the "three first," and it places its seed in the middle of its <term>Center<note>original: "Centri"</note></term>. For every seed lies in the middle of the center of its fruit; that is the nature of the *Aniadus*. This is also true in peaches and all others.

<margin>C</margin> But there is a difference, in that the kernels are covered with a hardness. In pears and apples, it is not so, because some trees let the seed shoot forth with a sharp wood-sulphur, but others do not. This also often happens with the fruits, as in <term>Almonds<note>original: "Amygdalis"</note></term>, <term>Hazelnuts<note>original: "Auellanis"</note></term>, etc., where the fruit grows out of the wood, and inside, the fruit and the seed are one thing. Nature works this way, which is known not in one way, but in many ways. Therefore, in <term>Chestnuts<note>original: "Kesten"</note></term>, such a nature is also wondrous: outside is the thorn, then the husk, then the seed and fruit.

It is also threefold in almonds, etc., and yet divided into many forms and shapes, none equal to the other. And also, every tree by itself bears a fruit unlike any other. There are many such kinds, and they are more gently revealed in the books *On the Nature of Things* and *On Transmutations*.

# PHILOSOPHY, BOOK III
<note>original: "PHILOSOPHIÆ LIBER III."</note>

<meta>catchword: Therefore</meta>

The upper part [of the tree] sends into the earth its <term>Yliadum<note>A Paracelsian term for the primordial matter or the basic matrix from which all things grow.</note></term>. Now its growth begins so that the roots hold what belongs to them and become large, as its <term>Aniadus<note>In Paracelsian thought, the Aniadus is the inner vital power or celestial virtue that determines an organism's specific form and development.</note></term> dictates. The upper being first emerges in a single shape, which is the stem; and once it establishes the stem—which is its house—it then divides into two parts: that part which belongs to the exterior of the stem, such as the blossoms, fruit, and leaves. Then, for the first time, the "middle kernel"—which is the soul to which the whole nature of the tree is entrusted—pushes forward the leaves. That is, whatever is within the soul that belongs to the leaves is a "Green <term>Sulphur<note>In alchemical philosophy, Sulphur represents the principle of combustion, growth, and the fatty or oily substance of a thing.</note></term>." Afterward, once the leaves are in their proper kind and have their "Matter" <note>the physical substance</note> to complete them, the power of the blossom follows. Then the flowers are generated according to the <term>Aniadus</term> of that specific tree. And once the blossom has received its time and its matter is enclosed within it, the fruit pushes forth afterward and grows out of the blossom, taking the shape and form of that same <term>Aniadus</term>. Such is the growth of trees, among which the <term>Mace<note>The spice derived from the reddish covering of the nutmeg seed.</note></term> also grows, which is the noblest tree of blossom and fruit, born from a most noble Sulphur, <term>Mercury<note>The alchemical principle of fluidity, spirit, and volatile essence.</note></term>, and <term>Salt<note>The alchemical principle of solidity, structure, and permanence.</note></term>, in which all taste and smell reside.

This is also true in <term>Cubebs<note>A species of pepper (Piper cubeba) valued for its medicinal and aromatic qualities.</note></term> and <term>Peppers<note>original: "Pipere"</note></term>, and all others that are like them in this form. To philosophize further on these things, philosophy exists solely to show that, just as the <term>Aniadus</term> finds joy in the wood—making one thing thus and another thing so—likewise it manifests itself in fruits and blossoms. It makes each specific power within its own fruit, mixing nothing together, but keeping each separate from everything else so that its nature may not be broken or diminished. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, the saying that "four elements" should be in one thing is false—meaning four qualities or "complexions." For there is now only one complexion, one quality, and one nature, which is great or small according to its "degree." That is its own strength, which is not broken by cold or heat, for they do not stand together as one.

### IX.
### On Grapes, Currants, and Barberries.
<note>original: "De Botris, Ribes, & Berberis."</note>

<margin>This chapter is faulty.</margin> <note>original: "Hoc caput mēdosū est."</note>
Similarly, there is an acidity in the first three of these trees, which has resolved itself from the liquor of Mercury into the body of Sulphur, and therein coagulated into the exterior, and afterward conglutinated <note>stuck together</note> what comes from the power of Salt. These liquors have their colors from Sulphur—red, yellow, and white—but not from the material of Sulphur itself, but only from the "resolving nature" that casts them out and does not allow them to be coagulated. Therefore, it is merely conglutinated and manifests in trees, some in colors, others in leaves. They also have their own special blossoms; namely, in the <term>Botris<note>Likely referring to grapes or plants that grow in clusters (from the Greek 'botrys').</note></term>, the best taste is found in that blossom. In the <term>Barberry<note>original: "Berberis"</note></term> there is bitterness because an entire acidity is in the berry. In <term>Currants<note>original: "Ribes"</note></term> there is no taste in the blossom or leaves, but only sweetness in the berry. In these is the liquor of Mercury, which is why they affect the urine and cause intoxication, through the power of <term>Narcotic Anodynes<note>Substances that both relieve pain (anodynes) and induce sleep or numbness (narcotics).</note></term> in the Mercury. For all "Anodyne" nature is in the Barberry, and all [intoxicating] nature in the <term>Botris</term>, and all "Narcotic" nature in the Currant. Therefore, the <term>Botris</term> grows the most because Mercury drives it; and the Barberry grows less because the acidity hinders the growth; and the Currant has the sweetness of Mercury, which carries its growth within it. The "Anodyne" nature is in the <term>Botris</term> in the form of wine, and it gives a poor wood, and its acidity is in its sprouts. The <term>acidity<note>original: "Acetositas"</note></term> is in the Barberry and is valued there because the <term>Aniadus</term> distinguishes the colors of those whose essences are contrary. Currants also have something of this and are sweet; therefore, they are compared to the Barberry according to color, and to wine according to the berry. But because it is a different thing, they carry the <term>Vneam<note>An obscure term likely referring to a specific botanical habit or self-growing quality.</note></term>, which is as much as a "self-growth" similar to the matter of <margin>C</margin> <term>Peaches<note>original: "Phersichken"</note></term>. These species are of many kinds because the <term>Aniadi</term> are of many kinds, and the [middle parts] are of many kinds, all of which are drawn into their special path by the <term>Aniadus</term>, and thus led into and coagulated according to the nature of trees. Although they do not grow exactly like trees, but more like plants, and are cast with similar care: the reason is that they are not on their own earth but on foreign earth, so they must be well purified so that they may remain. But where they are in their own place, they grow by themselves, as is further told in "On the Nature of Things" <note>original: "de Natura Rerum"</note> and "On Transmutations" <note>original: "Transmutationibus"</note>.

->End of the Second Treatise of Philosophy, Book on the<-
->Element of Earth.<-

# THIRD TREATISE.
<note>original: "TRACTATVS TERTIVS."</note>

## ON FOODSTUFFS.
<note>original: "DE CIBARIIS."</note>

### I.
### ON GRAINS.
<note>original: "DE FRVMENTIS."</note>

In the same way that trees go into the wood from the Element of Earth, there is now also a Sulphur in this element that separates itself from it and becomes a food, such as <term>legumes<note>original: "Legumina"</note></term> and <term>grains<note>original: "Frumenta"</note></term>. And there is a dry Sulphur and a moist one together—two kinds of "three firsts" in nature and essence: one that is useful to use, the other not. For instance, <term>Oats<note>original: "Habern"</note></term> is a Sulphur that is not to be eaten [as a whole]; but the grain, its seed, is for use.

# ON THE ELEMENT OF EARTH
<note>original: "DE ELEMENTO TERRÆ"</note>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, it follows from the beginning that among these **grains** <note>original: "Frumenten"</note>, as they grow, that which is not edible grows first, and afterwards that which is edible grows, following this path. First, the form grows, composes itself, and shoots upward. Once this form is ordered and brought into its growing shape, the edible part grows upon it. Thus, when the inedible <term>Sulphur<note>In alchemical philosophy, Sulphur represents the principle of combustion, growth, and the oily or fatty substance of a thing.</note></term> has completed its work, the edible part follows after it. In this way, the <term>Aniadus<note>The inner vital power or celestial virtue that determines an organism's specific form.</note></term> separates them from one another. If this were not so, the edible and the inedible would grow mixed together in one form and essence.

But the <term>Aniadus</term> first drives out the inedible Sulphurs; thereafter, once that is out, the edible part grows. The inedible part forms itself into a stalk, as in grains; into a reed, as in **winged seeds** <note>original: "Samara," referring to the seeds of trees like elm or maple</note>; into a little bush, as in **wild plants** <note>original: "Paganico," Paracelsus’s term for woodland or wild vegetation</note>; into a stem, as in peas. All of this consists of a Yellow and White <term>Sulphur</term>, which is of the nature of such a form, drawn and taken from the <term>Aniadus</term>.

But the edible part, which grows forth once the inedible is formed, has two edible aspects within it: that for humans and that for cattle. That is, the flour and the bran. The flour is a <term>Sulphur</term> that is equal to human nature and ordained for it. The bran is something human-like, yet not his food. Therefore, pigs—because they are most similar to humans—eat them, as they are most suitable for them.

Now, however, one must know from whence this edible nature comes, so that the <term>Sulphur</term> should and must become edible, though it is by itself only a coarse <term>Sulphur</term>. It is like this: in the first <term>Yliaster<note>The primordial matter or the basic "stuff" of the universe from which the four elements were separated.</note></term>, the four elements are so ordained that each is given its own <term>Aniadus</term> to complete this nature and essence. Thus, here too, the <term>Sulphur</term> is transformed into many essences, yet its ultimate matter is nothing other than <term>Sulphur</term>, a <term>Salt</term>, and a <term>Mercury</term>. Therefore, we may find and take the first matter from the last. Although initially <term>Sulphur</term> is <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Salt</term> is <term>Salt</term>, and <term>Mercury</term> is <term>Mercury</term>, it is also the case that in the end, their matter becomes that same thing again, returning to its first matter. Therefore, that which lies in between—that is, between the first and the last matter—stands in the power of the <term>Aniadus</term>. But the first and the last stand in the power of the Three First Principles, which is to say, in their own nature.

->II.<-

<margin>B</margin> Now that it is understood that the "middle" between the matters stands in the power of the <term>Aniadus</term>, and the matter itself runs back again into its first matter, it should be noted that in the first <term>Yliaster</term>, a division of essences occurred into the four elements. It never runs back into that same [undifferentiated] state, and here is how:

Into the **Element of Air** <note>original: "Element Aeris"</note> has run the airy nature, and it enters it again. Into the **Element of Fire** <note>original: "Element Ignis"</note> the firmament, and it enters it again. Into the **Element of Earth** <note>original: "Element Terræ"</note> the fruit, and it enters it again. Into the **Element of Water** <note>original: "Element Aquæ"</note> the minerals, and they go back into it. Thus, each thing goes back into its first [element].

But the four do not go back into that from which they first emerged <note>the Yliaster</note>, for that would be against all understanding, which nature cannot suffer in this way. If it were to go back into its first Monarchy, there would be a fragility or a future state that cannot be. Furthermore, these things were made out of nothing. If they were then to go back into their [original] matter, they would not be nothing, but something. Therefore, it is the conclusion of the **philosophers** <note>alchemists and natural scholars</note> that the **Daughter of the Elements** <note>the physical products or fruits of nature</note> shall remain without end for eternity.

This accords with the fact that we should know not only about these elements, but also about the others. For the "middle" between the two matters—in its form and essence—proceeds from the will and power of the <term>Aniadus</term>. This power has been so provided that it becomes what it is through the body that uses it. Then follows the power of humans, for the elements are directed and drawn according to him, and not he according to the elements; rather, he is provided for and <margin>C</margin> preceded them.

From this it follows that from this element and others, the food of humans grows—not only wheat, but rye and spelt, etc.—and all this in many ways according to the nature of the lands. They unite themselves with humans because he comes from and is of the same matter from which the other growing things come. Thus, the union is complete; that is, like leads and nourishes its like. That is to say, man is an "earth," and therefore he must eat the earth. Following from this are the four worlds, where each eats that from which it comes: the **Nymphs** <note>water spirits</note> eat the water; the **Gnomes** <note>here associated with fire, though usually earth spirits</note> eat the fire; the **spirits of the air** eat the air. And if man were not of the earth, he could not enjoy its food, for it would be contrary to him. But since they come from one origin, seed, and soil, the two join together as things that belong together, which man cannot separate. For he must live from that which he came from, and eat that which grows from that which he himself grew from, and drink from that which he issued from. Therefore, through the great <term>Yliaster</term>, the nature of the elements is divided so that they nourish and provide drink, having four elements within each single element.

->III.<-

### ON PEAS, OATS, AND BEANS.
<note>original: "DE PISIS AVENA ET FABA."</note>

The nutritional nature in <term>Sulphur</term> is of two kinds: one more noble, and one less noble. The more noble, such as **wheat** <note>original: "Weyßen"</note> and its like, is the Noble Sulphur. The other is the Lesser Sulphur; therefore, one is more [potent] in its kind than the other. From this it follows that...

### PHILOSOPHY, BOOK III.
<note>original: "PHILOSOPHIÆ LIBER III."</note>

<margin>▲</margin>
Humans cannot be noble without this; rather, they must have it daily for several reasons: In the same way that a fish is placed in water and has that as its food, and without which it can eat no food, and even without water eats nothing: So too is the human, who should more rightly be in the earth, placed like a fish in water, so that instead of the earth, he must have bread daily. Without bread, he can achieve no **digestion** <note>original: "dewung," likely meaning digestion or processing of food</note>; rather, it passes through with other food, just as water passes through with the bait of a fish. But a small amount of "noble" substance is also there which may turn out well, such as **peas** <note>original: "Pisa"</note>, **oats** <note>original: "Auena"</note>, and **beans** <note>original: "Faba"</note>. These come from a dry <term>Sulphur</term>, separated from the mild <term>Sulphur</term> from which the <term>Aniadus</term> <note>The inner vital power or celestial virtue that determines an organism's specific form.</note> ordered this fruit. It also unites with the body because it comes from the earth. From these **legumes** <note>original: "leguminen"</note> it is to be understood that two kinds of growth come from the earth: One growth is that which becomes flesh in humans without a "middle" <note>meaning: directly consumed</note>. Another growth is that which becomes flesh in humans only through a "middle" <note>meaning: consumed by animals first</note>. This should be understood such that there are two <term>Aniadi</term>: one of the earth, to procreate, and the other in the sensing beings, to prepare. Therefore, the <term>Aniadus</term> of the earth procreates toward two <term>Aniados</term>: the sensing one toward the <term>Aniadus</term> of humans, taking a <term>Sulphur</term>, a <term>Salt</term>, and a <term>Mercury</term> <note>The Three Principles of Paracelsian alchemy: Sulphur (soul/combustibility), Salt (body/stability), and Mercury (spirit/fluidity).</note> that is subjected to the <term>Aniadus</term> of humans without any middle, and goes into the flesh. Afterward, it procreates food for the cattle; that is under the <term>Aniadus</term> of the cattle, so that this same <term>Aniadus</term> makes flesh out of it. It follows then that this same <term>Aniadus</term> is subjected to the <term>Aniadus</term> of humans. Therein it is to be known that all growth becomes flesh, and everything that the earth procreates ends in flesh. But some into two kinds of flesh—that is, into the cattle and from that into the human; some into the cattle and not the human, for the reason that the cattle is grown from the poison of the earth, and therefore it is not suitable for humans for its own sake, not just for the food's sake. <margin>B</margin> There are also some growths that serve both humans and cattle without a "middle," such as all **legumes** and **grains** <note>original: "Frumenta"</note>. For their <term>Sulphur</term> is prepared with <term>Salt</term> and <term>Mercury</term> in such a way that they serve all eating animals that are subject to their <term>Aniadus</term>. Peas are made of much <term>Sulphur</term> and little <term>Salt</term> and <term>Mercury</term>. Oats have much <term>Salt</term>, less <term>Mercury</term>, and much <term>Sulphur</term>. Beans are composed of all three equally, and are the coarsest among the first three. <margin>On the various colors of the aforementioned.</margin> <note>original: "De variis coloribus prædictorum."</note> Likewise, one should note their colors. For from the nature of the <term>Sulphur</term> come many kinds of colors in food. All these colors are given to them in their generation and are not fixed. As in **red beets**, there is a red, dissolved <term>Sulphur</term> from the food; in yellow ones, a yellow <term>Sulphur</term>; in green ones, a green <term>Sulphur</term>. For all these colors come from the <term>Sulphur</term> alone. Although it does not have such colors in itself, they are nonetheless in it because of its own <term>Salt</term> and <term>Mercury</term>, which are full of such colors and change it.

<sig>i i i i</sig>

#### On Cabbages, Parsnips & Poppies: Also on Onions, Garlic: Also on Turnips, Radishes: Also on Lentils & Leeks.
<note>original: "De Caulibus, Pastinacis & Papaueribus: Item de Coepis, Allijs: Item de Rapis, Raphanis: Item de Lentibus & Porro."</note>

**Cabbages** <note>original: "Caules"</note> also come from the edible <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Salt</term>, and <term>Mercury</term>, as do **Parsnips** <note>original: "Pastinaca"</note> and **Poppies** <note>original: "Papauere"</note>, and all those like them. They have been divided in the <term>Aniadus</term> so that some eating-power is in the leaf, some in the root, and some in the seed. The plants that are food, such as **chard** <note>original: "Bleta"</note>, cabbage, and others, have the leaf-power from the <term>Aniadus</term> and the food-power from the <term>Aniadus</term>. Therefore, the cabbage goes into the form of a leaf and is a more dissolved <term>Sulphur</term> with much <term>Salt</term> and little <term>Mercury</term>. In the same way, in the parsnip, the <term>Aniadus</term> of the root keeps the same power of the food in the root. Thus, in the poppy and in lentils, it draws upward into the seed; the same in **millet** <note>original: "Milio"</note> also. <margin>C</margin> In these, there is a division such that many plants are for eating: **lettuce** <note>original: "Lactuca"</note>, cabbage, **purslane** <note>original: "Portulaca"</note>, and many other species. This happens because the plants are separated by their **complexion** <note>The combination of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a thing's nature and medical use.</note> according to the nature of humans. Therefore, in the element of Earth there are the four complexions, as in other elements; and the providence of the <term>Aniadus</term> is to be recognized there, such that coldness is in lettuce and purslane, and warmth in cabbage and chard, etc. For this reason the genera are separated; otherwise, they are not separated regarding the food itself. For if lettuce and cabbage were one plant, they would be of one kind; but because more use comes from them in two forms, two forms have been made of them. So also in the roots: in the parsnip is the leading power, and in turnips also; but they are separated for such reasons. And thus also the onion, the garlic, and the leek are kept apart, so that their power would not stand in a mixture with other beings. And in this separation it is further to be considered that Nature, for the sake of the "air," wants onions, garlic, and also radishes to be distinct, so that they are not to be cooked like turnips. For the Sulphurous nature is sometimes to be cooked and sometimes not. Therefore, this is a reason here that Nature wants each thing to be cooked according to its nature and belonging. Thus, garlic wants to remain raw and be separated from onions. For the onion wants to be cooked, and both of them are separate from the radish, which has a special preparation; and all are separate from turnips and parsnips, which want to be cooked separately. Thus has Nature put together that which has its own special cooking and its own special goodness, so that the **Great Wonders of Nature** <note>original: "Magnalia naturæ"</note> appear manifold and not simple. Such genera are many, which nonetheless all take their origin in no other way than as indicated by all things in this tract and booklet, wherein they shall all be understood.

# ON THE ELEMENT OF EARTH
<note>original Latin: "DE ELEMENTO TERRÆ"</note>

### V.
->Concerning Weeds, that is, concerning Darnel, Poppy, etc.<-
<note>original Latin: "De Zizania, id est de Lolio, Papauere, &c."</note>

<margin>A</margin>Regarding **weeds** <note>original: "Zizania," a term often used for darnel or tares in a biblical context</note>, it is to be noted that **darnel** <note>original: "Lolium"</note>, **cornflowers** <note>original: "Flores frumenti"</note>, **red poppies** <note>original: "Papauer rubeum"</note>, and everything of that kind which grows among the grain, takes its origin in this way: When the seeds of grain or certain **legumes** <note>pod-bearing plants like peas or beans</note> are sown, it must be understood that the <term>Tincture</term> <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a transformative vital force that imbues matter with its specific qualities.</note> of the Element of Earth, and of the other elements as well, is so diverse that it transforms the seed within the earth and turns it into weeds. For darnel, red poppies, and the like are born from wheat alone through the alteration of the seed by the power of the elemental Tinctures. This origin lies primarily in two elements: Fire and Earth. From this it follows that there are many fields where such weeds grow abundantly; this is due to the nature of the field, because it contains much of that specific Tincture. Similarly, there are certain places where whatever is sown is transmuted by the Heavens into weeds. It should be known that no wheat or fruit can be sown without weeds, of which there are many kinds. Thus, if a farmer sows and his seed fails, he finds wheat growing again, but mixed with **cockle** <note>original: "Ratten"</note>, darnel, poppies, and the like, rather than the fruits he actually sowed. These weeds also become "seedy," meaning they produce their own seeds and allow themselves to be sown as if they came from the first <term>Iliastro</term> <note>The "Iliaster" is the Paracelsian term for the primordial, star-like matter from which all things were first created.</note>, which is not the case; for they were never intended in the original *Iliastro*. Rather, through the Tincture of the elements, they take their birth in the same way as **worms from dung** <note>original: "Würm auß den Stercoribus"; a reference to the historical belief in spontaneous generation.</note>. In this way, such flowers and growths also come from wheat and corn. And if these are planted, they become more beautiful and lovely, but they do not lose their original nature. Therefore, whoever sows corn or wheat also sows all genera of weeds, according to the nature described.

<margin>B</margin>It also frequently happens that from certain grains and legumes, nettles grow, somewhat similar in nature to the others but distinct. Various grasses also grow from them, and many new plants. This is because the Tinctures are occasionally altered and varied. These weeds grow not only among these grains and legumes, but also among **cabbage stalks** <note>original: "Caulibus"</note>, so that many "bad" Tinctures flow in and corrupt the true nature of that seed. These misgrowths all come from the true main stocks that are planted in the fields and gardens; according to the nature of that land and sky, they are altered in their Tincture. Thus, there are unspeakably many genera of weeds, and they cannot be prevented or rooted out so that they never grow back. For the seed that falls into the earth is subject to the Tincture of the Earth and the Heavens that resides in every land.

->The End of the Third Treatise of the Philosophy of Theophrastus, concerning<-
->the Element of Earth.<-

# FOURTH TREATISE.
<note>original Latin: "TRACTATVS QVARTVS."</note>
## ON SIMPLES.
<note>original Latin: "DE SIMPLICIBVS." "Simples" are individual medicinal herbs used on their own.</note>
### I.
->(Concerning Saffron, Meadow Saffron & Safflower, also concerning the double Monk’s Head, Spearwort, and Globeflower)<-

<margin>C</margin>In the Element of Earth, colors exist separately, and **Taste** <note>original: "Gustus"</note> exists separately, as does **Odor**.
->Most [parts] of this chapter are missing.<-
<note>original Latin: "Deficiunt pleræque huius capitis."</note>

<term>Ariadus</term> <note>Likely a variation of "Aniadus," the vital celestial fruitfulness that determines the form of a plant.</note> means what is described in *The Nature of Things*: nothing of those colors and forms is understood here, for it concerns the generation of nature. But as for **speckled** <margin>*speckled.</margin> colors that come from nature, they come from the power of **Salt**. <note>In the Paracelsian system of the Three Principles, Salt is responsible for the physical body, solidity, and color of an object.</note>

### II.
->On the Taste of Herbs.<-

Likewise, Taste is divided into four parts: **Pungent**, **Bitter**, **Sweet**, and **Sour**. For example, Pungency is in **Ginger** <note>original: "Zinzibere"</note>, Bitterness is in **Rhubarb** <note>original: "Rheubarbaro"</note>, Sweetness is in **Polypody** <note>original: "Polypodio," a type of fern</note>, and Sourness is in **Sorrel** <note>original: "Acetosa"</note>.

Now, however, it is important to know that these have their **degrees** <note>original: "gradus," referring to the potency or intensity of a quality on a scale of 1 to 4</note>, one higher in degree than the other. For instance, **Pepper** is the highest, then **Cardamom**, then **Grains of Paradise**, then **Ginger**, then **Galangal**, and **Cinnamon** and others. The reason for this is that every pungent thing has a specific heat within it that is unlike any other and is a unique essence. It is the same with Sourness: **Centaury** <note>original: "Cen."</note> is the sourest, then **Mustard** <note>original: "Sinapis"</note>, then **Garlic** <note>original: "Allium"</note> and **Onions** <note>original: "Cepæ"</note>, then **Sorrel** and others. And as often as there is a "sour" in these items, there is a specific nature and virtue. So too with Sweetness: there is one kind in **Polypody**, another in **Gratiola** <note>original: "Graphoy," likely Hedge Hyssop</note>, another in **Turnips** <note>original: "Steckrüblein"</note>, and so on in many others. The same applies to Bitterness: there is one in **Rhubarb**, a great one in **Gentian**, and a great one in **Feverfew** <note>original: "Amarilla"</note>...

most of which is found in ***Colocynth*** <note>original: "Coloquintide," also known as bitter apple, a powerful purgative.</note>. These four **tastes** <note>original: "Gustus"</note> exist in many hundreds of variations within herbs, all of which arise from the <term>Three Primes</term> <note>Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury: the three fundamental substances that Paracelsus believed made up all matter.</note> in which so many essences are hidden. It is just as with silver, from which a goldsmith can create hundreds of different forms, yet they are all made of one single thing. These four types—namely, **pungency** <note>original: "das Näß," literally "the sharp/wet-biting taste."</note>—arise from **Salt** and overcome the **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note> of the plant. Thus, in the Salt of **ginger** <note>original: "Zinziberis"</note>, one must look for this pungency, and not in the **Sulphur** or the **Mercury**. <margin>*</margin> Similarly in **pepper**, **calamus** <note>sweet flag</note>, **cinnamon**, and all those that are sharp; in these, the Salt must be considered, and not the other two, for such is the <term>Herbal</term> <note>original: "Herbarium," here meaning the essential nature or classification of the plant.</note> in its specific property. However, that which is **sweet** comes from **Mercury** here, and the Mercury alone should be separated and extracted, for it gives sweetness to the Sulphur and the Salt and overcomes them. That which is **bitter** comes from Salt and Mercury when the Mercury has lost its sweetness and the Salt its sharpness; from what remains, a **conjunction** <note>original: "Coniunctio," an alchemical joining.</note> is formed, and that is bitter; therefore, it yields both Mercury and Salt. That which is **sour** is a **liquor** <note>a fluid or essence</note> of all three which has no **essence** within it and has evaporated within its Three Primes, much like a vinegar from which the **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus Vini," or alcohol</note> has escaped. Thus, these four stand within the Three Primes—Sweet and Bitter, Pungent and Sour—two by two. When one departs, the other remains; thus, the departure of one is the birth of the other, as is further explained in the book ***On the Nature of Things*** <note>original Latin: "de Natura Rerum"</note> in its own chapter.

<margin>* B</margin>
...that the seven planets inflict seven injuries upon the element of **Earth** <note>original Latin: "Terræ"</note>, and therein are seven herbs that may avert them. By this, it is also to be understood that the seven planets may also avert seven injuries on Earth if we know how to use them: just as the Sun may **purge** **melancholy**, **Mercury** may purge **cholera** <note>original: "Choleram," referring to yellow bile or a choleric temperament</note>, and **Saturn** may purge **fevers**, and so on. Therefore, it should be noted again that every star on Earth has its herb to fulfill the nature of its star and also to avert its harm. Such a nature is divided in the <term>Iliaster</term> <note>original: "Iliastro," a Paracelsian term for the primeval force or the "star of the matter."</note>, and the malice of each element is stilled by another; they do not cling to one another, nor are they born from one another. Similarly, there are twelve stars and twelve herbs; then other herbs and other stars. From this art is the physician born who wishes to be a true one. For ***Hypericum*** <note>St. John's Wort</note> is the Sun, and indeed the earthly Sun; **Peach-tree** <note>original: "Persic.," likely Persicaria (water pepper) or the Peach tree, both associated with Mercury.</note> is Mercury, and indeed the earthly Mercury. But what shall we call them, since those who suck the marrow from their art do not love us for it, and those who do not understand us despise us? Let everyone who wishes to be a philosopher consider this **concordance** <note>original: "Concordantã," the harmonious correspondence between the stars and earthly things.</note> well. For from it flows the **Physician**, the **Surgeon**, and every **Naturalist** who wishes to understand the body in its distress. For the stars teach one to recognize the disease, and the herbs teach one to heal it. These are the two paths upon which every physician should set his eye: if he knows the stars, let him then **speculate** <note>investigate/theorize</note> on the **origin of diseases** <note>original Latin: "principium Morborum"</note>; and if he recognizes the herbs, let him then **consider** what he should use. But to forget the influence of the heavens above and not to know the **operation** below is to act more than blindly. We show you this so that herbs may be better and more fully understood in their **generation**. But in ***On the Nature of Things***, the rest will be fully recounted.

## I. ON MUSHROOMS.
<note>original Latin: "DE FVNGIS."</note>

The origin of mushrooms is a single thing: they are a root without herb or seed, to be understood in this way. They ought to be a plant, but the botanical <term>Aniadus</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for the vital, spiritual power that governs growth and longevity in nature.</note> is not within them; therefore, there is no true root, no true stem, and no plant. It is a "misgrowth" of nature that grows from **Sulphur** that no longer has any **spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus"</note> in it, and similarly from **Salt** and **Mercury**. It is a dissolved thing of the three substances that is **conglutinated** <note>stuck together like glue</note> and not rightly **coagulated** or **prepared**; it is merely a conglutinated Sulphur. Therefore, there is little or no power in them. They also produce little flesh <note>nutritional value</note>, for they do not possess the true, whole earthly power; thus, they are not complete for any purpose. They grow in the shade of forests for the reason that they are too weak for the Sun; they cannot come forth before the Sun, for it consumes their conglutination, for it is...
