THE PHILOSOPHY OF THEOPHRASTUS <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note>

-># BOOK FOUR.<-
->### *On the Element of Water, together with its fruits*<-

->THE FIRST TREATISE:<-
->On the Form of the Element of Water.<-

### I.

<margin>A</margin>Initially, concerning the Element of Water, it is necessary to know how it is in its origin, into what <term>cataracts</term> <note>original: "Cataracten," referring here to the divisions or floodgates of the world's water system.</note> it is divided, and what its fruits are. It is thus: The Element of Water is a seed to the <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: "Yle," the primal, unformed matter from which all things are created.</note>, which produces from itself the trunks and the fruits upon or within it. This is the water, and within it is its fruit—that is, stones and metals, in as many varieties as there are of them. However, to philosophize about the seed of the Element of Water is to understand that this seed lies within the <term>Fabrica</term> <note>The "fabric" or structural workshop of the universe.</note> just as a seed lies in the earth. From this structure, the trunk emerges, then its branches, and then its fruit. Thus, from this seed grows a trunk that passes through the soil out into the light of day, yet it remains and exists within the earth. For in the same way that the Element of Earth holds its fruit within the <term>Body of Chaos</term> <note>original: "Corpus Chaos." In Paracelsian physics, Chaos is the atmospheric space or the "middle" element that provides room for growth.</note>, so the Earth is the body that sustains the growths, trees, and fruit of the tree of the Element <margin>B</margin> of Water. For there is no element that does not have a "body" in which it is carried. The Chaos carries the <term>Impressions</term> <note>The influences or "seeds" sent down from the stars.</note>; the element of Fire carries fruit for the Earth; the Earth carries for the Water; the Water for the Air; such that the fruit of each element is carried within another element. Now, just as the tree emerges from the seed of the element, so a flowing stream emerges from it, distributed through the whole earth. And all of this is but one single tree, one origin, one root, from a single trunk. All the streams that exist in the whole <term>Globe</term> <note>original: "Globul," the world-sphere.</note> are the branches of this trunk from this tree. And all the moisture of the whole globe is the "drippings" <note>original: "Abrißach," likely referring to the runoff or sap-like flow of the cosmic water-tree.</note> that fall from the branches of this tree and pass through all the pores of the globe by its distillation. This is nothing other than the small trickles from fir trees that fall down upon the earth; in this way, the "branches" of the water fall into the hollows of the earth.

In this manner, as has been shown, the origin of the Element of Water is understood. Therefore, all water and its fruit come solely from the Element, but they *are not* the Element itself. The Element has never been seen, and that is the <note>True</note> Element of Water. For nothing else comes forth from it but water; and it is called the Element of Water because of the water and its fruit, and not because of its <term>Complexion</term> <note>The balance of qualities like hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note> or quality, as is understood with other elements.

### II.

<margin>C</margin>Now, however, concerning its course and path, as well as its sites and locations, it is to be known that the tree itself has a beginning and an end; it springs up and dies, it comes into being and passes away. Thus, every flowing water is **New** and not old, never seen before, and this happens along the way. Just as the Element of Water lies in the middle of the globe, so it goes out toward all levels in a circle around the branches, from the root toward the day. And so many branches will grow from this root: the branch of the Rhine, the branch of the Danube, the branch of the Nile, etc. And other small branches, which are all branches of the root that grows from the seed in which the Element of Water rises. They are all trunks from one tree, growing out from the root according to the <term>threefold lengths</term> <note>original: "Trival Lingen," likely referring to the three dimensions or the longitudinal divisions of the sphere.</note> in the circle of the outer firmament of the two elements, Fire and Air. Thus, through these "threefold lengths," the tree is divided throughout the entire globe, out into the light of day. So the trunk and its branches grow from the center of the globe until it reaches the two outer elements; there is the limit of its length. For it goes no further into its "body," nor does its <term>Yliadum</term> <note>A Paracelsian term referring to the vital spirit of an element or the destined limit of its physical growth and reach.</note>. For if the *Yliadum* were not set at that place, every tree would spring toward heaven, further above the earth than it goes within the earth. This is also true of the fruits of the Element of Earth, which lie no further upon the earth than the height of the plants. Therefore, there are two types of Chaos: that which lies above this is the Chaos in which Fire is contained. And if the *Yliadum* were not there, the Element of Earth would send its fruit into the middle of heaven; and so would the Element of Water. Now, as the course and the path and the trunk of the tree are, it goes into its *Yliadum* upon the level of the earth; there it reaches its height, and that is its end. But to speak of where it eventually goes when it lies in the *Yliadum*: the philosophy is such that all branches conclude their *Yliadum* in the Sea, where they all come together. For just as it is one root, so it comes together into a single peak and <term>umbel</term> <note>original: "Dolden," the flowering head of a plant; here used to describe the sea as the "crown" of the water-tree.</note>, which is the Sea. The Sea itself is not a trunk nor a tree, but only the crown of the trunks; it does not grow from the root by itself, but only what it receives through the branches. That

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Alternative: moist.</margin>
...but where it is salty, it causes the place to be so, such that salt water also flows into it, as follows hereafter in the section **concerning salts**. And its rising and falling is taken from the fact that all * fruits go with the night and rise again with the day's heat; this is <term>Clisso</term> <note>original: "Clisso," a Paracelsian term for the hidden natural power that moves and directs the growth and cycles of living things.</note>. In the same way, things in the water rise and fall, go away and return, just as in other fruits.

### III.

Now, just as this is to be known, so also must its "death" be understood—that is, its **consumption** <note>original: "Consumptio," meaning the process of being used up or worn away.</note>—for nothing exists without consumption. This should be understood in such a way that when any thing enters its <term>Yliadum</term> <note>original: "Yliadum," referring to the specific span of time or the perfected state of a substance in its natural cycle.</note>, it becomes subject to **putrefaction** and decays. Every decay is a wasting away and a vanishing of the thing in which it exists, so that it is consumed just as if nothing had ever been there. This is the work of Nature: for just as Nature produces it, so she takes it away again; and as it comes out of nothing, so it returns again into nothing. In this, one must understand that the Element of Water is likewise subject to **corruption**. Thus, when it reaches the <term>Dolden</term> <note>original: "Dolden," referring to the sea or the "abyss" where all waters eventually gather and are transformed.</note>—that is, the sea—it decays there and consumes itself without any other help. Rather, out of its own essence and nature, it decays and consumes itself. Just as fire takes itself away and extinguishes itself, so also does water take itself away and consume itself. In this way, the "Tree" of the Element of Water and its branches are divided. What lies and exists within it regarding "fruits" follows hereafter, as does the nature of all of them, their growth, and their birth. It is its nature that it carries some of its fruits within it, casts some out, and throws some away entirely. Likewise, one must specifically know how many different paths, rivers, flows, kinds, and essences spring from it. However, so that all these things—whatever springs from the Element of Water—may be understood in its death: know that the branches, but not the fruits, come into the **Dolden**. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, one must specifically know about the death of the fruits: they all remain until the <term>Drachum</term> <note>original: "Drachum," likely referring to the ultimate point of transformation or the final "burning up" of a substance's life force.</note>; in that hour they are consumed, as will be understood and shown regarding the **Dracho** at the end.

### IV.

To proceed further to the origin of the fruits: know that all fruits of the Element of Water are these: **Salts, Minerals, Gems, and Stones**. Thus, there are four lineages of growth from the seed of the Element of Water. It is like this: the sweet water is the trunk; thereafter, the nature of its fruit is fourfold within the "Mother." One is the Mother of **Salts**, one of **Minerals**, one of **Gems**, and one of **Stones**. Each of these is then divided in many ways according to its essence. For instance, **concerning salts**, there are three fruits: Salt, Vitriol <note>A sulfate mineral, often green or blue, used in chemistry and medicine.</note>, and Alum. Each of these has many genera under it: there are many types of Salt, many of Vitriol, and many of Alum. So it is also **concerning minerals**: some are Metals, some are **Marcasites** <note>In this context, minerals like bismuth or antimony that resemble metals but were considered "immature" or brittle.</note>, and some are **Cachimiæ** <note>original: "Cachimiën," a term for metallic ores that are not yet true metals or are mineral-like "dross."</note>; and each specifically has more genera. Of the Metals, there are seven; of the Marcasites, there are nine; of the Cachimiæ, there are twelve. And again, each of the Metals is of various kinds for itself: such as Gold, which is "fixed" or "unfixed"; Silver, "fixed" and "unfixed"; while **Venus** is Copper and Zinc; and so on with the others, as will be recorded in their respective chapters. The Marcasites and Cachimiæ are likewise of many kinds within themselves.

Now, to know further of their origin, flow, "autumn" (harvest), and the like, one must know that all the fruits that come out of the Element of Water are divided into its branches and trees. For example, Salt has its own specific exit together with the sweet waters until the end of its **Yliadum**; so do the others. But to know of the division and separation of them all: all such fruits are in one root, <margin>C</margin> out of which each kind grows into its own specific essence. Just as a tree grows from one seed—the wood being separate, the bark separate, the fruit separate, the leaves separate, and yet it is all one tree—so also there, many hundreds of kinds of fruits grow from one root. Each fruit goes into its **Yliadum** and <term>triualkingen</term> <note>A difficult term related to the unfolding or "triple-distilling" of a substance's life stages.</note>, just as the **Fabricator** <note>The Creator or the Architect of Nature.</note> has ordered it. And so, when the division goes out from the <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: "Yle," the primary matter.</note> into its trunks and is born into a fruit of its kind, then many different things are found that come from the Element of Water: in one trunk Salt, in another Mineral, in the third something else. Therefore, just as on Earth every seed gives its fruit, so the seed of Water is a seed of many hundreds of things that grow from it. And when they come into their **Yliadum** and then await the time of **Autumn** (harvest), then the harvest and the "autumn" of each branch's fruit occurs, whatever is within it. Such harvest, birth, growth, and origin will follow specifically for each hereafter.

## Treatise II. On Salts

In the <term>Ares</term> <note>The specific power that gives things their unique taste and smell.</note> is all taste, flavor, and smell; these are separated by the **Archeus of the Elements**, each into its own essence and specific kind. This separation by the **Archeus of the Elements** <note>The "inner alchemist" or organizing spirit of nature that directs growth and health.</note> happens in the **Hyle**. From the sharp parts come the **Salts**; from the metals, the **Minerals**; from the resins, the **Sulfurs**; from the gems, the **Stars** <note>Referring to the celestial or crystalline light within gemstones.</note>, and so on.

# SECOND TREATISE.
## ON THE TYPES OF SALTS.
### CHAPTER ONE.
### Preface.

<margin>B</margin>
Now, however, to speak of the matter within this seed called <term>Ares</term> <note>original: "Ares," the Paracelsian term for the specific "seed" or vital force within an element that allows it to multiply and grow into different forms.</note>, from which then grows the fruit of the water—the <term>Salia</term> <note>salts</note>, <term>Mineralia</term> <note>minerals</note>, <term>Gemmæ</term> <note>gems</note>, and <term>Gluten</term> <note>resins or "glue-like" substances</note>: It must be known that sweetness and sourness stand together in one substance, as do moisture and sharpness, as well as the resins, and the matter of metals <note>original: "materia Metallorum"</note>, and of gems, and other such things. As in every thing, from which the other then grows, it holds them hidden within itself in such a manner. But the <term>Archeus</term> <note>original: "Archeus," the internal "alchemist" or invisible governing power in nature that separates and directs substances to their proper purpose.</note>, who is the divider of the elements and of all things that are within them, this same one separates each thing from the other and to its proper place, as much as is within it. Just as one who pours together ten kinds of colors, mixed into one mixture; although it is then only one color, it is nevertheless composed of ten, which only the Archeus is able to separate, each into its own essence. Thus the Archeus takes each thing out of the seed of the Element of Water and ordains it into its <term>Nedeon</term> <note>original: "Nedeon," a term used by Paracelsus for the internal "womb" or subterranean spaces where minerals grow.</note>, upon the <term>Yliadum</term> <note>original: "Yliadum," referring here to the destination or primeval space of the earth where growth occurs.</note> of the earth. Whatever is of a salty nature, he separates from all other essences; whatever is sweet water, the same; whatever is sour, or whatever is not like the others, or is unique, he separates from one another—such as two kinds of salt, two kinds of water, two kinds of metals of one name, and the like. Once he has thus separated them and directed them into the Nedeon, then follows the operation of that same Nedeon in the Yliadum, along with its ripening, in which it is ordained. How, however, each one has its essence and its path apart from the others, follows hereafter.

### CAP. II.
### On Sweet Waters.

<margin>C</margin>
Universally, the Archeus takes the trunk and divides it through the globes onto its Yliadum. Now, however, although it is the trunk, there is no operation toward the fruit within the water; it is only the house and the place in which the operation of the fruit happens. And water remains a water in every way, unmixed, and is nothing other than the watery ark <note>original: "Arch," likely meaning a vessel or container.</note> from the Ares, in which there is no power, but rather a <term>Phlegma</term> <note>In alchemy, "phlegma" refers to the tasteless, watery, and inert distillate of a substance.</note>, which is separated from all <term>Spiritibus</term> <note>spirits</note> and essences, except for sweetness, sharpness, <term>Buteri</term> <note>butters/oils</note>, and moisture, in which no further power should be sought. Rather, it is taken straight out of the Ares as a water that is raised up by the sun from its substance; thus it is empty and void. And it is the first separation in the Ares by the Archeus into the Yliadum, through his Nedeon: And it is the first separation, growth, and operation from the Element of Water, and it retains the name of its element as if it were the thing itself. Once it is thus separated into water, in which there is no further operation: then it grows like a tree from its seed, which rises up toward the Yliadum, out of the power of the Nedeonic nature. Once it thus reaches the Yliadum, it is the entirely perfect tree, together with its branches, and grows into its <term>Dolden</term> <note>original: "Dolden," literally a flower cluster or canopy, but here referring to the sea as the final gathering place of waters.</note>—that is, into the sea, in which it takes its consumption and disappears through the power of that same <term>Putrefaction</term> <note>decay/transformation</note>, so that the canopy does not grow larger, but rather consumes its excess weight and mass.

### CAP. III.
### On Sour Waters.

Thereafter follows the second easiest separation, and that is the sour water, and sharp water, and salt water, as follows. First, the sour, light water is separated in the Archeus of the element, in which there is no <term>Coagulation</term> <note>thickening or hardening</note>, and no substance of hardness or the like. Part of that same is a water in which the Ark of the Water exists, and it is empty, without power in it, and is the second easiest separation after the [sweet] water, and goes out in the Nedeon alone by itself into the Yliadum. Unless it happens that a cataract of sweet water falls into it and they go out as one, which shows the weakness of the sourness. This sourness is the phlegm of <term>Vitriol</term> <note>original: "Vitriol," a metal sulfate, often highly acidic.</note>. Thus, after the sweet waters, the salts <note>original: "Salia"</note> follow after: And initially, before the salts are gripped by the Archeus, the phlegm must first be removed—that is, that same sour water. And of it there are many kinds, for the reason that in the Archeus of the element, in some places more <term>Aluminous sourness</term> <note>sourness related to alum</note> is mixed in, in some more vitriolic, in some more salty, and the like, according to what is in each. And thus it is also only an empty water, and a phlegm, separated from the salty matter, with which the salty growths could not grow. And it goes out at special places, not at the ends where that from which it is separated arrives: For the reason that the true salts go straight upwards into the <term>Triual</term> <note>a Paracelsian term for a specific direction or celestial path of a substance.</note>. The water, however, falls out from its Triual to the side, because of its lightness and subtlety which is within it. From this arise the cold baths, from many strange springs with strange natures. Some which do not allow meat, peas, and the like to cook: The cause is found in the <term>Alumen</term> <note>alum</note>, which is so raw that when it is placed in a water together with the vitriol, it allows nothing to boil in its place, and does not even let sugar dissolve. Some waters do not dissolve salt, some bite, some clean ulcers <note>original: "Vlcera"</note>, some heal, some dry out...

It explains that pure water is an inert "phlegm" or container, while acidic or medicinal springs are the byproduct of the separation of salts and minerals like alum and vitriol.</summary>

<term>Itching</term> <note>original: "Pruritum"</note>, <term>Scabies</term> <note>original: "Scabiem," referring here to itchy skin eruptions or mange</note>, and the like: all these powers come from <term>Salts</term>, <term>Alums</term>, and <term>Vitriols</term> <note>metallic salts, often copper or iron sulfates</note> in which the power itself lies with a perfect nature; the waters then take after this nature to some extent.

### CHAPTER IV.
## On Warm Baths.

Regarding warm baths, it should be known that they arise in the same manner as the origin of the sour <note>mineral or acidic</note> waters: they differ only in that the <term>Liquor</term> <note>liquid or fluid</note> which separates from the <term>Gluten</term> <note>original: "Gluten," a resinous or "glue-like" substance in Paracelsian chemistry</note> flows with them. Or, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal "master builder" or natural force that directs growth and separation</note> begins to separate the Gluten and first takes its <term>Phlegma</term> <note>original: "Phlegma," the watery, inactive component of a substance</note> and purifies it so that the Gluten stands alone in its operation and form, as with Salts. From this it follows that when this Liquor enters the <term>Yliadum</term> <note>original: "Yliadum," the primordial chaos or the medium through which elemental forces manifest</note> and touches the common water of the <term>Seuri</term> <note>likely referring to a specific mineral spring or source</note>, the mixture causes an effect of boiling within itself. The Liquor from the Gluten is <margin>Lime-like.</margin> sticky, and its nature is much like the <term>Pitch</term> of the Elements; such Liquor and such water cannot remain together without the destruction of both their natures, the quality of which is that this mixture must boil, like water and lime; and it is as strong as sulfur and a magnet, and even stronger than <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "Aquafort," nitric acid</note> and <term>Tartar</term>, and many other things. Where such spirits come together, they create a boiling and a vapor, depending on how many of them there are, and they boil thus even into the Yliadum, for there is a vessel from the <term>Center</term> <note>the core of the earth or element</note> to the Yliadum. Therefore, it often happens that many baths first become warm in the Yliadum because of the mixing of the two <term>floodgates</term> <note>original: "Cataracten," referring to underground channels or flows</note>. And there are many baths that, if one were to dig two or three fathoms beneath them, would be destroyed; that is because, through this digging, the floodgates would fall away from each other or it would be found that two cold waters run together there, which only became warm upon their mixing. Thus the ancient <term>Pagans</term> found many such baths <sig>B</sig> which they enclosed so that the path of the Gluten and the sour water would not fall away from each other. There are many such various floodgates that could be made into warm baths in the Yliadum through such mixing, of which <term>Apulia</term> <note>a region in Southern Italy known for its volcanic activity</note> has many that are natural, but also artificial in the sense that they were brought together by skill. Many of them, like the Apulian baths, are made in the Yliadum through their being enclosed; otherwise, they would vanish into the air and lose their effect.

### CHAPTER V.
## On Salt Waters.

Now, as the separation by the Archeus proceeds out of the <term>Ares</term> <note>the specific "seed" or vital force within an element</note>, and nothing remains but the true foundation of the salty substances, the Archeus takes it upon himself to separate the <term>Salia</term> <note>salts</note>. He first sets apart the Salt from the Vitriol and Alum, then the Vitriol from the Alum, and finally the Alum itself. When he thus takes hold of the Salt and separates it, it is of a dry nature and growth; it first grows its <term>Bieli</term> <note>a specific stage of mineral development</note> in daily growth into the <term>Trapheoneum Year</term> <note>original: "Annum Trapheoneum," a Paracelsian term for a cycle of nourishment or maturation</note>. This same growth goes through the <term>Left Triual</term> <note>a directional term in Paracelsian cosmology</note> into the Yliadum. Then, as it pushes into the Yliadum, an ore grows from it, and it happens thus: it is a dry substance, and the moisture of the <term>Globe</term> <note>the elemental sphere of the earth</note> moistens it so that it enters the Yliadum in a moist state. While it lies in the Yliadum, its moisture settles back down and distills away from it, and thus the salt hardens there, along with whatever it had grasped while it was moist. For this reason, many <sig>C</sig> types of salt-earth full of soil and of many colors are found, which come from the Element of Earth in such a mixture. Some salt comes out pure and clear without mixture; this came out dry and not moist, and as soon as it reaches the Yliadum, it hardens into stone and is a stone of the nature of salt. For every salt is of the nature of <term>Hardening</term> <note>original: "Coagulation"</note>, just as water is of the nature of <term>Dissolving</term> <note>original: "Resolution"</note>. Therefore, the two natures are separated from each other: that which dissolves and that which hardens. Some salt-growth enters the fresh water and dissolves, emerging into the daylight as a spring; these waters mix together at their origin because the salt has not yet reached the perfection of its growth. And whatever other water—namely fresh water—runs into it in the cold cannot be mixed into it, for the pure salt in its course allows no other water near it, but runs separately from the other into the Yliadum. Such growths sometimes cut themselves off and sometimes not; the reason is that it often happens that there is only one thrust or an outpouring from the main path, which perhaps shoots alongside the <term>Triualkingen</term> into a Yliadum. Where the growths move from the true origin of the right substance, there is no long-lasting stay.

### CHAPTER VI.
## On Vitriol and Alum.

The origin of Vitriol and Alum is in this manner: just as Salt is drawn out alone in its essence, so too are Vitriol and Alum separated there. For within these three all salts consist, and every salt must be one of these three. Just as these two are separated and driven upward into the height of the Yliadum like the Salt, they then show themselves as an ore, in the same manner as the salt that is found in the earth or stones or the like. Therefore, from their nature alone is this understood. But of the form...

<header>ON THE ELEMENT OF WATER</header>

<margin>A</margin> The form that appears clearly in <term>Salt</term>, <term>Alum</term>, and <term>Vitriol</term> <note>metallic sulfates, like copper or iron sulfate</note> is understood such that all the fruits of the Element of Water are minerals and of the nature of metals. Among all these that arise from salts, there is none that possesses more mineral power than Vitriol. This is because these salts are mineral in nature, and all minerals lie within a single mass and <term>Ares</term> <note>original: "Ares," the Paracelsian term for the specific power within an element that determines the growth and form of its species</note>. Thus, Vitriol is the final stage in the separation of minerals. Immediately following it, the generation of metals begins, and <term>Venus</term> <note>the alchemical name for Copper</note> is the first. Therefore, Vitriol is attached to the nature of Venus. It is part salt and part mineral, for it carries a part of Venus with it; thus, copper is found in every vitriol. Because of this attachment to metals—namely Venus—Vitriol is a salt with a Venusian nature. Likewise, copper is mixed with Vitriol, and not without it; rather, as its generation shows, it is an entire Vitriol. Therefore, because Vitriol is so closely related to Venus, yet remains a salt, it becomes a mineral and takes its <term>Corpus</term> <note>physical body or substance</note> from the <term>Liquor</term> <note>liquid essence</note> of metals. This is why it appears pyritic and shiny, in strange forms and shapes, as is understood of <term>Marcasites</term> <note>metallic sulfide minerals like iron pyrite</note>. Alum, however, is not attached to metals, but is a free salt that stands alone in the fire and takes its body after the mixing of the earth. But Vitriol does not; it comes solely from the mixing of metallic bodies. Therefore, it appears as a Marcasite and as a <term>Cachymia</term> <note>original: "Cachinien," minerals that are "almost" metals but lack a metallic body</note>, which are the first growths in the birthing of metals. Just as water comes from salts, so Vitriol hangs upon Copper, and Copper upon Vitriol; their medium is the <term>Phlegma</term> <note>the watery, inactive component</note>, which unites and joins them together. Therefore, it looks and is like that medium and takes its body from it.

### CHAPTER VII.
## On Copper-water.

<margin>B</margin> Likewise, <term>Copper-waters</term> <note>solutions of copper sulfate</note> also come forth, which are nothing other than a resolved <note>dissolved</note> Vitriol that cannot be <term>Coagulated</term> <note>solidified</note> because it contains too much salt and moisture. It takes its power from the <term>Three Primes</term> <note>original: "dreyen Ersten," Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> of the salts and contains within it the most subtle spirit of the Copper <term>Tincture</term> <note>the coloring or transforming essence</note>. However, it lacks a body, unlike Vitriol or Copper, yet the Tincture of the same is within it; but being without a body, it is a pure water. When iron is placed into it, the water <term>tinges</term> <note>colors or transforms</note> it into copper. This is because iron has its body from the "mercurial" part of copper, but lacks the redness found in the Three Primes of metals. For the salt colors the iron. From this it follows that Copper-water—since it comes from the redness of the Three Primes of metals—tinges that same body which belongs to Mercury. Thus, iron becomes copper within it, for it is copper-like in its color through the Spirit of Salt.

### CHAPTER VIII.
## On Stony-waters.

<margin>C</margin> There are also waters that turn wood or clay into stone. This comes from the power of Salt when it is resolved; it cannot return to coagulation without a substance, and thus lacks its own body. Yet the water is made from the Three Primes from which stones grow and become, except that it lacks the body.

From this it follows that when these waters encounter clay, they permeate it and coagulate within it, and it becomes a stone. Namely, these become <term>Whetstones</term> <note>original: "Weststein," likely stones used for sharpening</note>. Likewise, when certain pieces of wood are placed therein, this water permeates them and fills their pores, coagulating within so that the wood appears as a stone. Thus, it is a coagulated salt from the Three Primes of stony matter, brought to coagulation through the wood. Many such stones come from clay, such as <term>Slate</term> <note>original: "Schifferstein"</note> and the like; also, any wood placed therein rots and turns green <note>likely referring to mineral staining or petrification</note>.

# THIRD TREATISE.
# ON MINERALS.

### CHAPTER I.
## On Marcasites.

<term>Marcasites</term>, as they are found in all varieties—whether in color, shine, form, or otherwise—are merely a superfluity of the metals. That is, they are the material that was "too much" in the metals, which the metals could not incorporate into themselves to become metal. From this it follows that first, when the Salts are separated from the <term>Ares</term> <note>the formative force</note>, the separation of the metals follows. Among these, the first is the Marcasite, as it is that which is not fit to be a metal, yet lies within the same matter. Thus, initially, the "matter of metals" grows out of the Ares. This is the <term>Materia Prima</term> <note>First Matter</note>, set into three parts: the <term>Spirit of Salt</term>, the <term>Spirit of Mercury</term>, and the <term>Spirit of Sulfur</term> <note>original: "spiritum Salis, spiritum Mercurij, spiritum Sulphuris"</note>. These three are one thing, in which all metals and minerals lie.

While they lie thus, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal "master builder" or natural force</note> initially works to procreate and separate the metals.

<margin>A</margin> ...into its form and essence. Before it attacks the metals, it throws away the excess that should not be present in the <term>Salt</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>Sulphur</term> <note>these are the "Three Primes" of Paracelsian alchemy: the solid/body, the fluid/spirit, and the oily/soul</note>, and purifies these three Primes of their excess just as they were generated. Once it proceeds purely in this way, the growth that is unfit for use passes out through the <term>Trival lingen</term> <note>original: "Trival lingen," likely referring to a threefold separation or a specific alchemical vessel/process</note> into its <term>Yliadum</term> <note>primordial matter in the process of becoming</note>, and initially divides into two parts: <term>Marcasite</term> <note>metallic sulfide minerals like pyrite</note> and <term>Cachimiæ</term> <note>a term for mineral residues or "imperfect" ores that are not yet true metals</note>. And when it thus enters the Yliadum, it coagulates into a mineral that consists of Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury. The yellow Marcasite takes its color from the Sulphur that lies powerfully within it; the white Marcasite from the Mercury that lies more powerfully within it. Then the Sulphur and the Cachimia take their color from the Salt: in the same way, they also take their form from the Salt, being shaped in that likeness—angular and smooth—which comes from the spirit of Salt; the weight comes from the Mercury in all three. And if they are correctly separated, then these three minerals—Salt, Mercury, and Sulphur—each stand particularly in their own place, for within these three Primes all minerals exist.

### CHAPTER II.
## Regarding Cachimiæ.

<margin>B</margin> Just as Marcasites are understood, so too must one know of Cachimiæ: when the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the "inner artisan" or vital force that governs the formation of things</note> is engaged in the work of the metals, he first casts out the excess of Salt, Mercury, and Sulphur, from which the Marcasite is formed, according to how each part joins together. That is: sometimes more Mercury than Sulphur, sometimes more Salt than the others, sometimes more Sulphur than the others. Whichever thus predominates, that one forms its mineral. Now, however, the three Primes are separated in this manner: first the Marcasite, thereafter the Cachimiæ. In Marcasites, Mercury and Sulphur prevail, being the two lightest which are the first to fly off and coagulate, as stated above, and they become the heaviest: the reason being the abundance of Mercury. After this, the excess comes out even more precisely, and it is mostly Salt, with a little Mercury and Sulphur—yet it is not without them, but has less of their substance than it has of Salt. From this follows another form which the Cachimia has, tabular and boat-shaped <note>original: "geschifftet," referring to a specific crystalline habit</note>, after the nature of Salt, which is thus in Sulphur and such a property. And yet it has all colors—white, red—like Marcasite: it has these same colors from the Mercury and Sulphur, whichever then predominates most. And it is fixed and more stable than the Marcasite, by reason of the fixed Salt that it is. It also fixes the colors within itself so that no fire harms it: for it becomes more fixed in its coagulation and is better coagulated together than any other mineral. This same powerful coagulation makes it fixed; as soon as that is dissolved, no fixation remains, as is also the case in the metals. Thus, Marcasite is nothing but the excess present in the first matter of metals in the <term>Ares</term> <note>the specific identifying force of an element</note>, which is separated by the Archeus into the Yliadum, from which Marcasites and Cachimiæ are born—over thirty kinds and forms, yet all comprised under these two names. And although there are many of them, and not just one form, they yet come from one matter: this is caused by the unequal weights of the three Primes coming together, one more than the other, which is why manifold forms spring from them.

### CHAPTER III.
## Regarding Copper.

<margin>C</margin> After the Marcasites and Cachimiæ are separated from the <note>original: "prima materia Metallorum"</note> first matter of metals, the first generation follows, and it is <note>original: "Veneris"</note> of Venus [Copper], such that the Archeus drives out from the first matter the greatest Redness that is in the Sulphur, and from Mercury the greatest lightness, and from Salt <note>Text uses alchemical symbol for salt</note> the greatest yellowness that lies in the Salt <note>Text uses alchemical symbol for salt</note>. Out of these three, he makes Copper, as he drives it out through the separation into the Yliadum. Thus it is a metal, and it is large: for in the reddest colors of Sulphur there is no subtlety, and it is the nearest color to Gold, but the coarsest color; where it remains in the Sulphur, no Gold can grow. And because it is a metallic matter, the Archeus separates it out and makes Copper from it. Now, it cannot become a pure native metal, because in the operation it is mixed with <term>Vitriol</term> <note>metallic sulfates</note> and joined so closely together that it yields an ore in which the Copper lies. Also, through the separation, as the nature of Marcasites and Cachimiæ are driven out, the copper-like generations run along too quickly and imagine themselves into it and coagulate together: all for the reason that it is the first metal after the separation of Marcasites and Cachimiæ. Therefore, in its proper separation, the Marcasites and Cachimiæ are found, and their three Primes from which they are born.

### CHAPTER IV.
## Regarding Iron.

<margin>D</margin> Iron is the second metal, taken from the three Primes with many additions, beyond that which is Iron; that is, in the birth of Iron, there is mostly Salt and Mercury, and less of the red Sulphur from which Copper grows. It also has copper-salt in it, only not the Mercury. Its composition is, for the most part in its <term>Corpus</term> [body], Salt, then Mercury, and then Sulphur. This is because malleability comes from <term>Mercury</term> <note>the "spirit" or fluid principle</note> and coagulation comes from <term>Salt</term> <note>the "body" or solid principle</note>. Therefore, if the Salt is too abundant, it makes the substance too hard, but with too much metallic nature: then it only results in brittleness. From this, it follows that in iron there is much ore, and much that is not iron, because there is more Salt present than there should be. In its initial birth, it happens that the <term>Spirit of Vitriol</term> <note>original: "spiritus Vitrioli"; historically referring to sulfuric acid or the acidic essence of minerals</note> flows through quickly and hardens the Mercury into <term>Steel</term>. That same Spirit of Vitriol makes iron rusty because it devours its own body due to the great sharpness it contains; it does the same to <term>Copper</term>, for it is a spirit. And they take their color from Sulphur and Vitriol; the birth of Copper, Iron, and Vitriol is one, sharing an origin through the <term>Spirit of Salt</term>. Therefore, Vitriol lies within Iron, Steel, and Copper, and Vitriol also contains those same metals and they can be drawn from it.

### CHAPTER V.
### On Lead.

Lead is a blackness of the three <term>Primes</term> <note>Mercury, Salt, and Sulphur</note>, which is not an excess but a metallic nature within it. For all metals lie within Mercury, and everything is but one Mercury—likewise with Salt and Sulphur. Just as Copper is the excess redness of the three Primes, so Lead is the blackness that lies within the three Primes. Namely, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal "chemist" or vital force of nature that directs growth and separation</note> casts out whatever blackness is most prevalent in Mercury, as well as the coarseness from Salt and Sulphur. Mercury provides the malleability, Salt provides the coagulation, and Sulphur provides the flow and <term>Tincture</term> <note>the coloring principle or essence</note>. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, four good colors lie in Lead: blackness, because it is the blackness of the three Primes; and redness, because it has a <term>precipitation</term> of Mercury within it. Although it is not equal to true redness in quality, it is as much as belongs to a coarse Mercury. Likewise, whiteness lies within it because whiteness comes solely from the <term>Calcination</term> <note>heating a substance to a powder</note> of Mercury; thus it becomes white through calcination solely by the nature of the Mercury from which the Lead is made. Yellowness also lies within it, which also comes to it from Mercury—that is, when it is driven to the first degree in calcination, a yellowness follows every Mercury, which is also in Lead. Thus, Lead is nothing other than the black Mercury that lies in the <term>Ares</term> <note>the primordial power of differentiation</note> and is separated by the Archeus, so that the coarseness and such colors come out of the Mercury.

---

### CHAPTER VI.
### On Tin.

Tin is a pure Mercury, coagulated with a little Salt and a larger amount of white Sulphur. Its Mercury is the <term>leprous Mercury</term> <note>original: "leprosus Mercurius"; an alchemical term for a "diseased" or imperfect form of the metallic principle</note> which lies in the Ares, and yet is metallic, drawn out by the Archeus and ordered into a metal. It also takes its colors from Mercury: white, yellow, and red. Its <term>Sublimation</term> <note>turning a solid into vapor and back to solid</note> also comes from Mercury; its <term>Resolution</term> <note>dissolving into liquid</note> comes from Salt, whereby it is sublimated and resolved through them.

---

### CHAPTER VII.
### On Mercury.

<margin>C</margin> <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Argentum Viuum"</note> is the Mercury that does not take on malleability and is contrary to malleability. The Archeus casts it out and lets it be a separate metal without malleability. Although it is more like the Principle of Mercury than all other metals, it is separated only in that it does not receive malleability from the Archeus because of the weakness within it from the Salt and Sulphur, which are too scarce in it. It follows that through <term>Spagyric Practice</term> <note>original: "Spagyricam Practicam"; the alchemical art of separation and purification</note> and by addition, it may be formed into malleability and into a metal, as the *Philosophy of Transmutation* <note>original: "Philosophia de Transmutatione"</note> shows. For it is in every way equal to every metal and can be transformed into them, because it remains behind from the metals during the operation—that which cannot be led into malleability.

### CHAPTER VIII.
### On Silver and Gold.

Now that the metals are thus procreated and separated from the Ares—where there is no longer anything of coarse raw colors or essence, but only the most subtle remains: purple and beauty—that is, the purest of Mercury, Salt, and Sulphur, in form, substance, and essence, and the clearest and best in all colors. In this, the Archeus works and separates the two essences from one another: a White and a Brown <note>likely referring to a deep yellow or reddish-gold</note>. The White, which is pure and clean, <term>Fixed</term> <note>resistant to fire</note> and <term>Subtle</term>, and all its filth and coarseness has been drawn from it. Tin and Lead...

### CHAPTER IX.
### On Zinc.

JUST AS the metals are born and exist in such a way that the true metallic flow and malleability are taken and divided into the seven metals, as stated above: so there remains a residue there in the <term>Ares</term> <note>the primeval source or "womb" of the elements</note>, acting as the <term>dregs</term> <note>original: "Fæces"</note> of the three <term>Primes</term> <note>Mercury, Salt, and Sulphur</note>. From these grows <term>Zinc</term>, which is a metal and yet not one; also <term>Bismuth</term> <note>original: "Wißmat"</note> and their like, which are fluid and partially malleable. And yet, although they are somewhat related to the metals by their flow, they are merely "bastards" of the metals—that is, something similar to them, and yet not them. Zinc is for the most part a bastard of copper, and bismuth is a bastard of tin. From these two, the most dregs and remnants are produced in the Ares.

<margin>B</margin>

### CHAPTER X.
### On the Archeus of the Metals.

AS has been stated above, regarding how all metals grow forth: it is further to be known that the Ares contains within itself the <term>First Matter</term> <note>original: "Primam materiam"</note> of all metals, as stated above. Now, however, as it distributes them into the <term>Earth's sphere</term> <note>original: "Globul"</note> apart from one another, it should be noted that in this process, it drives out the materials into the <term>Trivial Lines</term> <note>original: "Triual Lingen"; likely referring to the paths or veins in the earth</note> of the <term>Yliaster</term> <note>original: "Yliado"; the primordial matter from which elements arise</note>—those materials which are not yet "cooked" into metals, and are separated from one another in their distribution. In one place, there is a branch of copper; in another, a branch of tin; and likewise with other metals. As they come from the Ares into the Trivial Lines, an ore is formed from some—such as tin, lead, iron, copper—driving them out so that not all <term>Marcasite</term>, Bismuth, <term>Calamine</term> <note>original: "Cachtmien"</note>, and Zinc, etc., are purged out beforehand or remain in the dregs, but are instead pulled along with them. Depending on whether much or little follows, the ore is either rich or small in metal. And it takes its hardness in the Trivial Lines once the Archeus has brought it out of the Ares: then they are found in the Yliaster in many ways and forms. For in that same preparation by the Archeus, they are brought forth in many colors, so that no vein is like another. In the same way that among all fruits no apple is exactly like another, or no pear is like another: so too is this unequal in its form, as is philosophized regarding the <term>Thilma</term> <note>a Paracelsian term for a natural vessel or matrix</note>: for such is only the Thilma and its power, which is not fully grasped here.

But silver and gold are often found solid and pure: for the reason that the marcasite, bismuth, and other such ore-materials are well separated from the metals and brought forth into their own trivial lines. And thus the metal remains pure; this happens only to silver and gold. This is because all other metals are driven up beforehand, and all filth is cleaned from them; therefore they are found quite pure, according to how the Archeus has ordered them.

<margin>a</margin>

They are also often found like foam lying upon the rocks, such as "table-silver," and also in the meadows, as "flame-gold"; and in many other ways in the Yliaster. And most often in the waters, for the reason that such loose gold is pushed through the water with the sand onto the Earth's sphere, and is then found as small grains, as in the Rhine and elsewhere. For where the cataracts of the waters go through the Trivial Lines in which such gold lies, the water pushes it out into the daylight, depending on whether much or little of it lies there. And mostly with the floods and powerful rivers, they are washed out and cast upon the Earth's sphere, onto the shores and the ground. It also happens many times that two, three, or (more) metals are found among one another, such as in copper, silver, and gold; or in tin and the like, and in others. This occurs because in the Ares, the Archeus, through his operation in driving them out to the Yliaster, brings two or three together. This happens with metals that are otherwise similar and related to each other: as with silver and gold, it happens that in that same separation, gold often remains in the silver, and silver in the gold; so too with the others. And if it is thus mixed, when it comes to the <term>Coagulation</term> <note>solidification</note>, they can never be separated from each other and thus remain together.

# ON THE ELEMENT OF WATER
### FOURTH TREATISE.
# ON STONES AND GEMS
### *Of the Element of Water*
### CHAPTER ONE.
### PROLOGUE.

<margin>A</margin> In the first <term>Yle</term> <note>original: "Yle," the primordial matter or "Hyle"</note>, when the <term>Ares</term> <note>the primeval source or "womb" of natural forms</note> was established and ordered into its operation, the stony matter was also placed into the Ares by the three First Principles: by the <term>Liquor of Salt</term> <note>Liquore Salis</note>, the <term>Liquor of Sulphur</term> <note>Liquore Sulphuris</note>, and the <term>Liquor of Mercury</term> <note>Liquore Mercurij</note>. For these three are the beginning in all things, and the <term>First Matter</term> <note>original: "Prima Materia"</note> of all things. Stones take their hardness and <term>Coagulation</term> <note>the process of turning liquid to solid</note> from the Liquor of Salt, their body from Sulphur, and their weight—and in some parts their body—from Mercury. And the difference between them and the other three First Principles is that these are not metallic, nor water, nor <term>Cluten</term> <note>likely referring to "Gluten" or a sticky, intermediate substance</note>, but entirely stony, having been brought into that effect. In this Ares, initially, the purification of the minerals occurred; after that, the fruit of the stones; and finally, the gems were <term>procreated</term> <note>born or brought forth</note>.

In this, it should be known that some generations happened and will never happen again: that is, whatever gave up its purification in the first Ares—such as rocks and sand—nothing more of that grows. For initially, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the "internal alchemist" or formative spirit of nature</note> lay powerfully in the purification of the three First Principles, and <term>depurated</term> <note>cleansed</note> and purified them in their place; therefore, no further purification occurs. Thus, no more rock grows, nor any sand. But other stones and gems are born daily in addition to those that were
<margin>B</margin> previously born. But now there are some stones that do not come from the three First Principles, but are born <term>Impressionistically</term> <note>formed by the influence or "impression" of the heavens/elements</note> from the element of Fire. These same stones, such as crystals, beryls, citrines, etc., are accounted for by the element of Fire, and not here in this treatise.

### CAP. II.
### On Rocks.

Initially in the Ares, when it purged itself of its stony, superfluous matter, the body of the rocks came from it. For every rock is solely a Sulphur body, coagulated with Salt, and <term>tinged</term> <note>colored or imbued</note> and dyed with Mercury, in this way: When the three First Principles were cast out of the Ares, they <term>ebullated</term> <note>original: "ebulliert," boiled up</note> and seethed in the <term>Globule</term> <note>the earthly sphere</note>, and forced the earth apart from one another with power, making a path for themselves in the <term>Yliadum</term> <note>the primeval chaos or matter of the world</note> according to the <term>Triual Lingen</term> <note>technical term for the channels or veins through which matter flows</note>. For the Salt and the Sulphur that stood there could not reconcile themselves in the Globule with the earth, but were brought into conflict through the earth, coming into a rage and swelling up like the foam or yeast from a piece of meat or wine. For every rock is nothing other than a yeast of the three First Principles in stony matter, which has forced its way through with power, through the Triual Lingen into the light at the end of the Yliadum. And as soon as it came to the Yliadum through the upper two elements, it settled down and became <term>indurated</term> <note>original: "Induriert," hardened</note>, and thus remained standing as it stood in its yeast-form, and from this a rock was made in the ends and places where they are. Therefore, many rocks lie right upon the earth, and under the earth there is no rock: the reason being that all the yeast
<margin>C</margin> went up onto the Globule; some remained in the Triual Lingen and, being overtaken, hardened too quickly through the upper elements, coagulating while still lying in the earth. And they have their form, points, and corners, crags and peaks, from the yeast; as it blew itself up, it remained in that form. That they are not in all lands of the Globule is caused by this: a crack and a ridge were made, and as it first split, it went out accordingly, as it happened by chance, forming the valleys and Alps together. Therefore, in the valleys, the earth remained upon them: the reason being that in the foaming up, the earth remained upon the foam, and the Alps and valleys thus became fertile and were so made. Because of the earth that remained upon the foam, fertile valleys and Alps were made. But where the earth fell from the foam, there are dry and bare rocks.

### CAP. III.
### On Sand.

Sand comes from the body of the three First Principles that is too coarse for stones and does not accept the procreation of stones. Its body is Salt, its composition is Sulphur, its <term>compaction</term> <note>solidification</note> is Mercury: and it is that which is of no use for any stones, and is also not foam. Therefore, it follows after the foam, which is the yeast of the stony three First Principles: then the Archeus separates out whatever does not have a stony nature in it, or cannot be formed into stones. Such is the sand, which goes out immediately after the first separation, and goes into the Triual Lingen into the Yliadum along with the water, and coagulates outside the Ares into little grains, by the nature of the Salt; for it takes its form from the Salt, which coagulates in this way, and is driven into the Yliadum, mostly with the water-flows, onto the flat plains of the Globule. But what became of it in the first Ares immediately after the yeast, that same thing has [fallen] upon the earth

# PHILOSOPHY, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...laid down in the same manner as the rocks were driven out. For this reason, certain lands are found full of sand, because the Spirit of the Rocks has pushed the sand away from itself and separated it, so that it fell upon the plains: sometimes mixed with earth, sometimes beneath the earth, because the sand lifted the earth up with it and did not entirely pass over it through the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal "chemist" or vital force that directs nature</note> during the Operation. Within such sand lies the entire sea. This is because, initially, as it is written regarding the Element of Earth, the globe was first formed from the Element of Earth; and from the generations of the Element of Water, first came the purification of the fruits of the Element of Water, then the water itself. The water—and other "fruits" of water—was pushed through the sand and hollowed it out, settling within it. Thus the seas arose and were carved out, and they are maintained solely through the power of the Center, and not by any solid dam, but only by what the Center does. # CHAPTER IV.
## On Pebbles and Flint.

The birth of stones proceeds from the three First Principles of stones, following the separation mentioned before. Thus, the coarse <term>Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury</term> <note>the three "Primes" or fundamental building blocks of all matter in Paracelsian thought</note> resolve themselves into a clay and run according to the <term>Trialingen</term> <note>the threefold division or three Primes</note> into the <term>Yliadum</term> <note>the primordial state of matter or the "chaos" before taking form</note>—some through the water channels, some by themselves into the globe. Whatever forces its way out on its own, as soon as it leaves the Archeus, it hardens and creates 
<margin>B</margin> 
stone heaps of its own accord, which is how various kinds of stone quarries are formed, depending on how much Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury are held in the composition. Similarly, they take their colors from these components.

However, those that enter the water in the form of clay run out with the water into the Yliadum; these coagulate along the way in the water, attaching themselves through the power of the <term>Salt-spirit</term> <note>original: "Saltzgeists"</note> and becoming small grains. More and more slime clings to them over time, and they grow larger. Therefore, the further one is from the source of the water, the fewer stones are found, for in those places where the material of the stones flows out into the water, it coagulates immediately as it encounters the Yliadum and remains lying in that spot. In this way, all stones are born, and thus "tuff" stones <note>porous limestone</note> also take their beginning in the globe, being composed solely of a white sulfur that is fixed in both fire and water.

# CHAPTER V.
## On the Distinction of Stones.

Marble takes its colors from sulfur, for sulfur is the "body" of all stones, just as Mercury is the "body" of metals. This sulfur is red, from which all marble and other red stones are made. It takes its hardness from Salt and its weight from Mercury. The <term>Liquor of Mercury</term> <note>the fluid essence of Mercury</note> transforms itself <note>original: "musiert sich"</note> out of the blooming power that is within it and thus remains in the growth. However, marble that is a mixture of white and red has come together through two bodies—white sulfur and red—which ran together as liquids and were thus coagulated by their mixing in the Yliadum. And just as they come together unevenly into one color, they are found to be uneven and "flowered" <note>marbled or variegated</note>. Thus, white marble also comes from white 
<margin>C</margin> 
sulfur; it is the coarsest genus among all stones and is also the first work in the Archeus that occurs within the globe.

# CHAPTER VI.
## Chalcedony.

The lineage of Chalcedony is the hardest and coarsest kind among the stony <term>First Matter</term> <note>original: "Primâ materiâ"</note>, even beyond marble. This is because there is a more subtle Salt in it than in marble, yet it is better purified than marble; for marble has drawn the coarsest substance to itself, while the next coarsest is found in Chalcedony. Its types are many: some are clear, which mostly happens because of the fixed Salt and very well-purified Sulphur and Mercury. Some are thick, coming from thick Sulphur. It takes its colors—brown, white, blue, and the like—from the Salt-spirit. Whatever is red or its related shades comes from the Sulfur-spirit, and similarly from Mercury. It forms its colors in many ways: in dark varieties, it has two kinds of bodies, like marble. But in the clear varieties, the spirits of the three First Principles are present, and they * mix <note>original: "musiern," with a marginal note suggesting "miscieren" or mixing</note> together by the power of the 
<margin>* alternatively: Mix</margin> 
<term>Ares</term> <note>the "womb" of nature that gives form to things</note> as its "bloom." For there is no stone that does not have "bloom" within it with its colors and floral patterns; therefore, the nature of the Archeus gives it its "flowers" and its form.

# CHAPTER VII.
## Alabaster.

Alabaster and other soft stones—including some in the form of brittle amethyst—are created from the "brittleness" of the three First Principles in stones. Thus, all their frailty, which is not suitable for hard stones, is cast out by the Archeus from the Ares. From this, Alabaster is made; in it, there is no Salt-spirit, but only a brittle substance of Salt and white Sulphur, compacted with Mercury.

### CHAPTER VIII.
->Tuff.<-
<note>Dufftstein: Tuff or Tufa, a porous rock formed from volcanic ash or precipitated lime</note>

Tuff stones are those which are harmed by neither water nor fire. They are composed of a fixed <note>stable or non-volatile</note> Sulphur that does not burn in any fire, and a fixed Salt that does not resolve in any water, compacted together by the "liquor of Mercury." This is the coarsest substance, which cannot be polished nor does it take on a shine. For these are only born after the "shine" of chalcedony, marble, pebbles, and the like has been drawn out into their own beings. What remains is a coarse <term>arche</term> <note>the raw, primordial matter of a specific element</note>, which—like a coarse mold or as hollow as a sponge—coagulates into a stone in which there is no refinement at all.

### CHAPTER IX.
->Schist.<-
<note>Schifferstein: Schist, slate, or any stone that splits into layers</note>

<margin>B</margin>Schist and flagstones are formed from the body of Sulphur which contains the "salt-spirit" within it and has been separated from all other stones. Because of this, wherever this salt-sulphur lies, it allows no stone to remain whole, but splits it; therefore, it is drawn out separately. There are many types and varieties of it in the form of schist, and also in many colors. This all comes from the salt-spirit, according to how it is placed with the colors: the thinner and more subtle the color, the thinner the stone; the thicker the color, the coarser the stone.

### CHAPTER X.
->On Gemstones.<-

Gemstones take their origin in their <term>Ares</term> <note>the Paracelsian term for the source or "dispenser" of natural growth</note> in this way: Once all types of coarse stones have been drawn out from the *Ares*, and no more coarseness remains within it, there remains a pure subtlety of a diaphanous <note>transparent or translucent</note> nature, surpassing all other stones. From this, the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal "chemist" or vital force of nature</note> subsequently procreates and brings forth the noble gemstones. They are formed such that the greatest hardness and the most diaphanous nature are prepared first. Then, once the preparation has occurred so that the matter is sufficient and proper for gems, the gemstones are separated and prepared from it, each gemstone into its own form and being. This birth of gemstones is the greatest subtlety of Nature and the highest art.

### CHAPTER XI.
->Carbuncle. Color of light.<-
<note>original: "Carbuncul. Color lucis." A carbuncle is a deep-red gemstone, usually a garnet or ruby.</note>

First among all gemstones, the carbuncle is drawn out. This is the clearest nature that lies within all three Primes <note>Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury</note>, being the most diaphanous and the most brilliant. Its "body" is a Mercury, its color is a Sulphur, and it contains a little salt-spirit for the sake of coagulation. Within it is all light. This is because Sulphur has a radiant light within it, as Art <note>Alchemistry</note> proves through its transmutation: when all coarseness is removed from it, only the most subtle part of the entire Sulphur is brought into a gemstone. This happens through an excellent regeneration of "clarifying" by the *Archeus*, so that it rises like a subtle spirit through the "trivial passages" <note>small pathways or channels within the earth</note> into the pores of the globe, and immediately hardens in the <term>Yliadus</term> <note>the primordial matter or the chaotic "spirit" of the element</note>.

<margin>C</margin>There are many of its kind, such as hyacinths <note>zircon or orange-red garnet</note> and the like; whatever stones are shining and glowing belong to the lineage of the carbuncle. For every degree of light is separated specifically and made into a stone. This lineage is the rarest, for although all stones and gems come from this material, this is the most subtle among them all, and the most noble.

### CHAPTER XII.
->Emerald.<-

The emerald takes its origin from those same three Primes, and it is the "Greenness" that lies among the three Primes. Its body is a "stony Mercury," and its color comes from itself, coagulated with the salt-spirit. It rises through the trivial passages into the *Yliadus* drop by drop, which is why it is found in the form of <note>original: "Guttæ"</note> drops. For it distills from the center of the *Ares* upward, and only as it sinks back down does it first coagulate itself. During the ascent, it is not sufficient for coagulation, but only during the descent. Wherever it thus drips through the pores—be they stones or earth—it coagulates there according to the size of the drop. Sometimes there is a rapid operation where many drops come together into one mass, and thus large emeralds and other stones are found, according to how the spirit of the *Ares* goes out and spreads itself. In some places, many are found because, in the first operation, they fell more upon one place than another, and were thus drawn through the trivial passages toward certain lands located along these paths in the *Yliadus*.

### CHAPTER XIII.
## Ruby.

The Ruby, and all its colors among gems that are red, consist of the Redness of Sulphur and the "Body" of petrified Mercury. For Mercury is the "Body" of all gems; therefore, they must be heavy and cold in every respect, and translucent—this is what it means to be petrified. Thus, the *Archeus* draws out the Redness, and from it, he creates many lineages of red gems, according to the "degree" contained within, which determines whether a Ruby is formed.

Garnets are of the same kind, except they contain more Salt than Rubies, which is why they are four-cornered <note>referring to their crystal habits</note>. Thus also other categories are formed from the Redness of Sulphur within the Body of Mercury, in many forms and degrees, according to the nature of the Sulphur, the Salt, and the purity of the Mercurial Body.

### CHAPTER XIV.
## Diamond.
<note>original: "Adamas"</note>

<margin>B</margin>
The origin of the Diamond is the greatest hardness of all stones. It is drawn out from all of them and grows solely from hardness. Its Body is Mercury, its coagulation is solely the Spirit of Salt, and its color is its Sulphur. It is <term>diaphanous</term> <note>transparent or translucent</note> and pure, for they are all petrified and well-purified. This generation of Diamond takes the hardness of other gems that would otherwise be even harder; it is the hardness that is mostly absent from Alabaster and the brittle Amethysts, brought and set into a distinct being by the *Archeus*. This should be understood to apply to other gems as well.

### CHAPTER XV.
## Sapphire, and other Gems in general.

The blue <term>diaphanous</term> gems, such as the Sapphire, are formed from Mercury in both body and color. It is composed of white Sulphur and white Salt, but from a pale Mercury that has been petrified. For this reason, a white Sapphire is often found, because the Mercury runs white with it. Yellow is also found, because yellow colors also lie within the Mercury.

From this it follows that all gems that take their color from Mercury are the noblest and heaviest, and are called Mercurial gems.

Thus, in their form and whiteness, all gems are born from the three primes that are predestined for the nature of stones and gems.

<margin>☉</margin>
From this it also follows that some stones grow colored, divided, or speckled in so many various ways. This all takes its origin from the fact that sometimes two or three materials from two or three different gems come together, yet they do not mix into a single color, but remain in their own colors. Therefore, many colors are often found in a single gem. It also frequently happens that pure Mercury is colored by Salt with two, three, or more colors; then all those colors come solely from the Spirit of Salt—such as brown, blue, white, green, and the like, all grey. Sometimes it depends on the Sulphur; when it enters a pure Mercurial body and pure Salt (which are colorless), it creates red and many speckled colors. Also, if Mercury remains without color from Salt and Sulphur and emerges with its own color, it produces green, blue, white, yellow, and black. Or sometimes all three set colors speckled through one another and remain mixed; just as oil and water do not mix, so these three "liquors" <note>fluid essences</note> with their colors also harden and thus remain in their coagulation and are discovered, of which there are many without number.

# FIFTH TREATISE.
<note>original: "TRACTATVS QVINTVS"</note>
## Concerning the Glue of the Element of WATER,
<note>original: "De Glutine Elementi AQVÆ"</note>
### CHAPTER ONE.
#### Preamble.

Just as the First Matter is specifically ordered for each individual thing, so it should be understood regarding "Glue" <note>refers to *gluten*, or resinous, sticky, and organic-like minerals</note> that all such substances come from one Matter. These are: Sulphur, Corals, Amber <note>original: "Carabe"</note>, and *Entali* <note>fossilized dentalium or tubular shells used in alchemy</note>, all of which come from a specific First Matter, namely from the "liquor" of Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury. It has the property of a tough resin or glue, which remains as it is, just as it is found in itself. This first...

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of gemstones (emeralds, rubies, garnets) within the Element of Water. It transitions into the specific chemical and alchemical nature of "Resins"—a broad category of sticky, combustible, or oily mineral substances—and how they are refined by nature into substances like saltpeter, arsenic, and antimony.</meta>

# ON THE ELEMENT OF WATER
<note>original: "DE ELEMENTO AQUÆ"</note>

<margin>A</margin> This matter is a form and liquid of a **Resin** <note>In this context, "Resin" refers not just to tree sap, but to a category of oily, combustible mineral substances like bitumen, amber, or sulfurous compounds</note> which possesses something of a "star-like" nature within it. From this, something uniform is created, similar to gems and other stones, yet it is not of their same material. It is united from three materials: one part from the stony nature; the second part from the metals during their "resolution" <note>the process of breaking down or melting</note>; and truly, from the "salty" nature because of its transparent quality and its *gest* <note>the vital spirit or "yeast-like" essence</note>, which is somewhat like salt. Above all else, it is a Resin: a sticky substance with a burning power. Depending on what each specific type is, it is neither "fixed" <note>stable under heat</note> nor entirely departed from its source material like metals are; instead, these substances remain as the material from which metals might be made and into which they can be transmuted.

## CHAPTER II.
### Concerning Saltpeter, Plumofum, and Ochre.

<margin>B</margin> **I**nitially, within this matter, the *Archeus* <note>the internal "chemist" or formative power of nature</note> separates out everything that is not of the nature of Resins. He purifies it so that a pure Resin remains, which is ready to flow and "coagulate" <note>harden into a solid</note>. At the start of this separation, the impurity of the Salt—which exists within these "Three Primes" <note>Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury</note>—is cast out through the **three-fold separations** <note>original: "Triual lingen," referring to the alchemical process where the three prime substances are separated</note> into the *Yliadum* <note>the primordial, chaotic matter</note>, where it hardens. Sometimes, **Saltpeter** <note>niter</note> is formed from this, which is essentially the "foam" of the salt of the Resins. It shows itself most often on rocks because, in the earth, it is dissolved again and vanishes; but on the rock, it hardens and shoots out like icicles. Such is the *Archeus* of Salt. Following this separation, the Mercury purifies itself of its coarseness, and its *gest* <note>spirit</note> passes through the three-fold separations into the *Yliadum*. There it hardens and grows according to its nature, becoming **Plumofum** <note>also called "feather-white," likely referring to asbestos or feather alum</note>. This is merely the foam of Mercury, which in this state is not resin-like, but "fixed" <note>stable</note>, for within these Three Primes, nothing else remains fixed. Afterward, the waste is separated from the Sulphur, from which **Ochre** <note>original: "Oger," an earthy mineral pigment</note> is made, which resembles earth or stone, though it is neither. These three spirits take on many forms and shapes, all derived from the material of the Resins, yet they are entirely contrary to the resins in their actual essence. Therefore, wherever Ochre, Plumofum, or Saltpeter are found in a land, pure Resins of a particular type or shape will also be found there, many of which lie in the *Ares* <note>the natural dispenser of forms</note>, brought forth by the *Archeus*.

## CHAPTER III.
### Concerning Arsenic.

**N**ow that the three materials have been purified, the first separation of its true essence occurs, which is **Arsenic**, both White and Yellow. It takes a form that has something metallic about it, which is why it attaches itself to metals and commonly joins with ore, hardening alongside it. Through this separation, the "fruit of the metals" and the "fruit of the resins" come apart from one another. It also often happens that Arsenic rises alone during the three-fold separation into the *Yliadum*. This Arsenic creates its own special ore, for it is the coarsest substance residing within the Resin. In the workshop, it looks like a metal, but not in its actual form. All the "poisonousness" of the Resins is gathered together within it into one body. Among all the fruits of the Element of Water, there is no greater poison than that found in the matter of the Resins; therefore, a special growth emerges here from the "body" of the Salt.

## CHAPTER IV.
### Orpiment.

<margin>C</margin> **T**hus, after Arsenic, **Orpiment** <note>original: "Auripigment," a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note> emerges. It takes its body from Sulphur, its hardening from Salt, and its shine from Mercury. It is of a stony and metallic nature, yet it is neither; rather, it is the "subsequent poison" that follows after Arsenic. It passes from the Three Primes into the three-fold separations and settles into the *Yliadum*, where it generates in layers and plates. Much of its nature depends on the *Cachimiën* <note>a Paracelsian term for mineral-like substances or "half-metals"</note> in its form, and in its appearance, it mimics metals—namely gold. For it is a yellow Sulphur that has been beautifully prepared in a metallic fashion.

## CHAPTER V.
### ANTIMONY.

**F**ollowing these comes **Antimony** <note>original: "Spießglas"</note>. It takes its body from Mercury and is the coarsest type of Mercury after it has been purified. It retains all the power and virtue of Mercury. Therefore, among all the fruits emerging from the Three Primes, there is no fruit that retains the essence of Mercury more clearly than Antimony. It is nothing other than Mercury "coagulated" by the spirit of salt and sulphur; however, it is a coarse and brittle Mercury because it does not come from the pure nature of Mercury, but is ordered this way within this material. It rises into the *Yliadum* as an ore-like substance, for its body contains much of the nature of ore, even though it is not actually ore.

<summary>This page describes the alchemical formation of various mineral substances—Saltpeter, Ochre, Arsenic, Orpiment, and Antimony—from a "Resinous" base material through the actions of the Archeus and the Three Primes (Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury).</summary>
