<margin>A</margin>
What the eyes actually see is not the fruit; rather, the spirit alone is the fruit. However, there is a distinction between the natural spirit and the unnatural: the natural spirit is corporeal and material, embodied within a specific body <note>original: "Corpus"</note>. The unnatural spirit is entirely without a body. For although the redness of coral is the coral itself—and the physical mass is not—nonetheless, that redness is a body, but it is a body consisting so purely of the spirit that nothing foul or coarse remains. And because the spirit of fruits is neither tangible nor visible, nature has given it a special body to reside in, and that body is given another body from its own element. When people say that coral is good for something, they mean its redness is good for it; for the redness is a pure body in which all power lies. Understand the same regarding the **Heaven** <note>original: "Cœlum"</note>. The thunder that strikes—that is, the lightning bolt—is an essence drawn out and separated from all bodies, existing alone in its own narrow body. And because the **Heaven** is the most subtle element, and the only one that is purest and most refined, its **spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus"</note> is more vehement than any other. I show you all of this so that the **science of meteors** <term>Meteorica; the study of all celestial and atmospheric phenomena</term> may be fundamentally understood through the examples of the other elements. In this way, the element of **Heaven** <term>Cœlum</term> may be more easily understood. Without a fundamental grasp of the other elements, the understanding of meteors cannot be truly perceived; instead, one wanders in error, following the mistakes of others, which leads to a false understanding and interpretation of this knowledge.

<margin>* or, in its place.
B</margin>
Furthermore, know concerning the **Heaven** that God gave the Heaven the name **Firmament** <term>Firmamentum; from the Latin 'firmare', meaning to make firm or strengthen</term>, for the **Firmament** is the Heaven and all its being. Just as when one says "the Earth," one means everything that belongs to the Earth. Now, the Heaven is called the **Firmament**, and **Firmament** is the element's first name; **Heaven** is its second name. And God named it thus so that it should stand fast—that is, remain firm in its * nature for which it was created. Therefore, know now that it was necessary for God to give it this name. For wherever God gives a name, He also gives to that name its proper attributes. As He called **Peter** a **Rock** <note>original: "Petrum ein Felß... Petra"; a reference to Matthew 16:18, "You are Peter (Petros), and on this rock (petra) I will build my church."</note>: since the name was given to him by God and not by men, he remains a Peter, and is an invincible Rock. Likewise, know concerning the **Firmament** that God commanded it: "Stand fast." The name and the power that the name carries are great. For the other three elements are enclosed within the **Firmament** like an egg in a shell. Thus are the Earth, the Water, and the Air enclosed in this element, just as the yolk, the white, and the membrane are in an egg—that is, within the shell. By the word that God spoke—"Stand fast," which is the name **Firmament**—the three elements are prevented from shifting or falling out. For just as the shell holds an egg so that everything remains together, each in its place where it should be (the yolk in its place, the white in its place), if the shell were to break, they would separate from one another and would no longer be contained. Thus God proves through His own naming that He gave the **Firmament** the power to be a shell in which all creatures of nature are enclosed, and that the shell stands firm. This is because it is a great weight to carry the other elements, namely Earth and Water. Therefore, the word "stand fast" was necessary. By that word, every element remains in its essence and its nature; the Heaven brings this about. It is a wondrously made thing: that in such a **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note> which is **transparent** <term>Diaphanum; allowing light to pass through</term> and intangible, something solid and tangible should be carried, and that the light should carry the heavy. It is just like water carrying a ship full of stones, not letting it fall to the bottom.

<margin>C</margin>
But to speak of the Heaven and its substance and corporality, understand how it carries these things. You see the white in an egg; it is clear, pure, and thin, yet it has a property that allows it to carry the yolk so that it cannot sink, but must remain in the middle. If the white were mere water, the yolk would fall through the water onto the shell. But there is a difference between the white and water, in that the white has such a **chaotic** <note>original: "Chaostische"; referring to the 'Chaos' or primal gas/medium in Paracelsian thought</note> nature that nothing can fall through it. The **Firmament** is similarly disposed in its body, keeping what lies within it in the middle so that it must remain unmoved. And however the egg lies, whether up or down, it is always the same for the yolk, regardless of which part is at the bottom or the top. It is the same in the **Firmament**: wherever we are, we are both at the bottom and the top, whether we call it above us or below us. For a circle has no upper or lower part; everything is both bottom and top, one just like the other. I have seen fit to set down this Chapter with its six paragraphs solely as an introduction to **Meteors**, so that the elements from which they are made may be understood. And know that there are three species of **First Matter** <term>prima Materia</term>, and that the number three was present at the beginning of creation, and all things were created in three. These three species can be found through the Art: **Sulfur**, **Mercury**, and **Salt**. Why this is so has been sufficiently reported. What the **functions** <note>original: "Officia"</note> of these three are will be sufficiently explained and presented in its proper Philosophy. Following this, the chapter on the Stars will come hereafter: how those bodies arose within the three, how they are the fruits of the Heaven, and how they are the **Firmament**, so that in the following chapter it may be understood what their effect is upon the other elements and mankind, according to the meteorological way and explanation.

## CHAPTER III.
### ON THE FIRST MATTER and Essences of the Stars.
<note>original: "DE STELLARUM PRIMA Materia & Essentijs"</note>

<margin>B</margin>

Now, as you have heard regarding the **First Matter** <note>original: "Prima Materia"; the primordial substance from which all things are created</note> of the stars and the heavens, that there are three **Types** <note>original: "Species"</note> in one **Body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note>, under a single name: so now learn further of the heavens and how they are in their physicality <note>original: "Corporalitet"</note>. First, observe this example. The Earth is black, coarse, clumsy, bony, clayey, muddy, filthy, loamy, and so forth; it is so coarse that nothing is coarser. Now, the element of water is more subtle; it is clear, bright, pure, and so on, so that one can see through it several feet to the bottom. Thus is water clarified above the Earth. After that is the Air, which is entirely transparent, intangible, and so purely purged that one sees nothing in it at all. Now judge how unequal these **Bodies** <note>original: "Corpora"</note> are to one another—the Earth compared to the water, and the water compared to the Air—what a wide distinction exists. Now, look at the Heaven, which is above the Air: how far apart are the Heaven and the Earth from each other in their physicality? As coarse as the Earth is, so subtle is the Heaven; as dark as the Earth is, so bright is the Heaven. It is the clearest element, and yet it is a **Body**, for its fruits are **Bodies**, such as **RAIN**, snow, hail <note>original: "Schawer"</note>, lightning <note>original: "Strahl"</note>, and so forth. Where there is no **Body**, nothing is born; but where a body exists, something is born. Now one sees the **Body** of the lightning bolt, that it is a **Body** just as much as wood is from the Earth: but they are as far apart from each other as the elements themselves are. Just as you see how wood compares to a lightning bolt or to snow, or stone to dew, etc. And as much as the Heaven is more subtle than the Earth, so much more are its fruits above the fruits of other elements in their subtlety and **Operation** <note>their active power or effect</note>. For they are recognized by their fruits—from whom they come and what that thing is from which they have emerged. For every tree makes itself known through its fruits. And with the fruits **Philosophy** <note>here meaning natural science</note> begins; not with the mother, but with the child. The master is recognized through his work, and the work not from the master, but the master through his work.

<margin>C</margin>

Now further, since enough has been said of the Heaven, it is most necessary from here on to know of the stars and their origin: and namely in this way. You see that the Earth has nothing in itself; rather, whatever it has, it drives forth onto the Earth and keeps nothing within itself, giving everything out. Thus all trees and herbs are from the Earth and out of the Earth, and in the Earth there is nothing. So also know that out of the Heaven all the stars have grown and been taken from it: and that the stars do not stand before the Heaven otherwise than the trees upon the Earth. And just as trees are upon the Earth and have their feet in the Earth, so, by contrast, the stars have no feet in their element. For the reason is this: trees must stand **fixed** <note>original: "fix"</note> and not move from their place, but remain in the spot where they are set, sown, and planted. The stars, however, must not stand still, but must proceed along their circles. Therefore they are spheres that roll and revolve further and further, as if they were thrown by the hand of God: and thus they are distinct from the Heaven, and yet within the Heaven. Just as the tree is embodied in the Earth and cannot exist without the Earth, but must be in it and possess it, so the stars do not leave the Heaven, for they have their nourishment from the Heaven. And where they have their **Mansions** <note>original: "Mansiones"; their fixed positions or astrological houses</note>, there they are, and from those they do not depart, any more than a tree leaves its garden. Thus understand now regarding the stars, how they stand in their element, and how they are embodied with their element, and how they are fruits like the trees upon Earth. And it should also be noted that there are as many kinds and communities of stars as there are kinds of growths on the Earth. For every specific kind of tree, there is a specific kind of star: and not only of trees, but also of herbs and all earthly growths. For this is proven by the fact that there are as many **Influences** <note>original: "Influents"; the celestial forces acting upon the world</note> as there are kinds of stars and kinds of such growths on Earth. And every kind goes into its own like, and unlikes do not come together: as is sufficiently found and proven in **Philosophy** and **Astronomy**. For every Firmament is uniform to the other and equal in number.

Now you should further know, as you see that fruits come from the trees, and that nature in that place is a property and an essence—that is, a created gift—so that one tree bears pears, another apples, another nuts, etc. In such a property also stand the stars, so that to one star is given the rain, to another the snow, to another the hail, etc. And thus everything that comes from Heaven is born in such a manner: as will be shown in its chapters and **Paragraphs** <note>original: "Paragraphis"</note>. Now look at the Sun, what is in it: namely the heat that shines upon us, which is innate to it, and it is its property that it should be hot. Just as we see with the **Etnean** fires <note>original: "Ethnischen Fewr"; referring to the volcanic fires of Mount Etna</note> and the hot springs: so in those stars there is such a nature as well, and so much greater and stronger as the element is above the Earth and that which is earthly. Conversely, you see the coldness of stones, crystals, etc. So also are there stars that are endowed with such coldness and have it embodied within them. As you see that the **Magnet** attracts: so there are also attracting stars in the Firmament. Just as on Earth some things are of a dry nature, some of a moist: so also in the Hea—

through the entire firmament. Therefore, the **operations of the stars** <note>original: "Operationes Stellarum"</note> should be understood in such a way that they proceed from their own unique properties, which have been given to them for that purpose. And such <margin>A</margin> **operations** <note>original: "Operationes"</note> reside in the first three [elements]; they come from them, as will be recounted hereafter. Therefore, that **meteorology** <note>original: "Meteorica"; the traditional study of weather and celestial phenomena</note> is false which speaks of the heat of the sun, of its motion, or of other **formations** <note>original: "generationibus"</note>—how they arise by pulling [vapors] up from the earth, and so forth. For it is not as those people say; rather, it is a **nature suited and endowed** <note>original: "natura appropriata, dotata"</note> for its purpose, just as all other creatures on Earth are understood to have their own roles. There is no star that pulls rain to itself and then gives it back again, or any such thing; rather, it is its own nature, just as a pear tree’s nature is to produce pears. What the sun dries up is consumed in the air, just as all things are consumed in the earth. And just as the death of those things that come from the earth is in the earth—so that all things come to nothing and are entirely consumed—so too is there such a "burial" and consumption of all wet things in the air.

Now, know also regarding summer and winter: these also come from the stars. For in summer there are summer-stars that grant the summer, and there are other stars that grant the winter. The sun is the first and highest summer-star, and it has many other stars with it that provide heat. These begin at the start of summer and increase in their heat. Just as a dry tree has nothing in the winter, but towards summer it now has buds, then leaves, then blossoms, then its fruit, and so on; so there are stars of a kind that stand like dry trees in the winter. But when the time comes for the stars to rise, they take their power from the sun and ascend ever more firmly into the heat; and when they have reached the highest point, they thereafter decrease again in their heat. At that point, the winter-stars begin, just like the summer-stars, and "green" in their own nature, while towards summer they wither away. If such stars <margin>B</margin> are powerful, they produce a colder winter; if the summer-stars are powerful, they produce a hot summer. For just as one year is good, and another even better, while another is worse or not good at all, so too are those stars unequal in their rising and falling. Among the winter-stars, the Moon is the highest, and it has many others in its nature and company. Therefore, know that if the summer-stars were not there, there would be no summer; for the sun remains at the same heat, whether it be high or low. And if there were no summer-stars, it would be winter forever and ever, for the moon with its stars is cold forever and ever. Only this breaks the cycle: because both types of stars exist, they wither away—one part in winter, the other in summer. The height of the sun does not create summer, nor does its wide course; the summer-stars provide the summer, but they take their growth from the sun. The moon does not provide winter by itself alone; it provides a winter only with its stars, for it by itself is too weak—just as the sun is too weak without its helpers.

In the same way, know also of day and night: namely, that the day comes from the light of the sun, and the night from the light of the moon. This happens in such a way that God created a "day-brightness" <note>original: "Tagheitery"</note> in the sun, just as there is a brightness in fire, light, or the moon. And He made two kinds of light in the firmament—a day-light and a night-light—neither equal to the other; one is white, the other red. Now, when the day-light rises, the day begins and the night retreats; for the day-light has a brilliance that outshines all other lights. When the day-light then sets and has completed its path commanded by God, the night-light then begins—that is the moon and the darkness. Regarding the night, understand this: it is not the departure of the sun that makes the night simply because the sun has set. For its brilliance is so strong that even if the sun were directly beneath us at midnight, its reflection <margin>C</margin> would still be cast upon the earth, providing enough day-light that one could recognize the day and enjoy its light. But this is the night, and the "night-darkness" falls for this reason: there is a special kind of star that creates gloom and darkens everything to such an extent that, where the moon is not present, nothing can be seen at all. Just as a murky cloud in front of the sun also takes away the day-light, or when an eclipse comes which also takes the sunshine and makes a night. Thus there are specific **Shadows** <note>original: "Tenebræ"</note> in the heavens; as soon as the sun shines upwards and downwards, such **Shadows** <note>original: "Tenebræ"</note> fall upon them and bring such a completely dark night, in which darkness only the moon has its brilliance through the gloom. Yet it does no more than allow the darkness to provide and make a night until the sun overcomes this darkness again in its rising. Also, when the sun loses its brilliance through an **Eclipse** <note>original: "Ecliph i"; likely referring to an eclipse</note> and **Shadows** <note>original: "Tenebræ"</note> occur, it activates the night-stars so that it becomes entirely night, because the sun cannot shine through them.

Thus God has given the stars their course, so that they are cast by the hand of God into the circle of the whole firmament, each star into its own circle and path. The reason they must not rest is so that in the absence of one star, the others may also have their **operations** <note>original: "Operationes"</note>. Thus, in the absence of the sun, the night-stars may also be recognized. It is the same with all other stars: now high, then low. If one is high, the other is low; if one is in **Exaltation** <note>the point where a planet's influence is strongest</note>, the other is in **Declination** <note>the point where its influence fades or its position moves southward</note>. Thus, every star fulfills the work for which God created it, and it is ordered that each gives way to the other so that all things may be accomplished, as we see an example in the sun. For no star rests; no star stands still; they are all in daily exercise so that they may awaken nature and...

carry out a daily operation. And just as the stars are without any rest, so too are the things in Nature; that is, they work forever and ever. And although it is true that there is rest at night, such rest is given to the sensory creatures so that they may repose, for they cannot endure that which the stars and other non-sensory creatures do not feel. And although it is also true that winter is a rest for natural things, the reason for this is that they should rest after the yielding of their fruit. Yet, it is still no true rest; rather, they exert themselves forever and ever, preparing themselves again for summer toward a new birth and the offering of fruit. Thus, nothing in Nature idles; everything is in practice from hour to hour, from day to day, from night to night. Man alone idles at night and on the Sabbath <note>The day of rest</note> because of his commandment. The Spirit, however, shall be in work forever and ever, such that neither sleep nor the Sabbath makes it still or quiet. Thus are all the creatures; even though the **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note> rests, the Spirit does not rest—it is in daily, continuous operation.

<margin>B</margin>
Thus, regarding this, note that such **bodies** <note>original: "Corpora"</note> from which day and night come, from which summer and winter come, and all things (as has been said and will be said further) come from the Three Firsts <note>The Paracelsian "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>; these are the **bodies** <note>original: "Corpora"</note> of all those things. The Sun is **transparent and clear Salt** <note>original: "Sal perspicuum und diaphanum"</note>, clarified, extracted, and cleansed by the Three Firsts from all the gloom and **darkness** <note>original: "Tenebræ"</note> that were in that same mass. That same **darkness** <note>original: "Tenebræ"</note> was placed into a special kind, such that what is pure and clear is in one special mass, and what is dark is in another. It is just as when one mixes white and black together; it becomes neither black nor white, but a color that is in no way perfect: it becomes gray. But if they are separated from one another, it becomes again a good white and a good black. In a **pebble** <note>original: "Kißlingstein"</note> there is a light, in flint also, in marble also; but the darkness surrounds it so that it does not burn, and no light is seen at all. But if it is struck out, then the light is separate and gives its shine, and the stone remains dark. Thus, from the mass of the **First Matter of the Element of the Heavens** <note>original: "primæ Materiæ Elementi Cæli"</note>, the brilliance was taken, and the white brilliance was separated into the Sun, and the red brilliance into the moon and stars. And they are separated in such a way that the clarity and transparency of the white in the **Sulfur, Salt, and Liquor** <note>original: "Sulphure, Sale und Liquore"</note> was extracted like a spirit, and the Sun was created. Afterward, the brilliance of the red was placed into the **body of Sulfur** <note>original: "Corpus Sulphuris"</note>, and the red clarity and transparency were laid into the body of **red Sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphuris rubei"</note>. Thus, **Salt** <note>original: "Sal"</note> is a **body of the Sun** <note>original: "Corpus Solis"</note>, **Sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphur"</note> is a **body of the Moon** <note>original: "Corpus Lunæ"</note>, and the **Liquor** <note>original: "Liquor"</note> is a body of the darkness. In this way, we should also know that God created all things to exist in the first **First Matter** <note>original: "prima Materia"</note>; but He Himself separated them out again, each into that which it was meant to be. Therefore, God worked for six days until He had extracted, separated, and formed **Final Matters** <note>original: "vltimas Materias"</note> out of the **First Matter** <note>original: "prima Materia"</note>; that is, every creature that He commanded to remain until the dissolution of the world. Thus, God is the same one who first created and laid all things into one, and thereafter, in six days, drew out what was within the same.

Or as a carver has a piece of wood and may make out of it whatever he wants, provided only that he knows how to work and cut away from it what does not belong there. Therefore, He undertook to work for six days. And it is to be understood exactly as this example shows: The earth is black, brown, and foul, nothing beautiful or pretty; yet, within it is green, blue, white, red, etc.—all colors—there is nothing that does not come to be within it. When spring and summer come, all the colors come forth, which (if the earth did not prove it itself) would be impossible for anyone to believe were within it. Thus, just as from such black soil such noble, subtle colors go forth, so also have so many kinds of creatures gone forth from the first **First Matter** <note>original: "prima Materia"</note>, which in its mixture was also a foul thing. # The Book of METEOROLOGY

### CHAPTER IV.

## CONCERNING THE LIVING
## Species in the Stars.

<margin>A</margin>
As I have spoken until now concerning the unfeeling <note>non-sentient or inanimate</note> creations of the Meteorological region and its contents: So it is now further to be understood that there are also feeling—that is, living, moving, and rational—creatures in these same Meteorological regions.

For we should know this: that God has created living creatures in all the elements and has left nothing empty. He created not only the irrational, but also the rational. For instance, in the water you see the fish; in the earth, the mole <note>original: "Talpam"</note>. Just as you see them there, you should think no differently of the air and the heavens; there are similar animals <note>original: "Animalia"</note> that live there, such as the *Matene* <note>a Paracelsian term for atmospheric insects or flies</note> in the air, and the *Tortelleos* <note>creatures of the stars or firmament</note> in the heavens. Furthermore, there are living, sentient creatures in the manner of spirits: such as the Nymphs in the water, the Gnomes in the earth, the Lemures <note>spirits of the air</note> in the air, and the Pennates <note>celestial spirits or household gods of the heavens</note> in the sky. Whatever is shown to us by our coarse understanding in the lower sphere and globe serves as an example to us that in the upper spheres and the upper globe, there must also be a similar likeness. This is found to be true in the Work, in Nature, and in Art. Now, we shall not speak here of Nymphs, nor of Gnomes and Lemures, but rather philosophize on them in their own proper places. However, I say this so that we may know in Meteorology <note>original: "in der Meteorica"</note> that rational creatures with human reason and sensibility dwell and exist in such elements. For consider the many wonders that happen through the highest generations down into the earth, which could not happen without such reason. For <margin>B</margin> how could it be that a lightning bolt <note>original: "Strahl"</note> would strike so directly in one place and not another? From this, it is easy to gather and measure that such a thing happens through the intellect of those above—that is, the Higher Ones <note>original: "id est, Superorum"</note>. The Higher Ones are the Pennates. And I indicate this so that we may finally and thoroughly understand and know that such creatures are in the firmament, who carry such knowledge like a spirit. Whatever is in the world, knowledge of it also exists among them in the firmament. No one should wonder at this; it is as true as it is of Gnomes and Nymphs, and yet it is marvelous. Even if it has been beyond human understanding until now, it is nonetheless so, and the Work proves it.

<margin>* or: Joys.</margin>
Therefore, because this is so, and the works prove it: the Meteorologists <note>original: "Meteorici"</note> should know that the operation of the Higher Ones is at certain times guided and directed to this or that place—not just once, but many times, just like an archer shooting at a target. And although I do not describe their skill here, it will be shown in the specific Meteorological Chapters what power they have. Even more will be shown in Philosophy, from which the Meteorologist may take a very good report and sufficient understanding and wisdom. But so that I may be more easily understood in those same Meteorological Chapters regarding which Higher Ones <note>original: "Superis"</note> I speak: I indicate here that they are in the firmament and dwell in it with all wisdom, understanding, and arts, and similar operations beyond nature. They are in our globe just like the mountain-men <note>dwarfs or gnomes</note>, Lemures, etc. Thus we should know that we humans on earth do not possess such understanding alone, as if nothing else existed but man in his intellect. Rather, there are others in whom such understanding—and even greater understanding—exists than in man, in all that <margin>C</margin> concerns nature and natural understanding. For God is wonderful in His works and creations, He who is endlessly wonderful, and who commanded man himself—as the noblest of creatures—to philosophize and search into nature, so that he might bring forth the wonder-works of God. For what else do we have to do on earth but walk in Divine works and recognize them? We should not walk in things that are not God's work. For the works of God are divided into two ways: the works of Nature, which Philosophy encompasses; and the works of Christ, which Theology encompasses. In these we should spend the time we have to spend on earth, so that we may die in * peace.

However, you should also know that God created man and subjected all that He created to him. This is confirmed by the Psalmist, who says: *You have subjected all things to him,* etc. <note>Refers to Psalm 8:6</note>. But he does not mention in that same place what cattle, sheep, children, birds in the air, fish in the sea, etc. [are exempt], and of the four races of the elements <note>The elemental spirits: Nymphs, Gnomes, Lemures, and Vulcans/Pennates</note> that I presented in the previous paragraph, he mentions nothing at all. Therefore, they are not subjected to man in any way. Thus, those supposed artists are false who wish to force such *Saganas* <note>Paracelsus's term for elemental spirits</note> to their will—as do those who boast of the Black Arts and the like, claiming to have power over them. For once, man should know what God has not given him and what He has not thrown under his feet; he should not undertake anything concerning those things, for it cannot be—it is impossible for him. But whatever God has subjected to man, that is possible for him and turns out well for him. Now, as I have mentioned concerning the *Saganas* of the four elements: just as they dwell in them and not with us humans, so there is such a distinction between them and us: that we are humans created by God, inside and out, with a soul without death <note>an immortal soul</note>, which soul the others do not have. <summary>Paracelsus explains that the atmospheric and celestial regions are inhabited by rational, living beings like the Pennates and Lemures, who direct natural phenomena like lightning. He distinguishes these elemental spirits (Saganas) from humans, noting that while they possess great wisdom, they lack an immortal soul and are not subject to human command or magic.</summary>

# The Fourth Chapter.

<margin>A</margin> They possess reason and art, but they do not have a human soul; rather, they are "human-beasts" <note>original: "Menschviech"; beings that possess human-like intelligence but lack the eternal soul of mankind</note>. The Gnomes <term>Gnomi: elemental spirits of the earth</term> possess all the arts of men and demonstrate them, as do the Nymphs, and likewise the others: but there is no soul there for which Christ died. He died for man alone—for the man with whose blood and flesh He spoke. Although all of this is now more a matter of Philosophy than of Meteorology, it is nevertheless necessary to mention these philosophers <note>the elemental beings</note> here, so that in these paragraphs and chapters, their operations may be explained more thoroughly and without error. For much is attributed to Nature that does not actually come from Nature in that way, but happens through such *Saganis* <term>Saganis: a Paracelsian term for elemental spirits or beings</term>: as is openly demonstrated in mountains, valleys, the earth, in the water, and elsewhere. For God is truly wondrous.

And concerning Man, we should know that he is not of one single element, but is free, such that he does not belong to the earth, the water, the heavens, or the air alone. Instead, he lives out of them all and walks in them all; all things are created for his sake, and he is the one whom they must obey. But the Gnomes stay in the earth and can do nothing in the air, the firmament, or the water, much like a mole <note>original: "Schermauß"; literally a "shear-mouse" or mole</note>. The Nymphs stay in the water alone, like a herring. The Lemures <note>spirits of the air</note> are in the air, like a bird. Man, however, is not within the elements corporally <note>physically confined</note>, but is free upon the earth and not *in* the earth; upon the water and not *in* the water; under the heavens and not *in* the heavens; alongside the air and not *in* the air. And yet he is in all four as the Center, into whom all four operations deliver their reflux and all their rays within them. Thus, you may know the distinction between the understanding of Man and the *Saganis*—a distinction between their two types of wisdom, art, effect, and dwellings.

<margin>B</margin> But I mention all of this so that Man should not imagine that there is no "earth-man" other than himself, seeing as the Gnomes are even better at it and dwell right within the ore. Nor should he think that he alone knows what is in the water, since the Nymphs are actually inside the water and know much more. Likewise, he does not know more of what is in the air than the Lemures, nor is he the only philosopher of the air, for the Lemures know even more. So too do the "Superiors" <note>celestial beings</note> know more of the firmament than Man. Man only knows how to philosophize about what comes to him: such as what is upon the earth, like foliage and grass; what the minerals drive out of the water; and what the firmament and the air provide. That is where his philosophizing begins. But the *Saganæ* <note>elemental beings</note> know what is in the "First Matter" <term>Prima Materia: the raw, underlying essence of all things before they take physical form</term>, philosophizing and operating within it, which is more significant and to be more highly esteemed than the philosophers of the "Final Matter" <term>Ultima Materia: the finished, physical form of a substance</term>. Although Man also understands the First Matter, he is like one who watches a blacksmith at work from a distance; the one who is inside the forge is more certain than the one who stands outside it.

To further instruct you on what else is in the stars—that is, in the firmament—beyond what I have mentioned so far: observe that I present to you Vulcan <note>original: "Vulcanum"; the archetypal smith or "nature's craftsman"</note>, who is the fabricator and workman of all things. He is not only in the element of the heavens (the firmament), but is just as present in the other elements. Now I must first present this to you through an example. You see among us humans that we have nothing ready-made, but must first turn all things into a "Final Matter." For instance, if we want to have a house, we must arrange all the materials and build it ourselves. Thus, in all things, Man is burdened with labor, as the Prophet says: 
> You shall eat the labor of your hands, and in the sweat of your face shall you eat your bread, etc. <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 128:2 and Genesis 3:19</note>
This is now laid upon Man, and he does it. Furthermore, know that there is another who makes the things that Man later changes and uses. 

<margin>C</margin> There must be one who makes foliage and grass on God’s behalf. Just as a man must make a house for himself because God does not make it for him, so too is there someone in the earth who makes that which comes out of it. There is also such a one in the water who assembles such compounds. And likewise in the air, and in the firmament as well. For it is not enough for us to say, "God has ordained it so that it returns every year." It is true, but He has set someone over it to make, form, embody, and ordain it, and thereafter to let that work grow out through Nature. For just as God does not make a coat for a man, but has appointed the tailor for that task, so too will grass not grow or be brought into its form without a worker. The one who thus ordains things from the seed into their Final Matter is Vulcan. And though this is a "New Philosophy," it does not matter: for Aristotelian philosophy is heavily filled with lies and errors, and with many unmasterly, foolish fictions that can never be found in the Light of Nature. Therefore, one should not believe a man on his word alone, for the Spirit blows where it will—that is, not in one man only, but also in a second and a third, etc.

Know then of the Vulcan of the Firmament: he holds power within himself over the "Three Primes" <term>Tres Primas: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury; the three fundamental principles of Paracelsian alchemy</term> within the single First Matter. From these, he now makes everything in the firmament where he has his dwelling, just as God has commanded him to make. He composes, dispenses, and ordains the rain, the snow, the frost, the hail, the lightning-bolt, and all things that are heavenly operations. In these, he is the wood-carver, the smith, and the preparer. This Vulcan is not a spirit, nor is he a person (in this, he differs from the *Saganis*). Rather, he is a worker who does nothing more than...

# Of the Book of METEORS.

<margin>A</margin> ...to wait upon Nature and to bring out of her that which is within her, and what God has placed in her to be brought into the **Final Matter** <note>original: "Ultimam Materiam"; the completed or perfected state of a substance</note>. He is a craftsman just like fire; he works every thing that is placed within him. He melts the metals, he consumes wood into glass, he also prepares many things; and yet he is no spirit, no soul, no person. But he has within himself such a power to take hold, to intervene, and to prepare wondrous things: he is the **Vulcan** <note>In Paracelsian thought, Vulcan is the "inner alchemist" or force of transformation</note> who is subject to Man. For the Vulcan of the elements cannot be made to obey Man, but rather has his **Office** <note>original: "Officium"; duty or function</note> in Nature alone. However, because Man must finish his work entirely into the Final Matter—and the true Final Matter must come about through Man—the **Vulcan of the Elements** makes his Final Matter into nothing else than that which is **Intermediate Matter** <note>original: "Media materia"</note> for Man. And from this Intermediate Matter, Man makes the Final Matter; for this, he must have a Vulcan, which is the fire; this same fire represents Vulcan. He is the **Vulcan of Fire**, and is a servant of the natural arts which Man possesses; he thus stands in the place of the natural, elemental Vulcan. Therefore, as the example of the Vulcan of Fire demonstrates: so also is the **Elemented Vulcan** <note>original: "Vulcanus Elementatus"</note> understood, who completes all things without others. Just as fire melts the metal—Man cannot do it, the fire does it alone—and burns the wood—Man cannot burn it. Such an essence must be in Nature, which has a **Vulcan-like** property, otherwise nothing could come out of Nature, but everything would thus die away and not reach its end.

Now note further what else is in Nature. Although I have here taken only **Meteorology** <note>original: "Meteoricam"</note> before me, it is necessary to include other philosophy here for the sake of examples, and thus: There is yet another kind in the Firmament that shows itself in its **properties** <note>original: "proprietaribus"</note>, and works just like the Fiery Vulcan, namely this: You see that the rain from heaven makes the grass and foliage grow, without which rain such things could not be completed. Now, in this same <margin>B</margin> rain there is a power and a nature which immediately creates and drives things forward in the grass and everything that grows from the earth. Thus, what the **Vulcan of the Earth** forges has its prosperity through the rain, so that it proceeds and increases daily. Such an increasing, augmenting, and growing kind is another nature—not the Fiery Vulcan, but rather it is the **Iliaster** <term>Iliaster: the principle of life, growth, and the propulsion of matter toward its form</term>. And it is also not a created spirit, nor a person, <margin>Iliaster</margin> nor a soul, but a power—that is, a **Virtue** <note>original: "Virtus"</note>—that works in this way. 

So also, in turn, there is a kind in Nature that separates or extracts the flowers or herbs from other flowers, or the matter of iron from the matter of lead. Such a power is the **Archeus** <term>Archeus: the "inner master" or governing vital force that directs the development of an organism or substance</term>, who ordains all things into their essence, separates one from the other, and gives to every seed that which belongs to it: that is, he gives to the Vulcan of the earth his **instruments** and his gear for his necessity. Thus, know also that there is an Iliaster in the Firmament, and also an Archeus, together with the Firmamental Vulcan. So that the things which the heavens give birth to happen perfectly, the Vulcan is there, the Iliaster is there, and likewise the Archeus; they now complete the entire work until it reaches its place. In this way, the rain, snow, thunder, etc., are all forged. And when it is finished in its place, they send it down to us. For on our behalf, they are workers day and night, and care for us through the command of God. So that we might also be more provident in our Divine conduct and not be negligent, all these things come to us without our care, toil, or labor; and not a single flower would come to us if God did not give it, just like a sparrow <note>original: "Sperck"; likely referring to the biblical sparrow</note>, as **CHRIST** says in the **Gospel**.

And in addition to all this, after all things are made and delivered into the hand of Man, there is yet a following power that remains in the thing itself after Archeus, Iliaster, and Vulcan withdraw and give it over: That is the **Essence** <note>original: "Essentia"</note>. These are the miracle-works that lie hidden in Nature, which are of many kinds; yet "Essence" is its name, and it is also in the highest fruits in the Final Matters. But now, it is no less true that not everything serves Man without a means, but rather through <margin>d</margin> means: Just as the rain does not serve Man without a means, but through the means of foliage and grass, etc. Now, understand the same concerning all other **Meteorological Impressions** <note>original: "Impressionibus"; the "stamping" of celestial influence onto the physical world</note>. 

But there is another kind in the heavens; these serve Man and are not fruits that are tangible, visible, or material: but rather they enter into Man just like the sun with its shine. Although the sun proves its **operation** most noticeably, sensibly, and visibly above all stars, the other stars are of such a kind as well; and they demonstrate, like the sun, through their **rays** <note>original: "Radios"</note> within Man. But it is unnoticeable, insensible, and untraceable, yet powerful, as they then demonstrate, which is also sufficiently mentioned by the **Astronomers**. Now these are the same **Impressions**, because Man must suffer and endure them, and receive them by force—such as the heat in summer, the cold in winter, and likewise **Plagues** <note>original: "Pestes"</note>, fevers, and other things. After these come the **Inclinations**, which take hold. But because they do not "impress" <note>force themselves upon a person</note>, they are not "Impressions"; it is up to Man what he wishes to do. After these come the **Generations**, which are the meteorological fruits of the stars. And although everything is Meteorological and everything is Astronomical, there is nevertheless a distinction: the invisible things are commanded to **Astronomy** in their part, and the visible things in their part. Thus you now know what is in the stars and what is not. Let each person recognize that what he does not find in this **Meteorology**, he will find in **Astronomy**: so that all things come into and stand in their perfect order. What more is to be known of the Meteorological part follows hereafter in its subsequent **Paragraphs** and **Chapters** <note>original: "Capitibus"</note>.

# Chapter Five.
## CHAPTER V.
### ON THE GENERATION
### of Winds.

<margin>A</margin>
Now that you have heard enough concerning the beginnings of **meteors** <note>In the 16th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including wind, rain, and lightning, not just falling stars</note>, it is only right to write further of the things generated and the generations of meteors. First, we shall speak of the origin and birth of the winds, and of the **predestined circles** <note>original: "Prædestinierten Zirckeln"; fixed paths or zones in the heavens from which winds emerge</note> of the winds. Regarding this, know first: there are four parts of the cycle and circle—one toward the Sunrise [East], one toward the Sunset [West], one toward Midday [South], and one toward Midnight [North]. The circle stands in this manner: just as the two elements, Earth and Water, lie in the middle of the firmament, and the element of Air lies between the element of the Heavens and the lower globe. Just as the Earth lies in the middle and the Heavens go around it, so the circle goes horizontally around the middle of the Heavens, the Earth, and the Water, encircling them. For an example: take an **egg** <note>A common medieval and Renaissance analogy for the structure of the cosmos</note> and lay it on its side—not from the top down, but horizontally—and take the middle all the way around the egg so that the yolk also falls in that same middle, as it naturally divides itself. Now observe that the Heavens likewise go around the world with such a circle; in this same circle stand the "Mothers" and places of the winds, where the winds arise that are predestined. And when they wish to go forth, they travel from that same circle onto the globe through the element of air. When they reach the roundness of the world-spheres and strike against them, it may well be that the wind either strikes under the spheres to those who are beneath us, or onto the spheres to those who are upon them, or to both parts, as it divides itself toward the heights or the depths of the spheres. And so the wind travels through the air over the sea and earth, as far and as long as its substance lasts, until through long exercise and wide travel it consumes itself, is driven away, and vanishes, so that no **matter** <note>original: "Materia"</note> remains.

<margin>B</margin>
Furthermore, there are four parts, and each part has a special character within itself. Namely, the part from the **Orient** [East] is warm and dry. This is not because it receives such qualities from the Sun, or because it stands in the East—no—but because its nature is thus constituted in the **three primes** <note>Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury/Liquor</note>, to be so and not against its nature. Therefore, in the true **Eurus** <note>The East wind</note> and its companions, no other nature or operation is found but that which is warm and dry. Conversely, the **Zephyrus** <note>The West wind</note> in the setting of the sun is cold and moist—not because of the sunset or because it stands there (for the sunset has the same **complexion** <note>Temperament or physical constitution</note> as the sunrise), but because the nature of the winds' matter in the West was created to be cold and moist. Again, from the Midnight [North], those same "wind-bearers" are of a cold and dry nature, and thus they also create cold and dry regions where they are present; it is not that the winds take their nature from the regions, but the regions receive such nature from the winds. In the same way, in the Midday [South], the **Auster** <note>The South wind</note> is warm and moist, contrary to the **Septentrio** <note>The North wind</note>. This is not because it has much sea or stands in moist places, but because its nature is such, and it gives forth its generations accordingly. Understand, then, that the winds have no nature from the outside, but from within themselves. If the Auster were of a dry nature like the **Boreas** <note>Another name for the North wind</note>, no moisture would affect it to make it moist, but it would remain dry regardless of the sea, etc. Thus, if Boreas were given a moist nature, it would be moist and not dry, no matter what the region was like. You should also know that the birth of the winds stands in the "Wind-Circle" and in their own nature, and they are in the stars, and the stars are their mothers. There are many of these from the Boreal side, the Eurus side, the Zephyric side, and the Austral side—not just one, nor three, but several thousand, of which there is no number. These are the ones from which all winds spring that are placed in the main circle. Although winds are also created by other stars during rain or showers, they are not counted in the Wind-Circle, only those of the four parts.

<margin>C</margin>
As has been mentioned regarding the place of the winds and their origin from the furthest reaches of the Heavens, across the sea and earth through the air: know then that these same stars have within them the power to give birth to the winds according to their nature and property. In the same way as you might understand a tree that gives forth its fruit from its own nature, from its wood, and from its pith, so it is to be understood with such stars. Now the seed from which the winds are made is the <term>Prima materia</term> <note>First matter; the fundamental building blocks of a substance</note> of the three primes, namely from <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Salt</term>, and <term>Liquor</term> <note>In Paracelsian science, Liquor (or Mercury) represents the fluid/volatile principle, Sulphur the combustible/soul principle, and Salt the solid/body principle</note>. These three are the mothers from which grow those things we call winds: the **Sulphur**, **Liquor**, and **Salt**. In the Northern parts, they are of a cold and dry nature; in the Midday, they give warmth and moisture; likewise warm and dry in the East, and cold and moist in the West. As the nature of the three primes is, so is their fruit and produce—that is, so are those same winds. Furthermore, know that they have their growth in those same stars, a common progression according to their time. Though it may be sometimes less and sometimes more, they nevertheless rule in their seasons. When the winds become "ripe," they receive at that same time the development of their property and nature from the three primes, and they retain them. But because they have such a long way to travel, their powers become somewhat weak at certain times. For example, the Boreas [North wind] in summer may not hold its full property because the summer stars warm it; but in winter it does, for then it falls into the wind-stars and remains unbroken. But when the winter is about to depart...

Now, it is Sulphuric; therefore, it has a Sulphuric disease to cause: it is Salic <note>Related to the alchemical principle of Salt</note>, therefore it splits the mouth open and becomes just like salt-drops from salted meat in its property; for this reason, it causes many more cases of *scabies* <note>original: "Scabies"; a skin irritation or mange</note> and *alopecias* <note>original: "Alopitias"; hair loss</note>, etc. The midday Auster <note>original: "Auster"; the South wind</note> is likewise so in its time, best in its brilliance. Thus, each wind has its time in the year during which it is specifically born and operates without its own destruction.

Now, test the earthly examples of the origin of winds: for instance, you see that when water boils in a pot, it produces a wind from itself. You also see further that a wind arises from all things that ebulliate <note>original: "Ebulliren"; to boil up or effervesce</note>, whether they be dry or moist. A water that boils there gives a warm, moist wind, as the work itself bears witness. A dry boiling—as is known to the Alchemists—gives a dry wind. Now, know this: the Fiery Vulcan <note>In alchemy, Vulcan represents the transformative power of fire</note> in the stars boils the **Three Primes** <note>original: "die drey ersten"; Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury, the fundamental components of all matter in Paracelsian thought</note> according to their nature; from this the wind arises, and whatever its property is arises with it, just as the Fiery Vulcan does through wood. And the Fiery Vulcan is himself the wind, for he is placed within the Three Primes. Where the Three Primes are not, there is no fire; so he is also in the wind-stars. Upon this, it is now to be known that the Fiery Vulcan is nothing other than a Sulphur, a Saltpeter, and a Mercury. Now, when the spark of fire falls into these three, he is in action and does what pertains to him, according to how the three are ordered. For the Sulphur of wood is different from the Sulphur of the winds; the Saltpeter of wood is different from the Saltpeter of the winds; the Mercury of wood is different from the Mercury of the winds. As each species is, so is its fire, and so is its operation. For everything that grows, grows out of those three. Therefore, it is first of all necessary to understand the **Three Primes** <note>original: "tres Primas"</note> well; for according to their nature, they are the mother of all things.

<margin>B</margin>
Now you see well what a common fire does in common Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury. How much more is this **First Matter** <note>original: "Prima materia"</note> graded in the firmament—stronger and more powerful? You should note this: there is no other origin of the winds than when the Three Primes are moved by Vulcan into their operation; thus the Three Primes move into their action. This action then gives the wind and its nature with it—cold or warm, dry or moist, as mentioned above. Just as a wind goes out from a fire that it makes itself, so it is to be understood here. For thus God has set the generation of the firmament together, and in such a property, that the three should give and bear all things in their places where God has ordained them, and with their operations go into the center of the world.

So that you may understand this Vulcanian operation well, know an earthly example: You know that Sulphur is a fire that burns; also you know that Saltpeter burns, as does Mercury, and all three have a fiery nature until they come into their operation—that is, into their **Ultimate Matter** <note>original: "Ultimarn materiam"; the final, completed form of a substance</note>. Now the Sulphur receives the Fiery Vulcan, and because the others are embodied within it, for that reason one moves with the other, and all three go into a fire. The fire now "cooks" the wind. As you visibly see from the earthly versions of those Three Primes, how they make their impetus, motions, and tempests. From this it follows that in the birth of the winds, the stars are the **Vials** and **Flasks** <note>original: "Phiolas vnd Cucurbitas"; types of laboratory glassware used in distillation</note>, and the meteoric Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt within them are of an ethereal nature. These work through the ethereal Vulcan in those same vials; from those ethereal workings now grow ethereal operations, which are the winds that are driven out from such concavities onto the lower globe, according to the nature and strength of those same three primary things.

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, through the earthly example, understand the firmamental effect—not, however, in the same degree, but as far as the Heavens are from the Earth, so much more powerful is it above the Earth. And as much as it stands in clarity above earthly coarseness, so much higher is its operation graded, and so much is it changed in its three species or things. Therefore, the earthly example is sufficient to understand the **Meteorics** <note>original: "Meteoricam"; the study of atmospheric phenomena</note> and is also sufficiently proven by it; for all things that do not lie understandably before our eyes should be understood through that which is understandable. Just as the earthly operation is understandable to us and in sufficient understanding and knowledge, so is it an example and a likeness of that which is also thus, even though we do not see it. For even **Christ** proclaimed His word in parables, through which parables more should and must be understood. Thus, I give the earthly as a likeness for the firmamental, which is also transitory, just like the earthly.

Now know that the time and hour of the rising of such winds may, in part, be well known by astronomers and their species, quite fundamentally. Yet that same thing is not "Meteoric" but "Astronomic," to which I leave it. But when they go forth, know that they proceed according to their parts and agreement. For much concordance makes much strong wind; frequent concording and generating makes frequent wind; many species and a strong Vulcan make great, powerful winds, which is why they overturn houses and trees. For the wind is just as much corporeal and substantial in its kind as a matter or a stone that falls from on high. Although the stone has one kind of body <note>original: "Corpus"</note> and the wind another, there is nothing to marvel at in this. For the wind is also a body that can easily knock over another body, just like a visible body. For it is not only that which is visible that is a body, but that which is visible and invisible—whatever God has created is all corporeal. Yet in both forms, invisible and visible, they have equal power. For water carries a great weight of wood, however little it may seem; it moves great stones away in streams, just as...

# Fifth Chapter. 83

...even though it is thin and soft: know also that the wind has such power and might. 
<margin>A</margin> Now understand the origins of the winds: that they rise only in the **wind-stars** <note>original: "Windsternen"; specific stars believed to govern meteorological phenomena</note> and thus become ripe in their season through a **Vulcanic** <note>The transformative, fiery power of nature, named after the Roman god of fire</note> process, breaking out into the center of the globe. Thus, their nature and property affect whatever they touch, according to their essence: just as the **Boreas** <note>the North Wind</note> **Coagulates** <note>original: "Coagulirt"; to thicken or solidify</note>, the **Auster** <note>the South Wind</note> **Resolves** <note>original: "Resolvirt"; to dissolve or melt</note>, the **Eurus** <note>the East Wind</note> **Preserves**, and the **Zephyrus** <note>the West Wind</note> **Putrefies** <note>original: "Putrificirt"; to rot or decompose</note>. As they are able to perform their operations, they manifest them according to their kind. If it happens at a time when their **malice** <note>original: "Malitia"; the harmful or extreme quality of an element</note> is taken from them, then they can do nothing.

Thus, as the winds go out from their **emunctories** <note>original: "Emunctorijs"; vents or organs that carry off waste, here used for atmospheric portals</note> in the wind-circle—much like the **voiding** <note>original: "Assellieren"; the purging of waste from the human body</note> of a human—their first path is over the sea. Now, it is no less true that the circle does not stand so directly upon the sea that it only passes over the water; rather, it is so wide that it also reaches the lower circle of the lower globe, that is, the third **Peroledum** <note>a technical term used by Paracelsus to describe specific layers or zones of the atmosphere and firmament</note>, both above and below. Since the upper third Peroledum and the lower third Peroledum also influence the middle, know that it strikes the middle Peroledum in its body just as it passes by, whether upwards or downwards, toward whichever side—be it in the **Arctic** or **Antarctic** regions. When the third Peroledum is struck, the wind enters the water and moves it, so that it forces its way through the water—upwards or downwards as its **impetus** <note>force or momentum</note> is directed—while the other part remains upon the water. Now, that part of the wind does not remain in the water, but goes out of the water into the air. Through such passage, it creates **tempests** in the sea and in the water. For it should not have traveled in such a way, but rather upon the water; but as it uses its impetus in the air, it also uses it in the water, whereby it creates sea-waves and floods, more ghastly 
<margin>B</margin> and terrifying than those upon the water. For it throws the water up, thrusts it into the heights, and no one can know how powerfully it lies within the water; for its greatness overcomes the water, and the water must yield **cataracts** <note>floodgates or rushing channels</note> and **caverns** to it, so that it may exit into its body of elements. And it does not always exit the water entirely and make its caverns; rather, it is so subtle that it also passes through the **pores** of the earth. It passes through walls and through all barriers, as is visibly known; likewise through mountains and rocks, as it passes over the water.

And note this further: what remains in the water and comes out through the water, enters into the earth and travels through the earth until it finds its **exit** <note>original: "Exitum"</note> or is **consumed** within itself; from this, **earthquakes** <note>original: "Erdbidem"</note> arise. (Though these are not the only causes of earthquakes; there are many others as well.) For in such a form, the wind creates earthquakes just as it creates waves in the water; when something stands upon it, a ship or galley, they tremble and cannot stand still. Therefore, because they cannot stand still, it is a "water-earthquake." Thus, the wind can also move the earth through the pores of the earth—the large and the small, whether they be like cataracts or similar—though not as easily as water, which is much more willing and yielding to it. For everything that is born must be consumed and has an end; so it is also with the wind, which has its **limit** <note>original: "Terminum"</note> which it cannot overstep, but must die and take its death at that very point. Therefore, know that the earth of itself gives no winds, only what the winds drive into it. Although **Vulcan** <note>the transformative fire</note> is also in the earth and in the water, he is not **fulgurant** <note>original: "Fulgurisch"; lightning-like or flashing</note> in them; only in the firmament is he fulgurant and possesses a tempestuous impetus. This is the nature of the wind, which has the power to pass through all stone and metal, the earth and everything, with nothing excepted; and whatever resists it, it snaps apart and overthrows. By this example, 
<margin>C</margin> you shall finally understand it well, like **gunpowder** <note>original: "Büxenpulver"</note> that makes the gun and the ground tremble, and no one can withstand its storm. Thus, it is also like the gunpowder of **Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury** <note>the "Three Primes" of Paracelsian alchemy</note>, which nothing can resist. And although it is not fire, does not smoke, and does not flash, it is nonetheless an **ethereal gunpowder** that comes from the caverns and emunctories of the cataracts of the Vulcanic wind-stars. And it is thus a windy saltpeter, sulphur, and mercury, which accomplish all things wondrously; and without these three **species** it is impossible for this to happen. The only difference is that one is according to an earthly nature, the other according to an ethereal kind and property.

# Of the Book of METEOROLOGY <note>original: "Deß Buchs METEORORUM"; the study of atmospheric phenomena</note>.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, it should be as follows: what is commonly said—that rain is an extraction of the water from below, ascending and distilling up and down—cannot be. The reasons for this have been sufficiently demonstrated in the aforementioned sections. Rather, we should know that every rain comes from its own origin and is born anew, having never existed before; just as a pear has grown this year, and was never there in the years past or the years to come. So too are the seeds, where one follows the other and gives its fruit in its time, as God created it. Now, one should not attempt to count the rain-stars, for the entire firmament is full of them, divided among all lands as far as the globe extends. And although it happens that in some regions the effect of the rain-stars does not always manifest, or it rains seldom or not at all, this is not a defect of the stars—as if they were not there—but rather they are dried out by the winds and constellations of that particular land and region. Just as a tree is dried out, or a fruit that cannot ripen because of drought: so it also happens with the rain-stars in those same ends and places where they stand. Likewise, if they stand in moist constellations and wind-stars, they give all the more rain; that is, they apply themselves well, and nothing of them is lost. Know also that if they come late or early, or in great or small amounts, it is not because they are drying out, but because in one year they are more fruitful than in other years: just as we see in all growing things, so it is also in the firmament.

Now understand the beginning of rain in this way. When its etheric paroxysm <note>original: "Paroxylmus"; a sudden intensification or "fit" of celestial activity</note> comes, so that autumn is here and it is time to be ripe, then Vulcanus <note>the transformative power of nature's "inner alchemist"</note>, Yliaster <note>the primeval matter of the stars</note>, and the Archeus <note>the vital force that governs natural processes</note> begin to prepare within those same stars, as if in a pot, and operate toward rain, dispensing and preparing. Once they have awaited the time of digestion <note>the process of ripening or chemical maturation</note>, then the flowers <note>original: "Flores"; the first visible manifestation or "bloom" of a substance</note> come forth, as on a tree: <margin>B</margin> First a cloud, which increases according to the content of those stars—greatly or slightly, slowly, quickly, or nimbly, however it may happen and whatever material is present. For first the etheric smoke goes forth: and because it separates itself from common earthly smoke, it is called a cloud. Now, when that same cloud comes out from the stars, it settles downward toward the earth into the air, where it hovers. In itself it is water, but not yet fully prepared. And its material is Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury <note>The "Three Primes" of Paracelsian alchemy, believed to be the building blocks of all matter</note>, all three of which go into resolution <note>original: "Resolution"; the process of dissolving or liquefying</note> outside of the stars, like tartar <note>original: "Weinstein"; potassium bitartrate crystals</note> in a cellar or in water. Thus, the air is the cellar of this calcination <note>reduction to essence through heat or chemical change</note> and digestion, in which they dissolve and release themselves. Now, when the cloud stands in the air as in a cellar, if it is well-prepared for resolution, it happens all the sooner; if not, it remains longer in the air. Sometimes, when there is little of it, it vanishes entirely, or gives a rain or moisture that cannot reach the earth. But if it remains and is ordained for rain, then it resolves itself into water. And according to the nature of the rain, so is the resolution; the rain comes from the clouds, and the clouds from the stars. Thus it often happens that such rain lasts continuously, because clouds daily go out from the rain-stars and do not cease increasing, or one star follows another, or many work together, as the concordance <note>original: "Concordanz"; the harmonious alignment of celestial forces</note> strikes. For some give an hour, some more, some a day, some many days, some a week, some many weeks, and some are quite inconsistent and mingled, at irregular hours, etc. However it may be, the preparation is first made in the stars from the three primes, according to their nature; after that comes the cloud; after that comes the resolution in the air, by the air; and from that comes the rain upon the earth.

<margin>C</margin> Now the resolution happens in this way. As soon as the rain-cloud comes into the air, as into its cellar, and its time of resolution is at hand, it then resolves itself drop by drop, and not in a single mass, but exactly as if it were being distilled downward. This is alchemically <note>original: "Alchimistisch"</note> arranged by Divine Providence, so that one drop after another filters <note>original: "Viltriere"</note>, distills, and guttates <note>original: "Guttier"; to fall in drops</note> in the manner of drops, just as they then come down to us. It often happens that the resolution occurs slowly, and therefore the drops fall slowly; sometimes faster or more nimbly; according to the arrangement and dispensation, many or few, large or small drops, depending on the year and the season. Thus, every rain is nothing but a resolved Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, separated into the form of rain during the first extraction and separation <note>The initial creation or chemical refining of matter</note>. In the six days when God created all things, He also ordained every thing in its place with its own properties. These properties further prepare themselves in the fiery Vulcan <note>original: "Igneo Vulcano"</note> into rain, just as tartar turns to water and other such things, which in their final matter never resemble their first matter <note>original: "Primæ materiæ"</note>. From this, know also that such rain of which I speak is the mildest and best rain, which most perfectly fills, moistens, and drenches the earth, and is also the healthiest. For it springs from the mildest three primes of the first matter. For there are others that are more harsh, and therefore they are of a harsher nature than these. There are also rains that commonly overflow when they find a concordance, so that many of them come together and are prepared at once. Wherever such a concordance coincides, many kinds of rain occur together in that place, which can be recognized by the drops: some quite subtle like alcohol <note>original: "Alcool"; here referring to a highly refined essence or fine powder</note>, some a little larger, and so on up to the largest, as common experience itself proves.

But now there are other stars from which rain also goes out: but these have the property of bringing winds with them. This is the cause: the Salt in those rain-stars, and the Mercury as well, are not entirely prepared; that is, their impetus has not been taken...

### Sixth Chapter.
Vol. II. b

<margin>A</margin> A name has been taken from Vulcan <note>original: "Vulcano"; the Roman god of fire, here representing alchemical heat</note>: and that is a special kind. Where such a kind exists, those stars produce winds without rain for several hours or days, etc. Afterward, when the winds have died down, it is a sign that Mercury and Salt have united with Sulfur; then they go into the clouds and send them out into the air, sometimes with the wind—clouds and wind together. And such rain-clouds with their own winds are rare, because the wind is not resolved <note>the process of turning from vapor to liquid</note> in the same place where they fell, but in a foreign nation. So now, when these same clouds are resolved in the "cellar of ethereal resolution," the rains fall down in great quantities, as was mentioned before. It is also to be noted that when the wind is in the rain—that is, during the resolution—then the wind scatters the resolution and breaks its resolved <term>Guttas</term> <note>Latin: drops</note>, one into two or three parts: it also drives them to fall quickly, more so than they would otherwise fall. It thus throws the drops hither and thither, so that they cannot distill according to their nature, as it is meant to happen. To this, it is also important to know that where such clouds, as well as other rain-clouds, stand upon the mountains, they have more power for progression than on level lands. The reason is: the mountains have a coolness, and this coolness comes from the range. When these clouds come into this coolness, they resolve more quickly, whereas in other level lands they would be consumed. For there are many rain-clouds that are adorned <note>influenced</note> by other constellations, which cannot proceed in that place in the mountains. So, when the pot—that is, the star—has poured out its Autumn <note>original: "Autumnum"; the harvest season</note> and its reapers, then it has its time again until its three first parts of <term>Primæ Materiæ</term> <note>Latin: First Matter; the fundamental substance of all things</note> grow back according to their season. Then their operation begins again, as has been noted here with these rains.

<margin>B</margin> It also often happens that the earth and the water, within themselves, give off a coolness through their embodied springs and water and nature in their properties, such that the air also becomes cooler: as then happens many times. Where such coolness comes into the air, the air is also cooler, and thus many clouds are resolved which otherwise would be consumed. Especially in the mountains, such cold can rise to the heights. For the air is a cellar, and it is cold and damp in the heights—never warm, except only where the reflection <note>the sun's heat reflecting off the earth</note> is, and as high as it reaches. Thus two colds come together, where each refreshes the other and makes it like a cellar: although the higher the air, the colder it is. Also, the cloud often becomes so heavy that it falls very far down, quite close into the warmth, from which then warm rains follow; this is the fault of weight alone. But where they are few, they resolve high up and fall from a great height. It is also no less true that the same wind which comes out of those same stars is also damp in itself, like the Zephyrian <note>original: "Zephyrischen"; referring to Zephyrus, the west wind</note> wind. Therefore, when the Zephyrian wind blows out of the wind-circle, and the stars are in operation, rain will soon be there. For it passes through the air along with the rain-wind and makes it cool and damp; so when the cloud enters it, it soon resolves and melts into <term>Guttas</term> <note>Latin: drops</note>. But even if stars of a rainy nature were present and a dry wind blew, then the rain would not be very powerful in its operation; it would be driven away and consumed by the dryness. Therefore, special attention must be paid to this: for where such a concordance occurs in the dampness of the cellar—that is, in the air—many signs will appear in that place by which one may recognize it. Such as the little hands <note>likely weather vanes or star positions</note> and the <term>Cardines</term> <note>Latin: the "hinges" or cardinal points of the zodiac</note> which turn; people become heavy-spirited; the air becomes misty, heavy, and damp; the sponges, ashes, and sand in (raisins) and otherwise, and many more such things, not all necessary to recount; but the greater are the rains.

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, know that it also often happens in such clouds and in such conjunctions: when the Moon, the time, and the wind-stars harmonize and work together: and when the wind-stars are of fast operation and operate much: and that which is now born is well-prepared and quite firm, so that they begin the resolution too quickly, then great downpours result, many of which appear. But where it happens that such a resolution occurred just at the point when it comes from the <term>Athanar</term> <note>an alchemical furnace</note> into the cellar—as often happens, that the resolution begins in the <term>Aludel</term> <note>an alchemical condensing vessel</note> and is quickly completed in the dampness—where this also happens in such births, the entire cloud becomes all at once just one drop, like a body of water together. It does not have enough resistance to fall <term>Guttatim</term> <note>Latin: drop by drop</note>, so it falls all at once, and remains as a single drop. Whatever may happen during the pouring and falling, through wind and fall, it may be scattered: yet it falls down at once, one after another, in a swift resolution. It may well happen that a good amount of time passes before it stops. It may also be that rains come and have been before and after; those are of the correct <term>Distillation</term>. But these, which are cloudbursts <note>original: "Wolckenbrüch"</note>, have a different star and a different matter. With this, wind and other things may also come and happen, just as <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Sal</term>, and <term>Mercurius</term> <note>Sulfur, Salt, and Mercury</note> have in them a nature that is unequal—in one way in one, and different in another. Thus understand the origin of the natural, useful rain for the earth and for humanity; that they take their origin naturally as mentioned, and are thus ordained and created in their <term>Prædestination</term> <note>predestination</note> to moisten the earth. Now there are other winds and other clouds that are not of rain, but of a dry nature. How those are to be understood follows hereafter. What more is necessary to know of the stars, learn from Astronomy, for which reason I have omitted it here in this <term>Meteorica</term> <note>the study of atmospheric phenomena</note>.

Now regarding the dry clouds, know that there are also some stars that are not for rain and...
