### On the Thunderbolt.

<margin>A</margin>Regarding the thunderbolt <note>original: "Straal," literally a beam or ray, but here referring to a lightning bolt or "thunderstone"</note>, you should know that there are two kinds: Hot and Cold. They may travel together toward a star—that is, when the Cold and Warm separate, each according to its own nature, as is shown in the treatise *On Thermal Springs* <note>original: "de Thermis"</note>. This happens in the following way: This star, in its harvest, moves toward a concentrated expulsion <term>Egestion<gloss>the act of discharging waste or matter from a celestial body</gloss></term>. Now, the nature of such a bolt is such that it is rare, unless it is a very fast and nimble action; otherwise, it first sends forth its thunder following from the South. In this process, the Salts separate from the *earthy layer* and the earth-moisture, resulting in rain. Now, within such a star, there is usually a "Wind-spirit" <note>original: "Wündsch," likely a contraction of Wind-geist</note> and an attached nature of a wind that is also present. If there is a metallic nature there, or a chest-like, or marble-like nature from the Salt, the star compacts itself; whatever is of that nature turns into a stone, and what is not goes into the other expulsions. But that which turns into such a nature burns up the Mercury and a Sulfur, and it happens so quickly that through its operation and its contrary nature, it is cast out of the star into the earth—and so fast that it breaks through walls; that is its force <term>Impetus<gloss>violent energy or momentum</gloss></term> alone. Know also that these bolts are entirely stars: for many stars in the heavens dissolve again and enter into these and other generations.
<margin>* or.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>Or it is their bolt which is fast in itself, because the Mercury strikes it out of the narrow hole, as it cannot tolerate boiling Salt within it. For when its generation begins to move, the Mercury stirs and resists: that is, when it comes out of the Conjunction. But as soon as the stars come together—that is, when the matter goes toward generation—you see as in other things: first comes the budding time, then the stalk, then the <unclear>leaf</unclear>, then the fruit. As these things develop from one another, so it is here in the stars. First, the Sulfurous kinds are born, from which the lightning comes; then the Salt, from which the rain comes; then both together, from which the thundering comes; then the Mercury, from which the bolt comes. Thus they emerge from one another quickly, along with the windy nature. And then the Mercury strikes as soon as it touches something moist in its region; it strikes out through its vent <term>Exundatorium<gloss>an outlet or drainage point</gloss></term>, just as one sees a crack or bang: for it is in a narrow hole that it must pass through, and the wider it is, the louder its bang. Likewise, know that this hole is merely a swelling of water in which it lies; as soon as it resolves, as soon as it touches it, it strikes out through the dry swelling, whether it be wide or narrow. If it is very wet and resolves, it gives a harder blow.
<margin>* 41. Thereafter,</margin>
Know of such a bolt that one part is extinguished in water and comes to the earth cold; another part is cold by nature. Those which are hot and do not extinguish themselves come to the earth hot. In this part, a swelling is a compact vapor, held together without any coagulation. This vapor-salt is like a wind; it strikes into crevices, where a sweat comes out of a pore, or as a wind goes through a wall or partition—and there is much less in a bolt, and *yet* it grows. Thus it goes through the crevice, through the pores, and up again, as is the nature of wind. Because it is a dry wind, whatever it seizes, it overcomes or burns, according to its nature. For some burn gold, some the scabbard, some wood, etc. This is all due to the nature of the Salt within it. Also,
<margin>C</margin>this Salt melts keys together, irons onto one another, and makes locks corrode. For this is the true Borax for soldering, and a Salt equal to it. This <insert>can penetrate walls</insert>, for walls are all porous, and it all runs through. This vapor strikes the swords in the scabbard and leaves the scabbard without harm; this vapor strikes into the earth and other places and makes no hole. For it is merely a compact wind, gathered into a small space from a large mass. Thus you see how in the sun there is a great heat, more than in all the stars, and yet it is small. So there is a comparison with the wind—that is, the bolt—there is also a compact wind, which contains more than is otherwise in a thousand miles.

There are many such generations in the heavens, so that such a nature comes into a compaction where a few ounces <note>original: "loth"</note> outweigh 1000 hundredweight <note>original: "Centner"</note>, from which such strength comes. For as Saffron <note>original: "Crocus"</note> many times outweighs the Spearwort <note>original: "Flammulam"</note> in <unclear>potency</unclear>, so it is here. But the other bolts that are coagulated, those make holes and do more damage than the others, but their paths are seen where they pass through.

Thus the weather, and bolts, and hail are born, one after the other in time: like a herb, which first becomes the root from the seed, then the stalk, then the leaf, then the flower, then the fruit. Thus the lightning is the flower, the thundering the stalk, the rain the root, and the bolt its fruit. And so each has its special time, just as every herb has its special growth. And as manifold and strange as those are, and as many, so there is much to be known here as well.

### BOOK FIVE
### CONCERNING RAINS.

## On Rain.

<image-desc>Decorated initial D</image-desc>
**D**o know now concerning the rain-stars <note>stars believed to govern precipitation</note> that they are fixed and stand still in the same region in which they were born. For just as the lands lie still, so also do all their stars remain which are assigned to them. Their sheath <note>the surrounding environment</note> is the air of the entire world. Now, this air is of many kinds and plentiful, according to what the lands are. But it flows quietly from them; that is, the African air does not temper into Europe, nor the Asian into Europe. Likewise, all lands have their own air which stays with them: such as Hungary, Poland/Russia, Denmark, Swabia, etc. <note>original: "Pannonia, Sarmatia, Dania, Sueuia"</note> all have their air and do not change. For as you see the white in an egg—though the egg be turned however one wishes, yet the white does not change—so it is with the air. As this is so, it is also with the rain-stars at their first [origin]; that the rain-stars give their rain further than their region is, that same thing comes from the wind-star which runs therein and drives the clouds further than its [origin], for the sake of the fertility of that land. But the "edge-stars," which are not driven by the wind but by their own wind, also make themselves go further than their falling region. Thereupon know that there are special stars which go toward rain: just as some [plants] stand in the field, upon some Savin juniper, others Oregano <note>original: "Sauina, Origanum"</note>, and others next to them without harm. <insert>Seek the first Chapter of the Second Treatise.</insert>

# PROLOGUE

### Into the Books of METEOROLOGY, by THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM <note>Paracelsus</note>, Philosopher.

<image-desc>Decorated initial D</image-desc>
**T**o the end that we be not regarded as heathens for treating heathenish [matters] in our philosophizing, but rather that we present ourselves as believers, we wish to show you, as our students, two divisions of this error between the heathen and the believers. Before we explain the two divisions, we wish to declare a preface as an argument, thus: It is becoming and proper for a Philosopher that he know the beginning and end of that which he philosophizes about. In such writing on Meteorology <note>original: "Meteorischen"</note>, we know neither the beginning nor the end of things—how they came to be or how they are destroyed. Although we do not know such things, we yet know that which *is*, of which we write. As we know and see, yet [we know] not what the bodies <note>original: "Corpora"</note> are, nor what they contain, nor what is born upon them. For sight does not deceive, nor does experience. But upon what the bodies are made, that we also know; yet from what they are made, or enjoyed, that we know not. Therefore we leave the "Meteorics" blameless regarding that which we recognize through the fruits, and defend and indicate them, as a father through his child. This does not wish to be enough for us to lick from the Scripture or to believe. That is, believing and experiencing appear thus: that we know a creature exists; concerning the same, more is moved by the experience of the eyes and ears. So we let the Creation rest in these books and philosophize about that which is created, and remain silent and mute, like a closed mouth, as to how it was created. But while we speak of the creatures, it shall [behoove] us...

<header>ON THE BOOKS OF METEORS.</header>
<note>The "Books of Meteors" refers to the study of atmospheric phenomena, based on the Aristotelian tradition but here interpreted through a spiritual and medical lens.</note>
This same person shall be a philosopher to us, of which a part is the study of Meteors: for of this we have both a knowledge and a faith. Upon this, it is right for us to philosophize; and allow the objections or arguments of our treatment by other opposing parties, all of which points out, instructs, teaches, and provides more elegantly.

Now, someone might well reproach us and consider us a heathen because the first division is made as if we were treating this as an unbeliever, and that since we are a believer, we should speak from Faith: because such a speech is regarded by us as having very little wisdom or standing. We speak such things from the principle that a philosopher must be a believer: and he who is a believer is a philosopher, and he who is no philosopher is not wise in Faith. It is fitting for a believer to be a wise man and a man of skill, so that he may know what he believes. A fool who believes is dead in his faith. For causes—the works—make the faith; that is, the works of nature, of wonders; faith comes from signs, from works, from miracles. A philosopher should rightly philosophize as a believer, and not at all as a heathen, and call us a Christian. But we see there a distinction between faith and knowledge: he who wishes to believe must know. For out of knowledge, and according to what he knows, he believes. But since such knowledge comes from philosophy, and faith follows it, and thus one becomes blessed, so also might one become unblessed from it—such as he who knows all the signs and works of God and believes it all, but the fruit of his knowledge does not come forth, but dies away. This we call a dead philosopher. And he who knows much should bring forth much fruit; otherwise, he shall be regarded as a liar and not as a philosopher. For knowledge, then faith, then the fruit: that is the foundation of a philosopher.

<margin>b.</margin> Upon this, we divide philosophy into 3 types and into 3 faculties: Into the philosophers who treat of birth and origin, and are called Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophi Naturales"</note>. Into the philosophers who treat of the breaking down of things, and are called Medical Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophi Medicos"</note>. Into the philosophers who treat of wonders against nature, and are called Holy Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophos Sanctos"</note>. Since the ears of Christian Philosophy <note>original: "Christentlicher Philosophiæ"</note> serve faith alone, we wish to make a distinction: One type recognizes God through signs and nature; the others know Him and do not recognize Him, though they know to what purpose the works belong. A Christian philosopher knows that faith is from the work which He does and has done, in whom one should believe. Thus, as we should end in the One, and in Him from whom the works come: we encounter two kinds of works in the philosophers: the righteous and the false. The righteous are that leaves and grass grow, and all animals, and everything similar, and that the dead become living. The false are those who, as if through sorcery, make one sick and then healthy again, to mimic the appearance and deed of evil spirits; and they philosophize to us through them also for faith: through the others, nothing; thus in Him who has created the same, who can do such things.

## SECOND PROLOGUE

Thus it should be right for us that we are a believing philosopher, and that we ground and study our work comfortingly upon the works of nature, and meditate peacefully. For the more knowledge of the works of God, the greater the faith, and accordingly, the salvation. He who understands, recognizes, and knows many works of nature is high in faith, for the Creator is his teacher. He who knows much of the works of wonders is the greatest in salvation. Like PLATO, whom we regard not only as a natural philosopher but also as one acquainted with miracles. What made Peter <note>original: "Petrum"</note> blessed, but the works of Christ, which made him a believer? Otherwise, faith would have been dead in him. In Nature, the greatest is he who knows, teaches, and experiences nature and wonders: he who can do nothing, nor experiences, nor knows anything, is dead. All this we wish to let stand and serve you as signs. Let us leave the others to rest here and take up for ourselves the operation of nature, as the first prologue indicates. Since it is right and should be that every man is a wise man—that is, a philosopher—we wish to further show that which is to be understood for the body, and spoken regarding it, and not regarding the soul, as stated above concerning works for salvation. For the natural operation in man and the miraculous signs are the works toward salvation, through which the soul comes to heaven. But to philosophize naturally for ourselves, we indicate to you that his life may be an extension or a shortening, so that he does not deviate from daily experience while he lives, or the time of his blindness, or the time of loss in his hearing, until his tongue stands still and his reason is a child.

<margin>c.</margin> Upon this, every believer should be a philosopher, or have a neighbor who is one, so that he knows what maintains and preserves his life in health: since God has given him the medicine <note>original: "Artzney"</note>, only our free will is required. He should know what he eats and drinks, what it works and carries, and what may spring from it for the extension of his life. For the works that one does for the extension of his life are among the works toward heaven: he who looks to his health, so that no shortening of life may occur, is the true Emperor <note>original: "Kaiser"</note>: For...

# PHILOSOPHIA

When all our concerns should be directed toward long life, one should also recognize what was possible for Him <note>God</note> to create out of nothing. Such as the firmament <note>the heavens or sky</note>, that he may know its effects; of the earth, what grows there; of the sea and air, so that in all things he recognizes his Creator. He is a lame perceiver who merely believes that God created and then stifles his inquiry there. He is rich who recognizes Him through His works and believes in Him because of them. Not like a blind man describing colors: for God wants us to know Him well, and not in a drunken or meager fashion.
<margin>A</margin>

There is a powerful reason for His coming to the earth: that men might know Him well; and in that knowledge, which is seen in the works He has done. God has given man the understanding to judge that which he sees. Why else is he here, if not to judge the works of God in our knowledge, so that we know through our own judgment who God is, what He is, how He is, and entirely so—not just to suppose or have an opinion. The works of God are not for nothing; they are for us to recognize and weigh for our own good, to believe in Him who gives and has given them to us. Therefore, it is right for us to know the necessities, use, and advancement of the body, as well as those of the soul, for all happens through the works of God which make us blessed.

Thus, we wish to set down initially the four elements, and that which they contain and bring forth, and to recount all their impressions <note>term: Impressiones; refers to atmospheric phenomena or "meteors" like rain, wind, or lightning</note>, what is born upon them, such as the human body or his soul, as a work of God performed in the knowledge of man.

### The First Book
## OF THE METEORS BY THEOPHRASTUS OF
## HOHENHEIM, GERMAN PHILOSOPHER.
### Concerning the Element of AIR, Volume One.
<margin>B</margin>

<insert>First, we thank God that we are a native-born German man, and praise Him for the grace that we consumed our youth in poverty and hunger, and we rejoice in the day of the end of our labor and of rest. We also thank God that He has so kindly commended us to the Virgin, who makes perfect the Holy Trinity, to be our protection; and has ordained the Mother <note>The Virgin Mary</note> in whose grace, teaching, and name we begin our Philosophy of the four books of Meteors concerning the four elements, divided into two paragraphs <note>sections</note>, and each into two books: one separate section for the outer elements, and one separate one for the globe. These we wish to complete and philosophize upon in Her mercy: additionally, daily contemplating the eternal after this life, because the world and the body shall pass away. Thereupon we pray to Christ to stand by us, as His believer, and by you all. Amen.</insert>

It is a very well-founded philosophy if we say that there are only two elements: the Warm and the Cold. With the Warm, the dry is always understood; with the Cold, the moist; and thus a matter is comprised of two virtues. Disregard the philosopher <note>likely a reference to Aristotle</note> who speaks of four, such as hot and dry, hot and moist, or cold and moist, and dry: as if there stood four elements, which is not so. There are only two: wetness and heat are not together, nor are cold and dryness. It is like the likeness of a woman and a man: the two are only one human being; either alone is not a human being, but both together make the whole of humanity. Thus it is to be known in the elements: that Fire and Air are one, and Earth and Water are also one. Although it is true that we philosophize about the complexion <note>term: Complerion/Complexion; the combination of qualities like hot, cold, moist, dry</note> of the elements, that will not be necessary for further satisfaction. For we may philosophize that Fire and Air have no complexion, nor do Earth and Water, and thus: the heat from the Fire is a fruit of the Fire by which creatures live, as do those of the Air. The cold of the Earth is also a fruit, for the use of which the Fire has dried it through the summer; the same is moistened again through the winter for the next coming fertility. And there is no other philosophy than the philosophy of cold, as cold is indicated in its chapter. Although more or less cold and heat are found in the globe, yet one must act upon the other, and one prepare the other. Thus, it is more philosophical to speak nothing of complexion, but only of the house and the green <note>likely meaning the dwelling place and the living growth</note>.
<margin>C</margin>

That is an element, as long as it has the power to cool or to warm. Just as the Heaven <note>original: Cœlum</note> is one element alone, the Earth is also an element, and is also twofold. But this philosophy is to be recognized: that different fruits are born in each particular one. For that reason, two elements are understood, but only in their fruits, not in their nature. From such, two books are recognized and set upon the two elements: like a man alone and a woman, being only one human, but two fruits follow from them, as the birth of humans shows. Since two fruits come from the two elements, Water and Earth, they are rightly recognized as elements. For whatever gives fruit for the creatures to live, and which the creatures find useful, those are elements.

<summary>Paracelsus introduces his treatise on meteorology, arguing that true knowledge of God comes from studying His physical works. He proposes a binary system of elements (Warm/Fire-Air and Cold/Earth-Water) rather than the traditional Aristotelian four.</summary>

# ON THE ELEMENT OF AIR
<margin>A</margin> Heaven <note>original: "Coelum"</note> consists of two elements, and Earth <note>original: "Terra"</note> also consists of two. The greater is to be taken as a Man, and the other should be understood as a Woman, each within a single temperament <note>term: "Complex" (complexio) - the specific balance of qualities like heat or moisture</note>. What is the fruit or growth? Just as stones grow from water, rain from the stars, and herbs from the earth: so do the elements grow in the beginning, and they increase; the elements are merely the houses which the "genus" <note>the essential type or kind</note> makes greater, and that is the fruit which the philosopher should understand.

And finally, philosophy teaches that this exists only in Heat and Cold, not in Moisture and Dryness. For no hot thing is moist, and no cold thing is dry in Heaven, just as a vision is in the eye; the moisture in the face does not create the eye, but the eye creates the vision. Thus, each thing has that through which it becomes whole—as an eye is made perfect by vision—dryness is made perfect, and while it has moisture, no heat is present there. Just as little as a lightning bolt can be heard through the eye or seen through the ears, it is equally impossible for cold to be dry or heat to be wet. In this philosophy, life, heat, and moisture move into one element (which is not a true element) and dryness: but this is essential <note>pertaining to the inner essence</note> and not elemental. However, many call the substantial temperament an "Element," but nothing is substantial <note>meaning material or physical in the common sense</note>.

### ON AIR.
<margin>B</margin> But speaking of the element of Air, know that the Air holds all elements so that they remain in their course and persist in the Center—that is, in the circle and the ring. The earth and the sea, as two elements, are the center-point of the created things, like the center <note>original: "Centrü"</note> of the circle from which the element of Air goes out. This is not contained within itself as if something were there to displace it; it is to be understood thus: The globe is a sphere that rests upon nothing, but lies free on all sides. The philosopher should therefore not wonder that it does not fall or fall apart. Also, the physicist <note>original: "Physicus"</note> should not wonder at this as if it were miraculously sustained by God—as if a stone were held aloft or floated freely in the air. It is not so, but rather thus: The elements cannot fall, not because of any side or support, but for this reason: they stand free without miracle or falling down because the element of Air <note>original: "Aer"</note> surrounds them. This Air is nothing other than a visible substance, like an excellent Chaos <note>term: "Chaos" - here used in the Paracelsian sense to mean the atmospheric space or the "great void" that contains life</note>, through which one cannot see. The space of the element of Air, through which the air moves in all directions around the entire spherical globe, so encompasses everything comprised by the other three elements that they are locked within it. There is no other Chaos in the created world that is subject to the elements; rather, the earth and the sea fall into it, remaining in their center and not deviating from it. Understand it like this: Just as the yolk in an egg does not touch the shell because of the containment of the "clear" <note>the egg white</note> that lies between them; in the same way, a "clear" lies between the earth, in which the spherical globe is carried so that it lies still, just as no fat turns itself to fall or move. And although this is <margin>C</margin> visible, like the egg white which is thick and visible: it is caused by the fact that it is born from the Chaos, which stands in its order in that form. From the circle that encloses all creatures, or called Chaos, it goes out to the spherical globe; it goes from the Chaos to the spherical globe, so that the globe can neither fall nor be moved. Therefore, because the Air is an element and contains what is within it: through that same enclosure, all its operation <note>original: "Operatrum"</note> goes toward the center, that is, onto the spherical globe. This operation is the "clear" that holds the globe. And as long as the Air remains such a Chaos, whole and strong, there is no breaking. If the element of Air in its Chaos were to take a break <note>a rupture</note>—which stands in God's power—then the globe would have an exit. Upon that would follow the destruction of the elements and the breaking of all things, and not otherwise. As long as the element is whole, the "clear" is whole: thus nothing can fall, and thus the spherical globe stands in the middle of the element of Air, as a center of that same circle.

<margin>D</margin> To philosophize further on why all creatures float upwards, some standing above and others below according to the display of the spherical globe: the reason is that all things move from the center toward the circle by the nearest path. Just as when a circle is made with a center inside it, many hundreds of lines go from the center to the ring; likewise, all plants and animals look toward heaven, seeing more of the nearest line toward the Chaos, whether they are set above or below. Thus, everything on the sphere stands in a line toward the Chaos and has no other containment to keep it from falling over than the "clear": for everything stands sideways or downwards. But that such things do not fall downwards or...

# PHILOSOPHY

is considered a side, it is a creature and a work of God. For the causes that are beneath the **spherical globe** <note>original: "Sphaeraglobul," referring to the Earth or the material world</note> hang their heads downward, and yet they do not fall; they hang. But that this happens to them not as a downward motion, but as an upward one, and that the effect within them stands upward and stands in nothing: that is a special work of God, about which nothing can be philosophized, but is so ordained that all things are seen upward with their entire being. And it is a clumsy Philosophy <note>original: "vnbeholpff Philosophia"</note> practiced by those who philosophize that the Sun draws things to itself, and thus whatever the Sun draws to itself looks upward. Much remains unaccounted for and forgotten there, and it has a meager appearance compared to the foundation of the philosophers. For there is no power in such attraction by the **stars** <note>original: "Astris"</note> or firmament regarding their attraction. We wonder how they intend to justify that the stars do not pull the plants up entirely; what is there to hinder it? But the Spirit drives its fools.

## CHAPTER V.

And although we have established how God set the elements out of Nothing and made them as a God: we wish to philosophize on where He put that which was formerly in that place and occupied the position: accordingly, we shall further describe the element **Air** <note>Latin: "Aer"</note>. In the place where the four elements stand, there was once that which was cast out into **Hell**, and it occupied the place along with its followers. For that is the Heaven from which he <note>Lucifer</note> was cast out: and it is the place in which the four elements are contained. And what was not cast out into Hell at that same location is at the end that is reserved from perishability, which is **Paradise**, the other place of the elements. Now the elements are essentially created and filled throughout the circle, so that there is no further place within them that may be Heavenly or Hellish: unless there were something at the ends and places where nothing human is or can be, in which Hell were enclosed, where those lie who are cast out; or they must be among us, without any power or joy, or banned and bound into the substance of the elements. For that is the greatest Hell, that they must be and dwell in the perishable, and not as they were in their Kingdom. For such is indeed to be reckoned a Hell, when an angel of Paradise is thrust out into the world and robbed of Paradise. His Hell could not be greater than this: that he who is eternal and had nothing perishable about him should dwell in the perishable; he can have no greater pain. Thus we conclude that the place of the four elements was the Heaven of **Lucifer**: and he was not thrust out of it, but that same Heaven is perishable and set into the elements. That is his punishment, that he must remain therein. He did not expect that God would turn such a Heaven, such a delight, into elements: rather he intended that he should always remain thus in Heaven, therefore nothing could be taken from him. Now when God created the four elements without his further word, this creation and the creature was his casting into Hell: that is, out of the light of Heaven into the darkness, which is into the perishable world. Therefore some of his company dwell in the fire, in the air, in the earth, in the water: and no devil dwells outside the elements, but all in the four elements. And when the perishing of the world comes, then a sheepfold shall be made of all those who are enclosed in the four elements. Thus the beginning of the four elements is created out of Nothing: for the cause is that in the place where they are now, there was nothing perishable out of which the perishable could have been created. Therefore the imperishable had to give way into Paradise, and in its place the perishable was created by God: initially the Heaven, that is, the **Chaos**, which is the element Air, as stated above, and thereafter the other elements as stated above. Therefore, regarding the dryness of the air, we do not deny that there are many spirits, also in the "egest" <note>likely referring to the void or outward discharge</note> of the air, between the Chaos and the globe: but such is without prejudice to the elements. And as it has been shown how the element Air is created in three matters and set into three parts: how these same three parts perform their effects follows hereafter.

## CHAPTER VI.

To speak of the element Air, know that the Air encloses all other elements and all creatures within itself, and contains them so that they remain in their ordained order as they were created. For the Air is that into whose power the other three elements are given, so that they are contained by the Air. Just as a house is set upon a foundation, so are the elements set into the Air, which must lift and carry them. Since the Air now carries the other elements so that they remain in their places: it is to be philosophized what lifts and carries the Air. That same power which lifts it is the outward part of the element wherein God dwells in the **Trinity**; He lifts the Air so that it does not give way, nor can it give way, nor can it break. For it is impossible that the perishable should fall into the imperishable. Also, it cannot fall because the cause is that everything stands upward and nothing downward; it has no bottom or depth. Thus powerfully is the Air compacted and kept in a circle, so that it is as little possible for it to break or scatter as it is for the outer Kingdom to perish. But if it is to perish or break, then there is no other breaking than that everything shall and will fall into the **Center** <note>Latin: "Centrum"</note>: that is, the Air and the stars will fall into the globe, and the globe will be consumed by them, so that no ash will remain. Thus the breaking of the perishable heaven and the earth and all elements stands not to fall outward, but inward into the Center. For that is the highest in the secret...

# ON THE ELEMENT OF AIR.
<margin>A</margin> It is the agreement of the philosophers to seek why the ring should fall into the center: for the reason that there should be no depth there, neither to fall out nor to fall in. And that nothing stands downward on this, outward-facing, and internally everything stands downward inward-facing, and nothing upward: so that the center stands just as well as the Upper Heaven. Thus the Heaven is above in the entire circle, and nothing is below, although it stands below and above in the circle.

### CHAPTER VII.
### Concerning the Element of Fire, how it passes.
<margin>A</margin> But it is proper to philosophize on how the internal elements divide themselves in the aforementioned circle, and that is as follows. The Air is the first passage and the outermost; after that is the Firmament. These two hold the Chaos <note>In Paracelsian terms, "Chaos" often refers to the atmospheric space or the primordial matter from which elements are sustained.</note> within and encompass the globes and spheres. The Earth and the Water provide the globes, mixed and mingled with one another: yet each in its place as a perfect element. The upper two give their impression upon the lower two, that is, upon the globes; the two in the globe keep their impressions with them, do not cast them out, but receive them again: as the chapters on impressions <note>Refers to the "Impressio," the celestial influence or "signature" exerted by higher bodies on lower ones.</note> show for each in particular. Thus it can be seen how these same elements hold themselves, so that they do not [fall] out of their circle, nor stand above, but only inward, and thus nothing may fall in: for the globe lies at the bottom, and the heaven at the top. Also, what is beneath the globe, we let that be a wonder of God. But philosophy is this: how the globe is contained, and that is as follows. The Fire is thus ordered and divided into stars, so that it does not come out of the passage, just like a [bird], but does not fall onto the globe; the reason is that God [placed] the globe in the center under the Air, and it sustains itself from the Air, just like a bird. But the <margin>B</margin> inner parts are the heaviest and most material and substantial. That which holds the lower seas and the lower earths so they do not fall is this: [nothing] can fall, neither the earth nor the globe. For what is between the globe and [the heaven] is a clear element, and so perfect in its element that it carries, just as the [water carries a ship]. And just as the Earth is compact within itself, in that same [way it sustains] itself: so also is the Air.

---

## That the Heaven does not run around, and that
## it seethes from the Element of Fire, and gives the
## Clarity and air.
### CHAPTER II.
<margin>A</margin> But to philosophize concerning the element of Air <note>original: "Aer"</note>, what moves within it, or what that may be that moves the same, or whether it moves or not, is such: Accordingly, and firstly, consider that the Air, which is there, the circuit of heaven, is not such that it turns around and around in a circular manner. For the Air is the Clarity <note>The "Claar" or "Clarity" refers to the translucent, life-giving quality of the atmosphere.</note>, the brightness; the same takes itself out of [the center]. It does not run, as some think, but it arises from the egestion <note>The process of "voiding" or "breathing out" from a central source.</note> of the Chaos, so that in the element there is an outflowing and a digestion; this same process creates from itself the vapor, which gives us the air in the world, and is a Clarity of the world, to hold the center.
<margin>C</margin> But so that you may distinguish the philosophers from one another: the idea that the heaven should run or that the heaven runs around in a circle, and thereafter the same circle [moves] the world, is not so. For if such were the case, the world and the sea would [be destroyed]. Also, such a motion would create only a wind, not air, and wind has other origins, and air has others. For Air and Wind are two different things. [That the heaven] stands still is yet without harm: for if it stands still in its egestion, it gives the same air as the world must have, and not less or [more].

# PHILOSOPHY

This vapor occurred along the lines toward the Center, that is, along the lines in the growth of the world that stand toward Heaven. And thus, a uniform vapor rises from the Chaos upon the world; that is, the clear wind arises from the outer vapor, or the Air. Thus, this rising of the vapor does not come solely from the bubbling up, and it can possess no form, power, or virtue of the Chaos, so that one element hangs within the other, and none can exist without the others.

<note>The author uses "Chaos" here in the Paracelsian sense, referring to the atmosphere or the primordial matter from which elements are sustained.</note>

In this way, the element of Fire, which lies closest beneath the Air, is the very thing that—through its fire, acting as an element—causes the Upper Chaos to boil. And it is not the case that because more stars dwell in one place than another, it should boil more there, which would then produce more Air. Rather, the boiling is like a pot that seethes from every side; though it boils in particular spots, it is still only one pot that boils.

<note>The "pot" analogy explains that the universe functions as a single, closed system of heat and transformation.</note>

Thus, the distribution of the element of Fire was not created solely for the sake of pride or symbolic meaning, but for the sake of the <term>Nature-breath<note>original: "Naturkufft" - likely a variant of "Naturkluft" or "Naturkraft," referring here to the natural vital breath or power of the elements.</note></term>

### Follows:
#### A fragment, which perhaps also belongs to these philosophers' *On the Air*.

<sig>A</sig> The fall <note>literally "thrust" or "push"</note> of Lucifer was not that he was cast out of his kingdom into another kingdom of the spheres; rather, it is thus: He remained in his place, but that same place became transformed for him into the most impure state, contrary to his essence—that is, into the perishable. And thus he must, as an angel, dwell in the place of the second adversity, eternally and perishably locked within one.

Adam was not cast out of Paradise in such a way as if he had been moved from one country to another; rather, he was cast out in that Paradise was taken from him, and the world beneath his feet and before his eyes was transformed into the perishable world, into the mortal body, into sickness, and into adversity. He remained in his place, but the place itself was changed.

<sig>B</sig> Hell is not outside of the Center, but in the Center at the ends and places where man dwells. But it is different when the soul departs from the body; it remains where the body was and does not travel a thousand miles upwards or downwards. If it is blessed, it remains there; if it is infernal, it remains there. For thus joy and suffering are in one place. That which is preserved is in joy at that place; that which is damned is with these. The joy of one is the weeping of the other.
And to speak in conclusion, the interpretation is such: that everything which encompasses the Center with Heaven and Earth was once Paradise, and was thus transformed into that which has been described. And when Heaven and Earth shall pass away, then it shall once again be Paradise entirely, and shall be one Essence that is eternal, with nothing perishable within it.

To philosophize against us is difficult, and difficult to withstand us; unless it be that the Sophist <note>a term often used by Paracelsian writers to describe traditional scholastic academics who lack true spiritual insight</note> reads and notes the origin of perishable things and the origin of mankind. Then a reconciliation might occur, so that a philosopher might understand what we are speaking of here. We refer them to our books *The Fall of Lucifer*, *The Expulsion of Adam*, or *The Celestial and Infernal Kingdom* <note>original Latin titles: "Lapfu [Lapsu] Luciferi, Expulsione Adæ, oder Regno Cœlesti & Infernali"</note>, so that all things may be concluded most briefly for your understanding. For those same books begin from the first Essence and treat of the creation of perishable things, Heaven and Earth, and of Man, and there they end. Then this, our Philosophy, begins from the four elements. Therefore, we rightly direct you to the beginnings from which this Philosophy flows and takes its ground.

<sig>C</sig> And even if it does not suit the Sophist with his light of nature, he will not see a hole through it. For we give you to understand that in the beginning, men erred concerning the true ground of the cast-out Lucifer, and the expulsion of Adam and of Paradise. And they have persisted in that same error continually, and still do, only telling lies out of that error, commenting and questioning. And no one wants to consider whether the text he comments upon has come to light correctly or not, or whether some part of it is understood within you or not. For all such things must be tested by the Philosopher alone, and not the Sophist, who lies in such a way as he finds it in his calendar, which is full of every error.

### BOOK THREE ON METEORS, BY THEOPHRASTUS VON HOHENHEIM, GERMAN PHILOSOPHER.
REGARDING
METEORIC PHENOMENA FROM THE ELEMENT OF FIRE.
and the impressions thereof.

An introduction or preface by THEOPHRASTUS,
on the Impression of the Element of Fire, that is, from the
Firmament.
<sig>B</sig>
As we have mentioned in the first prefaces concerning the three Firsts <note>The "Tria Prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>, how all things of Meteoric action reside within them and are worked through them: the Firmament and the Elements stand within them, and the Impressions <note>term: "Impression" refers to celestial influences or atmospheric phenomena acting upon the earthly realm</note> come upon them. Thus, the same is to be seen in this Third Book of Meteors, since the first books have encompassed such things. Here it is to be understood that all Impressions have their origin from the stars and elements, as shall be mentioned and encompassed hereafter. But how these same Impressions are born out of them, we wish to recount in this *Meteororum*. As for the fact that other writers on Meteors have not shared in our philosophy—and still do not—but have described Meteoric matters differently: perhaps the spirit that directed their *Meteororum* brought forth some of their thoughts, yet it was not sufficient for the sense of an upright spirit to follow or respect his physics. Nature alone must give the right spirit and reach its foundation, otherwise no Philosopher is born. For the Philosopher is born in Nature and is proven through Experience <note>original: "Experiens"</note>, and not in the sharp-witted spirit of fantasies, which plays for its own amusement in its fantasizing. One who wishes to be a philosopher should look upon us with a friendly eye, in such a way that the Incorporeal Spirits are nothing else toward us all than as lords over their servants and people: and thus should it be understood. The lords create and command, and that same thing must be acted out: thus the servants are nothing but the lords' fools. For anyone would well like to be a lord himself, and not a lord's fool: but because that is the destiny, fools are also there. Thus the Incorporeal Spirits act, and in that we become fools: that is, we come out of our fantasies, art, and reason without any Experience—which should be a mother to our reason, wisdom, and arts. Then we are fools of the spirits, joking with us as a lord does with his like. Praiseworthy is the wise man who seeks his wisdom upon the [foundation]; [a fool] is he who makes himself wise, when the spirits above [make him] their fool. We must all confess that we have not been in the furnace nor in the heat in which we see the Impressions: will it not be a necessity for us to travel through them as from one city to another? It suffices us that we recognize the Other Nature, which is a mirror to us of an Experience that teaches us the essence and property of the Higher Nature. Therefore it is rightly recognized by us to [bring] Experience into the other: for our things signify and indicate the others. [We proceed] to describe the Impressions one after another, according to their origin, as shall be shown.
<sig>C</sig>

But the reason that the Hoarfrost in its form is not like frozen water, as the Dew [is]...

# CONCERNING METEOROLOGY FROM THE ELEMENT OF FIRE.

<margin>a</margin> Dew lies as if it were a smooth, frozen thing, like frozen water. However, hoarfrost is granulated and crinkled. The reason for this is that dew is a **dissolved salt** <note>original: "Resolutierts Saltz"</note> that has turned into water. It is the nature of this substance that when it is forced into **congealing**—whether by its own nature, by accidental artifice, or by the influence of mineral currents—it forms into small grains, corners, and stone-like shapes. For this reason, when the frost meets the dew, it forces the dew to congeal, and so it takes its natural form according to its essence, which is to crinkle and granulate.

### Concerning Dew.

<margin>b</margin> The origin of dew is as follows: When the winds of the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the sky or heavens as a physical and spiritual sphere.</note> go their way clear and dry, and the sun cuts across the earth with purity, then out of such powerful beauty, the **Three Primes** <note>The Tria Prima: Salt (stability/body), Sulfur (combustibility/soul), and Mercury (fluidity/spirit).</note> purify themselves. They become as pure and clear as a distilled substance. This same purification enters a state of congealing, so that it reaches a state of aridity and becomes entirely dry. But such congealed aridity lasts only as long as the heat of the firmament remains within it. When they lose their heat—as when the sun moves away from them and no longer touches them—then whatever is of **Salt** dissolves itself and falls upon the earth. It is so subtle that it cannot be noticed or felt until it touches the ground. For a Salt can be so clear and **rectified** <note>Refined or purified through a chemical-like process.</note> by the sun that no comparable subtle salt can be perceived. And the cold from below presses into this coldness. A portion of it mixes into the Salt, yet the Salt predominates. Whatever has not been sufficiently purified from the Three Primes by the sun remains in the **middle spaces** <note>original: "medijs Interstitijs"; the gaps between the atmospheric layers.</note>. Therefore, the reason is: the more completely the sun works, the greater the dew. Thus, it is a thing that does not come from the earth, but falls like a salt upon the earth, through which the earth receives its tempering, just as soup receives its flavor from salt.

### Concerning Manna.

<margin>c</margin> <note>The original text uses "Thron," likely referring to "Thau-reiff" or a specific form of Manna/Heavenly honey.</note> The origin of Manna is similar to what was told of the purification of dew. When the sun passes through and purifies **Mercury**, just as it does with the Sulfur and Salt in the Three Primes, this Mercury is held in the cold by the heat of the firmament, just like the dew. Mercury cannot contain itself for long when the cold seizes it as it occurs. And even if it is contained throughout the night like the dew, it afterwards falls to the earth in the same way. It is not spread out like the dew, but falls in certain patches and not on others. This is because Mercury is heavy; it does not allow itself to be scattered or blown by the air as the dew does, which is light and made salty after it has been refined. Mercury, however, is not so light, even though it lies mixed within the dew. It is an essence of Mercury without substance contained within it. It is like **Manna** <note>original: "Trott Reictern," likely referring to "Himmelstau" or Manna.</note>, than which nothing is sweeter among all things that come down from above to the earth; it is sleek, somewhat viscous, well-colored, and of pure white. It is separated from the Salt: the Manna comes from the Mercury, while the Sulfur is burnt away from its substance. Whatever essence remains within it mixes with the others.

### Concerning Mist.

<margin>d</margin> The origin of Mist is as follows: when the **Sulfur** of the Three Primes, due to the moisture of the Salt, cannot be burnt or consumed by the heat of the sun, it turns into a substance; that is, it becomes separated from the other two. For whatever becomes a substance is now a "born" thing, and what is a born thing is separated from the "unborn." Just as the Three Primes are unborn and gathered together in the middle spaces, whichever among them receives a substance through the firmament becomes a different "child" of the Three Primes. Thus, Dew is a child of Salt, and Manna is a child of Mercury. They are born into a substance through the celestial cycles. Therefore, they are the first to fall from the unborn state. In this way, **Mist** is a child of Sulfur, as has been indicated. It cannot become Dew, for it is too coarse and cannot be clarified. Nor can it become Manna, for it does not resolve into a juicy thing; rather, its essence is to produce a coarse vapor. When the cycles of the firmament give birth to something within it, it becomes nothing but a mist. Because the Salt does not allow it to be consumed, it separates from the unborn elements and falls to the earth's floor with a gloom, thickness, taste, and a certain dampness that comes to it from the Salt. And just as Salt is the mother of Dew in its properties, so is Sulfur the mother of Mist. Thus the three "born" things are fathered by the sun and shaped according to the properties of their origin. Such mists have no staying power in the air nor from the heat, but they fall every hour as soon as they are born. Although there are some mists born with very little Sulfur that are hardly felt on the earth, when they come from the water—since water is moist and the Salt is in the Sulfur—it becomes thick. The opposing force of the Salt, which is its moisture, drives the Sulfur; otherwise, without the moisture of the Salt, it would not be so gloomy. This occurs specifically according to the division of the Three Primes upon the ground and water.

<summary>This page explains the alchemical origins of dew, manna, and mist, attributing each to one of the Three Primes: Salt, Mercury, and Sulfur respectively. It describes weather as a process of celestial distillation and purification occurring in the "middle spaces" of the atmosphere.</summary>

# CLOUDS. <note>original: "NVBES"</note>

<margin>A</margin>The origin of clouds <note>original: "Gewülchs"</note> is thus: In the stars of the firmaments there is a contrary nature; when these collide with one another and pass through each other, births arise from them. In the nature of clouds, these are of the sulfurous form, as they pass into the essence of the sulfurous stars or mercurial stars. Thus occurs the assembly of the three primes in a contrary nature; this contrary assembly is the cause of the three natures of clouds: in Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury. Every star is powerful in its prime; and when the Salt-star enters the paths of the Sulfur-star, two things happen: for the sulfur burns in its star, and the saltpeter <note>original: "Saltzperer," likely referring to nitre or saltpeter as a reactive salt</note> fights in its star. So when these two come together, the sulfur-star ignites, and thereafter a storm is born out of the stars, according to the properties of the two stars. If it is a cold ignition, such that the sulfur is not pure in the saltpeter, then it does not ignite fully, but only in part. Just as when arsenic is placed in a fire, it is a salt but a dead salt, doing nothing but smelling; antimony <note>original: "Speißglaß," the historical term for antimony ore</note> is the same, and others more. Thus, just as there are many living salts here on earth, so too are there many kinds of stellar natures. From such things, when the sulfur-stars ignite a salt-star, according to what that star is, a smoke is birthed which is called a cloud. For every cloud is merely a smoke of its star. Therefore, a cloud is nothing other than an ignition by a sulfur-star into the salt and mercurial stars; for under these three, all stars are contained.

## RAIN. <note>original: "PLVVIÆ"</note>
<sig>B</sig>
<margin>B</margin>The origin of rain is thus: as the beginning of clouds was shown, so is the beginning of rain and the various kinds of clouds. For instance, an arsenic-cloud gives no rain, only a gray, thick cloud that dissipates again without wetness. There are many such arsenic-clouds, pure and dark white, and of other such colors, depending on whether the arsenic is much or little, according to how the sun purifies and ignites the stars. When the sun ignites the sulfur-stars well and lets them go on burning, then the stars are simple. But where one star, in its nature, touches the other two primes in its matter, the effect follows according to its properties. Thus, when it ignites salt—that is, the salt-stars—it turns into a wet cloud. That same cloud is a pure salt that comes out of the salt-stars. And as soon as it becomes a "birth" from the "unborn" <note>Paracelsian terms for the transition from potential matter to physical manifestation</note> out of the stars, then the wind carries it. And as soon as it comes out from the stars, it is heavy and falls toward the earth, or even upon the earth, if it is not a well-cooked salt of the heavy kind. And while it stands in the middle of the sky, if it does not come to the earth because of the lightness of the wind or air, it begins to resolve <note>term for dissolving or melting</note>, and resolves itself in the middle of the sky into water, just as a liquefied or watery salt does out of marble; not all at once, but gradually, one part after another. As it resolves from the substance of the cloud, it falls upon the earth, for it has no wind within it. And from the high fall down from the middle of the sky to the earth, it shatters and falls apart through the air and wind, which it creates for itself in its heavy fall, so that it comes down in drops. It is as if someone pours a bucket <note>original: "Schaff," a vessel or tub</note> of water down from a tower; it does not fall in a heap as it was poured out, but it scatters apart into drops. Thus the cloud resolves itself for as long as it takes for all the wet salt to come out. For there are many clouds that have more than ten kinds of stars in them, wet and dry: what is wet falls, what is dry remains a cloud.

### Cloudburst. <note>original: "Wolckenbruch"</note>
The origin of cloudbursts is thus: When the sulfur-star ignites a powerful salt-star of an antimonial kind, and this birth is then separated out from the star, if it was a complete salt-star, it has no air in it to carry it. These do not remain in the middle of the sky, but they fall toward the ground. If they do not fall to the ground in the manner of a driving rain <note>original: "Plageregenweiß"</note>, these have within them arsenic, antimony, and the like; these do not let [the water] fall [gradually], but whatever turns into water-cloud beneath them falls down all at once, following the resolution. Therefore, cloudbursts are nothing other than a swelling salt [driven] by the sulfur-star and through the firmament. This is from all other genera of salts and stars; and as soon as it catches the air, it has nothing to hold it up, for it is a compact, resolved water in a heap. Then it falls all together heavily toward the ground, because it is a hurried resolution, happening all at once and not one after another like other rain. The same applies to all other types of the three primes.

### Lightning and Thundering.

As has been mentioned regarding the properties of the stars—that some consist of Sulfur, some of Salt, and some of Mercury—so it happens that when a Sulfurous star <note>In this context, "stars" refer to invisible atmospheric forces or "astral" influences rather than distant suns.</note> brushes against a Nitrous star <note>Nitrous refers to Saltpeter (niter), associated here with cold and explosive force.</note>, and before the two come together substantially in their physical matter, they possess a contrariety toward one another. For the Sulfur and Saltpeter remain distinct until the Sun ignites the Sulfur through its heat in summer, or the Sulfur (being easily flammable) is ignited in winter. Thus, a Nitrous star breaks apart. Initially, they produce smoke—that is, a cloud—which goes forth before it catches fire. Then, as they do not "smell" <note>likely meaning "mix" or "harmonize"</note> together, the Sulfur drives the Saltpeter so strongly into motion that a wind is created by their repulsion; as they retreat from one another, it goes out with the wind.

As the Sulfur approaches the Salt more and more, and the cloud becomes longer and stronger, all of this grows out of the Sulfur falling so violently into the Saltpeter. The Saltpeter then blows the burning Sulfur out from itself through the cloud in a sudden thrust; and when this thrust from the Saltpeter occurs, then **Lightning** is born. For lightning is nothing other than a back-stroke <note>a recoil or sudden discharge</note> occurring in one or more thrusts. Note this: it has received its richness from the Sulfur so that it does not burn out immediately, but carries a fire within itself, and thus strikes the Sulfur into lightning through the clouds. It also breaks within itself, and the contrariety of these two forces shatters them apart; in that very clash, **Thundering** arises. And once the thunder has occurred, the cloud resolves itself into rain, according to the property of Salt. Thus the Sulfur is extinguished in its burning, the Saltpeter also dissolves, and a beautiful [calm] follows afterward.

The same also happens when a rain falls during such contrary workings of Sulfur and Saltpeter within the cloud. If such a rain rises above the first two and touches the vapor, the greatest and most notable thunders are produced, for water is the greatest opponent to such fire. Likewise, if a Mercurial star <note>associated with fluidity and volatility</note> joins them, the thunder and lightning are strengthened, becoming longer and more powerful. For therein is nothing but the contrariety of the Three Primes <note>Sulfur, Salt, and Mercury</note> when they meet in one path; none can stand by the other when they are in their fundamental state of damage or "burning." This is their "burning": when the Sun ignites them. When they come together while hot, they easily ignite one another, and as they attempt to mix, they shatter one another.

### Hailing.

<margin>The origin of hail is thus: when a Sulfurous star seizes a Nitrous star, etc.</margin>

As has been shown regarding the property of the Nitrous star: when it moves in a powerful path beneath the Sun, and the Sun drives it through the solar heat so that the Saline matter is digested <term>Digestion: a process of slow heating used in alchemy to mature or transform a substance</term>. Through this heat, it is in the nature of Salt that in all digestion it coagulates into small grains. When this occurs, the Salt drives itself into little stones, according to whether it is a "bad" Salt, wet or dry, sharp or sweet, according to its quality. Now, while it is in this state of "birthing," it is not completed unless a Sulfur-fire is present and lightning is underway. Then, in that same ignition—as is seen with thunder—the Saltpeter is struck apart. And although it is not yet perfectly made into stones or grains, this happens during the fall. This is the way of the Saline nature in coagulation.

However, if only a Nitrous star of that property is in coagulation, and the Sun shines through it and it takes in the light—igniting it without a Sulfurous star, yet not to the point of burning (for the stars ignite nothing to a flame among the Three Primes except Sulfur)—then, when the star is thus in the heat of the Sun and is as hot as if it were fire, Salt alone is born. It granulates into little stones according to the nature and shape of its quality. But the moisture still present with the Saltpeter prevents the coagulation from becoming perfect; rather, it hinders it. But as soon as a Sulfurous star is joined to it and touches the Saltpeter with its fire, it proceeds just as was said. As soon as the Saltpeter receives the flame from the Sulfur, they strike each other multiple times, and each time is a thunderclap. And as the shattering of thunder occurs, the effects fall down—that which the Saline nature has formed through the Salt-fire—and the rest resolves into water. Thus **Hail** and **Rain** fall together from one cloud. For it is one matter which has been extinguished by the burning Sulfur, specifically in the Salt-star; and this never happens except in great heat, because the Sun must powerfully digest it.

### The Thunderbolt and the Shadow.
<note>The term "Straal" (modern German: Strahl) here refers specifically to a lightning bolt or "thunderbolt."</note>

The nature of the thunderbolt is as follows. As has been indicated regarding the three stars <note>The "Three Primes": Sulfur, Salt, and Mercury, which Paracelsus viewed as the fundamental components of all matter</note> individually, it is to be known that the joining of these three stars together results in a single path and circle, with powerful force, and yet the sulfur does not burn. Then they lead the previous elements together so that they come into one matter—the sulfur, the salt, and the great powerful heat of the sun—and so they unite in a mixture. And although they stand together without conflict, this mixture is not harmful, and exists within a wind. Or, if a salt-water separates from it, or an arsenic, that goes toward the rain. But while they are in this state of action within a water, their matter is such that through the greatest ascent, it whitens everything from itself that may become water or rain. Thus, they remain stars in a compact assembly, which is compressed into one another with great motion.

Upon this, as the sun through its mighty compaction <note>The process of thickening or solidifying</note> then strikes, the Mercury, the Saltpeter, and the Sulfur <note>original: "Solphur"</note> are drawn from one place into another in the middle of the heavens, and do not break apart from one another; rather, their collective compact freezing <note>original: "Congelierung"</note> remains firm as one. And even if it breaks, the pieces still remain firmly together and burn. Such is the turbulence of the saltpeter and mercury that they make an unbelievably sudden crack from their position against one another, so that it drives all clouds and rain away before it. If the crack occurs in the heights, it is not noticed on the earth as it truly is, for it is stifled in the heights without a perceptible fire, and is extinguished and falls downward without turbulence. But if it falls through the rain, it strikes again, for the water in the rain and its great heat oppose one another, so that it comes to strike again and hits the earth according to how it is moved by the opposition. And gradually it works: and is thus called a "cold thunderbolt"; or if it is a "horn-bolt" <note>original: "Hewrin," likely referring to a specific sharp or piercing type of lightning</note> and extinguishes itself in the rain-clouds, it is also cold and not fiery. 

But initially, they are all fiery, and strike with a blow, and are joined in a powerful compact. And if it remains fiery and strikes toward the valley, it catches and burns, striking that which is like itself. For there is the greatest opposition within a compaction together that can be found, for these are the "Three Primes," and there is no breaker to melt them. Thus, there would be more to write of such signs and histories than of other descriptions of men.
<sig>B</sig>

## On Witch-Weather.
<note>original: "Herenwettern" (Hexenwetter). This refers to storms believed to be supernaturally conjured by witches or demons.</note>

The origin of witch-weather is as follows: Although witch-weathers are not natural, we did not wish to defile our five books of *Meteors* with them. But it is proper to treat them as meteorological phenomena, and thus: We shall leave aside the very first beginning of such weather. Secondly, we wish to note that the infernal spirits <note>Demons or fallen angels</note> create and make these same weathers above. For what reasons they do this to the detriment of man, we do not wish to reveal here. But their operation is such that they have nothing in themselves, but rather a sulfur and pitch and salt and mercury, and that in many hundreds of forms. For this reason, the cause is so arranged that they fulfill the will of man and, having prepared it, they come into their place in the heavens and erupt in such a form. Then the clear firmament does not let them remain, but strikes them every time out of the middle heaven toward their place. But their resistance is so strong in return that they make a roar and a revival. This roar is in their power, so that they themselves—upon their own sulfur, salt, and mercury—make a smoke, clouds, rain, and the like. For just as we show the "digestions" <note>The alchemical process of maturation or transformation</note> of the stars and how "egestions" <note>Waste products or discharges</note> come from them, so in the infernal spirits there is a similar digestion that gives its discharge. This discharge is of their nature, upon them; that is nothing but wind, hail, showers, and thunderbolts, and much more wicked and harmful than other thunderbolts from the firmament. Such an effect proceeds in parts and changes to create enmity, and ends in witchcraft as nothing other than a discharge from the infernal spirits, who then have power over their infernal nature to make all such storms, in which they lie full day and night. What further should be understood regarding such spirits, we have sufficiently mentioned through the nature and the causes—that is, how it happens in witch-weather.

This center is thus dedicated to colors, just like a salt that lies in the fire, and its vapor is of all colors; as that is changed, so its colors are displayed.

### Rain of Blood, Frogs, and other Animals
Humans (as giants).

<margin>A</margin> The origin of rains of blood, frogs, and similar animals is this. Every star is a seed of the one part, from the <term>Three Firsts</term> <note>The Tria Prima: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt</note>, and every [seed] of the firsts is manifold and in many forms: like wood, of which there are many kinds, stone, and other such things. From this it comes that in certain stars are born raw sulfur, yellow arsenic of all colors, and mercury of all colors. And when such has been born in it out of its own power: then it pours that out from itself. For what is born there, it can no longer endure within itself; and so, if a redness of its sulfurous or mercurial kind [arises] from the <term>Geyle</term> <note>Lust or fertile discharge; here used to mean a celestial seminal emission</note> of a star: then that same star [pours it] to the ground, and it is scattered to fall down from the height like a rain, and thus appears as a red rain like blood. This is not a rain [in the sense of] how rains normally originate, but it is like a [discharge] of a star, which thus pours its fertility out upon the earth. It should be noted that if a star [pours] its fertility from it, there are many that give a "corpse" <note>A physical residue or matrix</note> upon which something living may grow in the likeness of worms, frogs, and other such things. But such [creatures soon] die off. It is also possible that the greater stars give birth to humans; [these] rains are an ignition from one star into another, through their manifold nature: but such is a
<margin>B</margin> fertility of each star in particular.

### Falls of Metals and Stones.

<margin>A</margin> The origin of falling stones is this. Which stars have in them the clay-like kind of sulfur, that is, the saline sulfur, as those stars are which give birth to sulfur and the salt-flow: so when that same star bears the matter in itself, at the end of its operation, it throws the same out from itself: from such comes the seed of all stars. For the birthing of nature, or from growing of itself, or one from another, [comes from] the stars, which thus let their fertility fall; and this is like a stranger [in] a field where the seed was not sown: in this place there is no [root], but it has let its "corpse" fall, upon which such a plant stands. For only the stars bear them originally as a seed.

## On Earthquakes.
(The beginning is missing.)

Where the ground is sandy and reedy, or of a soft earth, and a portion of it is peeled away from the upper part of the earth by rivers, then the fall causes a trembling in that same place; or one may judge this by the great weight of its mass. Also, if the earth has a hollow beneath it and a crust: where a piece of the earth falls into those same hollows in that place, then earthquakes also occur there. Or if two crusts fall into one another: all this creates a great wind, which is pressed by the aforementioned cause and forced to yield from its place. Such wind breaks open paths and <term>cataracts</term> <note>waterfalls or floodgates; here referring to subterranean channels</note> near the piece that falls. For where there is no fall, there is no damage; but where there is a great fall, it drives the wind with violence into earthquakes. Many such earthquakes will occur when the cliffs and the mighty mountains see themselves, when their feet shall spark, which the whole world shall feel.

## On the <term>Lorindt</term>.
<note>Lorindt: A regional or archaic term likely referring to a "roaring" sound or a "water-boom" associated with ice or subterranean water movement.</note>
<sig>B</sig>
The origin of the <term>Lorindt</term> is thus. The <term>Lorindt</term> is just like the earthquake, and has such a beginning. When beneath great waters rich with ships, lakes, and flowing streams, a <term>cataract</term> <note>subterranean channel</note> goes, and a hole digs through the bottom of the lake—caused by the softening of the water from the lake into that same <term>cataract</term>—then the lake water falls through into the water below. And in that same falling, because of the air, it lets out a "plumb" sound, just as when one pours water from a narrow vessel so that it "glugs"; thus it glugs in the same way. This glugging, when it is in winter, we have heard it: for the cold gives the <term>resonance</term> <note>original: "Resonanz"</note> of the waters. Then the voice in the water changes, just as if it were another cry, like one who sings in a pot submerged in water: his voice is unrecognizable, and the place of it is unknown. Likewise, when the earthquakes of the waters happen in this way, or in other great waters such holes occur: then the water runs through the lake-water, and where it runs, it gives a voice, according to whether it runs strongly or weakly. Such a voice also goes through the water and is a <term>Lorindt</term>, which lasts as long as the hole remains open. Thus every <term>Lorindt</term> is a running water beneath itself; such water is heard most in winter and in great cold. The reason is that summer takes away the voice, for warm water breaks such a voice; the colder it is, the sharper the sound. Also, some <term>Lorindts</term> arise when a lake freezes over at the top, or in some parts: then the great steam that is in the water beneath the ice forces the ice to break where it is weakest. Thus when a hole or crack occurs, the vapor from the water beneath the ice goes toward that same hole. Then, as far as it can reach out, so far does it "shout": because the great <term>impetus</term> <note>force or momentum</note> moves the air that lies enclosed under the ice, which must go out with violence. This violence at the exit goes out with a cry, just as a covered vapor breaks the lid and bangs. Thus there is such power in the vapor that it goes out with <term>impetus</term>, and because of the great cold, it has a "cold cry," and the ice [vibrates] up to that same hole. And the nearer to the hole, the smaller the cry, because of the opening. Every <term>Lorindt</term> that comes from vapor is nothing but like a pipe through which the wind goes and makes a sound: thus it is also a piping, the air caught between water and ice.

<sig>C</sig>
The origin of the <term>wind</term> is thus. In the circumference of the world, upon its <term>planes</term> <note>original: "Planis" — likely referring to the flat surfaces or zones of the earth</note>, as the lines draw themselves, and in the <term>firmament</term> <note>the heavens or sky</note>, these same are fixed and constant, and have their own nature and periods, and are <term>elemental arches</term> <note>original: "Elementischer arch" — structures governing the elements</note>, so that they have the likeness of elemental effects. As one wind is warm, the other cold, the third moist, the fourth dry; such is written of them. These stars in the circumference of the <term>planes</term>, attached to the <term>firmament</term>, opposite the <term>planes</term>, reach over and over the earth and the sea. Thus the wind is a birth from such stars, of which there are very many in the circle of the circumference: for it is born out of them as an <term>egest</term> <note>original: "Egest" — a discharge or waste product</note> of that same star. And every wind is assigned to nothing else: when the stars cleanse themselves of their digestion, then the wind is driven. And every main wind is an <term>egest</term> of its star. Although otherwise it is from the weather, as from the discharge of water and rain: that same winds along with the main wind. For only the main winds are those that go out from such satisfactions through the <term>emunition</term> <note>original: "Emunition" — a cleansing or purging, like a biological "emunctory" organ</note> toward the earth, over the sea.
