within them. But who can escape this, or step outside of its path? Thus there is one cause above us, and one with us. The one above us hides itself; the one beneath us, its power is within us. From this it follows that death does not come through us, nor is it turned away by us. Therefore, the First Medicine <note>The "First Medicine" likely refers to divine or fundamental healing principles established by God.</note> must follow us in our blindness with watchful eyes. Thus it is proper to write of our own affairs, from one thing to the next: the beginning of which is caused by the water of physical springs, undertaken here among others in their proper order.

### III.
God has scattered and sprinkled such medicine here and there throughout the world: for He has also placed wonders in the world to meet the diseases of the fruits of the earth. And just as men are divided into particular kingdoms—he who has the French Disease <note>original: "Frantzosen"; a common historical term for syphilis.</note> upon him is the same as the one by the Danube <note>original: "Thonan".</note>: the one in Germany <note>original: "Teutschlandt"</note> is the same as others. Therefore, though they are not identical to one another, yet it is one and the same thing. So also, if another water is found that we do not describe here, it is to be considered similar in origin, beginning, and derivation to the water described. For consider yourselves how small a thing it is, and for one to seek the seat of a Jewish King, or for one to seek with such pride and pomp—which manner and way is not necessary to maintain in the description of our purpose.

### IV.
Now, in beginning such and other descriptions, it causes us no honor here to maintain a distinction of cities, or new circles, or places outside our region: that is, to write of foreign things. For you see that one cause, one foundation, and one consequence is one healing in the body wherever they wish: let them see it as they will, there is a cause at the foundation, and a knowledge, and among right physicians, likewise a healing. Thereupon, as is shown here, it is also to be written of, to recognize it in that same foundation: by this example, that he who has the French Disease upon him is the same as the one by the Danube: the one in Lower Germany is the same as the one in Upper Germany, and so with others. Therefore, though they are not identical to one another, yet it is one and the same thing. So also, if another water is found that we do not describe here, it is to be considered similar in origin, beginning, and derivation to the water described. For consider yourselves how small a thing it is, and how little the whole world is to be counted as a stool for his King, and even less. Therefore, as we do not proceed through the foundations of human divisions, nor do we lead in the Order of Ptolemy <note>Refers to the Claudius Ptolemy's geographical system of mapping the world.</note> or in the paths of pilgrimage: we wish to reject such things as unnecessary or as a pride, to seek with such pomp, which manner and way is not necessary to maintain in the description of our purpose.

### V.
Since God has thus provided for every land according to its necessity, and none can stand in complaint against Him: for we are all men, as far as the world goes, so man needs nothing more than food and drink, cold and warmth, and a roof for shade. Who is so deprived of this that he might attribute a fault in that place to God? For we speak of nothing regarding this here. Those who would unwillingly love, or love the Rhine because of its salmon: let those be satisfied who are so minded. We write of necessity and of the city of Nuremberg. Therefore our readers and followers <note>original: "Sequaces"</note> should understand us in a different way than such people desire. From this it follows that the Harz Forest <note>original: "Hercynia".</note> does not complain that it does not have Mount Etna: but it has wood and Riesling <note>original: "Rißling"; likely referring to the vine or brushwood.</note>. Why should those of Socotra <note>original: "Sucuterlandt".</note> complain for the sake of bread, since they reach the age of the ancients with their heathens and their wise men? Or the Allgäu <note>original: "Algew"</note> against Alsace <note>original: "Elsaß"</note> for the sake of wine, since it yields nothing to them in strength and beauty? Thus God has loved His wonders, for the Kingdom is His. And with all this, who can lead a complaint without being a glutton? The unlearned and inexperienced might say: Saxony <note>original: "Saxonia"</note> is superior. So mark how much more Alexandria boasts than these parts? Look at Bavaria <note>original: "Bavarian"</note>, its tranquility <note>original: "Reuhi".</note>, and the tranquility of the Alpine sides, and the land where pomegranates and oranges grow; if a complaint were to happen over that, the ignorant physician would have to file it, he who knows nothing but Rhubarb <note>term: "Rheubarbarum" (Rhubarb used as a purgative)</note> and Aloes-wood <note>term: "Xyloaloes" (Fragrant medicinal wood)</note>. What his signs are, they are revealed.

# The Third Book.

### VI.

<margin>A</margin> Thus has God, in His order, provided for both the health and the necessities of all mankind. And just as a balsam oil is better for cooking than harmful water <note>original: "Schad Wasser"</note>, or wine for drinking, and beef compared to pheasant, so these things stand. We recount this in praise of natural waters, so that you may fathom their kind and properties, and not allow yourselves to be alienated from the waters. For what gives such beauty, what is the fairest in the heights? Or what can equal the coarse, since a beautiful person and a churl <note>original: "dölpess," a clumsy or unrefined person</note> are both formed by His wonderful works? In such things, His majesty writes of the carbuncle, the ruby, the topaz, and the imitation of crystal, and the whale-stone <note>likely referring to ambergris or a specific fossil stone</note> likewise. Thus, the lesser stones remain gifted: as with wine, water also surpasses wine by far in the Scriptures; wine is here, but water accomplishes more than any wine ever could, despite wine's virtues. Since this is ordained by God, it requires explanation, so that even the least thing that grows in the Fatherland is not despised. For although it is true that foreign things are cherished, and held higher than the domestic, the common is often more noble than that which is brought from afar. Anyone would be criticized if he only loved the corn in his own field as fruit, and yet God allows this to happen; He gifts the earthly King’s finger with the best of the peasant's labor. For He wishes the peasant to be just as healthy as the King, and to have him be equally unspeakable <note>meaning: of inexpressible value</note>. In this, the Philosopher <margin>B</margin> is instructed in natural things, and they do not need to have their art in the field of the Penates <note>household gods or spirits of the home</note>.

### VII.

Furthermore, although the emerald is of greater color, greater beauty, and a feast for the eyes: what are they, however, more or stronger than what the common man has? Reason should rightly marvel at such beauty. But now, in earnest, when the body must be relieved: what is it then but virtues at which body and soul should marvel? For virtue should be sought, and not merely beauty. For what does it matter if one is beautiful or handsome if he is worth nothing? Therefore, seek not that which merely pleases the eyes or tastes good to the tongue. For the nose often has its pleasure and delight in others—that is, in people. Just as one who looks into a mirror profits himself little, so the carbuncle stone profits the necessity of man little. Since Nature does not consider the profit of man in such beauty, what is the task of one who describes what is useful to man? Therefore, as we look into the mountains <note>original: "Berck"</note>, we adorn them according to their worth: the good for appearance, for those who like appearance; and the good for utility, for those who love utility. Thereupon, I write these books concerning the natural waters of the earth: a book of the corporeal waters, and of the growing waters, how they come forth from the power of the earth and are separated into elements.

### VIII.

And now that Nature gives man his necessity and medicine from the earth in two ways, as stated above: the first to be written of is what the corporeal waters are, of which this book speaks. What is to be known of the other growing waters shall be presented in its own book. Thus, it is first to be understood here that the corporeal springs or waters receive their name from the fact that they come out of a "body" <note>referring to a mineral or metallic source</note>, and that this same body becomes water. Therefore, because the body becomes water, without being extracted and without other preparation, but entirely of itself, it is rightly kept under such a name. For you see that there is no stone, no metal, no <margin>C</margin> mineral, etc., that is not brought to a water by the hand of Nature: outside of its casing, and even more so within its casing. For see how everything on earth becomes water, as much as is made of it. First, it is made into use as iron; this is used and worn away, eaten by rust, etc., and thus comes into loss so that nothing more of it is seen. From this it follows that this same rust does not remain a body, but transforms itself by its own power into water, by which power the rust is formed. Thus, not only iron, but silver, tin, and lead all transform one another in such a manner. Gold and silver are taken away in the earth, and in those places they also become water; for they become nothing—that is, they become that from which they came: they grew out of water and pass away back into it. Stones and others are also to be understood thus, and all are called the corporeal waters, as stated above.

Thus, upon the aforementioned ground, many minerals are lost which are in perfect delight, and...

## X.

Although it is proper / according to the elements, to write of these waters / in the books of the Element
of Water: For the reason / that they are born from the metals / stones / rocks / and the like Element
of Water / and not out of the earth. But rightly it should
be attributed to the Element of Earth. For the labor and the work is not of the stones
or the wood / which have provided the heap / but the honor and labor belongs to its Master / who brought it
to that point. Thus understand of these waters / the body is from the Element of Water / and the nature
which makes the body into water / that same is from the Element of Earth. Therefore the honor and
the name remains / with the Element of Earth. And it happens in that way / just as when one master
breaks the work of another / for his own benefit. Therein out of iron comes rust / because it was of the Element
of Water alone. But they wander into other elements / there is its breaking. For when its shame
comes / then it belongs to another element / and nevermore its own. Then no death follows. As with the fruit /
as long as it stands on its tree / it is in its element: But when it is robbed of the tree /
then it is in another element / and then follows its rot and other things. Like a fish that must be in its
water / man [in] air. Thus each rejoices in its element. Thereupon know /
that the earth is in such a manner a destroyer of the ores / rocks, and metals / when they lie beyond their time / as
we shall further explain regarding the minerals. We also wish to have mentioned here / the specific destruction in the
element / to be further mentioned in its places: As of the rot of the fruit / on the tree / which might be
an inclusion / yet without harm a deduction. Now from this follows the ground / that we write here such
of the earth: However, in the manner of a robbery, broken from the other element.

## XI.

Such species of water appear in many ways: One which comes from the metals / and
is divided in itself into many forms: As from each metal a specific one / and also
the same stronger or weaker: Thereafter from the mixing of metals in weight / in number / in
age / ripeness or not: Also in the mixing of foreign additions / of gems / and other such
things. Thus as they now come from the metals / so also from the stones. For as often as there is a stone /
so often is there an origin of a spring. Additionally, as stated above / with the mixing / so also from all
other ores of the vitriols / the alums / the salts: Also of the <term>Marcasites</term><note>Iron pyrites</note>, sulfur, <term>Tarabe</term><note>Possibly a term for bitumen or a specific mineral resin</note>, etc.
For from these comes the same kind of springs / and the stones in the springs / and the metals / etc. And if it happens / that there were more of the water than of the sapphires: That same is from the
earth / so that in the destruction of the whole growth the tree runs with it / and a resolution <note>A chemical dissolving or breaking down</note> comes from it.
From this it also follows / that such water does not flow so high in degree / as the stones or metals.
For more runs over with it / than is in the stone / or metals: That is / the mother upon
which they grow and / somewhere with them. But such is to be reckoned no other way / than according
to the weight / and not to be attributed to weakness. For that / which a gem accomplishes with a hole /
so must the water have an inner quality / in time and in use. All this shall be commanded to the
physicians / who should experience themselves herein: As they then give themselves
out and regard themselves as such / to satisfy the [patients].

### XII.

There are also other kinds of waters which, after their resolution <note>The process of a substance breaking down or dissolving into its elemental state</note>, return healthily to their first essence. That is, when they enter the third element—which is out of the water and outside of the earth—and are not brought into a completely free resolution by the earth, these same waters are those that create pebbles, flint, and other stones in the streams. As has been written specifically regarding these waters: likewise, many waters come from gold, which is to say they become gold again. These are the streams in which gold is found, and the like. For Nature is not always of such a kind or power that she creates a free resolution everywhere, but often falls back again. For the garnets found in the waters are born for a second time; therefore, they are not as full of virtue and character as those that come from the first kind and have remained so. For the first breaking is a lessening of its powers. So it is also with many more such waters in which metals are found in grain-form, which allow themselves to be beaten or in some parts hammered; they are changed harmlessly from the metals so that they may not return to their first form. Also, the best part belonging to a metal flows away, from which also comes a hindrance of its perfection compared to others.

### XIII.

There also occur various waters that are not "corporeal" waters <note>Physical, tangible liquids</note>, but come from the true water and flow over the ores, from which they receive a character and a likeness, as if something corporeal were within them. These originate thus: when the water-springs filter through the pores of the earth and encounter an ore-vein—of whatever kind it may be—and the water must emerge and press through it, then in that same ore, it is just like water standing in a copper vessel, taking on the taste. Just as with this copper-leach <note>original: "Kupferlet"</note>, so it is to be understood of these. Although it is true that gold, silver, and tin do not give such a taste, the ore in which they lie gives the water its character; therefore, something of the metal clings to it, which is then esteemed as its own nature. Thus it also often happens that a vitriol ore, or glass, or other things run with it, and yet they are not corporeal; their powers are not perfect, but are a work of the element of water, or a branch—the root is to be considered water—and they are of little or no value, accomplishing nothing in the body. For they come from the outside of the ore, therefore they have no inward path, yet they display some character and essence as if they were something.

Thus, as stated above, regarding how many kinds of waters are known to us, we wish to show in the following the metallic, the gem-like, and the like, pertaining to the ores, vitriol, alum, and such; and herewith we have concluded the First Treatise.

---

## The Second Treatise.

Now, as the birth of metals arises in the element of water and takes its origin—as we must note in *the generations of metals* <note>original: "de Generationibus Metallorum"</note>—how they are born, or before they are seized by the element of the earth, it happens in this way: The element of the earth exists in a compaction <note>A state of being solid or compressed</note>. Just as you see that the earth does not retain [the fruits], but drives them into another element, which is the air; in that same element, the work of the element of earth is completed. So it is to be understood in the same way regarding water: that the roots of the water drive their birthing into the element of earth, and in the same, it is completed. Just as you see that the fruits growing out of the element of earth grow into the air, these are subject to destruction if they do not fall from their element. In one way, a work of the element of water or the trees of the earth may pass through and destroy it; so also from the air, worms may grow, or through the element of fire, through rain, freezing, etc. When such happens to the fruits of the earth's element, it is a destruction of the body into another transformation and form. Thus the earth is of such a nature and property that it falls into the work of the element of water wherever a joint <note>A gap or opening</note> may be; from such an intrusion, the corporeal waters occur.

Furthermore, it is to be noted what it is that stands above the other element. Know that in the earth alone resides the counterpart of the element of water. As you see: the fruit from the earth and the fruit from the water. Thus they are also contrary in nature. For just as the arsenic of the...

That is, that which is to resolve the minerals into their bodily water shall happen through no physical means, but without any addition: and yet they resolve the mineral bodies.
<sig>A</sig>

Now, so that you may grasp the understanding: all minerals are coagulated <note>term: coagulated; thickened or solidified from a liquid state</note> upon salt, whether it be jewelry <note>precious metals</note>, whether it be stone, or other visible ores; thus the salt gives each thing and ore its master <note>its governing form or solidity</note>. And if salt were not there, all metals would be water, as would all stones and the like. Since the water is now coagulated by the salt, and all metals, stones, etc., have their master from the salt: it follows from this, that by the breaking of the salt, metals and stones become water again. Since salt is the centerpiece of such resolution, and is found in salt alone by the power of the earth. Therefore, it follows from this, that from the earth such a resolution and dissolution <note>term: dissolution; the breaking down of a substance</note> of the bodily waters occurs. And if it were thought that a medium must be present through which a preparation occurs before the earth gains its power to resolve and dissolve: take as an example that you see that Tartar <note>term: Tartarus; potassium bitartrate deposits, often used in alchemical analogies for stony crusts</note> is resolved by the power of the earth, but such resolution happens in no other way than through a medium, that is, fire; subsequently, such a resolution occurs.
<sig>B</sig>

Regarding this, Nature should be understood in this way: she does not seek such a medium. For what is her medium through which she coagulates? Nothing but herself. If she is thus a maker herself, she is also a breaker herself. For you see, if a coagulation <note>original: "Coagulas"</note> is to happen through the manner of the hand <note>manual craft or artifice</note>, it must have a medium through which it happens. Likewise, if it wants to break a thing, it must have nothing. This, however, is not dependent on Nature, but only on the hand, which must rise from another. In addition, the elements act thoroughly and boldly in what they wish to do, and not with puffery <note>original: "Bleswerk"; empty or superficial work</note>, as is the manner and power of the hand. Thus understand that without any medium, out of the power of the earth, such a breaking occurs through the earth into the ores of the water. Just as you see from the sun that it melts the ice, and from the cold how it freezes the water together. As there is no medium there, but rather the power of the element: so also understand the powers of resolution, as is our purpose here. Upon which you should note, since salt is the centerpiece to be attacked in the destruction of bodies <note>original: "Corporum"</note>, and the earth is powerful to accomplish the same and to dissolve the salt: thus all metals, all stones, and all other ores are broken and made into bodily water, whatever is subjected to the earth.

Now, although it is also the case that it might be thought all ores must be resolved because they all lie in the earth: it is not so. For what comes from a perfect nature and keeps its time, that resists. For you see that no fruit falls from the tree unless it be autumn; therefore, in the first treatise, such a thing is explained. From this, note further the powers of the earth, how they are manifold in congelation <note>term: congelation; the process of turning from liquid to solid</note> as well as in resolution; and to congeal element water, so often there is a way in the element of Earth <note>original: "Element Terræ"</note> to break the same again. For if such an adversary were not in the earth against the water, there would be a progression of minerals in all lands and places, which otherwise do not appear in any other way, that is, in a broken state: concerning such minerals <note>original: "de Mineralibus"</note>, more will be shown. And it is to be noted herein also, that in such destruction of the body of minerals, the taste <note>original: "Gustus"</note> is also scattered. As you see from the resolution of Alum <note>original: "Aluminis"</note>, which is not like the Alum. Likewise from the resolution of Vitriol <note>original: "Vitrioli"</note>, which is also not like the Vitriol, and yet of the same ground and one matter. That is, just as a water that is distilled, how it separates from one another in its kind, so it is there also. Likewise a water that freezes and thaws again: just as the same is separated again in its powers, so is this also. For the breaking of every stone and the breaking of every metal must endure such a change. But in their powers, as was told at the beginning, they remain in essence.

Now, however, further concerning this resolution: know that the resolving power is nothing other than the thick-moistness <note>original: "dickalf feuchtich"</note> of the earth; from such comes the aforementioned resolution of metals. If the metal lies there for its time and is subjected to this cold moisture, like iron to rust, and rust to humidity: then follows the resolution of that same ore further and further, as far as there is resolution: and what is thus resolved, that centers itself toward the spring <note>original: "Bronnen"; the source or well-head</note>. # On Natural Waters.
## On Power Waters.
<sig>B</sig>

### On Power Waters.
<note>Power Waters (Krafftwasser): Waters believed to possess alchemical or transformative properties due to dissolved minerals.</note>

Thus, <term>resolutions</term> <note>dissolved substances or liquid extracts</note> grow within stones, which also come to light in the manner described above, appearing with a strange nature and character. Some are exceedingly soft, so that iron is brought to be forged (into iron); some are so exceedingly soft that iron is made comparable to lead, and the like. Such waters take their origin from the resolution of such metals. As you see, steel makes iron harder than steel; also lead almost makes gold softer, for every metal or ore has its own particular softness or hardness within it compared to another metal: therefore such waters are resolved from such metals. There also occur many waters that harden stones and also make them soft: these come from such a stony nature, resolved therein. As you see with the <term>Adamas</term> <note>Diamond or hardest mineral</note>, how it overpowers other stones, just as its <term>liquor</term> <note>liquid essence</note> likewise makes all gems harder; and conversely, <term>alabaster</term> <note>a soft sulfate mineral</note>, as much as it is, softens the diamond (with it). Thus one should not wonder at such waters. For when they are transformed into liquors, they bring about such wonders.

So also one finds waters that turn wood into stone, and the like into many strange hardnesses and softnesses: this comes from the nature of such stones that have resolved themselves, and are of such a subtle nature that they penetrate the <term>pores</term> of the wood and <term>coagulate</term> <note>solidify</note> therein, and thus the wood is recognized as stone. This is what <term>Beryl-water</term> does; if a piece of wood is placed in it for six weeks, it is entirely transformed into stone. This nature is also shown by rain waters. Thus also stones are formed from peas, from beans, and from the like, if such a water seizes them. For such waters are in themselves stone, and penetrate into such things as one cloth penetrates another and remains therein. For every piece of wood or bean, etc., is more than half empty; therefore, what is empty fills itself with these stones and coagulates in its own time.

There are also waters of such a kind that give stones another color and hardness or softness: these same waters are from metals, but they penetrate the hardness of the stones in such a way that they take on their form, color, and nature, and yet are not equal to the metals. You shall learn of many such waters from the natures of stones, for from that follows the character and nature of such waters. For to write here of the nature of those waters is not our purpose, but rather whether a water has such a nature and from whence its origin may be.

### On Tasting Waters,
that is, <term>Taste</term> <note>original: "Gustu" (Latin)</note>.

Now there are some waters that come from acidity, or are perceived in other ways by the taste of the tongue, such as <term>acid springs</term> <note>Saurbronnen: naturally carbonated or mineral-rich acidic springs</note> and the like. These take their origin from the resolutions of metals before they become ripe. Therefore, it is first to be known of them what taste each metal gives before its ripening. As gold and lead give acidity; copper and iron give acidity; tin and silver a middle-ground: and that in many ways. But concerning such waters of the <term>thermal baths</term> <note>original: "de Thermis" (Latin)</note>, it will be shown in the following books. It also happens that such waters spring from <term>vitriol</term> <note>sulfate minerals</note> and <term>alum</term>: but not with a good taste, rather only from the metals.

In such waters it also happens that they take the <term>metallic tincture</term> <note>the color-giving or transformative essence of a metal</note> with them, so that while they are in the process of tinting, they are broken and turn to water: then these waters are of the kind that bear metals, and sometimes tint metals: so that often <term>gold-ore</term> <note>original: "Golders"</note> is found in the waters, which has been transformed from other metals into gold by this "Power Water." Also such waters many times make other metals: as sometimes waters are found that turn iron into copper, and cattle <note>possibly a typo for "veins" or "ores" in the original, or a reference to organic matter</note> into copper, and the like. But concerning such <term>generations</term> <note>the creation or formation of minerals</note>, more will be revealed in the book on minerals: for it is not our purpose here to write of anything other than natural waters.

There are also some acid waters and aluminous waters that provide a physical acid-spring, and grow in another form: these are described in the book on thermal baths, for they are not bodily waters, and yet are waters of the earth.

### The Third Book.

A layer on both sides, or according to the species of the earth and the ores, there occurs a generation of a worm. Therefore, such genera <note>types or classes</note> are not to be described because of the multitude of worms, and because the mixing of rainwater and subsequent decay come together, or a skin <note>Häuli: likely a membrane or film</note>, or they are already rotten: then the ground-worms, etc., are formed from it. From the aforementioned causes and mixing, as stated above, all the worms grow that emerge from the earth, and all vermin <note>Anster: archaic term for pests or insects</note>, as we shall explain more fully in *On Generations* <note>original: "de Generationibus"</note>. Therefore, no land should wonder at such genera of worms occurring in their lands at times. They run out mixed in the well-waters, and if they are drunk, such strange kinds of worms develop in the body of the same, as is their nature in the earth. The difference is that the body, with its form and other things, creates a distinction compared to the elements. For here the physician should take note, that they recognize this origin as it occurs in the small gloss <note>original: "Glosell"</note>, so also in the body, when such a corruption begins, as is further indicated in *On the Generation of Worms* <note>original: "de Generationibus Vermium"</note>. What this is, is shown in *On Plants* <note>original: "de Plantis"</note>, that is, of those same worms that come from the herbs, that is, of the cabbage-worms.

### On Medicinal Waters.

B Furthermore, note now further concerning the medicinal waters, which are endowed with manifold virtues. These occur in the way that the gems—in which the virtues reside—dissolve, also the corals and the amber <note>original: "Carabe"</note> and others of the like; these provide the medicine which the waters possess of a physical nature. From this it follows, that these waters stop their sickness, and likewise take away the "mountain-sickness" <note>Bergicht: likely a reference to gout or a miner's ailment</note> from children. Enough concerning such waters is indicated in this little book: but the highest matter belonging to this should be described by the physicians, who say what the waters are good for, and yet have no foundation for it. From what ground they come, that is what they should experience, to recognize such an origin. As we also write in *On Thermal Springs* <note>original: "de Thermis"</note>.

So also the metallic waters have their nature in this way: therefore, in such things the highest thing to know is the nature of the stones, the metals, the ores, and other things: so that subsequently the waters, and what they are, may also be recognized. For there is no well, no brook, that does not carry such a kind of medicine with it: therefore, where such knowledge and testing exists, especially indicated by the powers of such things, we have herewith concluded.

Likewise, there are certain special waters that are healing, so that they cure every dropsy <note>original: "Hydropisin"</note> and paralysis <note>original: "Paralysin"</note>. We wish to write of these, and fulfill this little book by explaining what we write in the *Book on Gout* <note>original: "Librum Podagra"</note> <note>Note: Paracelsus often cross-references his own specialized treatises</note>, and with that, we wish to have finished this Third Book here.

### On Natural Waters.
## The Fourth Book.
### TRACTATUS I.

### On Growing Springs.

Just as we have recounted the physical waters in the aforementioned book, so here following, our purpose begins concerning the "growing waters." But to recognize the physical water and now the growing water, and with what distinction they differ from one another—that is, concerning the water entering into its body. Just as the first secrets, and the waters of this book are those which go from the water into their body. Since they are both physical, and in these two books only physical waters are treated: it is a sufficient distinction to know that in the previous book, they take themselves from the body and resolve into a body <note>i.e., solids becoming liquid</note>: those which go from the water into their body. Like the first secrets, and from iron into a water; this here is from a water into a tree. As is now to be understood here, how iron becomes water and other gems: so the waters of the earth, which we call growing springs, become a body, of wood, of herb, of sponge <note>Schwanum: likely fungus or sponge-like growth</note>, etc. And here is likewise to be understood an essence, a strength, and a nature, to describe the breaking down of the first body, and here of the second body—that is, how the resolution occurs from these bodies, so it occurs here. That is, we wish to treat further how wood, herbs, and the like come from water, and leave the first book—that is, the previous one we treated, where the grown bodies were broken down.

# Concerning Natural Waters

For you see that there is no resemblance at all that looks like wood, or like a tree; likewise, a tree has no resemblance that looks like an apple. <margin>A</margin> This happening is the fault of growth: of which power we wish to describe as much as is required here. For as we have previously indicated, the breaking of <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process by which a liquid becomes solid; here, the author refers to the alchemical breakdown of matter to allow for new growth.</note> is the way. You see that the metals and minerals look like their <term>corpus</term> <note>Latin: "body" or physical substance.</note>, that is, like that from which they were transformed. For the reason is that it is water; therefore, it cannot look like the metal. But as you see that a metal is fixed, so again this water compares itself to the wood and the grass into which it becomes. Understand this through such an example: you see that <term>vitriol</term> <note>A sulfate mineral, often green or blue.</note> is green, another is blue and highly colored; yet when it is resolved into a water, there is no color there. So also you see the colors: gold is yellow, and in its <term>transmutation</term> <note>The alchemical change of one substance into another.</note> it is brown, and when resolved in this transmutation, it colors no more water; thus, something becomes nothing. In this manner, you should understand here that, in the same way, colors spring from no colors: such as the green in the grass, and yet there is no green visibly in the earth—that is, tangibly. Thus, as one is in its origin, so is the other to be recognized equally on both sides. Although many such examples have been encountered, in my intention, the greater part shall follow hereafter.

It is indeed a great wonder to be marveled at, that a living growth with flesh and with sensibility comes out of nothing; for it is possible hereupon, as the <term>light of nature</term> <note>A Paracelsian concept referring to innate divine knowledge or intuition granted to humans to understand the world.</note> makes known, that we also see what is hidden. Just as a carpenter [has] no house physically before he makes it. And as we [see] a house that we [perceive] with our eyes in every way because it is made and how it is shaped, and then we carry it in our mind as if we had it; in the way that we see it, so we see from such possibility the things grown in the earth. And as it is invisible what we have in our mind, [so it is with] what we have in the earth. And yet they are in the earth and [visible] to us, as it is highest to be described: how the colors and the water hide themselves, and in what way it proceeds to growth. For as we have described such in the previous book of the breaking of grown things: so we wish to write here of growth, of the breaking in the substance. That is, so that you see that what it is, is broken before the eyes. We wish to describe what becomes whole again to satisfy the eyes; but in the mind—that is, in the ground and in the property—it is not broken, but whole. Therefore, the philosophers are to be understood more according to the light of nature than according to the outward seeing of the eyes, in which shall be described that: that is, we describe here the growing water, which is the water that gives foliage and grass.

Thus is the order: for in the wood sticks the <term>worm-spirit</term> <note>The vital force or "seed" that generates life, often associated in early modern thought with spontaneous generation.</note> from which sensibility grows. Also in the <term>cadaver</term> <note>Latin: "corpse" or decaying matter.</note>. And as little as that is in between or to be grasped, so little can we grasp the secrets of nature with the eyes. For these are the <term>mysteries of God</term> <note>Latin: "mysteria Dei".</note>, that out of nothing such strange things should spring, where no one can say that something was there. And there is as little to wonder at concerning the origin of metals or the growth of wood as how a <term>chafer</term> <note>A type of beetle.</note> comes from dung, or a worm from another pillar: how strange nature is in her working and freedom! Who would consider it outside the light of nature, that wood should give a living worm, and other such things?

<margin>* al. Origin. Nature proves that such is within her, that without her we can recognize nothing, and we can recognize just as much in that which we do not see.</margin>

Thus, as now * the cause is that which comes out of nothing and makes itself visible: so nature proves that such is within her, that without her we can recognize nothing, and we can recognize just as much in that which we do not see. For we see roses, meadow flowers, lilies, etc., grow out of a black earth. So it is possible hereupon, as the light of nature makes known, that we also see what is hidden. Just as a carpenter [has] no house physically before he makes it. And as we [see] a house that we [perceive] with our eyes in every way because it is made and how it is shaped, and then we carry it in our mind as if we had it; in the way that we see it, so we see from such possibility the things grown in the earth. And as it is invisible what we have in our mind, [so it is with] what we have in the earth. And yet they are in the earth and [visible] to us, as it is highest to be described: how the colors and the water hide themselves, and in what way it proceeds to growth. ### The Fourth Book.

To admit this—it is indeed in the other—so that it is within the human being. For all human labor, art, etc., is all but the labor and art of one human being. The fish have their time, the birds their time: and yet everything remains with them, whether they may choose to do it or not. But this growth is not so: it comes, and it has died, and it is that same dead kind, that is, the old kind and nature is there, but nothing in it is broken. For there is the color in the rose, there is the taste, etc., and it is the rose that would continue. But the human being is not so; another <term>Corpus</term><note>Latin: body or physical substance</note> comes, and although the body may resemble the body of the rose—that is, today's as it is not his father's—and that in which the most lies: as with the <term>Virtue</term><note>German: Tugend; in Paracelsian terms, this refers to the inherent power, medicinal property, or "soul" of a substance</note> in the roses, where more depends on that than on its color or body. For to have a body is something that does not concern the <term>Philosopher</term><note>The natural philosopher or alchemist</note>, but the virtue and nature is that which is being treated.

## The Second Treatise.

Further now concerning this water, know then that this water belongs to the earth alone, just as the ore belongs to the water alone: therefore it shall be ordered for itself without intermixing. But what concerns the differences that may be compared, that same difference is in the form alone, and not in the essence: also in the growth, it is a special kind. But that same thing does not apply here: for whatever power is in the earth, is also in the earth, and also in the water. In the same way, it is to be understood in the other two elements. For take this as an example: all the <term>Medicine</term><note>German: Arsney; healing agents</note> that the earth has, the water also has: and what the earth or water has, the fire and the power have just as well in one as in the other. You see that from the earth grows the power of <term>Southernwood</term><note>Latin: Abrotanum; a flowering plant in the wormwood family</note>: so it is also in the <term>Chrysolite</term><note>Latin: Chrysolicho; likely referring to the gemstone or a mineral of similar hue</note>. You see on the other hand the power of <term>Carnelian</term><note>Latin: Carniola</note>: so it is again in <term>Shepherd's Purse</term><note>Latin: Bursa Pastoris; a common medicinal herb</note>. So also it is in <term>Crystal</term><note>Latin: Crystallo</note>, and also in <term>Manna</term><note>Latin: Tereniabin; a Persian term for medicinal manna</note>, as stated above. Since there is now an equal power in the four elements, the explanation is: only what comprises the form and outward nature is different, while an equal power exists within the elements: thus their virtues are also understood as equal. For what we have written of the virtues in the properties, those same we also want to see as possible in the genera. As it is granted to the water to be stone. So conversely in the water of fire there is a possibility to also fulfill the genus, and so also with the genus of metals. So also with these of which the moisture of the earth is also in the possibility to give birth to the water, which in turn gives birth to earthly grass. Therefore, however, its power is such that there is no element: out of which it happens, just like a deformity of the sentient body.

Just as there is one power, so there is yet a description of the virtues. But it requires a special, great knowledge of the forms, and whether the power of <term>Corals</term><note>Latin: Corallorum</note> lies in the herbs, trees, etc., or compares itself to gold, or where the power of corals lies in the creatures of the earth. Likewise also the <term>Transmutation</term> that occurs from them, what their <term>Warmth</term><note>German: Therm</note> and their resolved waters are. For you shall not doubt therein—I mean you inexperienced ones—for when <term>Basil</term><note>Latin: Basilicon</note> decays and changes its body into a <term>Resolved Substance</term><note>Latin: Resolutum</note>, as described in the previous book concerning ore, that such a resolution has a similar restoration and a kind of its body, with the reasoning of the superfluity, in that way. You know that in the <term>Cypress</term><note>Latin: Cupresso</note> lies a small power, but there is a large body. Now it follows from this that the <term>Putrefaction</term><note>Latin: putrefactio; the alchemical process of decay to release inner essence</note> decays the body, but the virtue may be separated from the body and brought into its <term>Compaction</term><note>Concentrated form</note>. Thus a handful does more than a wagonload without the putrefaction. Regarding such, note further that such a putrefied body must have a large <term>Dose</term><note>Latin: Dosin</note> and a change. Therefore, because the body is putrefied, it should not be despised, even if the body is foul; it is the separator of the virtue, but the sustainer thereof. Therefore, in those same waters, as is written of the physical ones, to be used in their own right. For the power of the elements against one another is the body, and not in their virtues. Although there is a blurring of the virtues, it is in such a way as you see that a human being has a body. If now a limb is lost, he still has as much of a limb, and also a life thereafter; some to death, some not. Thus, seek no differently in the plants as well, as the <term>Anatomy</term><note>German: Anatomick; here meaning the structural analysis of natural things</note> and of natural things. Herein, however, note that the power of things is brought into a narrowness: but as for that which concerns the life of the body, they will provide no description of these things.
Henceforth, however, to know of the growing waters of the earth, these are the body...

### The Third Treatise.

To describe further concerning the Earth with its growing springs. First, concerning the <term>Matter</term>, what that thing is which grows there, as stated above. And yet it is one Matter, and it is the First, not only of the Earth but also that which is in the other three elements. Such a division, however, happens just as if you found four people who have one piece of wood, and it is divided into four parts: one makes a fire out of the wood; the second lets his rot until its <term>Resolution</term> <note>The chemical breakdown or decay into basic components</note>; the third carves an image out of it; the fourth dyes it so that one could no longer recognize what it was. These are now four ends, and there is one First Matter from which they come. And as unequal as the four are to one another, so unequally do the elements divide themselves from one another in their growths.

# On Natural Waters

Since the aforementioned times—as stated above—are divided in so many ways or points: you should also know that they have strange years, and one "year" should not be understood the same way in all cases. For a year is that which proceeds from its beginning until its exaltation <note>The point of highest potency or maturity in alchemy and astrology</note>. There are many kinds of such years: one is perhaps half a summer, such as the roses; another is a whole year, such as the saffron <note>original: "Crocus"</note>; another is a year such as the wheat <note>original: "Weisen," likely referring to grain/wheat cycles</note>; another is three years, such as the juniper, and so on with all the others.

And yet, a year in this context is not calculated according to our calendar year. Therefore, understand regarding the minutes—which we indicate here as "points"—that they should not be understood according to the year of our counting. Rather, they should be understood in this way: that every minute, that is every point, produces a generated thing <term>Generatum: a substance or being brought into existence through natural or alchemical processes</term> without ceasing, until the end of the world. Now note this: such generated things are not understood to be apart from the earth, but rather within the earth. For just as we indicate two times...

# On Natural Waters

<margin>Theory in Vol. 103. L. 32.</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
Since the body exists in a state of fragility, it must be generative; for as many accidents as arise within the body’s members, nature possesses just as many *Arcana* <note>Secret healing powers or essences</note>, and for every disease, there is a corresponding *Arcanum*. Note, therefore, that the true foundation of medicine lies here: every disease is healed in its *Specific Form* <note>The unique, essential nature of a remedy</note>, and not through the art of *Composition* <note>Mixing many ingredients together</note>. For every composition is a disruption of the true art. Observe the craftsmen and what serves them, or wherein their craft stands. The armorer must make armor from iron alone; the potter his pot from clay alone. If a physician is to be a master, he must stand against the enemy <note>the disease</note> in the *Specific Form*, so that through this, healing must and shall occur. Thus, in medicine, there is also an enemy. And if a middle ground were sought—such as mixing iron and copper together to make armor—it would not work; it must be steel.

The Theory in medicine concerns such *Specifica* which take away the *Morbus* <note>Latin: disease</note>, just as water extinguishes fire. There is no other way to handle the extinguishing of fire except through water alone. Otherwise, it would be a precarious thing to quiet it until it consumes itself. Therefore, it should be noted here that the theory <note>of the schools</note> is devised within nature like flying spirits. Truly, if they recognized nature in her *Potentia* <note>Power/Potential</note>, they would certainly be silent. But because the Theory is speculated upon, the secrets and *Magnalia* <note>Great works/wonders</note> of nature are forgotten. The aforementioned lies cannot compare to nature. Therefore, whatever is to be and must be fathomed from nature should be taught in such a way that every *Simplex* <note>A single medicinal herb or substance</note> is understood in its *Arcanitet* <note>Its hidden healing power</note>. For every disease, an equal number comes to both sides. For nature has no more weapons or spears than there are enemies against her. There are no more medicines than there are diseases, and no more diseases than there are medicines. A medicine should not be composed of many things, but should be driven through by a single power and full of its own essence. How diseases take their origin is explained in the *Iliad* <note>Likely referring to Paracelsus's 'Opus Paramirum' or his theories on the 'Yliaster' (prime matter), rather than Homer</note>. However, as much as is known here, so much is indicated.

<margin>B</margin>
Now, just as the fruit of the earth enters into a form—in which there are noble things like *Edleras* or *Cultus* <note>Paracelsian terms for refined or cultivated natural forces</note>, etc.—if this is to happen, it must have a form and a *Corpus* <note>Body</note> that is different from the first. From this, it follows that the earth is the mother of all growing things, and not the other three elements. Although the true power comes from the earth, the power of *Congelation* <note>Solidification/Freezing</note> is in the Element of Earth and has no body and no weight. But the body, that is Earth, and it is transmuted into another body, such as a tree, for which it is good. That is, it retains an anatomy in all species. There are *Arcana* in *Siphita* <note>A Paracelsian term related to the vital force or spirits of growth</note>. Now, the Anatomy of Coral and the Anatomy of *Siphita* are one. But they are not one body. Thus, in all other *Generatis* <note>Generated things</note>, it should be understood here that they should be kept in the same form. Therefore, nature now takes a form that looks like the disease and uses mastery like a soldier who carries his weapon according to how his enemy meets him. Thus, nature is better understood by physicians if they wish to offer a useful remedy. For Theory is Anatomy, and Anatomy is the Theory of Physicians—but I do not mean the Anatomy of the Italians, *id est* <note>Latin: that is</note>, of corpses.

<margin>C</margin>
Since the form now rises according to the form and the tree of nature, we shall also understand its growth from now on. When nature performs this, she doubles it coarsely. For you see that no craft exists on its own without another craft to help it complete its work. Like a goldsmith without a forge, or a smith without his tools, etc. Thus, it follows that the earth cannot accomplish such work without help; it must proceed in this way. It must have a builder who performs the work upon the appearance and prepares it. This happens through the outer elements, which are Air and Fire. The Air is that which nourishes it. For as soon as the seed is in the earth, it gives the same to the Air. Now, there are many kinds of air on earth that are hostile to man. Although the Air is considered one thing, it is not one, but as many species of generated things as there are, so many kinds of air are there. Thus are the herbs fed and guided, each according to its kind. For just as a man and all cattle keep their distinction in eating, so also the growing things have their own food. What they take serves the growing power, the body, and the nourishment.

Know further that the element of Fire must cook the same through the stars. Such cooking happens in this way: Firstly, if the element of Fire did not have the Heaven with its help, all plants would remain cold and would not grow. For nothing grows without the sun, and if there were no sun—that is, no heat from the heaven—and no day and night, and no equal being of time, then all plants would grow like a weed. But it would not become good—that is, *Clarified*. The grape would remain sour and harsh. But the sun is that which clarifies such coarse things and polishes the coarse into a pure growth. Just as a polisher scours the armor, so the sun is also a master of polishing. Thus, you should know that growth comes from the power of the earth and not the sun; but the sun is that which clarifies it for that reason.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine relies on the "Specific Form" of a single remedy (Simplex) rather than complex mixtures, matching the remedy to the disease like a weapon to an enemy. He also explains that while the Earth provides the body for growth, the Sun and Air are necessary for nourishing and "clarifying" plants into their final, useful state.</summary>

# The Fourth Book.

**A** **Clarified.** Time provides the second part, as we have recounted in the previous chapter. Therefore, know further that in the Sun, this power to clarify is manifold and not singular. It is not merely that there is one glow and one clarification; rather, as often as there is a *generaturm* <note>original: "Generaturm"; likely referring to a generative force or formative principle</note>, so often is there a special glow. And with that glow, and with the wheel of the *Acatia* <note>original: "Acatia"; likely Acacia</note> there is a specific power, and for the *Berberis* <note>Barberry</note> a specific power. Likewise, the White <note>possibly white flour or a specific white plant</note> has its own, and the Oats have their own. It is not the case that because there is one Sun, there is only one power; rather, in the single Sun there are as many powers as there are generations of things. Thus, the Sun is sovereign over the plants to ripen and to cook them, which would otherwise remain coarse and tough.

In the same way, know also that the growing springs divide themselves in many ways, as with wine, of which there are a thousand kinds on Earth. Here, note how subtle the *gradus* <term>degrees or stages of intensity/quality</term> are to recognize. For if wine is to be divided into at least a thousand parts, I look at the degrees of goodness in all things and skip over those that are merely trodden down. The Earth and the four elements do not give such degrees, for it concerns an equal *numerum* <note>original: "Numerum"; number</note>. That is: he who knows the number of the stars also knows the number of generation. For from there the degrees and the wonderful nature of things are derived. Not that the stars fulfill the number—that is, that the star is sovereign—or that it is what makes the Earth fruitful. Rather, the Earth is as sovereign as the Heaven; that is, from herself as much as the Heaven. And just as the Earth is not empty, so too the Heaven is not without stars, just as a field has its grass so that its soil does not stand empty. Such is the way of the Earth; and he who perceives one element also recognizes the others, for they are equal to it. Therefore, what is necessary to know—why this is in wood, this in herbs, this against that, and that against this—the same is made known by the foundation of *Anatomia* <note>Anatomy, used here in the Paracelsian sense of the internal structure and essence of things</note>, in which we shall conclude it.

**B** Also, if the process is lacking here, it shall be compensated for in *Iliado* <note>referring to the *Liber Azoth* or *De lliaster*</note>. And if the virtues are not described here, they are recounted in the fourth book of the *Archidoxis*. Likewise in others, where we speak of the nature of the beginning and the approach. And where we stop here, being hindered in this book, we wish only to describe the natural waters and their properties. It is not our intention here to show the *Arca Archidoxisch* <note>The "Archidoxian Ark" or secret medicinal treasury</note>, nor to display the Three Firsts <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> as a pure text according to the understanding of our Book VI, which we also understand to be included here as a particular. Thus, the virtues are to be further provided in a particular way, whereas here they are shown universally. Therefore, you shall recognize here what the elements work, how they are to be understood, and how they compare to our body, in what way and essence. For we wish to conclude the Fourth Book of Natural Waters, from which you shall learn one thing from another.

---

### TO THE READER.
The first and second treatises of the following fifth book are entirely deficient, as the original manuscript was not available, and no more was found in other manuscripts than what is present here. The third treatise, however, is complete.

### GREETINGS TO THE READER. <note>original: "LECTORI S." - a standard Latin greeting, 'Lectori Salutem'</note>

<image-desc>Ornate initial 'I' depicting a figure, possibly a scholar, reading a book.</image-desc>
The philosophical books that follow hereafter, Gracious Reader, have never before been printed exactly as the author himself described them. Rather, in many places, they were previously only short summary extracts, or otherwise prepared for print in a piecemeal and fragmented fashion. Now, however, in this edition, they are communicated for the common good from the author's own manuscripts, word for word, with nothing added. And what a difference there is between these and the previous ones, the diligent reader will well perceive through a mutual comparison <note>original: "ex mutua collatione"</note>.

However, these philosophical books should be twenty-three in number, the list of which was found on a special sheet in Paracelsus's own handwriting. Among these, only ten are present in a complete and perfect state, namely the 2nd, 4th, 7th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th, 13th, 19th, and 20th. Some are missing entirely, such as the 14th, 18th, 21st, 22nd, and 23rd. Of the others, only fragments and leaves were found, such as the 1st, 2nd, 5th, 6th, 8th, 15th, 16th, and 17th, which were perhaps torn apart by envious or ignorant people.

<margin>B</margin>
And because there is no hope that these books can be completed or their defects found, it was not deemed necessary to keep the order of the books as they were listed by the author. Instead, those which are present in full and without defect are arranged first, and the others follow. And because Paracelsus himself did not place a specific number at the beginning of any book, not much depends on the changing of this order. Here follows the *Catalog of Books* <note>original: "Catalogus Librorum"</note> as Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus's given name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim</note> recorded them.

### THE BOOK
### ON LUNATICS
### BY THEOPHRASTUS,
## Prologue.

<image-desc>Decorative initial S with intricate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>Diligent attention must be paid to the Spirit of Man, for two enemies beset him from birth. For according to the Spirit of Life, a man should be a Human, and not live according to the Spirit of the *Limbus* <note>The "Limbus" in Paracelsian thought refers to the primordial "great chaos" or reservoir of matter from which all physical things were created.</note>, which makes him merely a rational creature. For it is indeed true that Man is the image of God, and thereby he also has a divine spirit within him. However, he is otherwise an animal, and as an animal, he has an animal spirit. These are two opposing forces; yet one must give way to the other. Now, Man should not be an animal, but a Human: if he is to be a Human, he must live from the Spirit of Life of the Human, and thus cast away the animal spirit. Now it is necessary that the right of the Human be distinguished from the animal. This is the reason for writing this book, the title of which is *On Lunatics*. Although it is not the Moon <note>original: "Luna"</note> alone, it remains understood as a common name, encompassing Mania and *Velania* <note>A term used by Paracelsus to describe certain types of madness or frenzy.</note>. For it is my intention that the "deaf" <note>In this context, "deaf" or "taub" refers to those whose reason is numbed, senseless, or mentally clouded.</note> spirits and senseless people be recognized, and that they also be helped.

There are many who carry such a lunatic sickness who are not considered to be "lunatic." For there are many kinds of fools; they are not of one type, nor of one way, but in many ways, many types, many shapes, and forms. Fools have the animal spirit born within them; the "deaf" <note>senseless/insane</note> do not have it so inherently born—in this they differ in one way. Furthermore, fools act within the rational animal nature; the "deaf" act within the insane animal spirits—it is like this: Fools act with reason; what they do is animal cunning. If he is crafty and skillful, he has the animal nature of a fox; if he is fierce or wrathful, he has the nature of a wolf. For fools are divided according to the animals, as is described in the book on the birth and origin of fools. But the "deaf" have that same reason, yet it is shattered, out of its nature. This is just like a dog, which has two natures: one is the canine, naturally given dog-nature called barking, but done with canine reason. But the other nature is when he becomes rabid; then he uses that same animal dog-nature without canine reason—he is a frantic and mad dog. For there is a reason in animals and a cunning—in the fox, the deer, the magpie <note>original: "Egerstern"</note>, the woodpecker, etc. But a madness beyond that is the *Lunatic Disease* <note>original: "Lunaticus Morbus"</note>, about which I write here. That is, I write about the reason of those people. For human reason does not become "deaf," nor does it catch any disease. Therefore, nothing is to be sought in that human spirit, but only in his animal reason; that same reason is a great thing to understand in the "deaf" madman—he is nothing less than a mad dog. Farewell.

---

### FIRST TREATISE.
## CHAPTER ONE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial S with intricate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>Since Christ points out, "you are ravening wolves," and calls those people ravening wolves who are nevertheless humans, it is proper for me to reveal the wolves: for the reason that they rage like a mad wolf or dog. There is also reason enough to write about the single-minded, angry ones, since Christ says, "you generation of vipers," and also calls Herod a fox. Now, they are not animals in form, but in nature. If a man becomes an animal in his reason, it is only right—if he lives according to that same animal spirit—that he be named after it. But he who lives as a human in the human spirit shall keep his name as Human. Therefore, I begin to describe the animal spirits of men, which are called "deaf" or "insane" by the common man; and it is proper first to reveal the creation of man regarding the spirit of animal nature: one from the *Limbus*, the other from the word *fiat* <note>Latin: "let it be done," referring to the divine command of creation.</note>, which is the Human.

If these two spirits are recognized, one will be understood well enough to recognize every man—by which spirit he lives. Next, to describe the allegories of Christ, as mentioned, where he names man after the beasts. Thirdly, a further interpretation of these things. Fourthly, to indicate as much as the practice of natural medicine is able to do there. Although it is true that we know nothing of the animal creation—that is, from what the beast...

He classifies different types of madness by comparing human behaviors to specific animal traits (fox, wolf, dog) and cites biblical precedents for these metaphors.</summary>

# ON LUNATICS

<margin>A</margin> ...was made, other than through the Word. Now, however, nothing depends on that: for the reason that man is made from the *Limbus* <note>The "Limbus" in Paracelsian thought refers to the primordial "great mystery" or the material extracted from the universe to create man</note>, and the *Limbus* is nothing other than the mortal part of man that decays, with which death and decay the animal nature also dies and decays. Thus, it is enough to say once that man is an animal insofar as he is mortal: for that which dies and decays is the animal. Otherwise, man does not decay, for he must be present again in the Resurrection and must give an account there, receiving his reward, good or evil. For man must carry the animal within him, and the animal does not carry its own burden; rather, man receives and inherits it because he is a man and [spiritually] immortal. Now, however, his creation is such that in his animal nature and kind, all characteristics of animals are present—in one person this, in another that. Thus, every man—insofar as he lets his animal being rule—may be recognized as being like a beast or animal: one like a cow, another a sow, another a wolf, another a deer, etc. But if he puts that away, there stands a pure man, who can be compared to no beast. Now, this is the *Limbus* that gives us the body, which body is the *Limbus* in which are also Heaven and Earth, and the characteristics of all animals and birds. From this comes the condition that the beast and the man-within-his-beast resemble one another and share a characteristic: what is divided into species in the animal kingdom is also divided in man *in genere* <note>Latin: "in genus" or "by kind"</note>; but without the manifestation of the specific kind, it is not obvious.

What has been said concerns the common animals to which man compares himself and which compare themselves to him; this proves the animal nature on both sides. Now, however, know further that Heaven is also adorned with animal nature and characteristics. For who would say that Mars belonged to man? No one. Or who would be his master, his *Inclinator* <note>One who inclines or influences</note>, his *Ascendens* <note>The rising sign in astrology</note>? No one. For man is free without all these in his essence, having his nature from no one but God alone, in His image and Spirit. It is, however, quite true that the heavenly stars have an animal nature and kind. From this it follows that they belong to and are related to the animals by nature. If man is an animal [in his body], then he is also the one who has fellowship with the animals, in that he is twofold: animalistic and <margin>B</margin> human. As an example: I said man is subject to Mercury, and the like, as is found in the *Figura Coeli* <note>Latin: "Figure of the Heavens" or astrological chart</note>, and therefore this or that becomes of him. Now here is the distinction: man is not to be understood here, but rather the animal that he is. He who speaks thus of man speaks of the animal, not of the man. And thus the same art—as far as it pertains to Nature—is spoken to the animal and not to the man; for man is outside and above all that, nobler than them all. If he is then nobler, how can he be subject to the lesser? Thus, Heaven has its fellowship with man only so far as the animalistic touches the beastly, which man is forbidden to be or to use.

But how that same nature comes into us, know this: Just as the sun shines upon us and warms us, to the benefit of one and the harm of another, and hits the outer body; and just as the moon also shines in the same way, for the good of one and the harm of another; so you should also know that the animal stars likewise look upon the animal intellect in man, penetrating through the pores, the skin, the cell in which the animal intellect lies, just as their light goes through a glass. And thus, from this, that same animal intellect, sense, etc., becomes sick according to what that animal star is. These things—*impressiones* (impressions), *Influentz* (influences), *Constellationes* (constellations), etc., as they may be called—are all made solely for the beast and not for the man. If man lives as a man, it is all in vain; but if he lives as a beast, it happens to him as to the beast—that is, he goes along with the beast, and that which should be true for the animal becomes true for him. For just as fools are led by the stars, so also are led those who avoid wisdom, as is presented in their book. Now know that when the intellect becomes enraged, then <margin>C</margin> "madness" <note>original: "Doubsucht" (modern German: Tobsucht), referring to mania or frantic madness</note> is present, according to which beast is his master and has made him mad. Thus, madness is a raging beast, just like a dog that becomes rabid in the "dog days" <note>The hot period of summer associated with the star Sirius</note>. So also man becomes raging in his dog days. Now this is to be understood once and for all: that man [in his essence] is without any animal nature. Therefore, there are two of him: the *Corpus Physicum* (Physical Body) and the *Corpus Spiritus* (Body of the Spirit). The *Corpus Physicum* is dealt with in Astronomy and Astrology, and also in Medicine. Now, however, he has this distinction: that the things flowing from Astronomy should not be applied to the *Physicum Corpus*, but rather turned away from it into the other body, and explained and taught to the man. Therein you should know that medicine must be there, and that nature must be understood so far as it is animalistic to be maintained, and it is right. Thus, whatever can be "constellated" or "imprinted" by all external animals regarding diseases, the physician should know. But what concerns prophecy or augury should not be thought of, for they serve the beast; that is not Christian, but Heathen. However, know that for this and for medicine, these things must be used so that madness may be explained from its origin and ground. Thus, in conclusion, you should know that when a man becomes mad, the *man* is not mad, but only the animal in him. And he resembles a raging dog, which the course of the heavens makes frantic and mad; so also with man. Therefore, the name *Lunaticus* <note>Latin: "Moon-struck"</note> rightly stands, for the reason that it proves it comes from above: animal-star into animal-star.

Furthermore, know that just as our eyes, when directed into the sun, are surpassed by its light—even though our eyes are our sun—yet the sun above is so much greater than our...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and theological discussion regarding the dual nature of man—the animalistic/beastly versus the divine/human—and how the "beastly" intellect can be blinded by celestial influences if not properly governed by the spirit.</meta>

# BOOK OF PHILOSOPHY

appears that this light, or appearance, blinds our own light and takes it away. So it is also with the Moon and its light, and all of this in manifold ways. Now, however that may be, so it is also with the animalistic understanding, the reason and wisdom, which are within us like our eyes. Now, these also have suns in the heaven into which they look: so now the *concordance* <note>The harmonious correspondence between the celestial bodies and the human constitution</note> provides that the upper things shine into your understanding. Now a breaking occurs in our animalistic nature, and a blinding follows. And yet, in the same way that we have eyebrows and eyes to cover them so that the sun may not strike directly into them, so also there are *supercilia* <note>Latin: eyebrows</note> and *palpebrae* <note>Latin: eyelids</note> which likewise cover our reason, so that those same stars do not shine into them. But if the eyelids—that is, the <term>Tellküd</term> <note>An archaic term for the protective coverings of the eye</note>—stand open, now the *radius* <note>Latin: ray of light</note> strikes in, and the two cannot stand together, like wood and fire. From this overpowering, the "You" <note>The individual self</note> becomes mad and insane. For it cannot endure that its *temperamentum* <note>Latin: the balanced mixture of humors or qualities in the body</note> be overdriven. 

So also, if one uses the reason too much in an animalistic way, that same animalistic part in us also breaks. Therefore, we should stand still and remember that the "You" <note>The beastly nature</note> teaches man nothing—that is, the Spirit of Man—but rather we should learn as Christ says: *Every man shall be taught by God*, but not by the beast.

Now, so that you understand man rightly, know herein that man has his true spirit—of reason, wisdom, foresight, etc.—from Adam, and not from the beast. What that same spirit learns, it learns from God, for that same spirit is the image of God, and the body and its form belong to that spirit, so that the body and its nature are subject and obedient to it. Thus it will be: *Every man shall be taught by God.* Every enlightened person speaks from the spirit, not from the animalistic; nothing breaks in that spirit, it remains pure. It cannot become insane, for it does not worry, does not fear, and regrets nothing; therefore, it also does not repent <note>In the sense of having no cause for regret due to sin or error</note>. But the animalistic body worries; therefore, it becomes insane, furious, and clumsy. As a sign that we should not look upon, build upon, or use that same animalistic nature: we should use the one that cannot become insane. 

And if we use that same [divine] spirit, then we will be as if enclosed with eyebrows, in the same way as an eye that sleeps. But if we leave the [true] man lying there and go into the animalistic understanding, then those same eyebrows open and look at the heavens—at Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter—which they then grasp in their fantasy and imagine; and those whose *materia* <note>Latin: matter or substance</note> they look upon, it happens to them just like a fool who looks at the sun and is blinded by it: thus they also become mad. Therefore, note that man should not use the beast; therefore, for him to calculate by the astronomers is a shame and a vice, and also forbidden by Christ, and sufficiently indicated in the Scriptures. Therefore, we should not act in a Heathenish way, but in a Christian way, from which the true ground flows above all sects, faiths, languages, governments, and estates of the world.

### TREATISE II. ON ALLEGORIES
### DERIVED FROM CHRIST.
#### From Matthew III.
#### You Brood of Vipers.

<image-desc>Decorated initial capital 'J'</image-desc> John the Baptist first called the Pharisees a brood of vipers: But why? They lived animalistically and walked in animalistic understanding and did not use the Spirit of Man, which learns from God. Therefore, John called them a brood of vipers, that is, an <unclear>Aniser</unclear>. Now, the commandment from Christ is that we should not despise our brother—that is, not to say *Raca* <note>A biblical term of contempt</note> to him, much less call him a brood of vipers. Now know that John was also a man, and from Adam just as much as other men, and the Pharisees likewise from one father. Now, it would be unchristian in John if he had despised his own nature and called a man a snake, for that would be a mockery of God in His creation. 

But the reason is this: since man is created in the image of God, and has from Him that he is a man and no other creature, he should remain a man. And as long as he remains a man, no evil is done to him by his neighbor. But if he acts against his image and is a beast—a fox—then he receives the name of that same beast whose species he is, and is not worthy to be called a man. Though he looks like a man, he uses the beastly nature, not the human; therefore, the name is rightly his. Just as a pious man has the name "Pious" forever; but if he loses his piety, he who called him pious would do him an injustice. John did not want to flatter the Pharisees, but to tell them the truth as one who stood up for it and was no liar or <term>Dellerschlecker</term> <note>Literally "plate-licker"; a sycophant or parasite</note>; he called them not men, but a brood of vipers. For the reason that man is twofold: a beast and a man.

It also justifies John the Baptist's use of the term "brood of vipers" by explaining that a person who abandons their divine humanity for beastly behavior effectively becomes that beast.</summary>
