<page-num>187</page-num>
# ON PYGMIES AND SALAMANDERS.
<note>original: "PYGMÆIS ET SALAMANDRIS." The author uses "Pygmies" as a technical term for Gnomes or mountain dwellers.</note>

<margin>A</margin> Next are the little mountain-men and little earth-men <note>Gnomes and Pygmies</note>, who however are seldom married to humans, but are instead bound only by service. And the inhabitants of Etna <note>Salamanders or fire-spirits, named after the volcano</note> have no part with humans at all; they do not unite with humans, yet they are nonetheless subservient. Know also that they hover, and in part—especially the Etneans—are regarded as spirits and not as the creatures they truly are, as if they were merely an illusion or a ghost. Know this of them: as they appear, so are they flesh and blood, like any other human, and yet they are as nimble and fast as a spirit. As established at the beginning, they possess present things and those that have occurred which are not before our eyes but hidden; in this they may serve humans and preserve them, and the like. In this they possess reason along with humans (except for the soul). They have knowledge and understanding of the spirit (except for what pertains to God). Therefore they are greatly gifted, and they know and warn so that man may experience, see, and believe such things in these creatures. Therefore God has allowed them to appear, to make them known and to teach what God works in such creatures.

<margin>B</margin> Now, as has been said of the Nymphs, that they go out of the water to us and are found by the banks of brooks where they have their dwellings, where they are seen, taken, captured, and married as stated above. But the Forest-people <note>Wild people or Wood-wights</note> are coarser than they; they say nothing, that is, they cannot speak, and yet they have tongues and everything sufficient for speaking. In this they differ from the Nymphs, for the Nymphs are talkative in the local language, but the Forest-people are not, though they are capable of being taught. The Mountain-people <note>Gnomes</note> also have speech like the Nymphs, and the Etneans <note>Salamanders</note> say nothing, and though they can speak, it is harsh and rare. The Nymphs appear as stated above, in human clothing and with human desires, but are shy and do not show themselves for long. The Mountain-people are like humans, but shy; they are not tall, but short, though sometimes half a man's length or the like, and sometimes longer. In this manner the Etneans appear, fiery, and fire yearns in all their being and attire; they are those of whom it is said: "A fiery man walks in the house," or "A spirit, a burning soul goes there," etc. As it often happens that such forms are seen. They are also the "Zundeln" <note>Ignis fatuus or Will-o'-the-wisps</note> that are often seen, burning lights running across the meadows and fields, through one another and under one another; these are the Vulcans <note>Fire-spirits</note>. But they are not found living with humans. If they are found with old women—that is, with witches and the like—it is because the Devil possesses them in the same way he does a human, and thus travels about with them in such a form before the people as has been indicated. And thus they are led and brought, and many such things happen; it would be far too long to write here of how the Devil involves himself in these things. But know that it is perilous regarding the Fire-people, and the Devil rages in them to harm humans. Know also that he enters into the Mountain-people and makes himself subservient in that way, and likewise lets himself be found in the woods; that is, he takes on their form. And this happens in the same place they frequent. For if one has a wife who comes from them, he must keep her; but he must also keep his word to them in the manner that one should. For duty should be held against duty; then they are truthful, constant, and very inclined to be generous with money. For the Mountain-people have money; the reason is they mint it themselves. A spirit: what he wishes he had, he has. And their wishing and desiring—that is their work—so he has it, and it is good money. Thus they give money to many people in the crevices of the mountains, so that when they have gone away, the people run there. All this is Divine Order, that they become manifest in such a way, and that we see what is unbelievable for us to be told. Of all creatures, man is the most bound; what he must and will have, he must work for. But these creatures do not work for it; that is,
->without labor they have it.<-

<margin>C</margin> But if the Devil does not intervene in these things, they are human-like and seek alliance, as has been proposed. But they retain the nature of spirits in their vanishing. Just as one who has a Nymph who comes from the water should not offend her near water. So also with the others: do not offend them in such places where they might be lost. They are so far bound and obligated that they may not leave a human, except for the cause through which they came.

<margin>D</margin> For one who has a wife who comes from them must keep her; but he must also keep his word to them in the manner that one should. For duty should be held against duty; then they are truthful, constant, and very inclined to be generous with money. For the Mountain-people have money; the reason is they mint it themselves. A spirit: what he wishes he had, he has. And their wishing and desiring—that is their work—so he has it, and it is good money. Thus they give money to many people in the crevices of the mountains, so that when they have gone away, the people run there. All this is Divine Order, that they become manifest in such a way, and that we see what is unbelievable for us to be told.
